20891-itinerary-of-provence-and-the-rhon:
Plain, practical questions guide the Itinerary of Provence and the Rhone, made in the year 1819. Travellers with scant time can plan what to see and do with its help. Costs, roads, and sights are weighed for active use on the road.

John Murray's handbooks taught the British how to tour the Continent with sense. This tour down the Rhone covers towns, ruins, inns, and views in order. Provence's Roman stones and bright towns fill its pages. The book shows early guide writing at its most useful: exact, thrifty, and built for the hand, not the shelf.
abbott-primitive-industry-1881:
Charles Conrad Abbott, a doctor and keen digger in New Jersey, wrote this book on the Trenton gravels in 1881. He had found rough stone tools in the gravel beds near the Delaware River. The finds led him to a bold claim for the age of man in America.

Abbott held that the tools came from a true stone age race in America, as old as Europe's. His claim was the first of its kind for the New World, made in full print. Later men, led by Hrdlicka, took his proof apart stone by stone in the years that came.
actions-and-reactions-pg2381: Kipling's 1909 stories of actions and reactions: engineers, soldiers, and the empire's machinery. "The Power of the Dog" and its companions show his mature art. Strong, vivid, and very Kipling. Kipling's machinery age roars through these stories.
anania-de-natura-daemonum-latin-1581:
Gian Lorenzo Anania, an Italian priest, published De natura daemonum in 1581. The Latin work runs to four books on the nature, orders, and operations of demons. It belongs to the Counter-Reformation, the Catholic answer to Protestant reform, and it sums up demon lore in scholastic order.

Anania sorts demons by rank and task, as a naturalist sorts beasts. He explains how they act on bodies, minds, and the weather. Scripture and the church fathers supply his evidence throughout. The tone is calm, learned, and certain. Readers meet demons catalogued like specimens, in the most orderly demonology of its Italian moment.
annulus-platonis-oder-physikalisch-chymi: Annulus Platonis, 1781. The Platonic ring. This book preserves that work. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. It awaits future readers. The paper lasts as a quiet witness to its time.
arxiv-2510-00681:
Zhang, Li, Lin, and Lu introduce the first open-vocabulary object detection framework for event cameras in this 2025 arXiv paper. Event cameras report brightness changes with microsecond timing and no motion blur, which suits fast scenes. They capture no colour or texture, though, and detectors trained on fixed categories cannot name objects they never saw in training. Vision-language models such as CLIP solve that problem for ordinary photos, but their knowledge does not transfer directly to sparse event streams.

The team uses ordinary image frames as the teacher's input and distills CLIP's visual knowledge into an event-based student through spatial attention. A spiking neural network slices the event stream adaptively, choosing split moments that keep key temporal features instead of discarding them. A convolutional stage then runs the detection itself. In experiments the model consistently beat dataset-specific baselines and generalized to unseen categories.
arxiv-2510-00981:
Li and a large team from Microsoft, the Chinese University of Hong Kong Shenzhen, and Shanghai Jiao Tong University present FlexiCodec in this 2025 arXiv paper on speech technology. Neural audio codecs turn speech into tokens that language models can process. Lower frame rates shorten token sequences and cut computing cost, but low rates tend to lose semantic content. FlexiCodec attacks that trade-off with a dynamic frame rate.

The codec merges frames where the signal carries little information, and keeps more frames where speech is dense. An ASR-assisted dual-stream encoder and transformer bottlenecks help preserve meaning at low rates. At average rates of six and a quarter, eight point three, and twelve and a half hertz, it beat baseline codecs on semantic preservation and reconstruction quality. Users can choose the frame rate at inference time, between three and twelve and a half hertz.
arxiv-2510-01381:
Teetaert and co-authors estimate the full moving shape of soft continuum robots in continuous time, with uncertainty attached. Such robots bend everywhere, so state estimation usually leans on heavy dynamics or crude shape guesses. Disturbances that nobody modeled break both approaches easily.

Kinematics are corrupted by smooth noise inside a factor-graph formulation borrowed from navigation research. Fast sensing plus the simple model absorbs unmodeled pushes and survives sensor dropouts. Pose, velocity, and strain come out with covariances, queryable at any instant. Sparse structure keeps the computation linear in time, which real robots need. Gyroscope and pose sensors supplied the demonstration measurements. Interpolation during estimation admits measurements between explicit states. White-noise-on-acceleration style priors keep the curves physically smooth. Boundary factors at the robot's base anchor each solution. Soft robots need soft mathematics, probabilistically speaking, throughout the body.
arxiv-2510-01781:
Ding, Komatsu, and Liu count special primes in a classic coin problem in this 2025 number theory paper. Given two coprime coin sizes, some amounts can be formed in several ways and others in none. The authors fix a bound on the number of ways and look at the largest amount that stays under it. They then count how many primes below that bound need more representations than the bound allows.

For a fixed smaller coin size of at least three, they prove an exact asymptotic formula for that prime count. The count grows like a clean fraction of all primes up to the same bound. They also prove a positive lower bound under a mild size condition on the coins. Companion counts for primes with few representations receive similar treatment. The results sharpen what is known about primes hiding inside this Frobenius-style interval problem.
arxiv-2510-01881:
Krasucki and six co-authors probe the vibrations of a layered magnet in this 2025 physics paper. The material is chromium germanium telluride, a ferromagnet built from weakly bound sheets. They measured its Raman scattering spectra with high resolution across a wide temperature range. Calculations predicted ten Raman-active vibration modes, and the team identified all of them.

Cooling the crystal exposed a strong coupling between spin order and lattice vibrations. Spectral features shifted near two characteristic temperatures, one around one hundred fifty kelvin and one near sixty. Those marks signal local magnetic order appearing, then the full ferromagnetic phase locking in. One mode showed an unusual comb of very narrow peaks. Modeling explained that comb as vibrations of germanium pairs, split apart by the different germanium isotopes present. The work maps how magnetism and sound-like motion intertwine in this material.
arxiv-2510-01981:
Backis and eight co-authors test a modern readout chip for the T-REX neutron spectrometer in this 2025 instrumentation paper. T-REX, bound for the European Spallation Source, detects neutrons with Multi-Grid technology. Its grid of coated blades forms a voxelised proportional counter filled with gas. The open question was whether the VMM3A chip, built for other detectors, suits this readout.

The team measured a prototype at a finely collimated thermal neutron beam at the ISIS source. They mapped how pulse height and detection efficiency vary with position inside the voxels. Measurements were compared against two electronics schemes and against Garfield++ and Geant4 simulations. Corner regions of each voxel collect charge slowly, which can shrink pulses and lose events. The scans quantify that effect across the detector face. The results judge the chip's suitability for the final spectrometer and validate the simulation chain behind it.
arxiv-2510-02181:
Wu and Jain make live captions adapt to Deaf and hard-of-hearing speakers during conversation in this 2025 accessibility paper. Speech recognition often mangles the speech of DHH users, especially in real time. Older personalization demands piles of pre-recorded data and puts all the work on the DHH speaker. EvolveCaptions instead recruits the hearing partner into the fix.

While a conversation runs, hearing participants correct transcription errors as they spot them. The system turns those corrections into short, phonetically targeted prompts for the DHH speaker to record. About five minutes of such recordings fine-tune the recognizer on the spot. In a study with twelve DHH and six hearing participants, word error rates fell for every DHH user within one hour. Participants called the process easy, low-effort, and natural to use mid-conversation. Adaptation becomes a shared, in-situ activity rather than homework.
arxiv-2510-02281:
Kravchuk and Radcliffe study a new kind of defect inside a critical quantum model. Their 2025 physics paper works with the O(2N) model at its critical point. A defect is a line or surface where the rules change. Most studied defects keep full symmetry around them. This defect keeps symmetry only along itself. Across the defect, rotations must pair with an internal twist. The twist comes from a monodromy defect, which changes fields after a loop. A relevant operator then drives the system to a new fixed point.

The authors compute defect operator dimensions two ways. Large N expansion gives one set of leading values. A second expansion near four dimensions gives another. The two routes agree where they overlap. They also match older results for plain monodromy and pinning defects. Spinning defects widen the map of possible critical behavior.
arxiv-2510-02581:
Elghaayda, Rahman, and Mansour measure quantum coherence in expanding de Sitter spacetime without basis bias. Their 2025 physics paper studies two detectors moving with the expansion. Coherence usually depends on the measurement basis chosen. That dependence clouds what the quantity really means. Their framework splits coherence into total, collective, and local parts. Each part is defined without leaning on a basis. The detectors couple to a light scalar field around them. Two vacuum choices frame the analysis. One is the standard thermal style vacuum. The other adds squeezing through a tunable parameter.

Squeezing sharply boosted the coherence that detectors can extract. The boost survived even under strong thermal noise. Collective coherence also swung in a non-monotonic pattern. In the thermal limit, heat first suppresses coherence before it recovers. Such control knobs matter for relativistic quantum protocols. Curved spacetime becomes a resource, not just a nuisance.
arxiv-2510-02681:
Fronzi and co-authors predict heat-to-power material properties with networks that explain themselves. Their 2025 materials paper applies Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks. Such materials turn heat into power, so discovery matters. Standard machine learning predicts well but hides its logic. Black box models give little insight. The new networks split functions into readable pieces. They target the Seebeck coefficient and the band gap. Accuracy matched the usual deep network models. The difference lies in what comes out afterward. Plain formulas summarize each structure-property link.

Benchmarks against published models confirmed the robustness. The formula pipeline named the strongest input factors. It pruned redundant connections inside the network. Rebuilt formulas aligned with known physics. Designers can reverse the formulas toward target properties. Readable models speed up materials discovery cycles. Output plus reasons beats output alone in the lab.
arxiv-2510-02981:
Li and co-authors fix a timing flaw in ultra-low-power wireless links. Ambient backscatter devices ride on radio waves already in the air. They send data by reflecting those waves, using almost no power. Receivers must line up their sampling with each symbol. Delay and start-up lag break that alignment in practice. Standard sync methods fail here, since the ambient source will not cooperate. The team tackles the offset head-on.

A special pilot sequence at the sender creates a telltale error pattern. The receiver reads that pattern to estimate the timing offset. The estimator uses maximum likelihood reasoning on the signal statistics. Once measured, the offset is corrected before detection. An energy detector then reads the cleaned symbols. Bit error rates recovered most of what the offset had cost. That keeps it fit for cheap, massive Internet of Things rollouts.
arxiv-2510-03081:
Liu and co-authors argue that humanoid robots should evolve body and brain together. Most research tunes control software for a fixed robot shape. Nature took a different path, shaping limbs and behavior jointly. Their position paper calls for body-control co-design in humanoids. Form and policy would adapt side by side for each task. Resource limits would shape both, as they do in animals.

Three practical routes anchor their proposal. Clever exploration can search the joint space of shapes and skills. Simulation-to-real transfer can test designs cheaply before building them. Meta-policy learning can reuse lessons across many body shapes. The case is argued from methods, uses, and community needs. Benchmarks and design-aware control sit on that list. World models and reasoning systems mark the far end. Co-design, they conclude, is a cornerstone for the next humanoid generation.
arxiv-2510-03281:
Van Batenburg wrote a thesis that puts Shapley explanations of machine learning models on firm math ground. Shapley values split credit for a model's output among its input facts. They grew from game theory and were adapted for machine learning by Lundberg and Lee. Earlier papers stated the key results but left proofs sketchy or incomplete. The thesis goes back to the source claims and proves them with full care.

One result shows that Shapley values are the only explanation meeting four fairness style rules. The author also gives a case that disproves a past claim, showing that the symmetry rule cannot be dropped. A second result shows the values are the single best answer to a weighted fitting problem. These proofs matter because doctors, banks, and courts now ask why a model decided as it did. Sound math makes those answers safer to trust.
arxiv-2510-03681:
Majumder and Sahoo present a 2025 arXiv paper selecting which factors drive PFAS contamination in California groundwater, from a list of candidates, under data conditions. PFAS chemicals persist in the environment and threaten health, their drivers are entangled. Measurements are censored, since low levels go unreported, and wells correlate. The authors build a Bayesian hierarchical model that handles censoring inside a spatial process, approximated for scale. A global local shrinkage prior then separates signal variables from noise.

They compare three rules for declaring a variable selected: credible intervals, shrinkage weight thresholds, and a clustering method. In simulations, the credible interval rule proved most reliable. Shrinkage weights won in ultra sparse settings, while clustering stayed flexible. Applied to PFOS in California groundwater, the model picked a scientific set of demographic, industrial, and environmental predictors. Knowing which drivers matter focuses cleanup and monitoring money. The machinery transfers to censored spatial problems in science.
arxiv-2510-03781:
Asgari-Bidhendi and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper building a corpus of a million hadith narrations with an automated pipeline. Hadith, the sayings and reports about the Prophet Muhammad and the Imams, are Islam's second source of knowledge after the Qur'an, and they survive in collections. The pipeline segments texts, separates each narration's chain from its content, and validates the split. Enrichment layers add translation into twelve languages, vowel marking, summaries, thematic tags, and links between narrations.

Six experts graded a sample of twelve hundred narrations. Chain separation and summarization both scored about nine point three out of ten, near human quality. The corpus averaged eight point five overall, dwarfing a curated rival's score. Vowel marking lagged, with word error rates above fifteen percent. Work estimated at two hundred thousand expert hours was done in months at a fraction of the cost. Islamic studies gains a searchable infrastructure at scale.
arxiv-2510-04281:
Gao and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper introducing GROK, a multimodal model designed to reason from eye images and quantitative biomarkers to a clinical diagnosis. Earlier medical adaptations of multimodal language models often underexploited the complementary value of these inputs and produced weakly grounded explanations. GROK instead organizes its training around a quantitative-to-qualitative chain of reasoning resembling a clinician's workflow.

A CLIP-style module aligns OCT representations with biomarker concepts before supervised instruction fine-tuning teaches the model to explain findings and annotate lesions. The authors evaluate it on a new Grounded Ophthalmic Understanding benchmark spanning six disease categories and classification, report generation, and chain-of-thought quality. With LoRA fine-tuning of a seven-billion-parameter Qwen2 backbone, GROK surpassed comparable models, including a larger thirty-two-billion-parameter baseline and OpenAI o3, on report and fine-grained clinical measures.
arxiv-2510-04481:
Otis Chodosh wrote this 2025 survey paper on minimal surfaces and comparison geometry. A minimal surface is a surface that locally takes the least possible area, like a soap film. Geometers study how such surfaces reveal the curvature and shape of the space around them. The method echoes a classic trick: study shortest curves to learn about a space as a whole. Chodosh reviews what decades of work on area minimizers have shown.

The survey covers existence and smoothness results from geometric measure theory. It explains how first and second variation of area force a minimizer to have zero mean curvature and obey a stability inequality. Landmark results then use stable surfaces to limit the topology of spaces with positive scalar curvature. The Geroch conjecture and the stable Bernstein problem get detailed treatment. Recent progress has nearly settled the Bernstein question, with one case still open.
arxiv-2510-04581:
Anh Dang, Rick Nouwen, and Massimo Poesio wrote this 2025 paper on how language models read ambiguous plural pronouns. A word like they can point back to two things at once, or to a whole made of parts. People handle such choices with ease and show steady preferences. The team asked whether large language models share those preferences and can spot the ambiguity. They ran tests on pronoun production, interpretation, and ambiguity detection.

The models sometimes knew the possible referents of an ambiguous pronoun in the tests. They did not always choose the reading that people prefer, though. The gap grew when the favored reading was not stated in plain words nearby. Models also failed to flag ambiguity unless the prompt told them to look for it. Results shifted across test types in ways that lacked a clean pattern. The authors read this as shaky, surface level handling of reference.
arxiv-2510-04681:
Yang and nine coauthors at the Danish Meteorological Institute wrote this 2025 paper on a new climate record for Denmark. Denmark is a maze of coasts, with hundreds of islands and mixed land and sea in most districts. Global weather records blur those coastal features. The team built DANRA, a reanalysis that replays the weather from 1990 to 2023 on a grid of about two and a half kilometers. It rests on a proven regional forecast model fed with observations.

Against the leading global reanalysis, DANRA represented near surface weather more faithfully in their checks. The gains held in calm conditions and in extremes alike. Case studies cover a hurricane force storm in 1999, a heat record in 2022, and a cloudburst in 2007. Planners can use the record for adaptation and impact studies. Learning based forecast models can also train on sharp fields. The data set is free in a format from a public store.
arxiv-2510-05081:
Ronen Kamenetsky and five co-authors give image editors a finer dial in this 2025 arXiv paper. Text prompts steer modern image generators, but they offer clumsy control. Changing one attribute often distorts others. Editors also want smooth control over how strong an edit feels.

Their method, SAEdit, edits the text embedding rather than the image model itself. A sparse autoencoder lifts the embedding into a space where attributes sit apart. Moving along one direction changes just that attribute, such as adding a laugh to one chosen person. A scale factor adjusts the edit's strength continuously. Because only embeddings change, the trick works across many image backbones.
arxiv-2510-05181:
Ander Artola Velasco, Stratis Tsirtsis, and Manuel Gomez-Rodriguez police dishonest billing in the AI cloud market in this 2025 arXiv paper. Providers charge per token a model generates. That pricing tempts providers to inflate the token counts they report. Users cannot check the counts on their own.

The authors build an auditing framework on martingale theory. A trusted auditor queries the provider sequentially and watches for statistical inconsistencies. Theory guarantees detection of any misreporting strategy, whatever the provider tries. Honest providers are almost never flagged by mistake. Across Llama, Gemma, and Ministral models, cheating surfaced after fewer than about 70 observed outputs. False-flag probability stayed below five percent in their tests.
arxiv-2510-05381:
Yufeng Du and nine co-authors show that long inputs hurt language models even when nothing is hidden in this 2025 arXiv paper. The usual explanation blames retrieval failures inside long contexts. If a model finds every relevant fact, it should perform like it does on short inputs. The authors test that assumption directly.

Across five models and math, question answering, and coding tasks, performance fell sharply as length grew. Drops ranged from about 14 to 85 percent despite perfect retrieval. The failure persisted when filler tokens were replaced by whitespace or masked entirely. Even placing all evidence right before the question did not rescue performance. A recite-first prompting trick recovered up to about 4 percent for GPT-4o on RULER.
arxiv-2510-05581:
Ponkshe and Vepakomma make shared data embeddings private for the first time. Collaborative learning usually shares model weights between clients and a server. Sharing embeddings instead saves client compute, but no formal privacy guarantees existed for them. Their 2025 Power Mechanism learns embeddings with differential privacy built in.

A privacy encoding network works with a small utility generation network on the client. The resulting embeddings carry formal epsilon and delta guarantees. A powerful server then post-processes them for the actual task. The server model can be deep learning, random forests, or XGBoost. Clients need only one round of privatized communication. Experiments show better privacy-utility trade-offs and resource efficiency than baselines. The evaluations focus on tabular datasets, the enterprise workhorse format. Extending the co-design to text, speech, and vision remains future work. Split learning gains a principled privacy story from this design.
arxiv-2510-05881:
Chen and colleagues generate complete songs segment by segment. Full-song generation must stay coherent across minutes of symbolic piano music. Composers work from a theme and structure, consulting only relevant sections. Their 2025 Segmented Full-Song Model mimics that workflow directly.

Users supply a song structure and optionally a short seed segment. A rule-based algorithm splits the song into segments beforehand. Each segment is then generated attending only to structurally related predecessors. That selective attention beats uniform context encoding in coherence and motif awareness. A user study confirms the advantage over the prior WholeSong system. A web application wraps the model for iterative co-creation on a piano roll. Customizable structures and flexible segment ordering support the interaction. Stronger seed adherence rounds out the measured improvements. Generation also runs an order of magnitude faster, enabling real-time streaming.
arxiv-2510-06281:
Li and three co-authors enhance full-disk solar images toward telescope quality with deep learning in a 2025 computer vision paper. The GONG network watches the whole Sun in hydrogen-alpha light, but cannot resolve fine structures like filaments and fibrils. The Goode Solar Telescope delivers far sharper views over smaller areas.

They train a generative adversarial network based on Real-ESRGAN, with dense blocks and a relativistic discriminator. Carefully aligned GONG and GST pairs teach the model what sharp solar detail looks like. The enhanced images recover sunspot penumbra detail and resolve filaments and fibrils convincingly. Cross-correlation with ground truth reached about 0.78 on average. Small remaining misalignments capped the quantitative scores. The team plans better alignment and a larger dataset. Upgraded network images would give solar physicists fine-scale dynamics with full-disk coverage.
arxiv-2510-06381:
Cazenave proposes Monte Carlo Permutation Search, an improved tree search for game playing, in a 2025 machine learning paper. Deep reinforcement learning dominates headlines, but many settings lack its compute demands. General Game Playing needs strong search that works immediately on unseen games.

MCPS builds on the GRAVE algorithm for Monte Carlo tree search. Its exploration term also uses statistics from every playout containing all moves on the root path. Those permutation statistics capture move-order information plain node statistics miss. Cazenave derives the weighting formulas for the three statistics sources. The derivation removes GRAVE's bias hyperparameter, so less tuning is needed. Across Hex, Go, AtariGo, NoGo, and a wargame, MCPS almost always beat GRAVE. The result strengthens a classic approach to game AI. It matters where learning pipelines are impractical and decisions must be good immediately.
arxiv-2510-06481:
Khass and six co-authors couple risk-averse path refinement with active view selection for robot navigation in a 2025 robotics paper. Safe navigation in uncertain environments demands caution and curiosity. A robot must avoid risky routes while sensing what matters next. Separate planning and perception waste safety and information.

Their framework refines a coarse reference path using tail-sensitive risk maps. The maps derive from Average Value-at-Risk statistics over an online-updated 3D Gaussian-splat field. Locally safe, feasible trajectories emerge from that risk surface. In parallel, next-best-view selection becomes optimization on the pose manifold. Riemannian gradient descent maximizes expected information gain. The objective targets uncertainty critical for imminent motion, not curiosity in general. Scalable gradient decompositions keep the loop updating efficiently online. Extensive computational studies demonstrate effectiveness. Robots gain a principled way to look where danger and ignorance overlap.
arxiv-2510-06581:
Bo Li, Fangxiao Wang, and Shiji Xing study fair division, but for burdens instead of goods. Their 2025 paper asks how to split indivisible chores among people with unequal weights. A leading fairness idea is the weighted maximin share, which promises each person a fair worst-case portion. Nobody knew whether a constant-factor approximation to it was even possible.

The authors present the first constant-factor approximation algorithm for this fairness notion. Their method simplifies hard cases into canonical ones and bounds what agents can value. They also prove that no method can guarantee better than a factor of two. That lower bound improves the earlier best mark, which stood near one point three seven. The true best ratio now sits somewhere between two and twelve. Closing that gap remains an open problem in weighted fair division.
arxiv-2510-06681:
Leonardo Clarke leads a team studying how distant galaxies formed their stars. Their 2025 paper uses data from the James Webb and Hubble space telescopes. The sample holds 659 star-forming galaxies seen as they were billions of years ago. The team measures the star-forming main sequence, a tight link between galaxy mass and star formation rate.

They estimate star formation two ways, from hydrogen light and from ultraviolet light. Each estimate gets its own dust correction. The scatter around the main sequence grows toward lower masses in the hydrogen-based version. It shows no such trend in the ultraviolet version. Comparing the two rates reveals bursty histories in much of the sample. Between 41 and 60 percent of galaxies clash with a steady star formation story. Burst timescales may also shorten at earlier cosmic times. The results portray young galaxies as flickering builders rather than steady ones.
arxiv-2510-07081:
Fanheng Kong, Jingyuan Zhang, Yahui Liu, and Zirui Wu speed up a new breed of language models that write many tokens at once. Their 2025 paper studies diffusion language models, which decode text in parallel. Open implementations play safe and finalize only the single most confident token per step. That caution wastes many refinement rounds, a delay the authors name delayed decoding.

Their analysis found that confident tokens stabilize their neighborhoods. Nearby predictions lock in early and rarely change afterward. Their method, LocalLeap, exploits that local determinism. It finds high-confidence anchors and decodes relaxed neighborhoods around them in parallel. The strategy needs no retraining of the model. Across reasoning, code, and instruction benchmarks, throughput rose nearly sevenfold. Decoding steps fell to about fourteen percent of the original count. Quality loss stayed negligible in their measurements. Faster diffusion models could make parallel generation practical for everyday use.
arxiv-2510-07281:
Eides revisits the error budget behind one of precision physics' prized numbers, the hyperfine splitting of muonium. Its splitting once anchored key constants and still gives the best value of the muon-to-electron mass ratio. Recent global adjustments of physical constants quoted the theory uncertainty at a strikingly small figure. Eides argues that figure understates the true uncertainty by a large factor. 

Two earlier careful analyses put the uncertainty at several hundred hertz, not the fifty-one hertz now quoted. The smaller number, Eides shows, was misread as the full theoretical prediction error. Sharper measurements elsewhere have retired its old role in fixing the fine structure constant, which makes the remaining error budget even more pointed. He calls for an immediate correction in the recommended values. The note warns how one mislabeled number can spread through shared reference data.
arxiv-2510-07581:
Yue, Wang, Zhan, Li, and co-authors give language models new kinds of actions, so they can stop spelling out tool calls in prose. Their 2025 paper attacks an awkward bottleneck. Models reason in text, so every interaction with a calculator or simulator must be written in a special format, parsed by hand-built machinery, and routed externally. Language ends up doing two jobs, reasoning and control, badly entangled.

A reinforcement learning method with counterfactual rollouts teaches the model to explore rarely used but critical environment actions. On multi-turn tasks needing contingent planning, including calculator-based multitask problems and a partially observed sorting task, the approach beats strong baselines confined to vocabulary actions. Decoupling control from language removes a whole class of format errors and brittle prompt engineering.
arxiv-2510-08081:
Lan and four coauthors wrote this 2025 paper presenting AutoQual, a language-model agent that discovers interpretable features for ranking online reviews. Review quality is domain-dependent and shifts over time, so hand-built features do not scale. AutoQual mimics a human researcher. It proposes feature hypotheses through reflection, implements them itself as tools, and stores lessons in persistent memory.

Deployed on a platform with a billion-level user base, AutoQual raised reviews read per user by under one percent in A/B testing. Reader conversion rose by a fraction of a percent, large in absolute terms at that scale. Discovered features stayed explicit and computable. The authors frame the framework generally: it turns tacit knowledge in labeled data into features people can inspect, building trust in ranking systems.
arxiv-2510-08281:
Tianwei Li and co-authors tackle lifetime value prediction for mobile gamers in a 2025 arXiv paper. Ad platforms that sell space by real-time bidding need to know what each user is worth over time. Good estimates guide ad placement and raise returns for advertisers. Gamer spending is spiky and full of outliers, which makes direct prediction of total spend unreliable.

Instead of guessing the total at once, their model breaks the goal into smaller parts. It first predicts how many purchases a gamer will make at each price point. It then rebuilds the total payment from those counts, matching how in-app purchases actually occur. The team tested the model on a real industrial data set. They also ran it live on the TapTap ad system in an online A/B test. It was compared there with ZILN, a leading model for this task.
arxiv-2510-08481:
Yifei Xu and co-authors forecast hashtag popularity by letting language models reason about context in a 2025 arXiv paper. Viral hashtags steer campaigns, opinion, and large advertising budgets, yet predicting them is notoriously hard. Classic regressors use surface features and miss the story behind a tag. Language models reason well about context but estimate numbers poorly.

Their framework, BuzzProphet, assigns each job to the tool that does it best. A language model writes rationales about a hashtag's timing advantage, audience reach, and topical virality. Those rationales enrich the features fed into a standard regressor, which makes the numeric forecast. They release HashView, a benchmark of seven thousand five hundred thirty-two hashtags from social media. Across regressor and model combinations, BuzzProphet cut prediction error by up to 2.8 percent and raised correlation by thirty percent.
arxiv-2510-09081:
Kraaijeveld and co-authors render vast bundles of moving lines in real time without faking the lighting, in this 2025 arXiv paper on computer graphics. Line sets appear in flow simulations and in brain imaging, where thousands of fibers trace the wiring of white matter. Dense sets need honest transparency and soft shadowing to be readable, but those effects are expensive. The team's framework voxelizes the lines, boxing them into a three-dimensional grid.

That grid supports two tracing styles at once: true ray tracing for accurate see-through layering, and cone tracing for ambient occlusion, the gentle darkening where lines crowd together. A culling step rebuilds the acceleration data only for voxels the camera can actually see, slashing per-frame preparation. In comparisons, it beat the prior state of the art on quality and speed for mostly opaque dynamic line sets.
arxiv-2510-09481:
Walter van Suijlekom, Michael Wondrak, and Heino Falcke study particle creation by gravity in a 2025 arXiv paper. The Schwinger effect creates particle pairs in a strong electric field, and its derivation assumes the field switches on and off in the distant past and future. The authors pursue a gravitational analogue in an expanding FLRW universe, using a long gravity pulse to mimic a steady background.

They derive the production rigorously through the Heun equation, using new formulas linking its local solutions to read off probabilities for an infinitely long pulse. Production shows a lower threshold in the late-time frequencies, tied to how long the switching takes. At high frequencies in a spatially flat universe, the spectrum is Planckian, with a temperature inversely tied to the duration of the scale change. They compare the result with Schwinger's own for an electromagnetic pulse.
arxiv-2510-09681:
Sashank Makanaboyina, the sole author, presents NNDM in a 2025 arXiv paper, a hybrid model for finding brain tumours in MRI scans. Accurate tumour segmentation guides diagnosis and treatment planning. Standard network models such as U-Net often struggle on new data and on exact edges, and with narrow training sets.

NNDM couples NN-UNet, a strong self-configuring network, with a diffusion probabilistic model. The diffusion stage learns the pattern of errors between the network's predicted mask and the true mask. It then progressively refines the mask, correcting small flaws and sharpening tumour edges through iterative denoising. On the BraTS 2021 benchmark datasets, NNDM beat plain U-Net and transformer-based baselines on both Dice overlap and Hausdorff distance, two standard scores. The refinement also improved robustness across scan types and tumour parts.
arxiv-2510-09881:
Kim, Seungmin Lee, Junho Kim, and Young Min Kim present LTGS in this 2025 arXiv paper on 3D scene reconstruction. LTGS builds a long-term chronology of a scene from sparse view updates, using Gaussian splatting, a method that renders scenes from many soft 3D blobs. Everyday places change often, so a single capture goes stale fast.

The authors note that tracking such change the usual way needs dense observations in both space and time, which casual camera captures rarely provide. LTGS instead works from occasional new views of the same place. It updates the scene record so that each state reflects when things changed. The goal is photo-realistic playback of a place as it evolves over weeks or months.
arxiv-2510-09981:
Fan Zuo and co-authors scale traffic monitoring with AI cameras in this 2025 arXiv paper on transportation systems. Cities need accurate traffic data for both daily management and long-term planning, above all during disruptions like disasters, big construction, or New York City's congestion pricing program. Fixed sensors are costly to install and maintain, so coverage stays thin.

The team uses language model powered camera systems to extract traffic insights from video at scale. Cameras are already widespread, so the approach avoids new sensor networks. The system aims to turn raw footage into counts and patterns that planners can act on. Cheaper, wider monitoring would let agencies judge policy effects, such as pricing, with far better evidence.
arxiv-2510-10381:
Rodríguez-Falcón and Luciano Stucchi quantify emergence in agent-based models in this 2025 arXiv letter on complex systems. Emergent behavior, patterns that arise from many simple agents interacting, defines complex systems. Yet measuring emergence has mostly meant eyeballing space-time patterns and judging them by eye.

The authors propose mean information gain as a numeric metric of emergence. Information gain measures how much observing the system teaches an observer over time. A model whose patterns carry more new information scores as more emergent. A quantitative scale lets researchers compare models and parameter settings objectively. That could turn emergence from a talking point into a design variable for simulations of crowds, markets, and ecosystems.
arxiv-2510-10581:
Heng Zhang and seven co-authors build a tool for finding the true cause of failures in multi agent systems, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Agent teams excel at complex tasks but fail often in long, multi turn deep search. Existing methods blame steps by their order in time, which confuses symptoms with root causes when errors spread across agents. The missing piece is how information flows between agents, not just when actions happened.

Their framework, GraphTracer, builds Information Dependency Graphs that record how agents reference and build on earlier outputs. It traces failures through these dependencies to localize root causes. It also generates synthetic failure data aimed at critical nodes. On the Who&When benchmark, their 8 billion parameter model reached up to 18.18 percent higher attribution accuracy than state of the art models in the reported comparisons. Plugged into production frameworks, it improved performance by between 4.8 and 14.2 percent across deployments.
arxiv-2510-10781:
Douglas Hutchings, Luai Abuelsamen, and Karthik Rajgopal coordinate mixed drone and ground robot teams for hazardous material emergencies, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Standard coverage control spreads robots using Voronoi cells, territories built around each agent. In emergencies it struggles: aerial and ground agents move at very different speeds, teams start clustered, and response must be fast. Their two layer approach optimizes aerial and ground positioning separately.

Aerial agents airdrop ground sensors onto high priority locations, speeding deployment. The paper details bounded Voronoi cell computation, numerical integration for importance weighted centroids, and control strategies that keep agents from getting trapped. In simulations, the method cut response time by 88 percent compared with ground only deployment. It reached the target sensor coverage in 25 seconds, versus 220 seconds for ground robots alone, accepting a modest sensor loss. The full implementation code is publicly available.
arxiv-2510-10981:
Tomoya Wakayama and Taiji Suzuki prove that in context learning in language models amounts to Bayesian inference, in this 2025 arXiv paper. In context learning is the trick where a model learns a new task from examples inside its prompt, with no weight updates. Working in a meta learning framework that allows mixtures of task types, the authors decompose the total risk into two orthogonal parts. The Bayes gap measures how close the trained model comes to the best possible in context predictor. The posterior variance captures the task's intrinsic uncertainty and does not depend on the model.

For a uniform attention Transformer, they bound the Bayes gap in terms of how many pretraining prompts were used and how long their contexts were. The striking finding concerns the mixture: uncertainty about which task is at hand vanishes exponentially fast with just a few in context examples.
arxiv-2510-11981:
Yankai Zhang and Yoshitaka Tanimura build exact simulation tools for atoms bathed in heat. An atom governed by a Coulomb potential, the classic attraction between charges, never sits alone: a thermal environment keeps jostling it. Treating that influence without crude shortcuts is hard. Their 2025 arXiv paper derives hierarchical equations of motion tuned for atomic orbitals, called AO-HEOM.

Their math uses a rotation-proof three-dimensional model of system plus bath, so the setup respects the atom's spherical symmetry. The resulting equations are exact in their numbers within the model and handle strong coupling and memory effects that simpler theories drop. To test it, the authors compute the linear absorption spectrum of an atom in an isotropic thermal environment. They vary the coupling strength and temperature step by step. The spectra show how the environment reshapes the atom's response to light, checking a tool meant for realistic, warm quantum systems.
arxiv-2510-12281:
Wei characterizes a class of rough curves called t-quasicircles using a new family of mappings, in a 2025 arXiv mathematics paper. Quasicircles are images of circles under maps that distort shapes in a controlled way, and they sit at the boundary between smooth and fractal geometry. Classical results describe ordinary quasicircles through quasisymmetric boundary maps, which control how distances are stretched.

Wei introduces (rho, t)-quasisymmetric mappings, a broader class that generalizes the classical notion. With them he gives an analytic characterization of t-quasicircles, viewing the result as an analogue of a classical theorem of Tukia and Väisälä. He then studies conformal mappings from the unit disk onto t-quasidisks, the regions these curves bound. The boundary values of such mappings turn out to be almost quasisymmetric in the new sense, with the parameter squared. This extends the classical Quasicircle Theorem to the t-quasicircle setting.
arxiv-2510-12381:
Zheng, Takayasu, and Takayasu ask whether railway commuters choose routes rationally and consistently over time, using a year of Tokyo smartphone data, in a 2025 arXiv paper. The data cover over one million users in the Tokyo area during 2023. Few earlier studies had measured how stable route choice behavior is, or how it varies by origin destination pair.

The team built algorithms to extract commuting paths, transport modes, and transfer stations from raw position data. They then reinterpreted the standard route choice model through the canonical ensemble of statistical physics, treating rationality as a temperature like quantity. Route choice behavior in aggregate proved stable across the whole region through the year. However, behavior varied strongly by origin destination pair. Estimated parameters split into two groups with opposite preference signs, meaning commuters divide into two camps on what they value. They argue that transfer modeling in railway route choice needs more care.
arxiv-2510-12581:
Haghighi and colleagues make diffusion models teach themselves by aligning their weaker internal layers with their strongest ones, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Earlier work showed that guiding a diffusion model's intermediate representations with external supervision speeds training and improves output quality. LayerSync replaces the external teacher with the model's own most semantically rich layers.

The method adds a plug in regularization term with no training overhead and needs no pretrained models or extra data. Representation quality varies across layers, and LayerSync uses the best layers as intrinsic guidance for the weaker ones. On image generation it greatly accelerated training of a flow based transformer on ImageNet while improving quality scores by a large margin. The approach is domain agnostic and also improved audio, video, and human motion generation in their tests. The authors present self alignment as a general recipe for faster, better generative training.
arxiv-2511-00281:
Tristan Aurégan, Noé Daniel, Megan Mazzatenta, and Luc Deike study the drops thrown up when bubbles burst at the ocean surface. Those drops shape how the ocean and air exchange gases and particles. A lone bursting bubble is well understood: its cavity collapses into a fast jet that breaks into drops. Real bubbles, though, often sit in rafts with neighbors close by.

High-speed cameras show that neighbors change the cavity shape as it collapses. The result is drops that are smaller, faster, and more numerous. With up to six neighbors, drop size can shrink fivefold. Rafts therefore produce a much wider spread of drop sizes than lone bubbles, a fact ocean models should include.
arxiv-2511-00481:
Rahul Mishra and five co-authors propose a light anomaly detector for wireless sensor networks, the webs of small sensors behind environmental monitoring, healthcare, industry, and smart infrastructure. Faults, disturbances, and intrusions all corrupt readings, and heavy detectors strain tiny devices. Their framework rests on a first-order Markov chain: readings are binned into states, and a transition matrix learns how states normally follow each other.

An anomaly is simply an observed transition whose probability falls below a computed threshold, so detection runs in real time with no labeled data. On the Intel Berkeley Research Lab dataset, the system caught thermal spikes, voltage faults, and odd temperature swings with high precision. Against z-score, hidden Markov, and autoencoder rivals, it balanced accuracy, efficiency, and interpretability for large deployments.
arxiv-2511-00681:
Mehmet Yigit Avci and six co-authors give MRI scans a common language for contrast. Scanners, protocols, and hospitals all differ, and standard contrast labels are largely absent, which throttles large-scale machine analysis. Their approach, MR-CLIP, learns a shared contrast code by aligning each 3D scan with its DICOM scan settings, the header data every scanner already records.

The learned embeddings cluster MRI sequences distinctly and beat supervised 3D baselines at few-shot sequence classification when labels are scarce. The same embedding space doubles as a quality check: corrupted or inconsistent records betray themselves through a large image-record distance, with no hand labeling involved. Routine header data becomes a teaching signal, laying a scalable base for label-efficient MRI analysis across diverse clinical collections.
arxiv-2511-00781:
Purba Banerjee, Srikanth Iyer, and Shashi Jain tackle hedging for options whose payoff depends on the whole price path, not just the final price. An investor holds such an option to maturity but can trade only cash, the underlying asset, and plain options that expire earlier.

Their method is model free, borrowing its shape from martingale optimal transport. It chooses the static hedge portfolio that minimizes the expected worst case hedging error at the earlier expiry date. A numerical scheme handles the case where only finitely many plain option prices are known. Tests under Black-Scholes and jump diffusion prices show how the hedge performs, and the authors also prove bounds on the remaining error at final maturity.
arxiv-2511-01081:
Oleksandr Volkov, Yurii Volkov, and Nataliia Voinalovych study power series distributions, a broad family that generalizes many familiar discrete laws, including the Bernoulli, Poisson, and geometric laws. Their aim is constructive: how to build such laws whose covariance structure is fixed in advance.

They derive a first order equation for the law's generating function. It ties its settings to the chosen covariance function. Choosing an analytic or polynomial covariance then fixes the generating function's structure. That link lets them construct new groups that keep a set covariance and extend the classical laws. The approach serves random modeling, where the spread pattern must be set ahead of time.
arxiv-2511-01281:
Sahil Rajesh Dhayalkar writes a beginner friendly mini book on the particle filter, a method for tracking hidden states in noisy, nonlinear systems. Where the Kalman filter needs linear, Gaussian assumptions, the particle filter represents belief as a cloud of weighted samples, hypotheses that evolve with the system.

Step by step, the guide builds the intuition first, then the mathematics. A finite set of particles can stand for a full probability distribution. Prediction, measurement, and resampling then update the cloud in Bayesian fashion. Worked examples, numerical walk throughs, and Python code accompany each idea. The stated aim is that readers finish able to implement the algorithm and to feel how randomness and structure together make inference possible in real time.
arxiv-2511-01381:
Hitesh Kyatham, Arjun Suresh, Aadi Palnitkar, and Yiannis Aloimonos simulate event based cameras underwater. The underwater world defeats ordinary vision with poor light and high dynamic range scenes. Event cameras, which report changes pixel by pixel rather than frames, are an attractive alternative, but training vision models for them needs realistic data.

Their pipeline, EREBUS, generates synthetic event camera data from a camera mounted on an autonomous underwater vehicle, in environments with suspended particles and bad visibility. They show it on rock detection in poor visibility, a task where conventional techniques struggle. The approach is meant to generalize to other underwater tasks, giving researchers training data for a sensor that is hard to collect real data for.
arxiv-2511-20081:
Chen, Artola, Liu, and colleagues clean up noisy molecular MRI scans without knowing the noise. Their 2025 paper presents BALD for CEST imaging. CEST MRI visualizes scarce metabolites through proton exchange effects. Its noise varies across the image in complex ways. Standard denoisers can distort the very signals doctors need.

BALD first stabilizes the noise variance adaptively. Self-similarity inside CEST data guides that transform. Noise becomes uniform across pixels without prior noise knowledge. A two-stage cleanup then separates signal from noise. Local singular value decomposition prevents spatial and spectral artifacts. Hard thresholding kills random components first. Wiener filtering refines what survives afterward. Phantom tests and live scans validated the method. BALD beat leading CEST denoisers on quality metrics. Downstream concentration maps and cancer detection improved too. Plugging its stabilizer into rival denoisers also helped them. Accurate molecular maps may reach the clinic sooner.
arxiv-2511-20181:
Lee, Ricardo, and Tambyah marry high-order tracer transport to low-order fluid dynamics. Their 2025 paper targets the thermal shallow water equations. Weather models need both speed and faithful tracer motion. Low-order dynamics solvers converge fast and stay cheap. But crude transport smears tracers excessively.

A discontinuous Galerkin scheme handles material tracer transport. It provably conserves tracer variance, or damps it with upwinding. The dynamics core stays a low-order mixed finite element method. That core conserves energy by construction. Coupling runs through the dynamics solver's multigrid hierarchy. High-order basis functions sit at the low-order mesh's quadrature points. Standard test cases verified consistency and conservation. Turbulent thermal instability tests showed the payoff. Solutions stayed richer and less diffusive than pure low-order runs. Stability held without excessive tracer smearing. Overall accuracy remains capped by the low-order dynamics. The trick generalizes to other Hamiltonian transport systems.
arxiv-2511-20681:
Leonidas Mindrinos, Nikolaos Pallikarakis, and Nikolaos Tsitsas show in 2025 how neural networks can recover an object's hidden shape from scattered waves. Their test object is a coated cylinder surrounding an inner cylinder of any shape. The inner surface resists electric current, a property described by an impedance function. Only far-away readings of the scattered field are at hand, so the inner shape must be inferred, never seen.

The authors split the job among specially built one-dimensional convolutional networks. Circular padding in the networks respects the repeating nature of the readings. A first network sorts which shape family the inner cylinder belongs to. Later networks rebuild its exact boundary curve and the impedance function along it. In many tests, including versions with added noise, the pipeline stayed quick and robust. A peanut-shaped boundary, for instance, was recovered well with fewer curve coefficients than a kite-shaped one.
arxiv-2511-20881:
K. Ernest Bognini studies in 2025 the period-doubling sequences, infinite letter strings built by repeatedly replacing 0 with 01 and 1 with 00. Such sequences, born in chaos theory, can be generalised to alphabets of k letters, with k at least 2. Bognini asks how these strings split into repeating blocks. His tools are kernel words, special factors first used on Tribonacci words, and gap sequences, which record the spacing between them.

The paper first pins down the sequences' combinatorial and arithmetic properties. It then defines their kernel words and shows how a binary period-doubling sequence factorises into them. Gap sequences turn out to encode the same structure from another angle. Finally, for alphabets of three or more letters, Bognini gives a full factorisation built from kernel words and gaps together. The work extends a factorisation programme from Fibonacci-like words to the period-doubling family.
arxiv-2511-21281:
Boumediene Hamzi and Houman Owhadi give Gaussian process models of turbulent flow a firmer theoretical footing in 2025. Gaussian processes are flexible statistical tools used to fill gaps in fluid data, but their starting assumptions, called priors, are usually picked for convenience. For two-dimensional stochastic Navier-Stokes flow, a recent theorem by Coe, Hairer, and Tolomeo proved quasi-Gaussianity: the flow's long-run behavior matches a simpler linear Gaussian process in a precise sense.

Hamzi and Owhadi build their prior directly from that linear partner process, the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck model, using its stationary covariance set by the forcing spectrum and dissipation. The resulting kernel keeps the power-law energy spectrum of real turbulence across scales. It also supports fast spectral computation. Most importantly, its uncertainty estimates come with guarantees, including support alignment and posterior consistency, tying practical data assimilation to rigorous stochastic equation theory.
arxiv-2511-21481:
Lorenzo Carlucci and Giordano Celli compare two famous logic principles by the yardstick of computational difficulty, in a 2025 pilot study. Both principles, the Ordered Ramsey Theorem and a well-ordering preservation principle for exponentiation, match the same induction strength inside reverse mathematics. That program calibrates exactly how much logical power each theorem needs. Weihrauch reducibility gives a finer ruler, asking whether one problem can be solved by calling the other as a subroutine.

Carlucci and Celli show the Ordered Ramsey Theorem is Weihrauch-equivalent to running the well-ordering principle and the Eventually Constant Tail principle in parallel. A related principle, built by jumping the Limited Principle of Omniscience, turns out incomparable with the well-ordering principle. Neither reduces to the other. The equivalence is the first reduction of this kind linking a combinatorial principle to a well-ordering preservation principle, a template the authors offer for wider comparisons.
arxiv-2511-21581:
Alex Ning, Yen-Ling Kuo, and Gabe Gomes teach a language model to stop thinking when it has thought enough, in 2025. Latent reasoning lets a transformer reason in its internal states instead of written chain-of-thought words, compressing reasoning greatly. Existing versions use a fixed, forced number of latent steps for every problem, wasting compute on easy questions and possibly shortchanging hard ones.

The team adds a binary stop head so the model itself decides when latent reasoning ends, then applies reinforcement learning after supervised fine-tuning to shrink reasoning length while protecting accuracy. On a 1-billion-parameter Llama model solving the GSM8K-Aug math dataset, total reasoning length dropped by 52 percent with no penalty to accuracy. Adaptive stopping thus compounds latent reasoning's compression gains, pointing toward models that meter their own compute per problem. Code and pretrained weights are released for others to extend the approach.
arxiv-2511-21781:
Mlaweh and colleagues present BeeRNA, a computer method that designs RNA sequences which fold into a chosen three-dimensional shape. RNA is a chain of letters whose shape decides what it can do. Designing a chain that folds into a target shape is called inverse folding, and it is much harder for full 3D shapes than for the simpler flat patterns most older tools handle.

BeeRNA searches using an Artificial Bee Colony method, which copies how bees scout for food. It first filters candidates by base-pair distance, then scores survivors by how closely a predicted fold matches the target, while keeping the letter mix balanced. On the RNASolo test set it scored 2.50 angstroms of average shape error against 9.33 for the rival gRNAde tool, and it needs no training, which suits short RNAs under 100 letters such as microRNAs and aptamers.
arxiv-2511-21881:
Bilsborrow and Jeffrey measure how galaxies in computer simulations point in correlated directions, a phenomenon called intrinsic alignment. Galaxies are not randomly oriented, and their alignment contaminates weak gravitational lensing, used to map dark matter. The team searched for alignments in the CAMELS suite of hydrodynamic simulations, varying both cosmology and feedback settings across many runs.

They detected the alignment signal clearly. Its strength depends on the matter density, the clumpiness parameter sigma-8, and two supernova feedback parameters, but not on black hole feedback in these small simulation volumes. Quiet, quiescent galaxies, which have stopped forming stars, aligned about ten times more strongly than star-forming ones in amplitude in their samples. Supernova feedback also affected the two galaxy populations differently, suggesting distinct alignment mechanisms at work. Lensing analyses must therefore model baryon physics and alignments together.
arxiv-2511-21981:
De Villa and colleagues simulate ammonia-hydrogen compounds at Uranus and Neptune interior pressures, 100 to 300 gigapascals. At such pressures these ammonium polyhydrides, with formulas from NH7 all the way to NH24, were predicted by crystal structure searches to form exotic, metastable structures unlike anything at ambient conditions. They heated each compound in simulations, watching for solid, superionic, or liquid phases.

Every compound turned superionic on heating, with the solid-to-superionic transition falling between 350 and 700 kelvin regardless of composition in their simulations. Melting points varied far more, from 700 to 3,000 kelvin, dropping as the proton fraction rose, and above a proton fraction near 0.97 the materials should melt directly with no superionic phase at all in their results. All melting temperatures sit below ice-giant interior profiles, so these compounds would be liquids there.
arxiv-2511-22281:
Guo, Mao, Liang, Wang, and Cai, computer vision researchers, order an image's patches by how much each one reveals about the rest. Seeing a rooster's beak constrains the unseen remainder far more than seeing blank sky, a phenomenon they call patch collapse, by analogy with quantum measurement. They train an autoencoder that softly selects which patches reconstruct each target patch, and graph the learned dependencies. They rank patches by PageRank, producing a principled order in which to reveal an image to a model.

Respecting that order pays off twice. Retraining the state-of-the-art MAR autoregressive generator with collapse ordering boosts image generation. In a new classification setup, vision transformers shown only the highest-ranked patches still classify accurately after seeing just 22 percent of the image. Patch collapse, they argue, generalizes: spend computation where information is.
arxiv-2511-22381:
Lorini and Rozplokhas introduce a logic for what a group of agents believes together, and how strongly. Distributed belief is what follows when a group's separate pieces of information are pooled, even if no single member holds the whole picture. Their language can state that a group believes a fact with at least a given strength k, a graded version of the usual all-or-nothing notion.

The logic is interpreted through belief bases, the stored sets of facts each agent holds. A group's strength is computed after merging the members' bases, so the grade reflects the actual pooled evidence rather than an abstract scale. They use it to formalise epistemic disagreement, where agents' views conflict. They give a sound and complete Hilbert-style axiomatisation, prove decidability by filtration, and supply a tableaux decision procedure, establishing that satisfiability checking is PSPACE-complete.
arxiv-2511-22581:
Forkel and Foerster report a simple recipe beating algorithms at a hard coordination benchmark. Hanabi, a card game where players cannot see their own cards, is a standard zero-shot coordination test: trained agents develop incompatible conventions and fail together. Specialised algorithms were invented for this failure. The authors instead run standard independent PPO with one change, raising the entropy coefficient from the usual 0.01 to 0.05, keeping policies more random in training.

The result is a new state of the art for inter-seed cross-play in Hanabi, beating every specialised method by a margin. Higher entropy stops seeds locking into incompatible conventions. Two more tweaks help: a high advantage-estimation parameter around 0.9 in the reported setting, and recurrent instead of feed-forward networks. Care is needed: their counterexample games show entropy-tuned policy gradients still cannot always reach cross-play, so specialised algorithms remain necessary.
arxiv-2511-22781:
Agarwal and Chakraborti measure the AI boom's carbon cost and ask what drives it. Training and running modern models burns much energy, but emissions vary wildly between projects. They study models across language processing, computer vision, and audio. They examine model size, repository activity including commits and age, task type, and the organisation behind the model, to find what tracks higher emissions.

Two drivers stand out: model size and versioning frequency both correlate strongly with higher emissions. Domain matters too: language models tend to have lower footprints than audio systems. Most surprisingly, university-driven projects showed the highest emissions, followed by non-profits and companies, while community-driven projects showed a reduction. The authors argue for green AI practices, efficient architectures, optimised workflows, and renewable energy, framing the study as a first audit framework for innovation's hidden environmental ledger.
arxiv-2511-22881:
Chnaras and Kupinsky map polynomials computing square roots in a field. Over the p-element field, a polynomial computes square roots if its value at every nonzero square squares back to that element. When p is 3 modulo 4, one monomial does the job at minimal degree. When p is 1 modulo 4, the Tonelli-Shanks algorithm produces such polynomials, but minimality and the degree spectrum stayed open.

They prove structural results, including a rigidity result: a polynomial whose square has very few monomials is a monomial, and enumerate all minimal-degree examples. Tonelli-Shanks turns out not always optimal: for p equal to 41, a minimal polynomial has degree 17 while the Tonelli-Shanks polynomial has degree 18. Tree decompositions show the minimal example reducing degree at the last step where Tonelli-Shanks never does. Building on recent bounds, it gives the first picture of degrees in the harder class.
arxiv-2511-22981:
Mori and colleagues work on a counting question in geometry: how many flat faces, called facets, can a family of lattice shapes have? The shapes are twinned chain polytopes, built from partially ordered sets. And they belong to the reflexive family, lattice polytopes whose dual shape is also a lattice polytope, a class used in algebraic geometry.

They prove that a twinned chain polytope in dimension d has at most 6 raised to the power d over 2 facets. When d is even, the bound is reached for shapes built as free sums of d over 2 copies of the del Pezzo polygon. The result gives a partial answer to Nill's conjecture, which claims the same bound for every reflexive polytope. The claim is so far confirmed only in low dimensions, where the limits are 6 facets in dimension 2 and 36 in dimension 4.
arxiv-2511-23081:
Dwiputra and colleagues study a quantum battery, a small quantum system charged by a separate charger. It is built here from a bosonic oscillator, a vibrating mode that can in principle hold unlimited energy. In practice the stored energy sloshes back and forth between charger and battery in coherent oscillations, which caps how much power the battery can take up.

They show that slowly ramping the charger-battery interaction, a slow quench, suppresses those oscillations. The maximum charging power then grows as a power law in the quench duration, with an exponent between 0 and 2 set by the ramp shape. So slower charging paradoxically delivers more power. Adding charger dissipation restores a finite best duration. The same scaling appears when the system is mapped onto the Tavis-Cummings model of atoms coupled to light, hinting the effect is widespread.
arxiv-2511-23381:
Allen and Genao study how the field generated by the torsion points of a curve compares with the cyclotomic field generated by roots of unity, asking when the two can coincide. The p-division field always contains the p-th roots of unity. It is larger, and the authors prove that for every number field finitely many levels can give equality, with a bound that does not depend on the curve.

Their proof shows a curve at an exceptional prime has a point of order p defined over an extension of degree at most six. In the ramified case, that degree is at most six times the degree of the base field. This converts the problem into known torsion bounds. Assuming the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, they also bound the primes where the division field is abelian over fields without rational complex multiplication, generalizing earlier rational results.
arxiv-2512-00281:
Finding lung cancer early saves lives, but screening rules based on nodule size and growth can delay diagnosis. Sylvain Bodard and a large team present an AI system that rethinks lung cancer screening in 2025. The system works directly on low-dose CT scans.

Instead of waiting for growth, the AI performs both detection and malignancy diagnosis at the level of each nodule. The authors report performance beyond radiologists, leading models, and standards based on size and growth. If such results hold in wider trials, screening could flag dangerous nodules at the first scan rather than months later. Low-dose scans are noisier than standard CT, which makes nodule-level diagnosis harder.
arxiv-2512-00481:
Quantum error correction for continuous-variable systems runs into a no-go theorem: Gaussian tools alone cannot suppress Gaussian displacement errors. Fucheng Guo, Frank Mueller, and Yuan Liu propose a concatenated dual displacement code in 2025. Earlier schemes used GKP states to correct small displacements.

When displacements grow large, lattice-crossing errors exceed what a GKP state can correct. Concatenation layers codes so that one level catches what another misses. Optical and microwave quantum computers both use continuous variables, so stronger displacement codes would raise the fault tolerance of those platforms. GKP states encode a qubit in an oscillator, which is why they anchor this research line. Large displacements are the regime where protection is most needed and hardest to get.
arxiv-2512-00981:
Mateusz Oleszko, Ralf Hambach, and Herbert Gross work on optical design math in a 2025 paper. Designers of lenses and mirrors care about aberrations, the flaws that blur an image. Freeform optical surfaces, shaped without simple symmetry, are now common and demand tools built for generalized systems.

A standard method expands the total wave aberration into coefficients that depend on field position and pupil position. That expansion lets designers see which surface adds which flaw. The authors decompose the total aberration for generalized systems, surface by surface. Clearer attribution of flaws helps designers fix the right surface instead of guessing.
arxiv-2512-01081:
Stephen Fitz proposes a research program on machine consciousness in a 2025 paper. The Machine Consciousness Hypothesis holds that consciousness is a substrate-free functional property. In plain terms, what matters is the computation a system does, not the material it runs on. The key requirement is second-order perception, the ability to perceive its own perceiving.

Fitz proposes testing the idea in silico, inside simulated worlds. The plan studies how groups of learning systems build shared models of themselves inside simulated worlds that organize themselves. A testable program could move these debates from philosophy toward measurement.
arxiv-2512-01281:
Xuan Yang, Songbo Zhang, and Xuefeng Wu checked whether brief radio flashes in space ever repeat. These flashes, called fast radio bursts, last just a blink. Some seem to fire once and never again. The team picked a group first found by the Parkes scope in Australia.

They watched the same sky spots again with Parkes and with the FAST scope in China. They used many hours of new data for the search. No new flash showed up from those spots. A null result still helps. It sets limits on how often such bursts can repeat and how bright repeats could be.
arxiv-2512-01481:
Qisen Wang and co-authors build a way to make 4D scenes from video models. Camera-guided video tools can make fine film-like clips. Real 4D work needs more. Views from many angles must match in space and time at once.

Past fixes lean on data tricks or slow test-time tuning. Those paths are capped by weak spread to new scenes. The team's method uses diffusion sampling in a higher space. It aims for matched multi-view clips with high detail. Such clips serve in film, games, and robot training worlds.
arxiv-2512-01681:
Farzaneh Seyedshahi and co-authors test a pathology model on biopsy samples from many centers. Subtype sorting and outcome calls in mesothelioma guide therapy. Most models train on large resection samples. Real diagnosis rests on small biopsies instead.

Their model was trained by self-supervision on resections alone. They test it cold on multicentre biopsies. A pass would show resection training can transfer to biopsy work. That transfer saves the cost of building big biopsy sets for each new hospital. Biopsy tissue is scant, so a model that wastes none of it on training folds holds a real edge in rare cancer work.
arxiv-2512-01881:
Training a deep vision network means following noisy gradient signals downhill toward lower error, and the optimizer is the rule that decides each step. Ahmed Nebli's 2025 paper argues that today's rules force a fixed compromise: methods like AdamW trust the size of each gradient as a guide to the landscape's curvature.

Nebli proposes ThermoLion, an optimizer designed to unite two kinds of information, the sign of the gradient and its magnitude, instead of leaning on one alone. Framing training as signal recovery inside high-dimensional noise motivates the design. If the approach holds up, it could give vision models a steadier, more informative path through training.
arxiv-2512-02081:
Topological data analysis summarizes the shape of data with persistence diagrams, which track when features like loops appear and vanish. Dong Liu's 2025 paper proposes a hybrid quantum algorithm that computes these diagrams, going beyond what earlier quantum methods could deliver.

Existing quantum topological algorithms, such as the LGZ algorithm, efficiently produce only summary statistics like Betti numbers. Those totals hide the life story of each individual feature, which is what practitioners in drug discovery, materials design, and medical monitoring actually use. A quantum route to full diagrams could bring quantum speed to a widely used data tool.
arxiv-2512-02381:
Electric heavy equipment working far from the grid needs charging brought to it, and mobile fast chargers are trucks that do exactly that. Farhang Motallebi Araghi and three co-authors tackle in 2025 the joint problem of choosing the charger fleet and routing it under time windows.

Existing planning treated fleet design and routing as separate problems, fixing the vehicles before dispatching them. Joint optimization can pick a fleet that fits the actual routes, saving both capital and time. The work speaks to agencies electrifying off-road fleets at remote sites where fixed chargers cannot be justified.
arxiv-2512-02981:
Zhongyu Yang and four co-authors fight hallucination in multimodal language models by letting agents check themselves. Hallucination, fluent but false output, remains a critical barrier to reliable multimodal systems. Many fixes lean on human intervention, or underuse the agent's own ability to catch its errors.

InEx draws on how humans make reliable decisions, through introspection and cross checking. Agents examine their own answers, then collaborate across modalities to test them. Self correcting systems could make visual question answering and captioning safer for medicine, education, and public information. Self checks that run in the loop cost no staff time. They can guard each call, not just a test set run once a year.
arxiv-2512-03281:
A census of feeding black holes reaches deep into the early universe. Caroline Baccus and Xinfeng Xu present the sample in this 2025 work. They use spectra from the NIRSpec instrument on the Webb telescope.

The sample holds over two hundred broad-line active galactic nuclei. More than half are newly identified, and they span a wide range of cosmic time. Though faint and small, these sources accrete at high rates, the authors say. The census helps trace how black holes grew in remote eras. Broad lines signal fast gas near a black hole, a trait this census counts at scale.
arxiv-2512-03381:
Players in a co-op game must talk to solve puzzles together. Nicholas Tomlin and a large team study that talk in this 2025 work. Cooperative games yield rich language data, since players reason under uncertainty in complex settings.

The team collected the Portal Dialogue Corpus from the co-op mode of Portal 2. It holds many hours of spoken dialogue and tens of thousands of utterances. Such corpora help researchers see how people coordinate through words. They also give AI builders real examples of grounded, task-based conversation. Dialogue corpora from games offer natural talk tied to shared goals and visible scenes.
arxiv-2512-03681:
Quantum walks, where a particle spreads across a graph over time, offer one route to quantum computing. Lilith Zschetzsche and co-authors ask in a 2025 preprint how that route relates to one based on coupled masses and springs. Both problem families live on huge, sparse graphs. Both are known to capture the full power of quantum computation.

The authors build a direct translation between the two settings, not just a link through shared hardness. Their mapping keeps the graph geometry, the starting setup, the read-out step, and access to problem data intact, so overhead stays low. Algorithms written for quantum walks can therefore be converted into oscillator versions, and the other way around. The correspondence works for easier subfamilies that fall short of full quantum power. It also yields a clearer proof that the oscillator problem is equally hard.
arxiv-2512-04081:
Raising numbers to an irrational power scrambles their additive structure in ways number theorists are only beginning to chart. Joseph Harrison studies that scrambling in a 2025 preprint. Take a finite set of non-negative reals, raise each element to an irrational power, then ask how large the set of k-fold sums can be.

For sets drawn from an arithmetic progression, Harrison proves the sumset grows at essentially the fastest rate. It matches the count expected if all sums were distinct, uniformly in the power. The key bound leans on deep tools: a functional transcendence theorem and recent refinements of the Pila-Wilkie counting theorem.
