He also gives a Diophantine condition on the power guaranteeing a certain linear form in such powers cannot vanish. That yields a new proof that infinitely many powers keep a multiplicatively independent set linearly independent.
arxiv-2512-04981:
NaHyeon Park and five co-authors show how the hidden instructions inside text-to-image systems can skew who appears in the pictures. Modern systems use a large language model to read and expand a user's request, which improves the match between words and image. But when a request says nothing about age, race, or gender, the model often fills the gap with its own assumptions.

The team built a benchmark that varies how vague or detailed a request is, and tested eight recent systems. The language-model-based ones showed stronger demographic skew than simpler systems, and the hidden system prompts proved to be a main driver, bending the text encoding before any picture is made. Their fix, called FairPro, rewrites those instructions on the fly to ask for fair treatment while keeping the user's intent, and it cut the disparities sharply in tests.
arxiv-2512-05081:
Jung Yi and five co-authors introduce Deep Forcing, a way to make streaming video generators hold together over long clips without any retraining. Models that generate video frame by frame in real time tend to repeat themselves, drift, or slow down as the clip stretches. A tempting fix, borrowed from text models, keeps early tokens as anchors — but applied naively to video it degrades the picture and freezes the motion.

Deep Forcing pairs two training-free tricks. Deep Sink reserves half of the model's memory window for anchor tokens and re-aligns their timing so the scene stays stable during long runs. Participative Compression prunes the memory instead, keeping only tokens recent frames attend to and discarding stale history before errors pile up. Together they stretch a model trained on five-second clips past a full minute, with sharper, livelier motion than rival methods, still in real time.
arxiv-2512-05181:
Anh Tong and eight co-authors describe a modular instrument for optically detected magnetic resonance inside a standard helium cryostat. The technique reads out tiny magnetic signals through the glow of nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond, a sensitive quantum magnetometer. The challenge here is plumbing. The cryostat's insert is nearly two metres long. The light must travel that whole path, excite the sensor, and bring the fluorescence back without losing alignment or beam quality.

Their setup spans the full insert while living mostly outside the cryostat, so it drops into existing systems without major modification. To prove it works, the team measured how the resonance signal shifts with temperature and with small applied fields, and detected the magnetic transition of a strontium ruthenate sample. The demonstration shows nitrogen-vacancy magnetometry is feasible even in cramped cryogenic environments, widening where the technique can be used.
arxiv-2512-05581:
Vincenzo Aronica, Julian Bautista, Arnaud de Mattia, and Hector Gil-Marín measure how fast cosmic structure is growing by analyzing the same galaxies in two mathematical spaces at once. Galaxies' positions are distorted along the line of sight by their own motions, and the distortion rate encodes the growth of structure — a key test of gravity and dark energy. Analyses usually work in Fourier space or in configuration space and combine results afterwards; this team builds a joint framework from the start.

They validate it on the AbacusSummit simulations and on mock catalogues reproducing the BOSS and eBOSS luminous red galaxy samples. The validation uses an effective-field-theory clustering model of the kind behind the latest Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument results. The joint inference gives unbiased, robust constraints consistent with each space alone. Applied to the real data, their growth measurement agrees well with the official result.
arxiv-2512-05781:
David Jennings and six co-authors extend a quantum algorithm for simulating fluids that do not compress. The lattice Boltzmann method, which tracks particle packets hopping on a grid, is a favorite candidate for quantum speedup. A recent quantum version handled only idealized setups. Real flows have walls, inlets, outlets, and outside forces pushing them along. This team builds all four into the algorithm and checks what they cost.

The added machinery does not spoil the scaling: the cost grows as before, so the hoped for quantum advantage survives contact with realistic geometry. To support the theory, the authors run classical simulations of the method on standard test flows. These include the Taylor-Green vortex, the lid driven cavity, and flow past a cylinder. Accuracy and convergence behave as the analysis predicts. The paper maps a route from tidy quantum prototypes toward the flows engineers actually simulate.
arxiv-2512-06281:
Hengzhuang Li and nine co authors try to stop image aware language models from neglecting the pictures they are shown. Such models can chat about images, yet in their deeper layers the words tend to crowd out the visual signal. The result is weak sight based skill and, at times, made up details. The cause, they argue, is training that only asks the model to predict the next word.

Their fix, LaVer, adds a visual task inside the model's shared meaning space. Parts of an image are hidden, and the model must rebuild them from what remains, all in the same inner code it uses for words. After training this way, the models gave more of their focus to image content. Tests across many tasks showed clear gains, most of all on tasks that need fine visual detail. It offers a direct way to keep sight strong in such models.
arxiv-2512-06381:
Tao Wang and six co authors improve the first pass of a shopping recommender, the step that picks a shortlist of goods a user might want. Big platforms run many shortlist models side by side, drawing on behavior from many corners of the app. Adding samples from other corners helps, but only up to a point: many of those goods would have been picked anyway, so the gain fades.

Their framework, IncRec, hunts for the samples no current model picks, the true leftovers across all corners of the app. It then learns a representation aimed at just those leftovers, so the new model adds goods the old ones missed. A further step favors leftovers that stand a good chance of being shown to users. In offline tests and live trials on Taobao's home page, IncRec beat leading methods, and it now runs in the live product.
arxiv-2512-06481:
Tae-Hoon Kim and four co authors watch strain bend the magnetic spirals inside a chiral magnet, live under a microscope. Pulling on a material is a clean, low power way to steer tiny magnets, but how the spin pattern rearranges in space as strain builds was poorly known. The team applied a measured one way stretch while imaging helical domains with a Lorentz electron microscope.

Reorientation of the spiral's wave direction hinged on its angle to the pull, much as in metals that deform for good. Magnetic defects did the work of moving, by breaking and reconnecting, or by gliding and canceling like dislocations in a crystal. Simulations point to a strain driven change in a twisting magnetic interaction as a key driver. The findings map how strain steers magnetism at the nanoscale, a route toward low power magnetic devices.
arxiv-2512-06681:
Amartya Hatua opens up a small language model to see, causally, how it computes sentiment. Mechanistic interpretability aims to trace a model's behavior to its parts. Working with GPT-2, Hatua patched activations layer by layer, swapping in signals from other texts to test which layers carry the feeling of a passage. A two stage picture was on trial: early layers spot emotional words, middle layers fold in context like negation and sarcasm.

The first stage held. Early layers did act as word level sentiment detectors, stable and largely blind to context. The second stage failed in all three forms tested. Context was not concentrated in the middle, not split by phenomenon, and not as the theory spread it. Instead, late layers did the folding in, through one unified, non modular mechanism. The result is a caution: sentiment in this model is wired otherwise than the tidy hierarchy predicted.
arxiv-2512-06981:
Yuemin Wang and Ian Stavness improve how image models learn to label every pixel in a scene, a task called semantic segmentation. Training usually starts with a warm-up game: hide random patches of an image and make the model rebuild them. The authors argue random hiding wastes effort on easy patches. Their warm-up instead hides the patches the model currently finds hardest to rebuild, chosen round by round as training proceeds.

Tested on street scenes, general photo sets, and two farm data sets for spotting weeds among crops, the selective method beat random masking. It also beat the usual shortcut of pretraining on a giant labeled photo collection. Gains were largest for the classes the model otherwise handled worst, a valuable trait when rare categories matter. Using the same data for warm-up and training worked best on a small budget.
arxiv-2512-07181:
Ana Aguilar-Pineda and co-authors speed up a flexible simulation method used for three-dimensional engineering problems. The virtual element method handles meshes built from general polyhedra, which suits messy real geometries, but big problems need preconditioners that keep iterative solvers from stalling. Their construction is a two-level overlapping Schwarz method: the domain is split into subdomains that overlap, each solved locally, with a coarse global pass tying the pieces together.

What is new is the setting's roughness: the subdomains themselves can be irregular, extending earlier work that assumed tidier decompositions. Numerical experiments show the solver's effort stays robust as subdomains multiply and mesh parameters vary, with condition numbers on par with classical finite element results. Rival frameworks exist, the authors note, but the plainness of overlapping Schwarz is itself a virtue.
arxiv-2512-07781:
Leandro Abaroa, Gustavo Romero, and Valentí Bosch-Ramon wrote this 2025 astrophysics paper on mystery lights in the sky. A mountaintop observatory in China, LHAASO, keeps finding ultrahigh-energy gamma-ray sources. Many of them have no identified origin at all.

The authors propose a culprit that hides in plain sight: dead microquasars. A microquasar is a small black hole system that once fed violently on a companion star. When the feeding stops, the engine quenches and the system goes dark. Cosmic rays from its active years may linger inside its cocoon. Those particles later strike nearby molecular clouds and collide with their gas. The collisions shine in gamma rays of extreme energy. Remnants of the greediest feeders could release particles at PeV energies. Their clouds would glow at hundreds of teraelectronvolts in response. Several unidentified Galactic sources from LHAASO fit this picture naturally. Dark PeVatrons may be yesterday's microquasars.
arxiv-2512-07881:
Mikołaj Sienicki and Krzysztof Sienicki wrote this 2025 comment paper in the foundations of physics. A 2024 paper by Aerts and co-authors made a bold suggestion about language. Word frequencies in texts, it claimed, follow Bose-Einstein statistics from quantum physics.

That fit was offered as a clue to the origin of quantum statistics itself. The Sienickis answer with a modest but pointed critique. Three key steps in the argument blur physics with definitions, they say. A normalization issue is dressed up as bosonic enhancement in the first. Rank is identified with energy in the second, weakening the fit's diagnostic force. The third concerns a baseline comparison too weak for the conclusion drawn. A claim about the deep nature of reality needs a sterner test than that.  Reproducibility also earns a flag. Analogies can inspire without proving ontology.
arxiv-2512-08181:
Edward L Ned Wright, Joseph Masiero, Amy Mainzer, and colleagues, planetary scientists, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025 about the asteroid Torifune, also known as 2001 CC21. It is the flyby target of the Hayabusa2 extended mission, yet its size is uncertain because its brightness and reflectivity are poorly known. The team gathered every NEOWISE infrared observation from late 2021 to early 2024.

They fit the infrared data with a rotating, cratered thermal model shaped like an ellipsoid. The fit gives a diameter near three hundred forty meters, far below an earlier estimate of about seven hundred. Polarization data also point to a smaller body, though not quite this small. The model favors forward rotation with a modest tilt. Fitting older Spitzer data gives a larger size, and fitting both datasets demands oddly high thermal inertia, showing how hard this asteroid is to pin down before the flyby.
arxiv-2512-08581:
Huali Zhang improves the local theory for two dimensional compressible Euler equations, which describe a gas that can be compressed as it flows. The result gives local existence and uniqueness of solutions in Sobolev spaces for starting velocity, log density, and vorticity that meet set regularity conditions. A notable point is that vorticity needs less regularity than velocity and density.

The proof uses the Smith Tataru method and the wave transport structure that is built into the two dimensional system. A key observation is that Strichartz estimates still hold even though the gradient of vorticity appears as a source term in the velocity wave equation. That balance allows the lower vorticity demand to work. The theorem improves the known regularity threshold by a quarter order over prior results, sharpening what starting data are known to launch a unique local solution.
arxiv-2512-08681:
Alexey Gordeev and Lars Daniel Ohman give a new construction for triple arrays, a structured type of rectangular array studied in combinatorics. Their method combines a symmetric design with a resolution of another design. It is the first general method that can produce non extremal triple arrays, which the authors call resolvable in this setting.

With the construction, they produce the first examples of a previously missing array size and list all resolvable arrays of a smaller size, where only one example was known before. A known infinite family also turns out to fit the method. The authors introduce unordered triple arrays as a related object, propose a stronger form of a long standing conjecture, and support it with full counts for small cases. Several infinite families are built, with a link to finite affine planes.
arxiv-2512-08881:
Aysim Toker and coauthors present SATGround, a method to improve visual grounding in satellite images with vision language models. Visual grounding means finding the object in an image that a text instruction refers to. Satellite scenes are complex, so precise location is hard even for strong general models.

Their approach fine tunes a pretrained model on varied instruction tasks and adds a dedicated grounding module. Special control tokens link the language model to that module, allowing joint reasoning over words and spatial information. Tests on several remote sensing benchmarks show consistent gains over prior methods. The relative improvement on visual grounding is especially large. The authors argue that structured spatial reasoning is the key ingredient for reliable satellite analysis. Their results point toward more trustworthy tools for real world work with remote sensing data.
arxiv-2512-09081:
Arman Zarei and coauthors present AgentComp, a framework to improve how text to image models handle composition. Leading models produce striking images, yet they struggle to capture object relations, attribute bindings, and fine details correctly. A key limit is that models are not trained to distinguish prompts and images.

AgentComp uses language models equipped with image generation, editing, and question answering tools to build compositional data sets on their own. Those data sets pair similar cases that differ in a targeted detail. An agentic preference optimization method then fine tunes the image model to tell such cases apart. Results reach leading scores on a standard compositionality benchmark, without the loss of image quality seen in prior approaches. The gains even transfer to abilities that were not trained directly, such as text rendering.
arxiv-2512-09381:
Guram Bezhanishvili and Mashiath Khan settle a question in modal logic that had been open since 1998. Their subject is product logics, which combine two logics so that statements can speak about two dimensions at once. The specific combinations pair GL, the logic of provability, or its variant Grz, with S5, the standard logic of necessity and possibility.

Gabbay and Shehtman had asked whether these product logics can be captured by finite sets of axioms. The authors prove that the GL product with S5 is product matching, a strong structural property. For the Grz product, they show it can be axiomatized by adding a single extra principle, the Gödel translation of the monadic Casari formula, to the combined logic of the two components. Together the results give finite axiom systems for both logics, closing the question posed more than twenty-five years earlier.
arxiv-2512-09781:
Ian Descamps and five colleagues in physics education compare three versions of a pendulum lab activity. Each version was built by a different teaching team. The teams started from the same theory of how students learn and shared similar goals for the lab. Even so, their finished activities came out noticeably different from one another.

The authors trace the split to three causes. The teams held different expectations of students at their own schools. They carried different side goals beyond the shared ones. They also drew different lessons from their shared theory. The paper argues that course designers should explain the reasoning behind their choices, and that teachers may gain by adapting a lab to their own setting rather than following it exactly.
arxiv-2512-10081:
Kensuke Takii, Changhao Liang, and Hiroaki Ogata propose the first axiomatic theory of learning analytics. The field, which uses data to understand and improve learning, has grown through practice while its theory stayed vague. The authors derive five axioms from the psychological definition of learning and the field's methodological needs. The axioms cover discrete observation, experience construction, state transition, and inference. From them they derive theorems about what the field can and cannot know.

Among the results: learner states are inherently unobservable, the temporal order of learning is irreducible, reachable states are constrained, and future learning cannot be predicted deterministically. The authors define the field's structure and practice as formal objects. They prove the axioms are jointly sufficient and individually necessary. They also show that familiar approaches, from Bayesian knowledge tracing to dashboards, fit uniformly inside the framework.
arxiv-2512-10181:
Phuc V. Trinh and Shinya Sugiura envision a quantum internet that flies. Their concept puts quantum communication terminals on drones and satellites, linking distant nodes through free space optical channels, light beams through air and space rather than fiber. The article lays out the vision, contrasts aerial platforms with ground based ones, and works through the engineering challenges altitude brings: pointing stability, atmospheric effects, and moving terminals. Typical non terrestrial scenarios get detailed system designs and analysis, at several altitude layers from unmanned aircraft to orbital satellites.

The forward look is integration. The authors propose joining high dimensional, multipartite quantum communication with sensing, computing, and intelligence for many simultaneous users. That is the path they see from isolated quantum links to a fully operational quantum internet. The piece is a magazine style vision article, short and programmatic, meant to organize a research direction.
arxiv-2512-10281:
Florian Lengyel studies a family of algebraic objects that sit at the crossroads of simplicial algebra and higher category theory. Starting from a tuple of positive integers and a commutative ring, he builds a diagonal simplicial tensor module, whose components are functions on a cosimplicial index set. The construction extends Quillen's diagonal for double semi-simplicial groups by restricting a multi fold simplicial module along the diagonal. The central question is when these modules qualify as algebraic n-hypergroupoids, a notion going back to Duskin and Glenn. There, horns, the partial shapes a simplex's boundary can take, admit fillers in a controlled way.

His kernel computation yields exact thresholds for the hypergroupoid property.
arxiv-2512-10381:
George Leontaris and George Prampromis ask whether rotating black holes born in the early universe could be the dark matter. Their setting is the dark dimension scenario, a theory that predicts one extra dimension of space, about a micron wide, tied to the observed value of dark energy. In that setting, a black hole that reaches into the fifth dimension behaves differently from an ordinary one.

The authors show that such five-dimensional rotating black holes lose mass far more slowly than four-dimensional ones. So holes above a certain starting mass could still exist today and make up most of the dark matter. They then add the memory burden effect, which slows the decay further still, strengthening the case that these objects could account for all of it.
arxiv-2512-11581:
Salim B Ivars and co-authors solve a long standing problem with tiny rings of light called Kerr micro-resonators. These rings can make soliton pulses, which form the teeth of a frequency comb, a tool for exact light measures. In the usual setup, though, solitons are hard to start in a calm, controlled way.

The team adds a small local spot that breaks the symmetry of the ring. That one change reshapes the tangled map of stable states into a smooth path. By slowly tuning the laser, users can now reach bright or dark solitons of any width, step by step and in reverse. The states also turn pump light into comb light with record level yield.
arxiv-2512-11681:
Hai-Peng Li and co-authors take a close look at one particle reaction measured by the BESIII team in Beijing. The reaction turns a J/psi particle into a phi, an eta, and a neutral pion. Three puzzles stand out in the data.

First, a narrow bump marks the a0(980) particle, seen through a rare rule breaking path. Second, two peaks were labeled as a non phi background. Third, loop diagrams called triangle diagrams should spike at that same energy. The team shows those spikes are in fact tiny, due to how the phi is spotted through a narrow mass window. They suggest other ways to spot the phi so the loop effect can be seen.
arxiv-2512-11781:
Vineet Pasumarti, Lorenzo Bianchi, and Antonio Loquercio show that racing teaches drones to fly hard. Training one drone alone with shaped rewards, like points for following a line, gives tame flight. Racing, with the single goal of winning, forces bold moves.

Through contests, drones learned to fly at their physical edge and to block and pass rivals, with no one coding those tricks. In both simulation and real flights the racers beat line trained drones, most of all on cluttered tracks. Their skills also moved to the real world more reliably and coped with new rivals. Sparse goals plus rivalry, the work suggests, can grow rich real world skill.
arxiv-2512-11981:
Nima Laal and co-authors measure what pulsar timing arrays can teach us about pairs of supermassive black holes. These arrays sense a background hum of gravity waves from many orbiting pairs at once. That hum carries facts about the pairs that light based surveys cannot reach, like how fast they shrink at close range.

The team ran Bayesian inference on 200 simulated NANOGrav style data sets. There is a better than even chance of halving the uncertainty on the pair hardening rate, and lifetime errors shrink by 25 to 75 percent. Odds reach 88 percent for a solid gain on one galaxy mass function trait. Other traits gain little beyond what light already gives.
arxiv-2512-12081:
Semih Kara and co-authors ask where to place electric vehicle chargers so they ease, not worsen, traffic jams. More EVs mean more charging trips, and careless siting can clog the very streets the cars use. The team models driver route choice as a traffic equilibrium, a state where no driver gains by switching.

Two models are tried: a congestion game and an atomic queueing simulation. Both feed a greedy placement algorithm that adds stations one by one. The greedy picks prove optimal or near optimal on realistic networks, though a counterexample bars a blanket promise. The queueing version reads more realistic, and the paper unifies the two by calibrating game delays from queue runs.
arxiv-2512-12181:
Mohammad Taghi Dabiri and three co-authors speed up satellite tracking in a 2025 paper. Optical links with low Earth orbit satellites need beam aim set in milliseconds to keep fast data flowing. Older systems sweep many beams in sequence or steer parts by machine, which can be slow.

Their method scans with two crossed line shaped laser beams and no moving parts. A physics model covers air loss and turbulence, and a neural network turns light patterns into the satellite position. Tests gave typical errors of 7 to 10 meters and scan times of 1 to 2 milliseconds. Older two stage methods took up to 5 milliseconds.
arxiv-2512-12981:
Jonathan Wenshoj, Tong Chen, Bob Pepin, and Raghavendra Selvan present CoDeQ, a method that shrinks neural networks by pruning and quantization at the same time. Doing both together should beat doing them in sequence. But past joint methods needed extra side steps and much tuning.

CoDeQ uses a simple insight: the dead zone of a quantizer, a range treated as zero, acts just like magnitude pruning. By learning the width of that zone during training, the method sets sparsity and precision in one pass. On ImageNet with ResNet-18, it cut bit operations to about 5 percent. Accuracy stayed close to the full precision model.
arxiv-2512-13281:
Jiaqi Wang and co-authors introduce VideoASMR-Bench, a benchmark that tests whether AI can make and spot fake ASMR videos. Such videos rely on fine sound and touch-like detail, so small artifacts matter more than broad scene sense. Older benchmarks for generated video miss that fine grain.

The set holds 1,500 real ASMR videos and 2,235 synthetic ones from nine generation models. Vision-language models try to detect the fakes while generators try to fool them, an adversarial setup. Even the strongest model tested failed to reliably spot AI-made ASMR clips. Humans, by contrast, still found them relatively easy to identify.
arxiv-2512-13781:
Audrey Lindsay and Tomasz R. Taylor study symmetries of particles and scattering in de Sitter spacetime. De Sitter space is the fully symmetric expanding universe model, with isometry group SO(1,4). Their work links those spacetime symmetries to the quantum states of basic particles.

For the key unitary representations, they give direct transformation laws for symmetry generators on one-particle states. The basis is adapted to an SU(2) times SU(2) split of the Hilbert space. From those laws, they derive Ward identities that constrain de Sitter scattering amplitudes. In the large-momentum limit, the Poincaré algebra and flat-space Ward identities return. The paper offers a firm symmetry base for quantum field theory in curved, expanding space.
arxiv-2512-14081:
Yang Su and co-authors ask how cold gas gets loaded into the Milky Way's nuclear outflows, the Fermi and eROSITA bubbles. The origin of the bubbles' multiphase gas is crucial for understanding feedback from the Galactic Center. They use HI4PI data on high-velocity clouds toward that region.

The clouds show an asymmetric distribution tied to bar-driven tilted dust lanes and distorted overshooting streams. The authors propose that nuclear outflows strike these gas-rich, off-plane structures and strip cold gas from 0.5 to 1.7 kiloparsecs out, not only from the central molecular zone. Clouds are accelerated to about 230 to 340 kilometers per second over 3 to 6 million years. The estimated outflow rate near 1 solar mass per year matches the bar-driven inflow rate, a tight gas cycle.
arxiv-2512-14481:
Shizhuo Mao, Song Chen, and Yi Kang tackle the memory problem of large language models, which grow faster than graphics card capacity. Shrinking numbers to fewer bits helps, but adjusting those scales during use is costly, fixed scales lose accuracy, and retraining the whole model is expensive. Their framework, SASQ, trains only the activation scales and leaves the pretrained weights untouched.

Extreme activation values are trimmed in a controlled way so the remaining values quantize cleanly. Inference then runs with fixed scales, which suits small devices. On LLaMA2-7B the method posted lower perplexity, a standard error score, than both a leading rotation-based scheme and the full-precision model on WikiText2.
arxiv-2512-14881:
Nguyen Binh leads a large team studying galaxies that stopped forming stars very early in cosmic history. These massive quiescent galaxies, seen at redshift above 3, are a window on how the first galaxies lived and died. Theory made mixed guesses about their surroundings, from crowded neighborhoods to high rates of quiet neighbors nearby.

Using Webb telescope data in the COSMOS-Web field, the team built a sample of 171 such galaxies with masses above ten billion Suns. Around them they found plenty of star forming neighbors, the reverse of the conformity pattern seen nearby. Settings ranged from near empty to dense, and 4 percent showed signs of fresh cold gas flowing in along filaments. One find, nicknamed Saigon, is the most distant low mass quiet galaxy known, at redshift 4.55 inside a forming cluster.
arxiv-2512-15281:
Faima Abbasi and two coauthors give digital twins a shared language so their layers stop talking past each other. A digital twin mirrors a physical system with data, models, and simulations, and it supports monitoring, prediction, and optimization. In multi layered twins, mismatched meanings between layers cause inconsistencies and sync failures, and hand built mappings are brittle.

Their semantic grounding pipeline first builds the twin in a flexible framework with data, model, and metamodel layers. It then lifts the metamodel into an RDF graph, a unified web of facts. An alignment method called SSM-OM matches that graph to an ontology using semantic embeddings, lexical similarity, and language model reasoning. Tests include RDF checks, a twin use case, and OAEI benchmarks. The results show consistent meaning, cross layer traceability, and broad domain fit.
arxiv-2512-15481:
Shavbo Salehi and co authors present PENME, a method for sending video by meaning rather than by raw pixels, in a 2025 paper. Video dominates network traffic and costs much bandwidth and power. Semantic communication sends only the meaning needed to rebuild frames, which can cut that cost if motion is handled well.

PENME picks a residual motion extractor for each frame from three options, using a five step policy based on motion strength, consistency, sharpness, variety, and error. A diffusion based refinement step touches only hard to predict frames. On the Vimeo90K data set it reports 40 percent lower latency, 90 percent less data sent, and 35 percent higher throughput than baselines.
arxiv-2512-15581:
Shashank Mishra and co authors present IMKD, a knowledge distillation framework for camera radar object detection in 3D, in a 2025 paper. Radar camera systems can reach high accuracy without using LiDAR at run time if a teacher passes on what it knows. Standard distillation, though, often copies features straight into each sensor and blurs what makes each sensor distinct.

IMKD uses a three stage, intensity aware strategy. It enriches radar features with LiDAR structure, guides the fused features with LiDAR geometry, and aligns camera and radar features with intensity cues. On the nuScenes benchmark it reaches 67.0 percent NDS and 61.0 percent mAP, beating all prior distillation based radar camera methods.
arxiv-2512-15881:
Researchers present JWST observations of the most distant luminous quasar known, J0313-1806 at redshift 7.64, in a 2025 paper. Such early quasars test theories of supermassive black hole growth, much of it hidden by dense gas and dust. Spatially resolved spectroscopy can now separate the black hole's glow from its host galaxy.

From the nuclear spectrum, the black hole mass is 1.63 plus or minus 0.10 billion solar masses, accreting at 0.80 of the Eddington rate. The team detects an ionized gas shell reaching about 1.8 kiloparsecs, traced by hydrogen beta emission yet almost free of doubly ionized oxygen. Modeling shows a thin, clumpy outflowing shell where that oxygen emission is collisionally suppressed, a fossil of a recent blowout phase.
arxiv-2512-16281:
Vadim A Naumov and Dmitry S Shkirmanov revisit neutrino physics in this short conference paper, presented in Moscow in August 2025. Neutrinos change flavor as they travel, a phenomenon called oscillation. In a full quantum field treatment, the neutrino is a propagator between source and detector particles described as wave packets.

The authors expand that propagator for short and long travel distances using series in small dimensionless variables. In both regimes, the leading corrections break the classic inverse-square falloff and reduce the expected event rate. They discuss whether this effect could partly explain the reactor antineutrino anomaly, a persistent shortfall in measured reactor neutrino counts. The four-page report offers theorists a field-theoretic lens on a long-standing experimental puzzle.
arxiv-2512-16381:
Zhihao Wang and five co-authors build a test arena for network AI in research shared on arXiv in 2025. Language model agents increasingly help engineers configure networks and troubleshoot outages. Progress is slow because there is no standard, low-effort benchmark for judging agents on realistic, changing network failures.

Their benchmark, NIKA, is the largest public one for network incident diagnosis. It replays real-world scenarios with no setup effort and gives agents a clean interface for quick prototyping. The suite holds hundreds of curated incidents across five settings, from data centers to internet service providers, covering 54 representative issues. Trial runs showed bigger models detect problems more often but still struggle to localize faults and name root causes. NIKA is open-source and modular, so new scenarios and failure cases can be added.
arxiv-2512-16581:
Sullivan Castro and three co-authors pre-train ad models in this 2025 arXiv paper. Display advertising bids in real time on guesses about what a user will do next. Positive events are sparse and erratic, so models starve for signal, and hand-built counter features miss how user intent evolves.

Their method, Abacus, pre-trains a sequential model to predict the empirical frequency distribution of a user's events, teaching it counting statistics that ordinary sequence training skips. A hybrid objective then mixes that task with standard sequential learning, combining the stability of aggregate counts with sensitivity to order. On two real-world data sets, Abacus pre-training beat existing methods and sped up downstream convergence. The full hybrid raised AUC by up to 6.1 percent over baselines, a solid gain for production bidding systems.
arxiv-2512-16881:
Arhan Jain and a large team present PolaRiS, a real-to-simulation frame for testing generalist robot policies. Real robot trials are slow and hard to repeat, while plain simulators look and act too unlike the real world to trust their scores.

PolaRiS turns short video scans of real rooms into interactive simulation scenes with neural reconstruction. A simple co-training recipe mixes simulation data to close the last gaps, letting policies be scored in unseen scenes with no extra tuning. In paired tests, PolaRiS scores tracked real-world performance far better than older simulation benchmarks. The ease of building new scenes points toward shared, open testing for robot foundation models.
arxiv-2512-16981:
B. Trefoloni and coauthors use JWST NIRSpec spectra of eight bright quasars at redshift 5.9 and beyond to weigh their black holes and feeding rates. Quasars shine as gas falls onto supermassive black holes, and the most distant ones trace early black hole growth.

Fitting the rest-frame ultraviolet and optical light with accretion disc models gave black hole mass and disc brightness together, with tighter errors than standard single-epoch recipes. The mean feeding rate sits at a log Eddington ratio of minus 0.9, with small scatter. Only about 0.2 percent of such bright quasars should feed past the Eddington limit, proof that slow, sub-Eddington feeding rules even for these early monsters.
arxiv-2512-17081:
Ashley Colley and coauthors examine virtual reality as a service design tool for plastics recycling, through two cases at unlike stages of the recycling trip. Recycling hinges on daily sorting habits and on how services are explained and felt.

Clean Cabin Escape is a home-scale VR escape room where players sort waste into local categories with instant feedback. The second case simulates a planned recycling center in VR, used in workshops where stakeholders test layout, signage, and customer paths. VR made both home sorting and complex centers concrete for citizens and professionals. Trade-offs cover hardware access, onboarding effort, visual fidelity, and local rule differences.
arxiv-2512-17181:
Anuj Sethia, Nasser Gohari Kamel, and Daniel Oblak demonstrate on-demand storage of telecom photons for up to one millisecond in an erbium-doped crystal, a step toward quantum repeaters. Repeaters must beat the steep loss of fiber links by multiplexing in time, spectrum, or space, which demands big, long-lived memories.

Their Er3+ in Y2SiO5 platform stores and recalls weak coherent pulses on demand, ten times longer than past erbium results. Efficiency hit 10.36 percent at 300 microseconds storage with a signal-to-noise ratio of 10.9. Two spectral modes encoding a frequency bin were stored with 81.8 percent overlap, and 20 time modes times 3 spectral modes were held at once with selective recall.
arxiv-2512-18081:
Tudor Jianu's thesis builds a full stack for robot guided wires inside blood vessels. Doctors thread thin wires and tubes through vessels to treat heart and vessel disease, but hand control is hard and tiring. His framework joins a training world, a control policy, and fresh data to raise the level of self guidance.

The training world, CathSim, copies vessel shapes and touch forces in real time. A control network blends camera views, motion data, and force signals to steer the tool. A public data set adds over 8,700 marked X-ray images for rebuilding wire shapes in 3D, and a transformer model predicts the wire's curve directly. Together the parts point to safer, finer vessel work.
arxiv-2512-18281:
Ryuichiro Hada leads a large DESI team using quasar pairs to probe the gas around quasars. A quasar's fierce light should clear and ionize the gas near it, carving a proximity zone. With over 10,000 close pairs from the DESI Year 1 data, the team reads that zone sideways, through the light of a second quasar passing behind the first.

Extra gas near quasars won out over the clearing effect, so the rear light was absorbed more, not less. The crowding reached about ten times the average density near the brightest quasars. Oddly, the zone's shape barely changed with the front quasar's brightness, a hint that quasar light may flicker or beam unevenly.
arxiv-2512-18381:
George J. Bautista and four co-authors analyze a Rao-Nakra sandwich beam, a layered beam whose motion is described by three coupled equations. Two equations track lengthwise motion of the outer layers; the third tracks sideways bending. The system also has boundary conditions that move with time. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, asks whether such a system is well behaved and controllable.

For the damped version, with time-varying damping and delays, they prove solutions exist and are unique, using semigroup theory and a classical result of Kato. A Lyapunov argument then shows the beam's energy decays exponentially. For the control version, they prove well-posedness and, through an observability inequality and the Hilbert Uniqueness Method, show the beam is null controllable. Handling all three coupled equations at once is the paper's main contribution.
arxiv-2512-18481:
C. F. P. Avalos, G. A. Prataviera, and M. C. de Oliveira study two trapped ions that share one thermal reservoir. In such setups the environment does not drain each ion separately; it links them, and that link changes how they heat up and settle. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, works out the coupled dynamics from a microscopic model.

The team derives Heisenberg-Langevin equations and shows the shared reservoir creates collective decay channels. When cross-damping matches local damping, a decoherence-free mode appears that keeps memory of the starting excitations. Using Fisher information from motion measurements, they map where cross-damping sharpens estimates of system and reservoir properties. For nonclassical starting states, the reservoir link can also build or preserve entanglement, strongest near that protected condition.
arxiv-2512-18881:
İzzet Sakallı and three co-authors examine a Letelier black hole, an object wrapped in a cloud of strings, sitting inside an electromagnetic universe. Two parameters, the string cloud strength and the electromagnetic universe parameter, deform it away from the textbook Schwarzschild case. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, works out how the hole would look and sound.

They derive the photon sphere and shadow size analytically, then extend the shadow study to plasma surroundings, where the silhouette systematically shrinks, and compute light bending with the Gauss-Bonnet theorem. Ringing modes for scalar, electromagnetic, and Dirac fields come from a sixth-order WKB calculation, and the Hawking radiation spectra differ clearly between boson and fermion channels. Quasi-periodic oscillation models add observational constraints. The study maps a full observational profile for an exotic black hole family.
arxiv-2512-18981:
Jiaji Ren and seven co-authors fix a blind spot in direction finding: signals arriving along the array's own axis. Measuring direction of arrival underpins sensing and future communication systems. Yet fixed arrays suffer the end-fire effect, where accuracy collapses exactly along the line of the antennas. Their array, posted to arXiv in December 2025, is built from fluid antennas whose positions can shift.

Moving the elements in effect reshapes the array's steering vector, the fingerprint each direction leaves across the sensors. Combined with the classical MUSIC algorithm, the result is high precision estimation even in the hard end-fire region, confirmed in simulation. Radar, sonar, and 6G sensing arrays all fight end-fire losses; reconfigurable geometry offers a physical cure rather than another algorithmic patch.
arxiv-2512-19481:
Katharina Stengg, Christian Macho, and Martin Pinzger test GPT-5 on a chore every developer knows: predicting what else a code change will touch. Impact analysis is usually manual and slow. The team first built a dataset that records, for each commit, the seed changes, the change pairs, and the change types, data that older sets lack.

GPT-5 and its mini sibling were tried with the seed change and parent tree alone, and again with the diff hunks added. Both models performed poorly in both setups, though the full model beat the mini. The sobering result maps how far language models still sit from dependable change reasoning.
arxiv-2512-19781:
Avi Kaplan-Lipkin leads a nine-author theory effort on spin squeezing. Squeezing spins creates entanglement that sharpens measures past the classical limit. Dipolar spin systems can make it on their own, through their quench dynamics. Most past theory assumed neat lattices. Real systems are messy. They range from ultracold molecules to color centers in diamond, and their atoms sit out of place.

The team studies a two-dimensional lattice of quantum dipoles with random gaps. With large-scale Monte Carlo runs, they map where XY order and scalable squeezing live. The map turns on both disorder and Ising anisotropy. Squeezing holds up mainly near the Heisenberg point. Rare, tight pairs of dipoles heat the system and spoil it. For diamond centers, the team shows a fix. Cutting those pairs out of the dynamics is enough to save scalable squeezing.
arxiv-2512-20081:
Alolika Roy and Amarendra Sarma design a force sensor that beats the standard quantum limit, the precision ceiling set by quantum measurement noise. Their hybrid optomechanical platform couples a cavity with a movable mirror and a fixed semitransparent one to an ensemble of quantum dots, with an optical parametric amplifier inside the cavity. Radiation-pressure back action is the noise source under the microscope.

The quantum dots' induced response, working with the system's nonlinearity, reshapes the noise spectrum in the sensor's favor. Coherent quantum noise cancellation can remove the back-action noise entirely in this arrangement. Raising the amplifier's pump gain then pushes sensitivity beyond the standard quantum limit while actually reducing the laser power required, a combination aimed at detecting extremely weak forces.
arxiv-2512-20181:
Sadia Nasrin Tisha, Md Nazmus Sakib, and Sanorita Dey compare two kinds of student hackathons. One is a gender-specific event; the other is a regular institutional event run in the usual open way. Using mixed methods, they look at team dynamics, project themes, role assignments, and the physical settings of both formats.

The gender-specific event fostered a supportive, collaborative mood, with projects often centered on health and well-being. The regular event felt more competitive and outcome-driven, with projects leaning toward entertainment and environmental sustainability. The authors propose a hybrid format that balances competition with inclusivity. Educators designing hackathons get concrete guidance on how format choices shape student experience.
arxiv-2512-20681:
Andrea Addazi imagines gravity before geometry exists. In pre-geometric theories, spacetime and its metric are not fundamental inputs but emerge when a larger gauge symmetry breaks spontaneously. The starting point is a gauge theory of the de Sitter or anti-de Sitter group on a manifold with no prior metric at all.

An internal vector field triggers the breaking down to the Lorentz group, dynamically generating the metric. Two models illustrate the idea: MacDowell-Mansouri yields Einstein-Hilbert gravity with a cosmological constant and a Gauss-Bonnet term, while the Wilczek model yields the pure Einstein-Hilbert action. A see-saw mechanism explains the Planck mass and the tiny cosmological constant. The Hamiltonian formulation shows three physical degrees of freedom and recovers general relativity after the breaking.
arxiv-2512-20781:
Youjin Jung, Seongwoo Cho, Hyun-seok Min, and Sungchul Choi improve image search driven by an example picture plus a text edit. A shopper might show a dress and ask for it in blue, without the pattern. Zero-shot systems merge everything into one query, which dilutes key details and ignores what the user wants to avoid.

Their module, SoFT, needs no training and plugs into an existing retriever. A multimodal model extracts must-have and must-avoid constraints, and candidates are re-ranked by those rules. The team also rebuilt benchmark data to allow several plausible targets per query. Scores rose clearly on the CIRR, CIRCO, and FashionIQ benchmarks.
arxiv-2512-21081:
Karim Abdelsalam, Zeyad Gamal, and Ayman El-Badawy cut the data bill for learning to control nonlinear machines. Model-free reinforcement learning is sample-hungry, but a learned model can manufacture practice. Their Dyna-style framework identifies the system's dynamics from data with SINDy, a sparse-regression method that returns compact equations. Those equations generate synthetic rollouts. The rollouts are periodically mixed into the replay buffer of a TD3 agent training on the real system.

Tested on a bi-rotor rig, the hybrid beats direct reinforcement learning on both stabilization accuracy and trajectory tracking, and holds up better under disturbances. The identified model does double duty: it explains the dynamics in readable terms and feeds the agent extra experience. For control engineers with limited trial budgets, the combination offers a practical middle path between pure modeling and pure trial-and-error.
arxiv-2512-21281:
Amit Acharya re-reads the Hamilton-Jacobi equation as an act of deliberate forgetting. In his framing, the classical equation arises by trimming particle mechanics. The trimming discards the velocity degrees of freedom and keeps a leaner account that still fixes the motion. Once Hamilton-Jacobi theory is seen as model reduction, not a trick tied to energy conservation, its reach widens.

The same link extends to general Newtonian particle systems. It covers non-conservative and frankly dissipative forces, friction and drag too, where the classical one was not supposed to apply. One step further, a geometric-optics pass over the extended theory yields a dissipative Schroedinger equation. It relaxes to the familiar form when the forces are switched back to conservative. Mechanicians gain a unified bridge: one trimming principle linking Newtonian bodies, Hamilton-Jacobi theory, and wave mechanics, with dissipation allowed on both sides.
arxiv-2512-21381:
T. Rick Perche, Francesco Gozzini, and Markus K. Oberthaler connect two areas of physics that rarely meet: ultracold atoms and relativistic quantum field theory. They show that a bound impurity atom inside a Bose-Einstein condensate behaves like an Unruh-DeWitt detector. A condensate is a cloud of atoms cooled until they act as one quantum object. The detector is a standard model of a device that measures a quantum field.

The authors give experimental parameters for the setup. It uses potassium-41 impurities coupled to a rubidium-87 condensate, with a Feshbach resonance switched on and off for a finite time. As an application, they study entanglement harvesting, extracting entanglement that already exists in the vacuum state of a field. They find workable parameters for pulling entanglement from distant regions of the condensate. A tabletop cold-atom experiment could therefore test effects usually associated with relativity and empty space.
arxiv-2512-21481:
Sunith Vallabhaneni, Thomas Berkane, and Maimuna Majumder address a quiet problem in data-driven research: web-scraped datasets often contain wrong values. Language-model web agents collect data at scale, but they hallucinate or omit values, misread pages, and miss invalid entries. Checking their output by hand is slow and error-prone.

Their system, the AI Committee, assigns each agent a distinct quality job, from scrutinizing sources and fact-checking to fixing values and validating integrity. It works with any language model and needs no task-specific training, using in-context learning, chain-of-thought reasoning, and a self-correction loop. On three real-world datasets it reached completeness up to about seventy-nine percent and precision up to one hundred percent, beating baselines. An ablation study shows each agent's contribution, and the tool is open source.
arxiv-2512-21581:
M. A. Bunin and I. I. Geguzin improve a first-principles calculation of how lithium chloride absorbs light near its fundamental absorption edge. Their method works inside local density functional theory but corrects the crystal potential for self-interaction error, a known flaw where an electron spuriously interacts with itself.

The correction scheme keeps the unit cell divided into regions as in ground-state calculations, and its self-consistent muffin-tin potential satisfies charge neutrality in each cell. Applied to lithium chloride, the method yields interband transition energies with no fitting to experiment. Above roughly two and a half electronvolts from the edge, the calculated peaks match the measured spectrum in shape and position well. Closer to the edge, electron-hole interaction reshapes the ground state and must be included to explain the spectrum.
arxiv-2512-21781:
Zhimin Zhao, Bram Adams, and their co-authors compare the tool ecosystems behind the two dominant software bill of materials formats, SPDX and CycloneDX. A software bill of materials lists a product's components and dependencies, improving transparency and security response. Its practical value, though, depends on the tools that create, analyze, and manage the documents.

The study analyzes over one hundred open-source tools and dozens of proprietary ones. It also uses ecosystem health metrics, tens of thousands of issue reports, and the top projects using each format. CycloneDX projects often show stronger developer engagement and selected health indicators. SPDX counters with a larger, more mature tool ecosystem and broader industry adoption. Neither format wins outright; their strengths are complementary. The authors identify concrete opportunities to improve tooling across both ecosystems, which matters as software bills of materials become a regulatory expectation in more industries.
arxiv-2512-22481:
Zihan Weng and nine co-authors present SPECTRE, a self-supervised system for reading intended movements from forearm muscle signals, aimed at prosthetic control. Surface EMG sits on the skin but is noisy and shifting, and generic self-supervised methods waste effort copying that noise. SPECTRE instead pre-trains on a body-grounded task: predicting masked, clustered frequency-pattern labels derived from short-time Fourier transforms of the signals.

A second ingredient, Cylindrical Rotary Position Embedding, shapes the model's sense of position around the electrode array's ring geometry, splitting linear time from annular space to capture muscle synergies. Across multiple datasets, including recordings from amputees, SPECTRE set a new state of the art for movement reading, beating labeled baselines and generic self-taught approaches. Ablations confirmed both ingredients matter.
arxiv-2512-22681:
ZhenQi Chen, TsaiChing Ni, and YuanFu Yang present CritiFusion, an inference-time add-on that makes text-to-image diffusion models follow complex prompts more faithfully. Modern generators paint well but often miss what a prompt asked for. CritiFusion requires no retraining and plugs into current diffusion backbones as a refinement stage in two teamed parts.

Its CritiCore module uses a vision-language model and several large language models to enrich the prompt and produce high-level semantic feedback that steers generation. The SpecFusion module merges intermediate generation states in the frequency domain, injecting coarse structure while keeping fine detail. On standard benchmarks, the method improved human-aligned correspondence and quality scores to levels matching reward-optimization approaches, with qualitative gains in detail, realism, and prompt fidelity.
arxiv-2512-22781:
Hollis Williams drops cone-shaped intruders into granular material and measures how the resistance force depends on the cone's sharpness. Granular impact is usually described by a steady resistance plus an inertial drag that grows with the square of impact speed. Geometry was known to change force sizes, but its effect on when the inertial part switches on had not been mapped.

Peak acceleration measurements show blunt cones follow the speed-squared law at every speed tested, while sharp cones only join that regime above a higher crossover speed. That crossover grows roughly in step with the tangent of the cone angle. Once in the inertial regime, peak forces from all cones collapse onto one curve after the same rescaling. Cone shape thus controls both how momentum passes into the grains and the speed where inertial drag takes over.
arxiv-2512-23081:
Taha Saeed Khan proposes a different way to keep a power grid's frequency steady as inverter-based generators replace spinning machines. In the classic setup, devices synchronize by coupling through the network itself, swinging against each other until they lock. Slower secondary control tidies up afterward. Without a shared reference, disturbances can cause long transients and large phase swings between units.

Khan's design has every virtual synchronous machine inverter track one broadcast global frequency reference, assuming the total power balance is known and maintained. Sync then becomes a tracking problem rather than mutual locking. In a second-order swing model, adding a simple PI frequency controller greatly improves transient behavior. A washout filter removes the extra control action in steady state, so network-determined power sharing is preserved. Simulations on a three-oscillator network show smaller overshoot, no lingering oscillations, and lower angular stress than standard synchronization.
arxiv-2512-23381:
Lorenz Bielefeld and co-authors flag a flaw in over-the-air federated learning, a scheme where many devices transmit their updates simultaneously and the wireless channel adds them up. That analog aggregation relieves the communication bottleneck of federated learning. But the literature has ignored a fact. Radio power amplifiers are nonlinear, and signals whose peaks exceed the linear range get distorted in and out of band.

The authors analyze the remedy, iterative amplitude clipping combined with filtering, and study its effect in single-carrier and multi-carrier OFDM systems. Simulations show the signal in over-the-air learning breaches the amplifier's linearity limit under realistic settings. Applying clipping and filtering degrades learning performance to varying degrees, and the damage is worst in multi-carrier systems, where clipping creates in-band distortion that filtering cannot remove. The paper is framed as a first reality check for the field.
arxiv-2512-23481:
Wei Cui and four co-authors study two-dimensional supersymmetric theories with N=(0,4) supersymmetry, obtained by twisting and reducing four-dimensional class S theories on a curved surface. Such constructions are elegant but leave subtle questions open: what are the theories' central charges, which gauge symmetries survive, and what superconformal R-symmetry emerges in the infrared?

The authors propose conjectural formulas for the central charges and test them on theories with SU(2) gauge group, where a Lagrangian description is available. They examine two branches of the vacuum space, the special Higgs branch and the twisted Higgs branch, computing each branch's Hilbert series. The counts agree with the proposed formulas, giving evidence that the conjectured charges capture the infrared physics correctly.
arxiv-2512-23581:
Courtney Kyger and four co-authors introduce profile Bayesian optimization, a method for tuning expensive computer simulations. Their motivating problem is a diffuser in a rotating detonation combustion engine: the simulation reports energy lost through diffusion. Engineers want the lowest possible loss as a function of the diffuser's length, one control parameter, while other design parameters vary as nuisances.

Standard Bayesian optimization hunts a single best point and ignores most of the control parameter's range. The profile version instead maps the best achievable response at every value of the control parameter. A two-stage acquisition scheme balances exploring new lengths against refining known optima, with deep and shallow Gaussian process surrogates tracking uncertainty. On benchmarks and on the engine problem, it beat traditional Bayesian optimization and earlier profile methods. The point is to tune the whole curve, not just one peak.
arxiv-2512-23681:
Adam Harper surveys a subtle phenomenon in analytic number theory: averages of character sums that cancel more strongly than the square-root barrier suggests. The square-root scale is what randomness alone would predict, and for decades it was treated as a natural limit. Harper explains how connections with multiplicative chaos, a chance-based framework, showed much better cancellation in averages of multiplicative character sums.

The survey focuses on the number-theoretic side of the arguments rather than the probability machinery. It also discusses possible applications of the improved cancellation. The paper grew out of work connected with the International Congress of Mathematicians, where a version will appear in the 2026 proceedings. That makes it a guided entry point to an active research area for number theorists. It maps the field more than it proves new theorems.
arxiv-2512-23781:
Jackie Baek, Will Ma, and Dmitry Mitrofanov report what happened when a large online retailer let an algorithm hand out daily discounts. Working with the retailer's base of more than twenty million customers, they designed a policy that chooses each customer's promotion each day, ten to twenty percent off in five steps. Respecting global limits on how many of each discount can be given.

Deployed in an A/B test, the policy raised revenue by about four and a half percent, by aiming discounts at promotion-sensitive customers and learning timing patterns across customers. The data also inspired a new theoretical model: customers remember the best promotion they saw over the last several days as a reference. Buy more readily when that memory is poor. The authors tightly characterize the optimal policy under the model, which cycles between poor offers and one good one.
arxiv-2512-23981:
Sebastián Gutiérrez-Bernal, Hector Medel Cobaxin, and Abiel Galindo González propose a new yardstick for dimension reduction, the maps that squeeze high-dimensional data into pictures or compact features. Standard scores judge such embeddings by distorted distances or warped local geometry. Neither directly measures how much information the projection throws away, which is what matters in information-sensitive uses such as early-warning indicators.

Their Entropy Rank Preservation Measure works neighborhood by neighborhood, comparing the Shannon entropy of the singular-value spectrum of each patch before and after projection, summarized through the stable rank. Validated on a financial time series and a standard manifold, the measure correlated only weakly with distance-based scores but strongly on average with a geometric criterion, while disagreeing in specific local regimes. The authors conclude their metric complements existing ones by flagging exactly where severe information loss hides.
arxiv-2512-24081:
Sijin Li and Wei Wang address a weakness of quantum measurement. Squeezed light can estimate phases beyond classical limits. But the advantage fades fast when light is lost. It also fades when detectors miss photons. The authors build on an earlier remedy. They amplify the quantum state before measurement.

This work extends the trick to entangled states. It also covers estimating several phases at once. Two setups are worked through in detail. One uses a two-mode entangled state. The other uses a four-mode cluster state. In both cases, sensitivity stayed robust under loss. Imperfect detection did not destroy the advantage either. For builders of large quantum sensors, the result is practical. It offers a path to quantum-level precision outside ideal laboratory conditions.
arxiv-2512-24281:
Spyridon Syntakas and Kostas Vlachos keep small marine vessels safe and on course. Their craft is an over-actuated surface vessel with three degrees of freedom. Wind, waves, and current push it hard. Sliding mode control offers robustness against such matched disturbances. Safety constraints need separate enforcement, though.

High-order control barrier functions supply that enforcement. They keep obstacle-avoidance constraints forward invariant. The barrier functions adapt to the vessel's state. A fast half-space projection adjusts the control only when needed. Robustness is preserved while chattering stays low. The test model is nonlinear and realistic. It includes added mass and hydrodynamic damping. Full thruster allocation is modeled too. Simulations showed robust navigation with guaranteed obstacle avoidance. The computation suits real-time embedded hardware with limited resources.
arxiv-2512-24481:
C Pallis writes a personal memoir of George Lazarides, a physicist. Lazarides was Pallis's PhD supervisor. He later became a collaborator. Throughout, he remained an encouraging supporter. The piece honors that bond directly. It records memories rather than arguing a thesis.

Work shared between the two men is also summarized. Their joint research touched supersymmetric models and what they predict. Inflation in the early universe was the other shared theme. Related work of Lazarides receives mention as well. Memoirs like this preserve the human record of a research community. Students and colleagues appear alongside equations and models. Readers interested in Lazarides and his circle will find a first-hand account here.
arxiv-2512-24581:
Igor Tunev revisits Dejean's conjecture and stronger forms about threshold words, sequences that avoid too much repetition. A word's root is its shortest repeating prefix, and a threshold word keeps every subword's length over its period at or below a set bound. The manuscript, in Russian, edits his bachelor and master work from the early twenty nineteen decade with improvements.

Circular threshold words and other strengthenings are developed beyond the conjecture proved in two thousand nine. New proof methods from his student work anchor the account. Combinatorics on words readers get both history and stronger constructions, presented as a revised collected version of earlier theses.
arxiv-2512-24881: Mykola Khrypchenko covers totally matching structures on the Jacobson radical of the incidence algebra of a finite poset over a field. Incidence algebras encode order relations of a poset in matrix-like form, and their radical captures strict order relations. Compatible structures are extra actions that couple well with the algebra product. He shows such structures are in general non-proper, meaning they do not arise from the simplest expected building. Algebra readers get a sorting for a concrete finite-dimensional setting.
arxiv-2601-06681:
Maciej Tadej and two co-authors study plant patterns on dry land in a 2026 paper. Their model is a grown form of a known water-and-plant model. Plants in it spread seeds far, not just to spots close by.

The land in the model is flat and has a fixed edge. They first show the model is well set: it gives one path, not many. Then they work out the terms on which plants live or die out. Rules for both death and life come out of their work in strict form. Dry-land plant groups form shapes that hint at health or near collapse. Far seed spread shifts which shapes can last on a small plot of land. Land care teams gain math that speaks to the loss of dry lands.
arxiv-2601-06781: Research by Huatao Xu and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with AutoTour. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. The authors present AutoTour , a system that enhances user exploration. By automatically generating fine-grained landmark annotations and descriptive narratives for photos captured by users. The key idea of AutoTour is to fuse visual features extracted from photos with nearby geospatial features queried from open matching databases. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-06881:
Debashis Panda and seven co-authors wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on waves where two fluids meet. The paper deals with two kinds of drag at that surface. One kind acts when the surface grows or shrinks. The other acts when one part of the surface slides past the next.

The two kinds of drag tend to move in step, so their effects are hard to pull apart. Past work used flat flow or flows in one plane, where the split stays blurred. The team turns to waves that stand in place in three dimensions. In that setup, each kind of drag leaves its own mark. The marks let the team split the two effects and weigh each one on its own.
arxiv-2601-07081:
Irina Kmit, Nataliya Protsakh, and Viktor Tkachenko wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on a wave equation with strong damping. The wave is almost periodic, which means its shape comes close to a repeat but not quite. The task is an inverse one. In an inverse task, the team works back from effects to find a cause in the equation.

The edge of the region is held fixed, a rule called the Dirichlet boundary condition. The work is set in Sobolev spaces, which hold functions with weak rates of change. The functions in view are bounded. Some are almost periodic, and some are fully periodic. The team finds a weak solution to the equation. It also pins down a source term on the right side of the equation. That term is part of what the inverse task must find.
arxiv-2601-07681:
Sayani Bera and Kaushal Verma prove a rigidity result for the chaotic regions of certain complex maps. They study polynomial automorphisms of complex two-space with positive entropy and degree at least two. For such a map, the escaping set collects points that run off to infinity under iteration. Its complement is the non-escaping set. Their 2026 preprint shows this set is rigid under holomorphic automorphisms.

Rigidity means symmetries of the whole space cannot deform the escaping set's structure. Positive entropy signals genuinely chaotic dynamics. Results like this classify how wild these maps can be. Complex dynamics in two variables is far less understood than in one variable. The paper serves dynamicists working on Hénon-type maps. It pins down one more invariant of their behavior.
arxiv-2601-07781:
Klaus Zollner and coauthors map tiny magnetic hot spots where cobalt touches graphene through a boron nitride layer. Proximity effects let a magnet stamp spin traits on a nearby nonmagnet. The team studies a cobalt, hexagonal boron nitride, and graphene stack with first-principles math. They find strong local change in the spin polarization brought on in graphene's Dirac states. Their 2026 preprint details that pattern.

The exchange coupling, magnetic moments, and tunneling spin polarization that result all hinge on atomic registry. Registry means how the atomic lattices line up at each interface. Small shifts in alignment therefore change the magnetism a lot. Such sensitivity matters for designing graphene spintronic devices. Those who build devices may use the hot spots or need to tame them. The paper speaks to physicists who work on flat, thin magnetic devices. The three thin sheets shift in traits from spot to spot.
arxiv-2601-08081:
Lavinia Heisenberg, Shayan Hemmatyar, and Nadine Nussbaumer prove a non-renormalization result for vector field theories. Their 2026 arXiv paper covers ghost-free local functionals for massive vector fields. These fields are coupled to dynamical geometry, so spacetime itself responds.

The proof assumes locality, Lorentz invariance, and a valid effective field theory below a fixed cutoff. Under those terms, quantum corrections do not create local operators of a certain kind. In particular, they do not renormalize the derivative self-interactions behind the theory's constraint structure. For theorists, that protection keeps a delicate classical structure safe from quantum damage.
arxiv-2601-08181: Aviral Gupta, Armaan Sethi, and Dhruv Kumar peer inside TabPFN, a foundation model for tabular data. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that such pre-trained models perform strongly across many table tasks. Still, their internal representations and learned concepts remain poorly understood. Weak interpretability makes it hard to trust or debug these models in real use. The authors study how TabPFN processes and transforms input features layer by layer. Their findings help readers judge what the model has truly learned from tables.
arxiv-2601-08581: Mir Alimuddin, Jaemin Kim, Antonio Acin, and Leonardo Zambrano wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on a key step for quantum networks. The step is entanglement swapping, a way to spread a quantum tie. In standard forms, a middle read decides the final state. That makes the step a matter of chance, and forces teams to drop failed rounds. The authors sort the reads where the step stops being a gamble. For pure inputs of any kind, each outcome gives a state equal to the rest up to local unitary shifts.
arxiv-2601-08781:
Stefan Guttel and Kaustubh Roy extend a fast group sorting tool called CLASSIX. The tool puts like data points in one group and odd ones apart. It is fast, and a user can see why each group formed. At first it used plain straight line distance to judge how near two points are.

The pair adds two more ways to judge nearness. One suits city grid like moves, where you go along streets, not across blocks. The next suits data made of traits, such as chem traits of a drug. Both forms keep the speed and the clear logic of the first tool. A reader who sorts data gets more reach from a tool they can still explain.
arxiv-2601-08981:
Fredrik Lohne Aanes seeks to lift a tool that tells how much each trait in a model adds to its call. The tool is called KernelSHAP. It tests groups of traits in samples to weigh each trait. Past sample picks could draw the same group twice, which wastes runs. Aanes picks group sizes from a skew count law, then draws with no repeats.

He also adds two resample tricks to gauge how firm each weight is. Both tricks re-run the weights on split or flipped samples. In his tests, the new gauge does as well or more well than old ones. A reader who must explain a model call gets a leaner SHAP, with a clear doubt range.
arxiv-2601-09181:
Parameshwaran A and Bhaskar Sen Gupta sim how an active near point fluid splits in a thin tube. The fluid is near its gas and liquid split point. Its bits can move on their own and tend to line up, like a flock. In a plain fluid, split zones grow by known laws. Own motion may shift those laws when walls close in.

They run atom scale sims in a round tube pore. They track zone form and growth speed as own motion is tuned. The tube is near one way in shape, so growth may jam or rush in new ways. A reader in soft stuffs gets a case of life like split in a tight space.
arxiv-2601-09381:
Martin Grohe asks what a good query language for machine learning models would look like. His 2026 arXiv paper turns to logic, treating neural networks as weighted graphs that can be queried. He discusses two logics built for weighted finite structures: first-order logic with summation, and its recursive extension.

These logics grew out of foundational work by Grädel, Gurevich, and Meer in the 1990s. With co-authors, Grohe has tested them as languages for asking structured questions of trained models. A query language could let users probe a network's behavior in a precise, checkable way. The paper maps how far logic can go in that role.
arxiv-2601-09581:
Dorsa Fathollahi, V. Arvind Rameshwar, and V. Lalitha analyze an error-correcting decoder's chance of failure. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies the recursive projection-aggregation decoder for Reed-Muller codes. The channels covered are general binary memoryless symmetric channels.

Ye and Abbe proposed this decoder in 2020. A 2025 result showed it achieves vanishing error for low-rate codes on the binary symmetric channel. The new work extends that guarantee to the wider channel family. Reed-Muller codes are old, elegant codes now back in focus for modern links and storage, so stronger guarantees on their decoders carry real weight.
arxiv-2601-09781:
An unnamed author argues for a principle that keeps certain quantum theories apart from gravity. The 2026 arXiv paper presents the topological equivalence principle, on decoupling topological field theories from gravity. Such theories describe the deep infrared behavior of many gapped quantum systems.

They also encode the global symmetries of quantum field theories once gravity is removed. In curved anti-de Sitter space, though, sectors that look decoupled still feel Newton's constant. The sensitivity enters through sums over distinct saddle-point shapes. The paper frames how equivalence should be stated so the decoupling claim stays honest.
arxiv-2601-10081:
N. Sherlekar and a large team study light given off by a clean chip joint. The joint pairs gallium arsenide with its alloy kin. It holds thin gases of electrons and holes in a plane. When the two meet, they give off light.

The team built side by side joints with no added dopants. The light is bright. Its hues show free pairs that roam the plane. One peak is the heavy hole free pair. A second peak sits at a high band named the H band. A drift trait named the tidal effect also shows in the hues.
arxiv-2601-10381:
Calum Robson builds a phase space on Clifford algebras. A phase space pairs each place with its push. That pair form is base to classic physics. In Kähler form, the pair comes from a rich metric frame. Robson seeks a like frame in more dims.

He uses the Hodge frame on a Euclidean Clifford algebra. In his build, pairs link forms of dual ranks. A k form pairs with a form of rank n minus k. That swaps points and planes for slabs of each size. The work lifts phase space ideas to high dim algebra.
arxiv-2601-10481:
Michael Bleher, Denis Brazke, and Sebastian Nill build a curve match tool for the round sphere. Match tools gauge how like two shapes are. On a sphere, the tool must bend with the space. It can then drive non local costs that push sets to a best form.

Their cost pulls a set to be round in a broad sense. The match tool is the kernel of that cost. It comes from a Helmholtz law with a small length term. The team study how the cost acts as terms shift. Such costs shape drops, films, and cells that sit on curved skins.
arxiv-2601-10581:
Kimia Abedini, Farzad Shami, and Gianmaria Silvello work on question answering over genome data. Gene and genome facts sit spread across many large databases. Pulling the right facts out is slow and hard, even for experts. Large language models could help, but they have limited access to these special databases.

The team extends GeneGPT, a system that lets a language model query genome resources. Their new design moves from a single agent to several agents that reason together. Each agent can take on part of the search task. The goal is more accurate answers to biomedical questions. The work points toward tools that help researchers query gene data in plain words.
arxiv-2601-10781:
Kanchana Ranasinghe and co-authors present FOFPred, a model that forecasts future optical flow. Optical flow maps how each point in a scene is about to move. Such maps are gold for robot control and for video generation. Yet forecasting dense motion that holds up in the real world is still an open challenge.
