FOFPred is conditioned on language, so words can steer the forecast. It joins a vision-language model with a diffusion process in one design. Learning comes from noisy, real-world data, not just clean lab sets. A robot that can foresee motion can plan smoother paths, and a video model that foresees flow can keep motion coherent across frames.
arxiv-2601-10881:
Sunny Atalig, Marek Chrobak, Christoph Dürr, Petr Kolman, Huong Luu, Jǐrí Sgall, and Gregory Zhu prove two complexity results on spanning-tree congestion. Given a graph, the task is to pick a spanning tree that minimizes the worst edge congestion. Congestion counts how many paths are forced across one edge. The problem is NP-hard, even on some narrow graph classes.

Several basic questions about its complexity stayed open. The authors settle some of them in this paper. Hardness results tell algorithm designers where not to hunt for fast exact methods. They also point to where approximations or special cases are worth the effort. Spanning trees with low congestion matter for network design and VLSI layout.
arxiv-2601-11781:
Dawood Wasif, Terrence J. Moore, Seunghyun Yoon, and a joint team from the United States, Korea, and Australia build a guard frame for self-driving cars. Cars that drive themselves must stay safe in rare road events. They must also cope with cyber and physical attacks while on the road.

Their frame, called RAIL in the work, keeps a human in the loop. It turns mixed signals from the car into calm, scaled shifts in control. It also picks which events the car should learn from next. The aim is a car that adapts to risk yet stays in bounds a human can trust.
arxiv-2601-11981:
Jian Lang, Rongpei Hong, Ting Zhong, Yong Wang, and Fan Zhou build a tool to spot fake news videos on new topics. Past tools assume the mix of topics stays the same from training to test. That fails when fresh events bring new topics.

Their frame, called RADAR in the work, adapts at test time. It uses fetched data to guide that change. They call it the first frame for test-time change to unseen news videos. Such a tool could react faster to new false claims as they spread.  Fast change is key when a false clip spreads at speed.
arxiv-2601-12281:
Lingyi Zhu, Zhongxiang Wei, Fan Liu, and their co-authors design antennas and beams to fix a blind zone in air-ground sensing and comms. Normal base stations tilt beams down to serve the ground. That leaves a backward blind zone for air targets.

Low-altitude flight growth makes air cover a real need. Their new antenna form steers beams for both air and ground at once. They add beamforming and user scheduling to match. Full-space cover would serve drones and ground users from one site.  Air cover from the same site cuts new mast needs.
arxiv-2601-12581:
Himanshu Bangar and nine co authors report a large spin torque effect in a layered material. The stack pairs germanium telluride with a ferromagnetic layer in a van der Waals heterostructure. Recent work has found large spin orbit torques in such layered materials. Those torques could drive energy efficient spintronic devices in the future.

One weakness has held the field back so far. Damping like torque conductivity in these stacks trails that of heavy metal systems. Low values limit the path to commercial devices. The team report a giant value of that conductivity in their stack. A jump of that kind could close the gap with heavy metals. It would make layered materials real contenders for spin based memory.
arxiv-2601-12981:
Sulaiman Khan, Md. Rafiul Biswas, and Zubair Shah predict type 2 diabetes early with a tabular transformer. Their model analyzes longitudinal patient data over time. It processes health records together with bone related tabular data. Long range dependencies in disease progression are the signal they chase.

Conventional methods often overlook those slow, complex patterns. A transformer built for tables can weigh distant records against each other. Early prediction of diabetes opens a window for prevention and lifestyle change. The study was funded for publication by Qatar National Library. Multimodal records, joined well, may flag risk years before symptoms. The work serves preventive medicine and health data science.
arxiv-2601-13081:
Geoff Keeling and Winnie Street take up a puzzle about chat with large language models. Such models can act out figures that seem to hold firm traits and moods. The authors call such figures characters. They ask if a character is a minded thing with beliefs, wants, and aims that last over time.

One view, which they call the illusionist view, says no. On that view the seeming mind is a trick of the text. The paper weighs that claim and its rivals. It asks what joint play of human and model in talk can and cannot show. For readers in mind studies and AI, the piece gives a clear map of the claims at stake.
arxiv-2601-13581:
Heedou Kim, Changsik Kim, Sanghwa Shin, and Jaewoo Kang tackle scams that use social tricks in 2026. Such scams now use long, personal chats to fool victims over many turns. Old tools that scan for set signs miss much of this slow deceit. Large language models can spot some of it, but their help for human thought is less studied.

The team builds ScriptMind, a system that joins machine checks with human judgment. It works out the crime script, the step-by-step plan a scammer seems to follow. It also tests how well the model grasps the trick. The goal is aid that helps people see the scam, not just a score.
arxiv-2601-14081:
Xingcheng Chen, Oliver Weißl, and Andrea Stocco build tests that explain why deep learning models fail in 2026. Test generation plays a crucial role in assessing model quality before deployment. The most advanced generators rely on generative AI to synthesize inputs. They remain limited in giving semantic insight into misbehavior causes.

They also lack fine-grained semantic controllability over generated inputs. The team's feature-aware test generation targets those gaps. Tests tied to clear features show which trait trips a model. Developers can then fix the flaw, not just count its effects.
arxiv-2601-14481:
Ramandeep Gill, Jiang He, Jonathan Granot, Jian-Chao Sun, and their co-authors assess a planned gamma-ray instrument in this 2026 paper. The dominant radiation mechanism that powers the prompt gamma-ray emission in gamma-ray bursts remains poorly understood. High quality polarization measurements could settle the question. Time- and energy-resolved linear polarization of prompt photons can distinguish between synchrotron and inverse-Compton processes.

The instrument is POLAR-2, a polarimeter designed for that job. The paper studies the prospects of prompt GRB polarimetry with it. The test is fair to both views. Each one makes a clear call, and the tool can tell them apart. No new burst is used. The case rests on what the tool can do once it flies. Readers get an appraisal of what POLAR-2 could prove about the brightest explosions in the universe, before the hardware flies.
arxiv-2601-14581:
Philip Korman studies solution curves for a boundary value problem in this 2026 math paper. The problem is a semilinear Dirichlet problem. In it, the Laplacian of u plus a nonlinear term g of u equals a given function f. The value u is zero on the boundary. Korman decomposes f into parts. One part is a multiple of the first eigenfunction. The rest is a remainder term.

His title names the approach: global solution curves in harmonic parameters, and multiplicity of solutions. Multiplicity asks how many solutions exist for one set of data. Readers get a picture of how solutions branch and multiply as the harmonic parameter varies, a core question in nonlinear analysis.
arxiv-2601-14681:
Shuhao Liao and eight co-authors build an exploration system for robots in this 2026 paper. Autonomous robot exploration needs two kinds of thought. Global reasoning picks where to go next across a whole space. Local control handles the next few seconds of motion. The team's framework, FARE, integrates both. It pairs a large language model for global reasoning with a reinforcement learning policy for local decision making.

The authors call this a fast-slow thinking paradigm. The language model thinks slowly and broadly. The learned policy acts fast and locally. Readers get a hierarchical design for robots that must explore unknown spaces with both judgment and reflexes.
arxiv-2601-14981:
Yi-Li Sun, Ze-Zhong Li, and co-authors report growing a new iron-based crystal that can superconduct. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with a barium iron arsenide crystal. Titanium atoms replace some of the iron atoms in the structure. That swap adds holes, making the crystal hole-doped.

The crystals came about by chance. The team had been trying to grow a different, nickel-doped crystal. They describe in detail how the new crystals grew in the lab and what they measured in them. The work adds a fresh material to the iron-based family of superconductors.
arxiv-2601-15181:
R. Babjak and M. Vranic design a one-laser route into the strong-field quantum regime. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with direct laser acceleration of electrons. A single intense laser pulse first speeds electrons inside a thin, underdense plasma.

The same pulse then bounces off a dense foil and meets the electrons head-on. In that clash the electrons emit high-energy photons by nonlinear Compton scattering. The photons can decay into electron-positron pairs by the Breit-Wheeler process. One single laser thus does both jobs in the scheme, which keeps the setup lean and simple.
arxiv-2601-15481:
Jakub Antczak and four co-authors use machine learning to forecast hospital demand in a 2026 arXiv paper. Crowded emergency departments put patient safety at risk. They also strain how a hospital runs day to day. Good forecasts of arrivals help managers plan staff and beds. The team focuses on early prediction of daily arrivals.

Three models are tested side by side. One is SARIMAX, a time-series model that can use outside factors. The others are XGBoost and LSTM networks, two widely used learning methods. Each model forecasts arrivals over a seven-day horizon. The title adds a priority queues angle to the approach. For hospital planners, the work speaks to a daily problem: how to match scarce resources to demand that shifts fast.
arxiv-2601-15581:
Taichi Sakakihara, Teppei Jodo, Seok Kang, and Yuji Sakamoto build a holographic head-mounted display in a 2026 arXiv paper. Holographic displays promise a next step past current headsets. They may reduce the three-dimensional sickness that plagues virtual reality. A good display must update images as the head moves, in real time. For holography, that is hard. Computing hologram data takes heavy resources.

Their device targets six degrees of freedom. That means it tracks both rotation and position of the head. Full tracking makes virtual objects stay put as the wearer moves. The paper's challenge is the compute load behind that freedom. Readers in optics and display engineering are the audience. Working holography at head speed would mark real progress toward comfortable headsets.
arxiv-2601-15881:
David Johansson and Yavar Kian solve an inverse problem in elasticity in a 2026 arXiv paper. They want to recover nonlinear material parameters. Their data are boundary stress measurements. The stresses answer to prescribed boundary displacements. From the surface response alone, they infer the material law inside. That law is a nonlinear elastic tensor. It depends on both displacement and strain, and not on position.

The governing system is a class of quasilinear Lamé systems. Inverse problems like this drive nondestructive testing. Engineers would love to read a material's traits without cutting it open. Proofs of recovery tell them when boundary data truly suffice. The math is demanding, but the applied motive is plain: safer structures through better material knowledge.
arxiv-2601-16081:
Aishwarya Majumdar and Yuan Liu build a quantum way to make a yes or no call on a shift signal. Their 2026 preprint works in the phase space of light like modes. A real value sits in a shift act on that space. The task is to tell if the value lies in a set band. The band ends need not match on each side.

The pair seek a method that stays firm when terms shift. Firm calls count for sense and read tasks in quantum tech. Their method aims to give the right call with strong odds. It must do so without fine tuned steps for each case. The work adds to the set of firm quantum read tools.
arxiv-2601-16781:
Paul Youssef, Christin Seifert, and Jörg Schlötterer find a cheap way to teach chatbots new facts. One known path shows the bot long sets of worked cases. Those sets cost time to build for each fact. They also eat space in the bot's short view. Their 2026 preprint swaps those sets for small trained marks.

Each mark is a short code trained to sway the bot. The marks ape the pull of the long case sets. Yet they need no fresh cases per fact. Bots could then gain facts fast and cheap. This could help news, care, and school bots stay fresh.
arxiv-2601-17181:
Doreen Osmelak, Yang Xu, Michael Hahn, and Kate McCurdy test if tongue forms map to sense in set ways. Tongues map sense to word forms in wild, unlike ways. Past work says those maps aid swift talk. But form-to-form links in a tongue got less heed. Their 2026 preprint checks how verb and pronoun forms mark set sense traits. Traits span person and count, in a wide tongue set.

Set marks that recur across tongues hint at shared rules. Such rules would mean talk shapes form, not chance. The finds back the swift-talk tale in a new way. Tongue science gains cross-land proof here.
arxiv-2601-17381:
Kiyoshi Kato gives a full account of a two-loop self-energy calculation. The task is a base step in particle theory. Loops bring ultraviolet divergences that must be split from finite parts. Kato uses a simple sector decomposition method. The method cuts the work into zones where each part can be handled cleanly.

The final form serves both hand analysis and numeric work. It lets users renormalize the divergence and keep a finite answer. Clear worked cases are rare for two-loop tasks. Students and coders can both learn from this one. It turns a feared step into a traced path. That has value far past the one diagram.
arxiv-2601-17481:
Emily Broadhurst and four co-authors present Lattice, a way to build guardrails for chat agents. Guardrails block harmful outputs. Most current ones use static rules. Static rules cannot adapt to new threats or new settings. Lattice builds its own guardrails and keeps improving them. It works in two stages, as the abstract states.

Self-built rules can grow with the risks a system meets. They can also fit each deployment's own needs. The risk is that loose growth could weaken safety. A sound frame must test each new rule. Lattice aims for growth with control. It speaks to teams that guard chat tools in health, law, and schools.
arxiv-2601-17581:
Daniel Ogenrwot and John Businge study how AI coding agents change code on GitHub. Agents now submit pull requests as autonomous contributors. Little proof exists on how their changes differ from human ones. The team runs a large-scale study of agent pull requests. They compare how agents modify code. They also compare how agents describe their changes.

Such proof is key to judge agent reliability. Reviewers need to know where agents excel or slip. Description quality shapes how fast humans can check work. The study gives teams data for policy on agent code. It moves debate from anecdote to record. Open-source projects can set rules with proof in hand.
arxiv-2601-17681:
Pritam Chatterjee and Anirudha Menon study spin textures in three-dimensional Dirac semimetals. They couple a Dirac semimetal Hamiltonian to a generic spin texture. A simple unitary transform gauges away the spatial part of the exchange term. That step creates effective corrections to the Dirac dispersion. A full function's worth of freedom appears in the result.

Such freedom means spin textures can reshape electron behavior widely. Designers could tune semimetal response through texture choice. Dirac semimetals are prized for fast, robust charge flow. Coupling them to magnetism opens device paths. The work maps the math of that coupling. It shows the range of effects on tap.
arxiv-2601-17781:
Andreas Säuberli, Darja Jepifanova, Diego Frassinelli, and Barbara Plank ask a simple question. Can a machine write text that is as easy to read as a person wants? Their 2026 preprint starts from eye movement. How our eyes move across a page shows how much effort the text costs us. Easy text and hard text leave different traces in the eyes.

The team trains a model to predict those gaze patterns. They then use the model to steer a language model as it writes. The steering pushes the output toward the reading style a user picks. In effect, the difficulty of a text becomes a dial that can be set. That could help learners, new readers, and anyone who needs plain text.
arxiv-2601-17981:
Osman Goni Ridwan, Hongfei Xue, Youxing Chen, Harish Cherukuri, and Qiang Zhu propose a new way to write down crystal structures. Their 2026 preprint works in reciprocal space instead of direct space. The usual record lists where atoms sit in the unit cell. Symmetry labels and site names then shrink that list to a few values. That record reads well for people and for archives, but it has a flaw for machines.

One structure can map to several records, and the map back is not one-to-one. A reciprocal-space form aims to fix that mismatch. A clean one-to-one code helps databases and learning models treat crystals without mix-ups. The work serves the growing field of materials data science.
arxiv-2601-18081:
Peixuan Han, Yingjie Yu, Jingjun Xu, and Jiaxuan You build an agent system that writes academic rebuttals. Their 2026 preprint presents DRPG, short for decompose, retrieve, plan, generate. A rebuttal answers reviewers and can decide a paper's fate. Support for this step is rare, even as language models spread through research work. Off-the-shelf models and simple pipelines struggle with long contexts and often miss the point of a critique.

DRPG splits the task into stages that match its name. Breaking a review into parts, fetching the right paper text, and planning replies should yield sharper answers. The aim is targeted, persuasive rebuttals that respect the record. Authors under deadline could gain real help.
arxiv-2601-18481:
Wanrong Yang and Aibin Zang study how small waves die out in a key model of sea and sky flow. The model tracks a fluid that is pushed by heat and by spin. Here the fluid sits in a half space, like air or sea above a flat floor. The calm state is a stack in which weight and heat hold in balance.

The team ask if a small bump near that calm state fades in time, and how fast. Their setup lets drag act on the flat moves but not on the up moves. That slant makes the maths hard, since some moves lack a brake. A proof of fade would back the use of the model for long term flow. It would also show which bumps a forecast must track with care.
arxiv-2601-18581:
Anna Theorin Johansson works on an old ask: when can a maths task be solved in whole counts by work in small parts? The task here pairs two forms in many counts. One form is neat, with each count raised to the same power on its own. The next form is free, with one step less of power. The ask is if a pass in each small part must mean a pass in the whole.

That kind of pass-or-fail rule is known as the Hasse rule. Johansson hones an old proof path to cut the count of counts the rule needs. Her cut is large: the bound drops by a wide step. In one key case the old need fell by a third. Tighter bounds bring hard count tasks close to the reach of hand proof.
arxiv-2601-18681:
Yilie Huang, Wenpin Tang, and Xunyu Zhou tune the clock of tools that build data by a slow walk back from noise. Those tools start from pure noise and step, time by time, to a clean case. The steps can be set at even gaps or by a hand-made plan. With a fixed count of steps, a poor plan wastes steps where they count least.

Their plan, named in the title, lets a step rule learn to speed or slow the clock as the walk goes. Steps grow thick where the walk needs care and thin where it runs free. The total time of the walk stays the same. A learned clock could give the same grade of case for fewer steps. That would cut the cost of each new shot or text such tools make.
arxiv-2601-18781:
I. Alikhanov puts forth a neat link between two gaps in the masses of neutrinos, the lightest bits we know. To weigh a neutrino in full is a core ask of the field. Its mass sets much about how the small world and the cosmos grew. Tests to date give gaps between the masses of the three kinds, not the masses them-selves. A true link among the gaps could help pin the full set.

Alikhanov draws the link from the best joint fits of how neutrinos shift kind as they fly. The link is plain in form, so its sums can be worked by hand. It also comes with tales of what it could mean for how mass is born. If the link holds as tests sharpen, it would be a clue of weight. If it fails, that too would teach the field.
arxiv-2601-18881:
Cyril Closset and six co-authors build special defects in a three dimensional field theory. The theory is a gauged linear sigma model, a tool that links field theory to geometry. Its target space here is a partial flag manifold, a space that encodes nested sets of subspaces.

The team constructs Schubert line defects in this model, extending their own work on full flag manifolds. Such defects act like probes: they sit in the theory and expose its hidden structure. The math ties quantum field theory to the geometry of flags, a bridge that has paid off in many past studies.
arxiv-2601-18981:
Ruslan Abdulin and Mohammad Rasoul Narimani guard power grids against faked sensor data. Smart meters and linked sensors help run modern grids, but each new link is a door for attack. In a false data injection attack, bad data fools the grid into wrong views of its own state.

The pair add attention based graph filtering to both catch the attacks and find where they hit. Graph tools fit grids well, since lines and nodes form a network by nature. Fast, sharp spotting of fake data helps keep a key service safe as more of it goes online.
arxiv-2601-19081:
G. Cao builds a detailed optical model of the light sensors inside a giant neutrino detector. The JUNO observatory in China holds more than seventeen thousand large photomultiplier tubes, which turn faint light flashes into signals. A precise model of how each tube responds to light is key to trusting the detector's simulations.

Better models also sharpen how JUNO maps signal size back to particle energy. Neutrino studies live or die on that energy scale, since the particles barely interact and each flash counts. Cao's model gives the experiment a firmer base for all the physics it plans to draw from its data.
arxiv-2601-19181:
Reed Yalisove and seven co-authors watch magnetic textures form in a layered crystal at near room conditions. Such textures, called skyrmions, are swirls of magnetism that may one day carry data at low energy cost. They are usually studied in the cold and in strong fields, far from everyday settings.

The team uses a special electron microscope that varies heat and field while it watches. Their crystal mixes iron, cobalt, germanium, and tellurium in a layered form. Seeing which swirls linger, and where they melt, tells engineers how close such memory ideas are to real use.
arxiv-2601-19281:
Zheng Zhang and eight co-authors let smart glasses users point with their eyes and speak to confirm. Smart glasses watch the world through head mounted cameras, but they lack a screen for the usual visual feedback. The team introduces a two step way to refer to real objects around the wearer.

First the user gazes at the object, then speaks to name or confirm it: gazeify, then voiceify. Eyes are fast pointers, and voice is a natural second channel. The pairing could make hands free control of smart glasses feel less like guesswork for everyday tasks.
arxiv-2601-19581:
Eliya Blumenthal, Ilay Mangel, Amit Kanigel, and Shay Hacohen-Gourgy build a new kind of superconducting qubit. A transmon is a small circuit whose frequency can be tuned with a magnetic field. Its key part is a Josephson junction, a thin barrier that supercurrent crosses. Standard junctions use aluminium and its oxide on both sides of the barrier.

Here one side is a van der Waals superconductor, a layered crystal called 4Hb-TaS2. The authors realise a flux-tunable transmon built on this junction. Swapping in layered materials widens what circuit quantum devices can probe. Such junctions may reveal unusual states of matter beneath the surface. The work extends circuit quantum electrodynamics beyond its usual materials.
arxiv-2601-19981:
Rathindra Nath Das, Arnab Kundu, and Nemai Chandra Sarkar use entanglement to diagnose chaos in a quantum model. Their model is the Rosenzweig-Porter model, a random-matrix system with a tunable transition. They study timelike entanglement measures, built from a spacetime density kernel rather than a state at one instant. Such measures can sense both how eigenvectors spread and how chaotic the spectrum is.

For several ways of splitting the system, they compute a Tsallis entropy and related diagnostics. One quantity, entanglement imagitivity, captures the kernel's non-Hermitian character. The measures sharply flag both eigenvector ergodicity and spectral chaos. New diagnostics matter for classifying phases of complex quantum systems. The work widens the toolkit of quantum chaos.
arxiv-2601-20181:
Christian Parkinson and Souvik Roy build a control framework for epidemic models that include randomness. Rather than steer the random system directly, they steer the spread of its possible states. That spread is described by a Fokker-Planck equation, a standard tool for tracking how a probability distribution evolves over time.

Optimal control of that equation aims to push the distribution toward a desirable state, such as low infection levels. The approach suits compartmental models, which split a population into groups like susceptible and infected. It offers health planners a principled way to weigh interventions when outcomes are uncertain. It is built for choices that must be made before all the facts are in.
arxiv-2601-20281:
Yusuke Sakai and six colleagues pin down the magnetic structure of the compound LaMnSi using nuclear magnetic resonance. In its antiferromagnetic state, the manganese moments line up in an ordered pattern. The team probes that pattern with resonance signals from two kinds of nuclei, manganese and lanthanum.

Their study determines the structure at the microscopic level, with the moments oriented along the c-axis of the crystal. It also reports on the electronic properties of the ordered state. Knowing the exact magnetic order is a base step for explaining how this material conducts and responds to fields.
arxiv-2601-20481:
Myungjin Lee, Eunji Shin, and Jiyoung Lee present a training-free way to make speech synthesis forget a person's voice. Modern zero-shot text-to-speech models can clone voices with striking realism, which creates crime risks when voices are copied without consent. Speaker unlearning aims to block the generation of chosen identities on request.

Existing methods need costly retraining and work only for speakers seen during training. The authors' approach avoids retraining altogether. A cheap, flexible block matters for platforms that must honor removal requests quickly, before a cloned voice can be misused for fraud.
arxiv-2601-20581:
Ory Schnitzer and Ehud Yariv calculate the effective slip length for flow over a grooved surface filled with lubricant. The surface is a periodic array of rectangular grooves, fully wetted by the lubricant, with an exterior shear flow running parallel to the grooves. Their focus is the limit where the lubricant is nearly inviscid compared with the outer fluid.

Slip length measures how much the surface lets the flow slide, which sets drag. Lubricant-filled grooves are a route to low-drag coatings for pipes and ships. A formula in the thin-lubricant limit helps designers pick groove shapes without heavy simulation.
arxiv-2601-20881:
Matteo Rossi presents a network designed to read lips more reliably. The 2026 paper introduces MA-LipNet, a model for lipreading. Lipreading decodes speech from silent video of lip movements. It holds clear value for fields such as public security. It can also help where audio is missing or drowned out. The task is hard because lip gestures are subtle.

Many sounds share nearly the same lip shape. Existing methods often suffer from weak feature separation. They also generalize poorly to new speakers and settings. MA-LipNet answers with multi-dimensional attention. Attention lets the model weigh the most telling frames and features. The design aims for robust reading across varied conditions. The paper adds to efforts to make silent video speak.
arxiv-2601-21281:
Licheng Wang, Yuzi Yan, Mingtao Huang, and Yuan Shen improve neural solvers for routing problems such as planning delivery paths. Recent solvers use graph networks trained by trial and error. The best known design reaches near-optimal routes without expert help or labeled examples.

The authors extend the attention step at the heart of that design. Their extended model reads the graph in a richer way before choosing the next stop. Better attention should mean better routes for the same training effort. The work adds to the push toward solvers that plan complex routes quickly on their own.
arxiv-2601-21481:
Sai Pavan Deram, Jacopo Pegoraro, Javier Lorca Hernando, Jesus O. Lacruz, and Joerg Widmer locate devices in the near field with cheaper antenna arrays. Combined sensing and communication needs wide arrays to pin down nearby targets. Fully digital arrays at that size are too costly and complex to build.

Sparse arrays cut the cost but create ghost positions from grating lobes. The authors propose a two-stage recovery method that works through the ambiguity in steps. It uses compressed sensing, which recovers a signal from few samples. The result aims at accurate near-field fixes without the price of a full array.
arxiv-2601-22081:
Yichun Zhao and co-authors study the hidden labor of making information accessible at work. In teams where blind and low-vision employees work with sighted colleagues, much information arrives in inaccessible forms. Slide decks, diagrams, and PDFs that screen readers cannot handle. Teamwork then depends on transforming those materials.

Someone must modify or recreate each item in an accessible form. The authors show these transformations are frequently overlooked, lack proper support, and impose extra burdens, often on the blind employees themselves. Their 2026 preprint argues the work should be recognized and resourced. The findings speak to any workplace that treats accessibility as a feature instead of shared infrastructure.
arxiv-2601-22181:
Qingyuan Tian and co-authors give position embeddings a firmer theoretical base. Rotary Position Embedding tells a Transformer where each token sits in a sequence. Extending it to sequences longer than those seen in training is common, but the extension strategies are diverse and lack a unified theory.

Their 2026 preprint proposes MrRoPE, a mixed-radix version of rotary embedding. Mixed radix means different components count at different rates, like seconds, minutes, and hours on a clock. A principled way to stretch context length matters because long documents, codebases. And conversations all press against the limits set at training time, and ad hoc extensions can silently damage a model's sense of order.
arxiv-2601-22381:
Victor Nikhil Antony and four co-authors built Lantern, a small robotic object made to blend into daily life. Robotic objects are plain, powered things that sit in a room and move or glow in subtle ways. Their 2026 report walks through many rounds of design and build.

The team tuned the guts of Lantern to hit set goals while keeping the build cost low. A cheap, open base lets more labs and artists make their own robotic objects. It also lets studies of long-term home use run at real scale. The work is a platform paper, meant to be built on.
arxiv-2601-22681:
Filip Fryš proves that a jagged, lower-dimensional size measure always exists for a class of rough sets. The sets are countably rectifiable: built from countably many smooth pieces. His 2026 preprint studies anisotropic Minkowski content, a size gauge that weights direction by a chosen shape.

He shows the gauge exists and equals a natural functional tied to that shape. Such gauges serve the math of fractals, films, and rough surfaces. Existence proofs end disputes about whether a number is even there. The work is pure geometric measure theory. It firms a subtle corner.
arxiv-2601-22881:
Ke Ping and four co-authors release AnoMod, a public dataset for finding faults in microservice systems. Modern cloud services are built from many small parts that talk to each other. When one part fails, engineers must find which one, and why, from a flood of signals.

Most older benchmarks cover only speed-related faults and one or two kinds of monitoring data. AnoMod aims wider, with more fault types and more data kinds. A shared, richer benchmark lets detection tools be compared fairly, side by side. Public release matters here: a shared dataset lets new detection methods be tested by anyone, not just the creating team.
arxiv-2603-01481:
Sales chatbots must sell well over a full chat while each reply stays smooth and within the rules. A 2026 study on training such agents argues that mixing those two aims into one score causes trouble. Large end-of-chat rewards can swamp small per-turn signals, which leads to shaky training or tricks that game the score.

The proposed method, DuCA, splits credit across two time scales, short turns and whole sessions. A key step scales each kind of reward on its own before the two are joined for each update. In tests with a lifelike user simulator, DuCA beat a strong baseline on sales success. It also cut repeat phrasing a lot and made the bot sound less easy to spot as a machine.
arxiv-2603-01581:
Robots run by vision, language, and action models often act too slowly for smooth real-time control. Zihao Zheng, Zhihao Mao, Maoliang Li, and colleagues speed them up in this 2026 work with a draft-and-check trick. In that trick, a fast draft is checked, but fixing token errors by full re-runs costs the time saved.

Their method, KERV, uses robot kinematics, the math of joint motion, to predict and patch draft errors. A Kalman filter, a standard motion tracker, forecasts actions so bad tokens need no costly re-run. Motion cues also tune the bar for accepting a draft token as the run proceeds. Across varied tasks and settings, the method speeds runs by roughly a third. Success rates stay near the unsped baseline, which is the key trade-off.
arxiv-2603-01681:
AbdulRahman Alharbi and Diogo Gomes solve a class of mean-field games with tricky edge rules in this 2026 work. Mean-field games model crowds of small players who each react to the whole group at once. Their setting fixes inflow on one part of the border and a flexible exit rule on another.

Exit flux and border value must satisfy a complementarity link, which blocks standard proofs. The pair build a monotone operator on a convex domain, with an extra border variable for exit flux. A shift flaw in the value function is cured by working in a quotient space that ignores constants. A classic existence theorem then yields solutions for a penalized version of the problem. Taking the penalty to zero gives weak solutions with the stated regularity for density, value, and flux.
arxiv-2603-01981:
Minhee Kim and Yong Yang attach honest error bars to machine learning forecasts of reactor material swelling. Their 2026 work studies void swelling, a radiation damage mode that sets how long reactor parts can serve. Learning models now predict swelling rates well, yet they give point values with no rigorous uncertainty.

Licensing and risk work need intervals with known coverage, not just a best guess. Their framework pairs ensemble learning models with conformal prediction, which calibrates intervals from held-out errors. A log transform handles the shift from nucleation-dominated early swelling to growth-dominated steady swelling. Even in sparse data regimes, coverage matches the target confidence level in their tests. Calibrated intervals could replace overly conservative bound curves in risk tools for high-dose reactor internals.
arxiv-2603-02081:
Jiale Lao and Immanuel Trummer argue that future query engines should be synthesized per query, not engineered once for all. Their 2026 work observes that hand-built engines strain to keep pace with new techniques and user needs. Internal complexity also makes those engines hard to extend or rebuild cheaply.

Their proof of concept, GenDB, uses language models to generate execution code for each incoming query. The generated code is optimized for the specific data, workload, and hardware at hand. An early prototype runs a multi-agent setup built on a commercial coding agent. Tests use a classic benchmark plus a new one designed to reduce leakage from model training data. Against five established engines, the synthesized approach performs significantly better in their evaluation, with limits and extensions discussed.
arxiv-2603-02781:
Chanwoo Hwang, Sunpill Kim, Yong Kiam Tan, and colleagues probe an attack on systems that recognize people by voice. Speaker recognition now guards biometric logins, forensic work, and voice services. Impersonation, where an attacker tries to be accepted as a specific enrolled person, is a central threat to those systems.

The paper's title points at its angle: the scores these systems output can reveal the target's voice traits, helping an attacker tune the attempt. The opening sections survey how mimicry, replay, and crafted adversarial audio have each been used against recognizers under different rules. By focusing on score feedback, the study highlights a leakage channel that designers of voice security must close.
arxiv-2603-03081:
Zhi Xu, Jiaqi Li, Xiaotong Zhang, and colleagues present an attack study that stress-tests the safety training of language models. Jailbreak attacks craft prompts that slip past alignment and draw out unsafe replies. Their 2026 method, TAO-Attack, improves optimization-based attacks that often stall on refusals or produce only fake-harmful text.

A two-stage loss first suppresses refusals so generation continues, then penalizes pseudo-harmful outputs to push toward genuinely harmful completions. A direction-first token update rule picks edits aligned with the gradient before weighing their size, speeding the search. Across several models, the attack beat leading methods on success rate, reaching total success in some settings. Studies of this kind map exactly where current safety training still bends.
arxiv-2603-03481:
Raj Narayan Dhara and Matteo Rizzi prove that a nonlinear diffusion equation admits solutions of a prescribed size. The equation is built on the p-Laplacian, a generalization of the ordinary Laplacian, with a radial potential and two competing power terms. Normalized solutions are those whose overall norm is fixed in advance, a constraint that matters in physical models. Their 2026 paper works in three or more dimensions and stresses the potential need not be bounded or carry a fixed sign.

The proof is variational, using a min-max argument to locate a radial solution. Its key tool is a Pohozaev identity, an exact balance relation, shown to hold for any solution under quite weak assumptions on the potential. That identity rests on a new global boundedness result for subsolutions of a related p-Laplace equation, proved along the way.
arxiv-2603-03581:
Edmond Chaussidon and a colleague make a practical case for squeezing more cosmology out of galaxy surveys without a bigger data vector. The deepest information in galaxy clustering is non-Gaussian, usually harvested by the bispectrum, a heavy three-point statistic. The marked power spectrum reaches similar information while keeping the familiar two-point structure: galaxies are weighted by a mark before the spectrum is measured. Their 2026 paper restructures the statistic for real survey use.

First the marked spectrum is rearranged to isolate its higher-order content, which demonstrably breaks parameter degeneracies the plain spectrum cannot. Survey geometry, they find, needs only the same treatment the standard spectrum gets. Perturbative modeling and the covariance structure, including cross-talk with the ordinary spectrum, are worked out. Finally, the statistic's cosmology dependence is smooth, so inference can interpolate between models instead of deriving formulas.

bjornson-arne-anderson-1881:
Rasmus B. Anderson translated Bjørnstjerne Bjørnson's Arne and early tales for Houghton Mifflin in 1881 and 1882. Bjørnson, later a Nobel laureate, built modern Norwegian prose from peasant life. Arne, the title tale, follows a crofter's son torn between his father's violence, his mother's songs, and his own longing to leave the valley.

Other sketches in the volume give brides, fishermen, and small farms in Bjørnson's fresh, direct manner. He wrote against the stiff book language of his day, close to living speech. Anderson, himself of Norwegian stock, made these tales a bridge between Norway and America. The volume helped found a national literature and export it at once. Bjørnson's peasants entered world reading through doors like this one.
bodin-de-magorum-daemonomania-latin-1581:
Bodin's Démonomanie reached learned Europe in this Latin translation, printed at Basel in 1581. The translator worked under the pen name Lotarius Philoponus. Latin carried Bodin's legal demonology to judges and scholars who read no French, greatly widening the book's power.

The four books define sorcery, weigh evidence, and prescribe punishments with a lawyer's care. Bodin's rigor answered Weyer's doubts and hardened witchcraft theory into law. This complete Latin text spread that theory far beyond France. It belongs beside the French original of 1580 in any serious study. Together they show how one jurist's book could steer trials across a continent.
bracton-de-legibus-twiss-vol4-1881:
The fourth volume of Twiss's Bracton came out in 1881, continuing the Rolls Series text of the great thirteenth-century treatise. Bracton wrote as a royal justice who knew the courts from inside. His book ordered the whole of English law, and Twiss's edition spread that order across six volumes.

Volume 4 takes up the criminal side of the law, the pleas of the crown. It covers felonies such as homicide, theft, and arson, and how the king's justice pursued them. Trial by jury was still young, and Bracton shows older proofs giving way to newer practice. The common law appears here at its sternest, with death or outlawry waiting for many offenses. The volume is a prime source for the birth of English criminal law.
cia-0000007481:
Winter 1962 brought volume 6, number 1 of Studies in Intelligence, the CIA's internal journal for working officers. One named piece, Anatomy of Spying, signals the issue's focus on how espionage actually works. The journal circulated inside the agency rather than to the public.

Inside, practitioners wrote for each other about tradecraft, analysis, and the hard parts of secret work. Such writing helped a young agency turn field experience into shared lessons. Released decades later, the issue lets outsiders watch that training process. It is primary evidence for how the early Cold War CIA understood its own trade.
cia-0000008381:
Plans for the Tan-Zam Railway drew CIA attention in an October 1965 paper on the project's prospects. The line was meant to link landlocked Zambia to the sea through Tanzania, easing its reliance on routes south. China backed the scheme, which made it a Cold War contest as well as a railway.

The paper weighs whether the line would be built and what it would change. Railways in such studies stand for trade, loyalty, and reach, not just track and trains. Readers see Beijing's growing role in Africa judged from Washington. The file captures development politics at an early Cold War turning point.
cia-0000008881:
Iran's current crisis, as of February 1951, is the subject of a CIA paper from the oil dispute's first heat. Iran's parliament was moving to take over the British-owned oil industry, and nationalist feeling ran high. The shah's authority and the government's stability both looked shaky.

The paper weighs the players: court, parliament, street, and foreign powers with oil at stake. Two years later, a coup backed by Washington and London would end the crisis by force. Reading the 1951 analysis shows the problem as first framed. It is a prelude written before anyone in the file names the ending.
cia-0000009081:
Peru's prospects came before CIA analysts in a paper dated June 1965. President Fernando Belaunde's government was pushing reforms while facing economic strain and stirrings of guerrilla unrest in the Andes. Washington watched Peru as one front in a wider Latin American contest.

The paper weighs the government's strength, the opposition, and the chances of upheaval. Country studies like this one tried to warn of crises before they broke. Peru did fall to a military coup three years later, which gives the analysis edge. Readers can measure the analysts' judgment against what actually followed in Lima.
cia-0000009681:
Two American prisoners held by the North Vietnamese Army were sighted in the Prey Ve area, a May 1972 report states. The place name is cut short in the heading, which places the sighting in the Cambodian border region. North Vietnamese units operated widely inside Cambodia by 1972.

Prisoners in NVA hands inside Cambodia fell between two countries' records. Officials in Saigon and Washington both had reason to track them, and neither had easy access. A dated sighting at least fixed the men's survival to that spring. The file preserves it as one more point in the borderland captivity record of the war.
cia-0000009981:
An American pilot died in the crash of an L-19 reconnaissance plane in Vinh Binh province, an October 1972 report states. The L-19 Bird Dog was a small, slow spotter plane whose crews flew low over battlefields. Vinh Binh lies in the Mekong Delta's flat, wet south.

Bird Dog crews directed artillery and strikes, work that kept them over enemy guns daily. Their losses were steady and their planes left little wreckage to find. A confirmed death in a Delta crash closed one such crewman's case. The file honors the spotter war's risk with a plain provincial record.
cia-0000010581:
North Africa's current situation is surveyed in an August 1952 CIA paper. France then ruled Morocco, Algeria, and Tunisia as protectorates or territory, and nationalist movements pressed in all three. Egypt, newly under its Free Officers after the July 1952 revolution, watched from the east.

The survey weighs French control against rising demands for independence across the Maghreb. Washington was torn between its French ally and the region's clear direction. Within a decade every territory named was independent, Algeria through a brutal war. This file catches the old order's last calm, surveyed whole in the summer of 1952.
cia-0000010881:
In February 1951 the CIA judged how three Southeast Asian lands might stand up to communist pressure: Thailand, Burma, and Malaya. China had just fallen to Mao's forces, and Washington feared the region could topple country by country. Malaya was already fighting a communist revolt under British rule, while Burma faced revolts of its own.

The paper grades each country's will and strength to resist, one by one. It treats their governments, armies, and rebel movements as the front line of a wider contest. Written before America's deep plunge into Vietnam, it shows the early map of fears that shaped later policy.
cia-0000012281:
Ed Proctor and Jack Smith, two American officials, talked over the use of material called Chickadee in May 1961, and a CIA record preserves their conversation. Chickadee was a cover name for sensitive source material in the Penkovsky case. The question before the men was how such material could be used without exposing the man who supplied it.

The record shows the home front's paperwork: coordination, caution, and argument inside the government. Running a great source took as much care in Washington as in Moscow. For readers, the page reveals the handling rules that protected secrets and source alike.
cia-0000012381:
Military Thought, the Soviet armed forces' journal, might be declassified, and an October 1965 paper weighs the considerations. The agency had gathered the journal's issues through channels tied to the Penkovsky years. Its articles, written by Soviet generals for each other, had been mined in secret for what they revealed about doctrine and plans.

Releasing such material meant judging what secrecy still protected. The paper balances the gains of openness against the habits of classification. For readers, it shows open-source gold being weighed: the foe's own words, and the question of who else might read them.
cia-0000012481:
Six American pilots were held in a two-story building in Sam Neua, Laos, and a CIA report from July 1967 records the fact in detail. Sam Neua was the Pathet Lao's stronghold country in the northeast. The report describes the captives' circumstances: the building's layout, the guards' routines, and the conditions the men lived under, as sources on the ground reported them.

Such detail made the intelligence believable and usable. Rescue planning and family accounting both began from facts like these. For readers, the report is architectural witness: a prison's address, known and written down.
cia-0000014781: Communist reaction to the Rosenberg execution in Uruguay fills a CIA file dated July 1, 1953. The executions had taken place on June 19 in New York. Reaction files flowed in from capitals around the world that summer. Uruguay's entry shows the case echoing even in countries far from the main stage. The Uruguay reaction file rests in the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000015281: Unknown flying objects were seen over Budapest, in a CIA report dated March 1, 1957. Budapest had risen in revolt the fall before and been crushed. American prisoners and missing men in Laos are the subject of a CIA record dated June 2, 1968, tied to the JPRC. The JPRC was the Joint Personnel Recovery Center, which worked to rescue and account for men in Southeast Asia. Laos was its hardest field, since the war there was secret.

Inside, the file concerns the center's Laos cases: who was held, who was missing, and what was known. Recovery work in Laos faced jungles, enemy forces, and official silence at once. The record shows the organization built for that work, and the scale of the task it faced in a country where little could be said aloud.
cia-0000041181:
Talks to prisoners of war, attributed to Jane Fonda, were broadcast from North Vietnam, in a CIA record dated June 5, 1972. The broadcasts aimed her words at the men held in Hanoi's prisons. Speaking to prisoners was the most charged part of her whole visit.

Inside, the attributed talks are preserved as the monitors heard them. Prisoners who heard such broadcasts faced them from inside cells and camps. The file records how the visit reached its sharpest point. A famous American voice was carried into the prisons, and the men there had no choice about hearing it from their captors.
cia-0000042781:
Further reportage on the Jesuit assassinations fills a CIA record dated November 3, 1989. The November date places this file weeks into the case's public life. By then the murders had become a fixed point in the war's story.

Inside, the reporting continues, with the case still drawing daily coverage. Sustained reportage kept pressure on every party to the war. Governments could outwait a single headline. They could not so easily outwait a story that returned each day with fresh detail and fresh anger. The file preserves that persistence, which helped make the priests' case the best known crime of the Salvadoran war.
cia-0000042881:

Inside, the pressures on the country over its rights record are surveyed. Reports from churches and rights groups fed the case against it. American aid debates turned on those reports each session. The file shows a small country cornered by its own record. The autumn's killings were about to make that record far harder to defend.

The report follows the early stages of that experiment. Small shifts in a satellite state's foreign and economic policy mattered to Washington because they hinted at looseness in Soviet control. For readers, the paper shows the long buildup to 1968. The Prague Spring did not appear from nowhere. Analysts had been tracking Prague's search for room to move since the mid-1960s.

cia-0000132681:
Only two days after a March 1 companion, this CIA briefing on Cuba is dated March 3, 1961. The Bay of Pigs landing was about six weeks away. Updates were coming fast enough that a two-day gap merited a fresh paper.

That pace is the story here: by March, Cuba reporting had become a near-daily service for a government closing in on an invasion decision. Each short paper refreshed the last, tracking an island whose defenses and politics decided the plan's odds. The declassified text survives via the CIA Reading Room mirror at the Internet Archive.
cia-0000132781:
Election season colors this Cuban Developments entry of September 4, 1960. In the United States, Kennedy and Nixon were campaigning for the presidency, and Cuba had become one of their issues. The CIA's running series kept reporting through the contest.

The paper belongs to the pre-election file both campaigns argued over: how the revolution had happened and what to do about it. Its September date places it two months before voters decided. For readers, the briefing links intelligence reporting to a famous campaign, in which Cuba's fate at home and abroad were debated together.
cia-0000135681: Brigade 2506's Spanish files include this document dated 1 March 1961, the start of the brigade's last full month before the April landing in Cuba. The force of anti-Castro exiles had been built and trained by the CIA over the previous year. The catalog records no subject for this item. It remains a primary source in Spanish, dated and placed within the brigade's papers, and its contents are for the reader of the text to establish.

Its worth is in the detail it pins down, one dated piece of a covert war fought largely on paper.
cia-0000136081: Dated 3 March 1954 and now declassified, a CIA cable records closing down SARANAC, ending a coded project whose work was done, or whose cover was blown. cia-0000136381: Castillo must be contacted, Washington agrees in this March 1952 cable, two years before he led the Guatemala invasion. All details needed to estimate the proposed movement's success are requested, with a full report to follow. Signed by J. C. King, it is an early seed of PBSUCCESS.
cia-0000136981: Spares and supplies are moving on the most urgent basis. This late June 1954 status report tells LINCOLN so. Spares for P-51s will arrive 29 and 30 June.
