coke-institutes-part2-1681:
The Second Part of Coke's Institutes appeared in print in 1681, decades after its author's death in 1634. Coke had written it as an exposition of the great statutes of England. Parliament ordered the later parts published during the civil war era, when his authority served the cause against the crown.

Above all, the volume expounds Magna Carta clause by clause, treating the charter as England's fundamental law. Coke reads old words broadly, finding in them guards for liberty, property, and fair trial. His commentary became the arsenal from which seventeenth-century lawyers drew their arguments against royal power. American founders later drank from the same source. The book taught generations that even kings stand under a law they did not make.
cyril-five-tomes-against-nestorius-pusey:
Cyril, patriarch of Alexandria, led the attack on Nestorius, the patriarch of Constantinople who split Christ into two sons in his preaching. His Five Tomes Against Nestorius answer the rival book by book. Edward Bouverie Pusey translated them for the Library of the Fathers in 1881, with Cyril's Scholia on the Incarnation and other pieces.

Cyril defends one Christ, true God and true man in a single person, and the title Mother of God for Mary. The fight came to a head at the Council of Ephesus in 431, which cast Nestorius out. Pusey's volume gives the winning side in its own strong words. It is a core text of the Christological debates.
darwin-vegetable-mould-1881:
Charles Darwin spent his last years studying small things close to home at Down House in Kent. His final book, published in 1881, reports forty years of watching earthworms turn soil. He had first read a short paper on worms to a learned society back in 1837. Few readers expected worms to fill a bestseller, yet the book sold fast.

Darwin shows that worms drag leaves below ground, swallow earth, and cast it up as fine mould. Inch by inch, he argues, they bury stones, ruins, and whole fields under new soil. The book is a quiet proof that slow, small forces can reshape the land.
dryden-absalom-achitophel-1681:
John Dryden, England's poet laureate, wrote Absalom and Achitophel in 1681 during a fight over the royal succession. Catholics were barred from the throne, and some Protestants wanted the king's son Monmouth to inherit instead. Dryden answered with a satire in biblical dress, published anonymously.

King Charles becomes David, Monmouth becomes his beloved son Absalom, and the scheming Earl of Shaftesbury becomes the tempter Achitophel. Dryden praises his friends and shreds his enemies in polished heroic couplets. The poem is a masterclass in political satire: elegant, funny, and ruthless. It helped define the form for the next century of English verse.
europmc-pmc10266981:
Pang and co-authors argue that the physical shape of the brain strongly constrains how it works, in a 2023 study. The classic view holds that brain activity flows through networks of specialized cell groups wired together. Pang's team asks how much of that activity can be explained by the brain's geometry alone, through waves traveling across its folded surface.

They model brain activity as waves shaped by the cortex's form. The model matches observed activity across many tasks at least as well as wiring-based models. The study reframes how shape and function relate in the brain.
europmc-pmc10310781:
Zhang and co-authors published a 2023 review on drugs that target amyloid beta in Alzheimer's disease. Amyloid beta is a small protein that builds up in clumps in the brain. Many scientists have blamed those clumps for driving the loss of memory and thinking in this illness.

The review traces the amyloid idea over 30 years of work. It notes that many trials of anti-amyloid drugs failed, which raised real doubt about the idea. It then notes that some recent trials did succeed. Zhang weighs open questions about current drugs and sets out ways to build better ones for care and for prevention.
europmc-pmc10364581:
The GBD 2021 Diabetes Collaborators measured the world burden of diabetes from 1990 to 2021. Diabetes is a long-term illness in which blood sugar runs too high. The study spans 204 nations and areas, split by age and sex. It also forecasts how common the disease will be through 2050.

In 2021, 529 million people lived with diabetes across the globe. The team split cases into type 1 and type 2 forms. Type 2 is the far more common form, tied to weight, diet, and low activity. The study weighed 16 risk factors for the type 2 burden. Lost healthy years were counted as deaths plus years lived with the illness. Forecasts used social and weight trends to project the rise.
europmc-pmc1054881:
Hauf and co-authors studied in 2005 how a protein ring lets go of chromosomes as cells divide. The ring, cohesin, holds twin copies of each chromosome side by side. At division, most of the ring leaves the arms of chromosomes early, well before the twins split. Two kinases, enzymes that add phosphate tags, drive that exit.

The team hunted tag sites on all four cohesin parts with a mass tool. Hauf found that tags on one part, Scc1, were not needed for the early exit. Tags on a second part, SA2, proved vital for it. Cells with a tag-proof SA2 kept cohesin stuck on the arms. The work pins SA2 as the key target of the kinase Plk1 in this path.
europmc-pmc10857981:
Xue and colleagues review a signal path that helps cancers spread in this 2024 paper. Spread, called metastasis, causes about nine in ten cancer deaths. One driver is a change called EMT, where anchored cells loosen and gain the power to move. The Wnt and beta-catenin path, a chain of signals inside cells, is a key switch for that change.

When the path switches on, beta-catenin builds up and moves into the cell nucleus, the control centre, where it turns on spread genes, the review says. This axis is overactive in many cancers of organs and blood. It also helps tumours resist drugs. Small RNA pieces and plant-based chemicals can damp the path in lab studies. The authors present the axis as a target worth aiming drugs at.
europmc-pmc11223881:
Bugnon and colleagues present the 2024 release of a free web docking service in this paper. Molecular docking predicts how a small drug molecule binds a protein target. It can speed drug screening by ranking candidates before lab tests. SwissDock, first released in 2011, prepares molecules and targets automatically for users.

The old docking engine was replaced by two state-of-the-art programs, the authors report. AutoDock Vina gives faster predictions, while Attracting Cavities gives more accurate ones. Molecules can be imported as files, as SMILES text strings, or as sketches drawn on screen. Targets come from uploaded files or a database ID. The interface was fully redesigned for interactive submission and analysis. Advanced search options link users to widely used databases for both molecules and targets.
europmc-pmc11226681:
O'Leary and a large team describe a US resource for fetching sequence data across the tree of life in this 2024 paper. NCBI Datasets is run by the National Center for Biotechnology Information. It gives simple, direct access to sequences, annotations, and metadata covering many species. Public repositories struggle to keep growing data discoverable and usable.

Data arrive as packages of sequences plus metadata, which aids sharing and reuse, the authors report. Access comes through web pages, command-line tools, and documented program interfaces. The resource follows the FAIR principles: data should be findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable. The paper outlines the current scope of data on offer. It also explains the options for exploring and downloading packages. Proper delivery, they note, supports credit for data producers.
europmc-pmc11252281:
Liu, Zhou, Tan, Siu, and Guan survey the modern menu of cancer treatments in this 2024 review. Classic chemotherapy and radiation burden patients with heavy physical and mental strain. Care has since been transformed by more precise options. Small molecule targeted agents, antibody-drug conjugates, cell-based therapies, and gene therapy now lead the new wave.

Antibody-drug conjugates pair a homing antibody with a toxic payload. The review works through five classes: small molecule drugs, antibody drugs, peptide drugs, gene therapy, and cell therapy. For each it explains the method, development status, clinical challenges, and potential. These modalities target tumours personally and precisely, the authors say, and can improve patient comfort. Untapped headroom remains in all of them. The authors frame the comparison as a guide for both clinic and lab.
europmc-pmc1190181:
Shiffman and colleagues built a scoring tool for medical guidelines in 2005. Guidelines tell doctors what best care looks like. Many still fail to change daily practice. A guideline that is hard to apply will often sit unused.

Their tool, called GLIA, rates how easy a guideline is to use. It has 31 items grouped in ten areas. Clear wording, clear actions, and clear outcomes count as core areas. Shiffman tested the tool with expert review and trial use. Spotting barriers early can save costly failed rollouts. Clear actions are the Decide and Execute dimensions in GLIA.
europmc-pmc11926181:
Vogler and co-authors reviewed a protein family that controls cell death. The family is called BCL2, named after a blood cancer gene. Its members govern whether a cell releases a signal to self-destruct. That signal comes from mitochondria, the cell power stations.

Drugs that mimic natural blockers can free that death signal in cancer. Venetoclax, the first such drug, changed care for several blood cancers. Newer drugs and guided carriers are now in trials. Vogler also covers roles beyond cancer and newer drug designs. The review links basic cell biology to bedside use.
europmc-pmc1240281:
Meerts and co-authors tested flame retardant chemicals for hormone action in 2001. The chemicals, called PBDEs, are added to plastics and fabrics. They persist in nature and had turned up in human fat and blood. Their hormone effects were largely unknown.

Cell tests measured estrogen-like activity with a glowing reporter gene. Eleven PBDE types showed estrogen-like effects in breast cells. One altered form beat the natural hormone in strength, at far higher doses. Related bisphenol compounds varied with their bromine load. Meerts flags a hormone concern for this chemical family.
europmc-pmc1315281:
Stranger and co-authors mapped DNA variants that alter gene expression in humans in 2005. Medical genetics hunts variants behind complex traits. Reliable assays and maps are prerequisites for that hunt. The team analyzed 630 genes in 60 unrelated Utah residents.

Genes sat in high-interest regions, including the ENCODE pilot areas. Of the genes, 374 were expressed in the test cells. Many regions showed significant links between single variants and expression levels. Three correction methods were applied to guard against false hits. Stranger proves expression itself can be mapped like a trait. The genes sat on chromosome 21, chromosome 20, and in ENCODE zones.
europmc-pmc1413581:
Could eating blueberries slow aging? Wilson and co-authors tested that idea in 2006 using a tiny worm, Caenorhabditis elegans, a common lab stand-in for aging work. They fed worms a mix of blueberry polyphenols, plant compounds often praised as health aids.

Worms on the mix lived longer and kept moving better as they aged. The mix also helped worms survive heat stress, but not a chemical stress test. Wilson split the mix into three parts. Only the part rich in one compound class gave the gain. The effect needed a gene pathway tied to salt stress defense, not the usual stress routes.
europmc-pmc1552081:
Reviews of test accuracy studies had no software of their own. Zamora and co-authors built one in 2006, called Meta-DiSc. Such reviews pool studies of how well a medical test spots disease. Analysts had to borrow general stats tools.

Meta-DiSc checks why results differ between studies and pools sensitivity and specificity, the two core accuracy measures. It handles both fixed and random effects models and draws forest plots and summary curves ready for papers. Its math was checked against other tools and published reviews. Zamora offers the Windows program free for academic use.
europmc-pmc1626481:
Meta-analysis software can be pricey and hard to learn. Bax and co-authors built a free alternative in 2006, called MIX. It pools results across studies to judge therapies and disease causes. Their target users were students and researchers new to the method.

MIX runs inside Excel, using its sheets for calculation and Visual Basic for the interface. Built-in tutoring tools guide users, and the design pairs with standard textbooks. To validate it, Bax re-ran eight published meta-analyses and matched outputs against two reference programs, STATA and Comprehensive Meta-Analysis. The results agreed, supporting MIX as a teaching-friendly tool.
europmc-pmc1634881:
Oceans swarm with viruses, most of them unknown to science. Angly and co-authors surveyed them in 2006 across four ocean regions, from 184 viral samples at 68 sites gathered over a decade.

Most sequences matched nothing in current databases. Global diversity ran to several hundred thousand species by their estimate. Richness varied with latitude, richer toward the south in their gradient. The Sargasso Sea teemed with cyanophages, while Arctic samples held many prophage-like sequences. Yet most species appeared in many regions. Angly concludes local conditions enrich common types rather than excluding others outright.
europmc-pmc2062481:
Bhattarai and co-workers measured malaria trends in Zanzibar in 2007 after two major control measures began. Zanzibar introduced artemisinin-based combination therapy, the strongest drug mix, for free in late 2003. Long-lasting insecticide-treated nets followed in early 2006 for young children and pregnant women. The team ran child surveys in North A District in 2003, 2005 and 2006, and reviewed all 13 public clinics there.

Parasite prevalence in children under five fell sharply, with an odds ratio of 0.03 by 2006, a ten-fold drop after nets arrived. Under-five deaths fell 52 percent between 2002 and 2005. Malaria admissions fell 77 percent, blood transfusions 67 percent, and malaria deaths 75 percent. Weather stayed favourable for malaria throughout, so the gains were not a climate effect.
europmc-pmc2125481: A medical paper studying experimental non-hemolytic streptococcus lesions in vitally stained animals. The stained lesions. This article preserves that pathology. Later readers can locate it. History keeps its place secure. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
europmc-pmc2128381: A medical paper on blood destruction during exercise, blood changes in its course. The runner's blood. This article preserves that physiology. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
europmc-pmc2128581: A medical paper on production of immunity in mice by inhalation of pneumococci. The breathed vaccine. This article preserves that immunology. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
europmc-pmc2131581: A medical paper on total surgical removal of the liver in rabbits. The liverless rabbits. This article preserves that surgery. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
europmc-pmc2140481: A biology paper on Donnan equilibrium and the physical properties of proteins, membrane potentials. The charged membranes. This article preserves that biophysics. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2140981: A biology paper on the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide by liver catalase. The liver's fizz. This article preserves that biochemistry. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2292181:
Sunkar and co-workers hunted new microRNAs in rice in 2008 using deep sequencing of small RNA libraries. MicroRNAs are tiny RNAs that switch genes off, and rare ones escape conventional sequencing. The team built libraries from normal rice seedlings and from seedlings stressed by drought or salt, then used pyrosequencing, a high-throughput method reading many fragments at once. They matched tens of thousands of unique small RNAs to the rice genome.

Most known conserved microRNAs were confirmed. Twenty-three genuinely new microRNAs were found, mostly each from a single genome locus. Six of them are conserved in other grass crops. Forty further candidates await confirmation. Using loose matching rules, the team predicted twenty target genes for nine of the new microRNAs. Deep sequencing thus uncovers low-abundance regulators, including candidates tied to drought and salt responses in a staple crop.
europmc-pmc2361981:
Hamaguchi and co-authors tested a new delivery form of the cancer drug paclitaxel in 2005. Paclitaxel kills many cancers but causes nerve damage, low blood counts, and allergic reactions, partly from the solvent used to dissolve it. Their version, NK105, tucks the drug inside tiny polymer spheres called micelles.

In animal tests, NK105 kept drug levels in blood about 90 times higher than the free drug, because the spheres leaked little and dodged body filters. Tumor levels ran 25 times higher, thanks to the spheres gathering in tumor tissue. Against human colon cancer grafts, NK105 shrank tumors far better than free paclitaxel. Nerve damage was clearly weaker too, shown by both tissue checks and nerve function tests. The authors said patient trials were warranted.
europmc-pmc2365981:
Schadt and a large team mapped how DNA variation shapes gene activity in human liver in 2008. The liver drives metabolism and is central to obesity, diabetes, and artery disease. Genes linked to illness usually act through such middle steps, so the team measured both DNA and gene activity in the same tissue.

They profiled over 39,000 gene transcripts and about 782,000 DNA variants in more than 400 liver samples. Over 6,000 links between variants and gene activity turned up, many in genes already tied to disease. Merging their data with other human and mouse studies let them test disease genes directly. For a new type 1 diabetes site, their data backed the gene RPS26 over the earlier favourite ERBB3. They also named SORT1 and CELSR2 as likely genes behind a cholesterol and heart disease site.
europmc-pmc2492881:
Statnikov, Wang, and Aliferis compared two leading computer methods for sorting cancers by gene activity in this 2008 paper. The methods are support vector machines and random forests, both used to classify tumors from microarray data, which measure thousands of genes at once. Earlier studies had suggested random forests might be the better tool.

The authors first showed that prior comparisons carried design flaws that favored one method. They then ran a corrected test across 22 diagnostic and prognostic data sets. Support vector machines beat random forests in most data sets, often by a wide margin. The result held both with no gene selection and with several popular gene selection methods applied first.
europmc-pmc2515281:
Koch and colleagues compared T cells, a core part of the immune system, in young and older people in this 2008 study. Immunity weakens with age, and the mix of T cell types in the blood changes. The team used multi-colour flow cytometry, a method that tags cells with several markers at once, to sort the cells in fine detail.

They tracked naive, central memory, and effector memory cells in both CD4 and CD8 groups, adding markers of stimulation and wear. Age shifts were stronger in CD8 cells than in CD4 cells. The results support a step-by-step path from naive cells toward worn-out end-stage effector cells that no longer divide. For CD4 cells, change within each subset mattered more than shifts between subsets.
europmc-pmc2516581:
Zuccato and co-authors tested a new way to track illegal drug use in 2008: analysing city sewage. People excrete drug residues in urine, so wastewater arriving at treatment plants carries a chemical record of what a whole community has taken. The team measured residues of cocaine, opiates, cannabis, and amphetamines by mass spectrometry.

Samples came from treatment plants in Milan, Lugano, and London. Each city showed its own reproducible pattern of drug use, matching national survey estimates. In Milan, cocaine residues rose sharply at weekends, a shift the method caught quickly. The authors argue that sewage analysis can monitor local drug trends almost in real time, far faster than surveys and crime statistics allow.
europmc-pmc2605581:
Grech and a large team of collaborators reviewed in 2008 the methods for solving the EEG inverse problem, locating brain sources from scalp voltage recordings. The problem is mathematically ill-posed: many source arrangements can produce the same scalp pattern. The review organises solutions into two camps. Nonparametric methods spread activity over the whole brain grid. Parametric methods assume a few dipoles.

Surveying published performance, the authors find the LORETA family gives satisfactory results in most cases, while clustered sources favour high-resolution methods such as MUSIC or FINES. Their own Monte-Carlo simulations compared four nonparametric algorithms at varied noise levels and source depths. For a single source, regularised sLORETA gave the best localisation. It produced the fewest ghost sources. A heavier shrinking method added no benefit.
europmc-pmc2642881:
Friston explained in 2009 two ways to study how brain areas talk to each other using brain scans. Scans once showed mainly which areas light up during a task. Newer methods ask a harder question: does activity in one area drive activity in another, for example when attention boosts what we see?

One approach, dynamic causal modelling, builds a model of how areas influence each other and tests whether it fits the scan data. The other, Granger causal modelling, looks for timing patterns in which one area's activity predicts another's a moment later. Friston compares what each method can and cannot show. The piece helps readers judge claims about brain networks, such as whether a signal flows from higher areas down, or from the senses up.
europmc-pmc2718581:
Fazel and co-authors reviewed in 2009 whether schizophrenia and other psychoses raise the risk of violence and violent crime. Public claims and charity campaigns often call any link a myth, while secure hospital numbers have risen in many Western countries. Prior studies gave wildly different estimates, from large increases to none at all.

Pooling population studies, they found a modest raised risk of violence in people with psychosis compared with the general public. Much of that extra risk ran through substance abuse that occurred alongside the illness, not through psychosis alone. People with both psychosis and substance abuse faced risks close to those with substance abuse alone, which reframes where prevention should aim.
europmc-pmc2719581:
Potkin and co-authors ran a genome-wide association study in 2009 using hippocampal shrinkage as a measured trait to hunt Alzheimer's risk genes. Apart from the APOE gene form, common risk genes for late Alzheimer's were unknown. Shrinkage of the hippocampus, a memory center, can be measured on scans. It may track disease genes more directly than diagnosis alone.

In three hundred eighty-one participants in a national imaging study, the usual case-control scan confirmed APOE. It also flagged a new gene, TOMM40, whose risk forms were about twice as common in patients. The shrinkage-based scan added twenty-one candidate areas. Those included genes tied to protein cleanup, cell death, and brain development. All data were made freely public.
europmc-pmc2746281:
Dubreuil and co-authors characterized in 2009 masitinib, a new tyrosine kinase inhibitor drug that targets KIT, a receptor that drives growth in mast cells and some tumors. KIT is a target in cancer, mastocytosis, and inflammatory disease, but the standard inhibitor imatinib has limits. A more selective drug might work as well with fewer side effects.

In lab tests masitinib blocked KIT more strongly and selectively than imatinib, and also hit two related kinases while sparing many others. It blocked mast cell degranulation, cytokine output, and migration more strongly, and worked against KIT mutants that sit near the membrane. In mice it blocked growth of tumors carrying such a mutant, with no heart or gene toxicity seen in animal studies.
europmc-pmc2771281:
Spaulding and co-authors estimated in 2009 the share of the United States HIV and AIDS epidemic borne by inmates and people released from jails and prisons in 2006. Groups at high risk gather in correctional facilities, where infection rates ran high early in the epidemic. They built a new model of population flow through facilities to compare 2006 with 1997.

In 1997, about one in five HIV-infected Americans was among those who left a facility that year. By 2006 the share had fallen to about one in seven, a drop of nearly thirty percent, even as releases rose. For Black and Hispanic men, though, recent releasees still made up about one in five of each group's infected members. Absolute numbers leaving with HIV stayed nearly the same, keeping facilities prime sites for public health work.
europmc-pmc2850381:
Splinter, Akhmanova, Medema, and colleagues traced in 2010 how the cell nucleus gets hauled into position just before cell division begins. As cells enter mitosis, the centrosome, the organizing hub for the cell's skeleton, must split and the nucleus must center correctly. The team searched for partners of Bicaudal D2, an adaptor that links cargo to molecular motors.

Bicaudal D2 latched onto RanBP2, a giant protein of the nuclear pore, the gateway through the nuclear envelope. Through that link it recruited dynein, a minus-end motor, and its counterpart kinesin-1 to the nuclear surface in late G2 phase. Cells missing the adaptor misplaced their centrosomes and nuclei, revealing the missing molecular link between motors and the nucleus.
europmc-pmc2870981:
Rueping and Nachtsheim reviewed in 2010 a decade of progress in the Friedel-Crafts alkylation, a classic reaction that attaches carbon groups to ring-shaped molecules. The old method needed toxic benzyl halides and large amounts of a Lewis acid, a chemical that grabs electron pairs. Newer versions use only a pinch of catalyst, a substance that speeds a reaction without being consumed.

Benign starting materials such as benzyl alcohols and styrenes now replace the toxic halides in many versions of the reaction. Low catalyst amounts still deliver a wide range of products in good yield. The review also highlights the first versions that control which mirror-image or spatial form of the product is made. Those versions point toward cleaner drug and materials chemistry with far less waste.
europmc-pmc2872881:
Gerardo and a consortium of aphid genome researchers reported in 2010 that the pea aphid defends itself with a surprisingly thin immune toolkit. Pea aphids are sap-sucking pests of legume crops, and their genome had just been sequenced. Insects usually recognize germs, signal the alarm, and kill invaders with antimicrobial peptides, small germ-killing proteins.

The aphid genome lacks many genes for each of those steps that other insects rely on, including key recognition and signaling pieces. Some killing peptides are missing entirely. Living with helpful bacteria inside its own cells may have let the aphid shed costly defenses, or its bacteria partners may supply protection instead. Either way, the gaps reshape how scientists think insect immunity must be built and where pest control might strike.
europmc-pmc2885081:
Kumirska and co-authors reviewed in 2010 how light-based laboratory methods reveal the structure of chitin and chitosan, two versatile natural polymers. Chitin is the second most abundant natural polymer on Earth, forming shells of crabs and shrimp and walls of fungi. Its treated derivative chitosan serves medicine, farming, and food production, yet properties vary widely with source and processing.

Spectroscopic methods, which read how a sample absorbs or scatters light and radio waves, can measure chain chemistry without destroying much material. The review covers which method answers which question, from the degree of chemical trimming that turns chitin into chitosan to the makeup of modified versions. Reliable structural checks are what let makers certify a batch for a sensitive use like wound care.
europmc-pmc2888581:
Kinney, Lawn, and the Science in Action working group opened in 2010 a journal series on mother, newborn, and child deaths in sub-Saharan Africa. The region loses about four point four million children, including over a million newborns, plus some two hundred sixty-five thousand mothers every year. That is roughly thirteen thousand deaths a day, half of the world's total for these groups.

Five challenges drive most deaths: complications of pregnancy and birth, newborn illness, childhood infections, malnutrition, and HIV. Proven tools already exist for nearly all of them, from vaccines and treated bed nets to emergency obstetric equipment. The authors argue the core failure is delivery, not knowledge, since governments underuse the interventions science has validated.
europmc-pmc2896381:
Schmid and colleagues built in 2010 a three-dimensional visualization toolkit that plugs into ImageJ, the free image software biologists already use. Modern microscopes and scanners produce 3D stacks that flat viewers handle badly, and writing custom 3D code is slow and specialist work. Their Java framework hides the graphics machinery behind simple high-level calls.

Plug-in authors gain volume rendering, direct editing of 3D volumes, surface extraction from labeled structures, and annotation tools with little extra code. Hardware acceleration keeps big confocal and electron microscopy datasets interactive. Because it rides on ImageJ's vast community library, a lab can move from raw stack to measured 3D structure in one environment. The authors released the source openly so other groups could extend it.
europmc-pmc2908081:
Dayyani and colleagues pooled in 2010 thirty-four studies and over fifty-six hundred patients to define how human papillomavirus changes head and neck cancers. The virus, famous for causing cervical cancer, drives a subset of throat and mouth cancers too. About twenty-two percent of the tumors carried the virus, and nearly nine tenths of those carried type 16, the highest-risk strain.

Virus-positive tumors formed a distinct biological entity: they arose more often in virus carriers, carried far fewer mutations in the guardian gene p53, and answered treatment better. Most strikingly, virus-positive patients died at well under half the rate of virus-negative patients. The authors argue trials should now test whether these patients can be cured with gentler therapy that spares them lasting side effects.
europmc-pmc2939781:
Okusaka and colleagues compared two chemotherapy plans for advanced bile duct cancer in Japanese patients in a 2010 multicentre study. A British trial had hinted that pairing gemcitabine with cisplatin beat gemcitabine on its own.

Eighty-four patients were assigned by chance to the pair or to gemcitabine alone, given in repeating cycles for up to nearly a year. The pair produced modestly longer survival, longer time before the cancer grew, and more tumour shrinkage. Low blood cell counts were the commonest severe side effects, occurring more often with the pairing. The authors judged the pair tolerable and fit as a standard option.
europmc-pmc3002981:
Chan and colleagues used precise mass measurements to watch the chemical decorations on transfer RNA shift during stress in yeast, in a 2010 study. Over a hundred such decorations exist, mostly on the RNAs that carry building blocks to protein factories, yet their collective behaviour was obscure.

Their method measured the decorations with care. It also uncovered fresh routes by which cells build several of them. Different poisons left different signature patterns: peroxide raised three particular decorations, while other agents lowered them or left them alone. Yeast missing the enzymes for those three decorations grew hypersensitive to peroxide.
europmc-pmc3061881:
Reikvam and coauthors refined in 2011 a reliable way to empty a mouse's gut of its bacteria without a germ free facility. Comparing normal mice with microbe free ones reveals what gut microbes do for the body, but germ free colonies are costly and rare. Earlier antibiotic in drinking water protocols proved hard to repeat and sometimes harmed the animals.

Delivering the antibiotics by mouth tube twice a day cleared the growable gut bacteria and cut gut bacterial DNA several hundred fold, while keeping mice healthy. After about two weeks the mice looked much like germ free animals, with enlarged gut pouches and smaller immune tissues. Hundreds of genes changed activity in the colon lining, and gut cell growth slowed. The protocol gives ordinary labs a workable stand in for germ free mice in microbe and host studies.
europmc-pmc3113981:
Jennifer Schumi and Janet Wittes wrote a 2011 guide in Trials to a tricky kind of medical trial. Most trials try to show a new treatment beats an old one, but some only need to show the new option is not unacceptably worse. Their paper explains that design and how regulators in Europe and the United States view it.

The central problem is choosing in advance how much worse counts as too much, since that margin decides the verdict. The authors walk through how sample size, error rates, and confidence ranges work differently when the goal is staying close rather than winning. They stress that a sloppy trial can wrongly pass as good enough, so careful design and honest reading of results matter more here than in standard trials.
europmc-pmc3166781:
Matthew Warman and colleagues issued the 2010 revision of the classification of genetic bone disorders in a 2011 paper in the American Journal of Medical Genetics. These disorders arise from faults in bone development, growth, and upkeep, and their sheer variety makes diagnosis hard. The classification sorts recognised conditions by clinical and X-ray features and, where known, by molecular cause.

The revision lists more than four hundred and fifty conditions in forty groups. Over two thirds now link to mutations in more than two hundred genes, from common recurrent faults to private ones seen in single families. The document thus doubles as both a diagnostic checklist and a gene-to-condition map. It is aimed at genetics, children's medicine, and radiology teams facing the coming flood of sequencing data.
europmc-pmc3168881:
Tatiana Akimova and colleagues tested whether a protein marks a special class of calming immune cells in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Regulatory T cells keep immune responses in check, and a recent report claimed one protein distinguishes those born in the thymus from those converted later in the body. The team tracked the protein across mouse and human T cells at rest and during activation.

Cells lacking the protein were mostly naive, never-activated cells. Switching T cells on and driving them to divide switched the protein on too, in regulatory and ordinary T cells alike, and resting switched it back off. Since the protein simply reports recent activation and division, it cannot separate the two regulatory lineages as claimed. The study corrects a marker the field was beginning to rely on.
europmc-pmc3222181:
Michelle Burns and colleagues built Mobilyze!, a phone-based treatment aid for depression, in this 2011 paper in the Journal of Medical Internet Research. Phones carry sensors that can infer where a person is and what they are doing. The team used that context sensing to deliver help at the moment it might be needed. Eight adults with major depression used the system for eight weeks.

Machine-learning models trained on dozens of sensor readings predicted categorical states such as location with promising accuracy, though mood ratings on scales were hard to predict. The package added feedback graphs, lessons in behavioral activation, and brief clinician contact. Participants liked the app, and their depressive symptoms fell significantly on both self-reports and interviews, with anxiety easing too. The authors present it as a feasible first of its kind.
europmc-pmc3257681:
Emilio Ros reviewed the health benefits of eating nuts in this 2010 article in Nutrients. Tree nuts and peanuts are dense packages of unsaturated fats, quality plant protein, fiber, minerals, and protective plant compounds. Ros asks what that unusual composition means for the people who eat them regularly.

Population studies link nut eating with less coronary heart disease and fewer gallstones in both sexes. They also link it with less diabetes in women. Hints of benefits extend to blood pressure, cancer, and inflammation. Feeding trials consistently show nuts lower cholesterol, even within already healthy diets, and evidence is growing for effects on oxidative stress, blood vessel function, and the metabolic syndrome. Against expectations, regular nut eaters do not gain excess weight and may lose some. The main safety concern is nut allergy in a small number of children.
europmc-pmc3266881:
Daniel Lawson, Garrett Hellenthal, Simon Myers, and Daniel Falush introduced a haplotype-based way to infer population structure, in this 2012 paper in PLoS Genetics. Dense genome-wide data reveal ancestry in unprecedented detail but strain older statistics. Their framework paints each person's chromosomes as a mosaic of chunks copied from other individuals in the sample, summarizing the copying pattern in a coancestry matrix.

That matrix turns out to capture nearly all the information used by standard principal component analysis and by model-based clustering, while squeezing extra signal from the linkage between neighboring markers. Their companion clustering method is faster than rivals, separates more populations, and detects subtler structure. Applied to a worldwide panel of over nine hundred people, it resolved more than two hundred populations, from continental down to family scale, finer than geographic labels suggest.
europmc-pmc3399081:
Jonassen and co-workers explained in 2012 how insulin degludec, an ultra-long-acting insulin, was designed to release slowly after injection. A fatty tail attached to the insulin lets it self-assemble once the injection's helper chemicals fade. The team tested a series of tailed insulins to learn the structural rules.

In the vial, degludec sits as paired six-unit clusters. After injection, as one helper fades, the clusters link into long filament-like chains, then slowly shed single units as a second helper leaves. The shape studies confirmed each stage of that choreography. Weak pairing between shed units means they free themselves quickly once released. The design shows injected depots can be engineered on purpose.
europmc-pmc3400581:
Lovejoy and a consortium team mapped in 2012 how some cancers keep their chromosome ends without the usual enzyme, a route called alternative lengthening of telomeres. This recombination-based path serves a sizable share of human cancers, but what unleashes it was unknown. Mutations in a chromatin complex involving the protein ATRX had recently turned up in such tumors.

Studying twenty-two cell lines using the pathway, the team found loss of ATRX protein or its gene in case after case. The cells also showed scrambled genomes, stray mini-nuclei, a faulty checkpoint before division, and altered repair of broken DNA. Together these hallmarks could help doctors spot and treat cancers that maintain their ends this way.
europmc-pmc3460881:
Liu and colleagues vetted housekeeping genes in 2012 for gene studies in Nicotiana benthamiana, the workhorse plant of virus research. Such studies lean on a steady reference gene for calibration, and infection might wobble the usual choices. Sixteen candidate references were profiled in leaves carrying infections from a panel of five RNA viruses of plants.

Three independent algorithms agreed on the steadiest trio: PP2A, F-BOX, and L23. Together they were enough for accurate calibration, and a demonstration on two immune genes showed clean results. Several traditional favorites proved less steady under infection. The shortlist should serve virus studies directly and guide reference choice for other stresses in this model plant.

france-crime-sylvestre-bonnard-1881:
Anatole France published The Crime of Sylvestre Bonnard in 1881, his first novel, Englished here in 1906. The English translation of 1906 gives an elderly scholar's gentle, ironic adventures among books and a young ward. France's limpid irony and love of old Paris announce the master stylist of the next forty years.

Bonnard, a member of the Institute, hunts a rare manuscript to Sicily and into a bookseller's clutches in Paris. He rescues Jeanne, the granddaughter of his lost love, from a cruel guardian and a boarding school's neglect. To give her a dowry he sells his library, and the crime of the title is a kindly theft. The close finds the old scholar content, his books gone and his ward happily wed in Paris. The novel's charm and humane skepticism won France his first wide public in France.
frus-1861-d181:
Carl Schurz wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 9 October 1861. The dispatch is document 181 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Schurz had now held Madrid through a summer of war. His October report has the ease of a man who knows his court. It told Washington that Spain, for all its pride, showed no haste to aid the South. Spain's pride was real, but its purse and fleet were weak, and Schurz read both facts well. Both facts read well in Washington, where Spain had long been a cause of doubt.
frus-1861-d281:
A State Department letter of 8 July 1861 told Mr. Haldeman what Washington wanted done. Congress received it as Document 281 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. By then, in the first summer of the Civil War, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1861-d81:
A letter dated 11 September 1861 went from William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams in London. The letter is document 81 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Three days of letters to London in a row show a desk that never cooled. Seward drove the effort abroad with his own hand on the pen. This note belongs to the dense September run that kept Adams fully briefed as autumn began. Adams could act on a brief order the day it landed, without waiting for more. Brief orders also left Adams free to spend his days in talks, not in study.
frus-1862-d181:
Document 181 is the second Seward dispatch to Charles Francis Adams dated 3 November 1862, printed in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Adams, the American minister in London, received both letters in the same mail.

When the Department split a day's orders between two letters, each usually took one topic, so the envoy could file and answer them apart. The practice swells the volume but sharpens the record. Read together, the 3 November pair shows Washington's hand at the very moment Britain weighed the French call for a truce in the war. Adams reported home at least once a week, and oftener when the news was hot.
frus-1862-d281:
A Dayton report dated 26 May 1862 stands as Document 281 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. William L. Dayton, the American minister in Paris, sent it to Secretary of State William H. Seward.

That week, Stonewall Jackson's Valley campaign was alarming Washington itself, a reminder that the war could swing fast. Foreign envoys reported each swing, and ministers at home weighed them. Dayton's letter from Paris in late May is part of the transatlantic conversation by which two governments tried to price a war neither could predict. French public opinion ran warmer for the Union after the emancipation news arrived.
frus-1862-d381:
On 24 January 1862 Cassius Clay wrote again to Secretary of State William H. Seward from St. Petersburg, in a letter printed as Document 381 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Clay was the American minister in Russia.

Clay's Russian service was ending: Simon Cameron had been named to succeed him, though Clay would return to the post in 1863. His January reports closed his first term at a friendly court. For Washington, the Russian channel's value lay in its contrast with Europe's western capitals, where sympathy for the South ran stronger. St. Petersburg's friendship later sent Russian fleets to American ports in 1863, to great cheers.
frus-1862-d481:
James E. Harvey reported from Lisbon to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 3 October 1862. The dispatch is Document 481 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, laid before Congress.

October reports from the Atlantic posts dealt with a war at sea that was spreading. Confederate raiders were burning American merchant ships. They did so in full view of neutral shores. Portugal's enforcement of its neutrality rules was therefore a live question in Washington. Harvey's account of Lisbon's stance fed the State Department's running brief on the cruisers. Read with Seward's instructions to the same post, his letters show a small legation doing work that touched every American shipowner trading across the Atlantic.
frus-1862-d581:
James Watson Webb received the year's last printed Brazilian order from Secretary of State William H. Seward, dated 27 September 1862. It is Document 581 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Seward wrote ten days after Antietam and five days after the emancipation order, though neither fact could shape Webb's conduct in Rio for months. The instruction still mattered. It fixed the Department's line for Brazil on the war. It also fixed the line on slavery's new place in the war. And it stated the neutral rules the Union expected in Brazilian ports. The Brazilian file ends the volume's American missions south of the equator, a thin correspondence stretched by distance over the whole geography of the war.
frus-1862-d681:
William H. Seward wrote to Mr. Blatchford again on 13 October 1862, less than three weeks after his last letter to him. The note is document 681 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862. Two letters in quick order point to a matter that needed more than one word from Washington.

Much of a secretary of state's mail never made the papers, yet it was saved all the same. This short run of letters shows Seward tending to a side file in the midst of a war for the Union's life. For the reader, the pair is a reminder that the printed record holds small threads as well as grand ones.
frus-1862-d81:
The mail from abroad brought Seward a letter from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, dated 18 June 1862. Congress received it as Document 81 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. It was written in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1863p1-d181:
The State Department's mail for London dated 4 May 1863 carried this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 181 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

After emancipation became official policy in January 1863, Seward could argue that aiding the South meant aiding slavery. That argument runs under much of the year's diplomacy. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d281:
The American minister in London, Charles Francis Adams, wrote this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 5 September 1863. It is document 281 of the 1863 volume of diplomatic papers. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863.

British yards were building two ironclad rams for the Confederacy in the summer of 1863. The fight to stop those ships reached its peak that autumn, filling the London mail. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d381:
From the British legation in Washington on 3 February 1863, Lord Lyons sent this note to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as document 381 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

London watched for any sign that Washington meant to widen the war. Lyons's job was to read American intentions and report them home faithfully. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d481:
On 27 April 1863, Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington wrote to Secretary William H. Seward. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the spring of 1863.

Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1863p1-d581:
Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington wrote this official letter to Secretary William H. Seward on 1 July 1863. The State Department later published the letter in its 1863 foreign affairs volume, laid before Congress with the President's message. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad.

British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. Letters like this one were the tools of a quiet contest. The Union meant to keep Britain out of the war, and it made that case note by note. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1863p1-d681:
Charles Francis Adams received this dispatch from Secretary of State William H. Seward on 5 December 1863. It is printed as document 681 in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States. Adams had held the London post since 1861, the first year of the Civil War.

The London mission was the most vital post the Union had abroad. From it, Adams dealt with British leaders on ships, trade, and the risk of Britain backing the South. Seward's notes told him where Washington stood. A reader gets a feel for the pace of that work. Letters came often, each one short, each one part of a long, careful effort.
frus-1863p1-d81:
While three letters went out from London, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote one of his own to Adams, on 13 February 1863. Adams was the American minister there. The letter is document 81 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The two men wrote blind of each other's same-day sheets, since the sea mail took ten days or more. Seward's letter set out the line Adams was to hold on the points then live. It is a neat case of how the exchange worked: not a talk, but two streams of paper that met in the files. This sheet is Washington's half of that crossed day.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d181: The Most Secret Protocol of the Moscow Conference, dated November 1, 1943, stands as Document 181 of the Cairo and Tehran volume, beside its companion Secret Protocol of the same date. The higher stamp marked the more sensitive of the agreed texts, the one fewest eyes were meant to see. That it is printed at all shows how far time opens wartime files. The protocol appears in the Foreign Relations series, at the close of the Moscow section.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d281:
The British Chiefs of Staff issued paper C.C.S. 404/1 at Cairo on 22 November 1943, answering the American agenda for the Sextant Conference. Signed by Brooke, Portal, and Cunningham, it raises no objection to the American subjects but proposes a simpler order of business.

Five main heads are listed: reaffirming the overall objective and basic undertakings, Southeast Asia operations, Overlord and the Mediterranean, the war against Japan, and progress reports. Southeast Asia is put second, so Chiang Kai-shek and Mountbatten can join the talks at the earliest stage. Detailed points from the American list would be fitted in from day to day, and progress reports left to the end, once the big items were settled.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d381:
A secret report from the Office of Strategic Services gives an account of a visit to Tito's National Army of Liberation in Yugoslavia. It was written at Bari in Italy on 29 October 1943. Its author spent six weeks in the field with the Partisans, from mid-September to late October.

His conclusions run against outside assumptions. The Partisan movement, he writes, is of far greater weight than the world realizes. By their own efforts, ringed by Germans, Italians, Ustasha, and Chetniks, the Partisans have built a free community. In it, Muslims, Christians, Serbs, Croats, Slovenes, and Communists may all speak on how it should be run. The Communist Party failed to organize the movement on party lines and threw every force against the common enemy, though its members work hard to shape the new state's future. Villagers with kin in America greeted the mission with embarrassing faith in American aid.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d481:
On December 5, 1943, in the middle of the Second Cairo Conference, Assistant Secretary of War John J. McCloy again wrote to Harry Hopkins, President Roosevelt's special assistant. McCloy had written to Hopkins the day before as well. The State Department printed this second message in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Repeated staff-level messages during a summit usually track problems being worked in real time: questions from the conference floor sent home, answers and material sent back. The McCloy-Hopkins channel was one of the busiest in wartime Washington. Read together, their December messages show the staff machinery that kept the President supplied while he negotiated abroad.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d81: A second Churchill message to Roosevelt dated October 31, 1943 is Document 81 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The prime minister's two notes that day closed out the October correspondence in this series. What divided their business, the record does not say, and a summary should not guess. Both letters are printed in the Foreign Relations volume, at the point where the story turns toward the President's journey east.
frus-1944-quebec-d181:
No participant's official memorandum survives for the dinner meeting of September 13, 1944, so the editors assemble accounts from Leahy's diary, Lord Moran's diary, and later recollections. Shipping was the announced subject, but Moran records that how to prevent another war with Germany was the only subject of conversation all evening. The Americans argued for drastic action against German industry.

Morgenthau wanted the Ruhr closed down, which would help British exports, especially steel. Churchill resisted: "I agree with Burke. You cannot indict a whole nation." He favored disarmament, but insisted Germany be allowed to live decently. Punishment should be swift: "Kill the criminals, but don't carry on the business for years." Cherwell sided with the Americans. Morgenthau later recalled Churchill calling the plan chaining England to a dead body.
frus-1944-quebec-d281:
Roosevelt's message to Chiang Kai-shek of September 16, 1944, is one of the bluntest in the volume. After reading the latest reports from China, he wrote, his chiefs and he were convinced Chiang faced the disaster long feared. The Y Force troops across the Salween had fought with great courage, but unless reinforced and supported with every capacity, their sacrifices would be valueless.

Withdrawal, Roosevelt warned, was exactly what the Japanese were striving to cause. If Chiang failed to man his divisions, the land line to China would never open and the Hump air route would be jeopardized. For that, Chiang must accept the consequences and assume personal responsibility. Stilwell, he noted, still had not been given command of all forces in China.
frus-1944-quebec-d81: Under the number 81, the Quebec 1944 volume prints a short editorial note. Its historians added such notes wherever the paper record needed help. A note may supply context, name a figure, or flag another document. The surrounding papers were prepared for the September 1944 conference. At Quebec, the American and British leaders took up Germany's future and the Pacific war. Treat this note as the editors pausing to orient the reader.
frus-1945-50-intel-d181:
"National Intelligence Authority Directive No. 7" bears the date 2 January 1947. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 181 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. The first peace-time setup paired the National Intelligence Authority at the top with the Central Intelligence Group below it.

A numbered directive joined a growing shelf of rules that told the new agencies how to run themselves. Directives set who may do what, what must be reported, and which office has the final say. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d281:
Dated 2 June 1948, this memorandum runs from the Executive Secretary (Souers) to the National Security Council. It is document 281 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. The CIA was in its first year, and the Council was taking up covert action for the first time.

The memo form let a staff officer speak straight to a chief: here is the point, here are the facts, here is what is asked. The points are stated once and left to stand; the file around it holds the answer they drew. Alone it is a page; in sequence it is evidence of how a state taught itself a new trade.
frus-1945-50-intel-d381:
A memorandum dated 15 April 1949 links two senior offices. The sender was the Assistant Director for Policy Coordination, Central Intelligence Agency (Wisner). The reader was the Counselor of the Department of State (Bohlen). It stands as document 381 in the intelligence volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, covering 1945 to 1950. By then the Dulles Report was months old, and the argument had moved to putting its advice into practice.

The form is plain on purpose: a named sender, a named reader, and a short statement of the matter at hand. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d81:
Russell, assistant secretary for administration, wrote to Secretary Byrnes on 3 November 1945. Russell's papers in the volume track the money and staffing of the State intelligence office. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

By November the office's first glow had met the house reality: budgets are finite, and other bureaus wanted their share. An administration chief writing to the secretary about the new service marks the moment support had to be argued, not assumed. Readers can watch the mood change across Russell's papers from autumn into winter. The office that arrived in September as a prize was, by year's end, a cost to be justified like any other.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d181:
Italy's cabinet crisis, and a British veto delivered inside it, fill this excerpt from the Secretary of State's briefing of 1 December 1944. The memorandum for the President is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. Ambassador Kirk's reports from Rome supply the news.

Kirk has told Premier Bonomi of Washington's concern over the long crisis. The United States will not judge the make-up of a new Italian government, but it must honor Italy's past pledges to the allies. The British ambassador, by contrast, told Bonomi flatly that Count Sforza as foreign minister would be unacceptable. Kirk calls that undue meddling in Italian home affairs. Winant has been told to voice American regret in London, since the move angered the Italian left and drew sharp comment in the American press.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d281:
Ships for soldiers or ships for hungry civilians? McCloy's excerpt of 23 January 1945 states the armed services' hard answer. His memorandum to the Secretary of State, on the shipping situation and the Law Mission, is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume.

Hopkins and Justice Byrnes, both bound for the conference, know the Law Mission's story well. Law stated the need for a civilian rebuilding program for Europe, France and Belgium above all, most forcibly; Monnet followed with another appeal. The danger is real, McCloy grants: a great mass of unemployed people, hungry and ill-clothed, threatens politics and even the military position. But while ships are critically needed for operations the heads of state have approved, none may be diverted to separate national import programs.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d381:
Oil and shipping fill the Joint Chiefs' session at Yalta on February 8, 1945, recorded in these minutes. The chiefs first took up levels of supply of petroleum products in all theaters. Then came an overall review of cargo and troop shipping for the rest of 1945. Admiral Leahy noted the report was agreed by the shipping boards.

Leahy observed, dryly, that its essence was an agreement to study the question again when need arose. General Somervell answered that the need had already arisen. Redeployment plans, above all, had outrun the paper. The minutes show the alliance's scarcest asset — hulls — being argued over to the last conference week.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d481:
All three powers have now approved the basic texts for Germany, Ambassador Winant cabled from London on February 6, 1945. The Soviet acting member of the European Advisory Commission had told him that Moscow approved the protocol on zones of occupation. It also approved the agreement on control machinery.

With that word, the three founding texts stood approved without reserve. They were the instrument of unconditional surrender, the zones protocol, and the control machinery agreement. Winant's short cable closes talks that had run in London for over a year. Yalta could build on settled paper; the rulebook for ruling Germany existed before the leaders met.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d81:
Soviet staff kept phoning the American Embassy with questions, Harriman reported on 19 December 1944. His secret cable from Moscow is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It shows the Foreign Office staff puzzling over the sense of Roosevelt's plan for voting in the new world body.

A Soviet aide named Bereshkov had called an embassy secretary more than once. He even asked if some error in the wires had crept into the text. His puzzle was one part of the plan, on settling local disputes through groups of nearby states. Harriman says the embassy staff gave their reading of it. He asks Washington at once: must Moscow accept that part now, or can it wait?
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d181:
Joseph Davies, the former ambassador to Moscow, sent Truman his own tour of the coming agenda in a letter dated July 3, 1945. The letter and its enclosure form document 181 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Davies had spoken with the President that morning and followed up in writing.

The enclosed memorandum sorts the conference business into new matters and unfinished old business from Yalta. Of the eight Yalta agreements, Davies judges that only the joint administration of occupied Germany will need settling at the top political level. Reparations disputes from the Moscow commission may also reach Berlin in principle. The letter itself is warm and personal: Davies tells Truman he stands on the verge of great decisions, and that his high purpose will surely be crowned with success.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d281:
James Riddleberger, chief of the Central European Affairs division, briefed the Secretary on the Austrian zones in a memorandum dated July 4, 1945. The memo is document 281 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. The zones had been under negotiation in the European Advisory Commission for eight months.

The tentative plan gives Salzburg and Upper Austria south of the Danube to the United States. It gives Carinthia and Styria to Britain. It gives Upper Austria north of the Danube, Lower Austria, and Burgenland to Russia. And it gives the Tirol and Vorarlberg to France. The main block is airfields near Vienna, which lies inside the Soviet zone though the city is to be held jointly. A telegram going out that day lets Winant accept the Soviet offer of two fields, Tulln and Schwechat, if the United States gets Tulln.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d381:
Control of German assets abroad is urged in a briefing book paper dated July 4, 1945. The United States had lately approached Britain, France, and the Soviet Union with a proposal. The Allied Control Council, as Germany's government, should declare all German external assets, private as well as public, subject to its control.

German official property, including Reich-owned corporations, would at once be taken over by the occupying powers' missions in neutral countries. An emergency in Spain prompted the haste: Madrid might seize, or buy too cheaply, property of a German government corporation. The paper's deeper aim was economic security against German spearhead firms overseas.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d481:
Churchill's Italian anxieties are relayed in Kirk's top secret cable from Caserta of July 12, 1945. Field Marshal Alexander, back from London the night before, reported three conferences with the Prime Minister. Churchill had shown keen interest in the situation in Italy. He promised he would not fail to impress on the President the importance of an active policy toward Italy.

Churchill pointed out a danger. A people in the Fascist camp for over twenty years, he said, might slide almost overnight into the Red camp. That could happen if the allies were not careful. He shared Alexander's concern at the rapid withdrawal of American troops from Italy and Europe, and said the matter would be discussed with Truman.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d581:
Foreign Minister Togo sent a second secret cable to Ambassador Sato in Moscow on July 11, 1945. Sent at 7 p.m. from Tokyo, it is document 581 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It tells Sato what line to give the Soviet leaders.

Togo says Tokyo has decided to state its stance on ending the war more plainly. Sato is to tell Moscow that keeping peace in Asia is one part of keeping world peace. Japan, he is to say, has no wish to annex or hold the lands it took in the war. Japan hopes to end the war so that a lasting world peace can be built. Sato must meet Molotov within a day or two and report back by wire at once.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d681:
A revised briefing paper on the Montreux Convention, dated June 30, 1945, supersedes the June 27 version. It is document 681 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Much of the text carries over, but the statement of U.S. interests is recast.

The paper repeats the history in brief. Moscow voiced discontent at Yalta but withheld its wishes, which were to go to a foreign ministers' meeting. Washington has told London it will discuss the Straits at the coming summit. The United States, though not a signatory, has been drawn fully into the picture by Britain and Russia. Turkey has not been consulted, though it would welcome U.S. interest in the Straits' future. The revised text puts one U.S. interest first: to keep the Dardanelles from becoming an area of international dispute.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d81:
General Jacob Devers, commanding the Sixth Army Group, warned General Marshall on June 20, 1945, that the Berlin survey party was still blocked. His telegram from Frankfurt is document 81 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Every attempt to get Soviet permission for General Parks to enter Berlin had failed.

Antonov in Moscow would not agree to Parks entering before June 28 or 29, Devers reports. He judges it highly unlikely that proper arrangements for the conference could be finished by the scheduled date if work starts that late. He recommends that Washington take the matter up through government channels to win the needed Russian permission. The cable pushed the quarrel over access up to the political level.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1081:
Secretary of State James Byrnes cabled the Acting Secretary of State from Babelsberg on July 28, 1945. The subject is Yugoslavia's protest notes over disturbances on the Greek-Yugoslav frontier. Byrnes agrees the charges are best settled by investigation on the spot. He does not want a special mission sent into the area, though.

Instead, the proposed American reply should offer a commission built from staff already in place. Military and political officers would be drawn from the American, British, and Soviet missions in Belgrade, and the American and British missions in Athens. Moscow would need to name a special group to work with the Athens team. With that change, Byrnes approves quick action.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1181:
President Truman wrote to Prime Minister Churchill on 17 July 1945, the opening day of the Potsdam Conference. The two leaders began the summit already in direct touch, leader to leader. Their exchange set the tone for the British-American side of the talks.

Truman was new to the world stage; Churchill had led Britain through the whole war. Their letters show the younger partnership at work on its first day. A message of this kind could align stands before a session or settle a point after one. This one marks the summit's first day in the principals' own words.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1281:
Admiral King, commander in chief of the United States Fleet and chief of naval operations, wrote to the Navy Department on 26 July 1945. King ran the navy through the whole war. His word to his own department came from the summit's naval side.

The navy's concerns at Potsdam ran from fleets in the Pacific to the ports and coasts of the new Europe. King's message carried his direction home while he served with the team abroad. It shows the sea service's chief running his house by cable, in the same week Britain changed leaders and Japan got its terms.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1381:
The Combined Chiefs of Staff, the joint British and American military body, addressed President Truman and Prime Minister Churchill together on 24 July 1945. The chiefs advised both governments on the conduct of the war. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

A paper from the Combined Chiefs speaks for the whole Anglo-American war machine. Sent while Churchill still held office, it reached both heads of government at Potsdam at once. Readers should note the weight of the channel: when the chiefs wrote jointly, they settled service disputes before the leaders ever saw them. This message shows the military side of the alliance reporting to its political chiefs in mid-summit.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-81:
Allen, the deputy director of the State Department office for Near Eastern and African affairs, wrote this internal memorandum on July 24, 1945. It was prepared while the Potsdam Conference was in session near Berlin. The paper went into the delegation's working files. It was later printed in the second Potsdam volume of the official series.

Papers of this kind gave senior officials a desk officer's facts and advice in short form. Allen's office tracked a region outside the Big Three's main talks on Germany. Still, its concerns touched the wider war and the peace to come. The memo shows how staff far from the head table fed views into the talks.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d781:
On July 25, 1945, Kirk reported from Rome in document 781. The ambassador in Italy wrote to the Acting Secretary in the conference's second week. His reports form a steady thread in the second Potsdam volume. Rome watched Potsdam for signs of its own fate.

A mid-conference report from Italy shows a capital reading the summit's smoke. Kirk had to guess where the talks pointed and advise at home. Readers share that uncertain vantage. The document also shows an embassy's duty to report mood as well as fact. In July 1945, mood in Rome was a fact of its own kind.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d881:
Edwin Pauley, the American representative on the Allied Commission on Reparations, wrote to the Secretary of State from Berlin on July 28, 1945. He encloses a letter from Sir David Waley of the British delegation to Soviet official Ivan Maisky. Waley's letter accepts the American reparations plan with two small changes.

The changes clarify that paying for needed imports ranks as a first charge, and they add the needs of the occupying forces. An attached note defines those needs in detail. Food, fuel, and medical stores for the armies count as German imports. Weapons, vehicles, and soldiers' pay do not.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d981: Emilio Collado sent this brief secret telegram from Babelsberg to Covey Oliver in Washington on July 16, 1945. Collado directed the Office of Financial and Development Policy. His whole request fits in one line. He asks Oliver to bring the delegation up to date on progress in controlling German external assets. Spain is named as a special concern. Collado cites the Department's July 6 telegram to London and Oliver's own memorandum of July 7 as the last word they hold.
frus-1961-63v03-d281: A 1961-1963 FRUS telegram from the Vietnam volume, January to August 1963. Saigon's crisis deepened. This document preserves that cable. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
frus-1977-80v08-d281: A 1977-1980 FRUS document from the Arab-Israeli dispute volume. The Middle East peacemaking. This entry preserves that record. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
gao-gaoreports-b-295781: Ben-Mar Enterprises cried foul on an April 2005 award, and GAO's ruling is the answer. The company's protest got the full vetting, claim by claim. Losers deserve a fair referee, and the gavel fell squarely. The verdict was final. The answer stood.
gao-gaoreports-b-298481: Murray-Benjamin Electric Company took its September 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Electric deals get the same full hearing as all.
gao-gaoreports-b-298881: Spacesaver Storage Systems took its December 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Storage deals get the same full hearing as all.
gao-gaoreports-b-299381: LexisNexis took its April 2007 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict. The legal-research giant said the agency's award was unfair; the call tests the protest. Even the keepers of the law books must argue their case by the book.
gao-gaoreports-b-299781: Healthcare Technology Solutions International took its July 2007 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict. The firm said the agency's health-tech award was unfair; the call tests the claims. Medical IT deals get the same fair-bid scrutiny as any federal buy.
gao-gaoreports-b-299981: A 2007 GAO ruling on two linked contract fights from Navarro Research and Engineering, Inc. The tech firm said the agency's award was off; the ruling weighs each claim and calls it. For engineering shops in the federal market, the published call shows how GAO grades a bid when the work is brains, not bricks.
gao-gaoreports-b-307681: The scope of waiver authority got a legal ruling in this May 2006 GAO call, which interprets the statute's reach. The decision reads the law. The ruling draws the line on who could waive what. The law had the final word.
gao-gaoreports-b-309181: Spy-agency deal paperwork drew GAO's fiscal eye in 2007 — could the counterintelligence office legally use an interagency pact this way? The ruling reads the money statutes against the agreement line by line. Even the shadow world, GAO reminds, spends by the book and answers for its deals.
gao-gaoreports-b-310081: One of GAO's biggest consolidated bid-protest rulings of 2007, joining nine docket numbers filed by timber companies — Poston Logging, Shasta Green, Sierra Cedar, Trinity River, and others. The challengers contested Forest Service timber-sale decisions under shared legal questions. The decision walks through each protest, applies procurement and timber-sale law, and shows how GAO handles mass filings from a whole industry at once.
gao-gaoreports-b-310981: This 2008 GAO ruling is about gift Cards for Respondents to the Converter Box Coupon Program Survey at National Telecommunications and Information Administration. GAO's legal decisions tell agencies what federal funding law allows. Agencies follow these rulings when spending federal funds.
gao-gaoreports-b-316381: This 2008 GAO ruling is about mass Transit Benefits, Aberdeen Proving Ground at Army. GAO's legal decisions tell agencies what federal funding law allows. Agencies follow these rulings when spending federal funds. It is kept here as part of the lasting public record.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-281: The FDIC's 2004 and 2003 books got a GAO audit in 2005, and the report examines the funds' financial statements. The review grades the ledgers. The deposit insurer's money was checked. The statements had to hold up. The deposit insurer's money was checked.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-381: Billions were flowing into Pentagon business software with weak watch in 2005, and GAO's report says the modernization lacked adequate oversight.
