The review flags the money trail. The taxpayers' billions deserved eyes on them. The oversight had to tighten. The taxpayers' billions deserved eyes on them.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-681: Foreign-tied defense firms got a GAO glare in 2005, and the report says the Pentagon's watch over them fell short. The findings demand the vigilance. The report warns that the secrets deserved guarding. The secrets deserved guarding. The watch had to tighten.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-781: Flight crew security training was strengthened in 2005, and GAO's report says the training improved, though better planning was needed. The findings balance credit and need. The report warns that the cabin crews deserved good preparation. The planning had to improve.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-881: Federal money systems kept flunking the bar in 2005, and GAO's report says the compliance goal stayed hard. The findings take the measure. The report warns that the agencies' books deserved modern standards. The agencies' books deserved modern standards. The bar had to be met.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1081: Insuring against terror attacks was a guessing game in 2006, and GAO's report says measuring losses from unconventional weapons was hard, though industry experts weighed in. The findings map the uncertainty. The report warns that the unthinkable needed a price tag. The policies had to be priced.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-381: Political hiring conversions got a GAO count in 2006, and the report tracks employees moved from noncareer to career posts. The findings do the counting. The report warns that the burrowing deserved daylight. The conversions had to be transparent. The burrowing deserved daylight.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-781: Tribal land deals were stuck in red tape in 2006, and GAO's report says the BIA's time frames and better data should speed the processing. The findings press for the deadlines. The report warns that the Native landowners deserved faster answers. The processing had to improve.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-281: Spare parts were taking too long to buy in 2007, and GAO's report says the Pentagon could better manage its acquisition lead times. The findings target the delays. The report's logic: the war machine should not wait on its own supply chain.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-781: Nobody was steering the flu ship in 2007 — GAO's report says federal outbreak leadership stayed fuzzy and the national plan stayed thin. The findings demand named leaders and a real playbook before the big one hits. Another warning the nation would wish it had heeded sooner.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-881: Fish rules needed better math in 2007 — GAO's report says the fisheries service owed sharper economic analysis for its proposed changes. The findings press for numbers that hold up before nets get restricted. Conservation, the report argues, is strongest when its economics are honest.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-281: The Government Accountability Office dug into bank Fees: Federal Banking Regulators Could Better Ensure That Consumers Have Required Disclosure Documents Prior to Opening Checking or Savings Accounts in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
geikie-prehistoric-europe-1881:
James Geikie, a Scots rock scholar, wrote this sketch of the ice age and man's place in it in 1881. Its full theme is the rocks of Europe in the time before writ history. Geikie knew the signs of old ice work in the field at first hand.

He reads scraped rocks, stray blocks, and gravel beds to map how far the ice sheets spread. In that cold frame he sets the stone age folk, their tools, and their beasts. The book gave the men of the stone age a firm time scale for the first time.
gibbon-decline-fall-vol-2-1781:
Edward Gibbon published Volume 2 of his Decline and Fall in 1781. This volume moves from Constantine to Julian and the later 300s. Christianity triumphs as the state religion, and Gibbon tells the story with unmatched irony. Councils, heresies, and imperial courts crowd the pages.

Julian the Apostate, who tried to restore the old gods, receives a rich portrait. Gibbon also treats the rise of monastic life and the Goths pressing on the frontiers. His footnotes mix deep learning with dry wit. Readers prized the volume for both narrative and character sketches. The History was becoming the standard against which English histories were judged.
gibbon-decline-fall-vol-3-1781:
Edward Gibbon published Volume 3 of his Decline and Fall in 1781. This volume runs from Theodosius to the fall of the Western Empire in 476. Barbarian invasions, court intrigue, and religious strife fill the story. Attila and the Huns sweep across Europe in famous chapters.

The sack of Rome by Goths and Vandals marks the end of an age. Gibbon treats saints and emperors with the same cool, ironic eye. His account of the last Roman emperors is both sad and scornful. The volume closes the Western story while the East endures. Gibbon's grand design now spans a thousand years. Its scale still awes historians.
giorgio-ferrera-cabalistic-exposition-of: Giorgio Ferrera, Cabalistic Exposition of the Biscione, 1481. The serpent exposition. This book preserves that work. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Coming generations can find it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
green-making-of-england-1881:
Anglo-Saxon England takes shape in Green's The Making of England, from 1881. English settlers cross the sea and carve kingdoms from Roman Britain's ruins. Missionaries then bring the Christian faith, and Alfred the Great defends the land against Danish invasion.

Green taught Victorian readers where their country truly came from. He writes of plowmen and monks beside kings and war bands. Settlement, conversion, and learning form his triple theme throughout. The book's humane warmth set it apart from drier chronicles of the age. It remains a beloved account of England's birth, written for the people whose story it tells.
hallywell-melampronoea-1681:
Henry Hallywell was a Cambridge scholar and clergyman whose Melampronoea appeared in 1681. The Greek title names his subject: a discourse of the polity and kingdom of darkness. He wrote in reply to John Webster, who had doubted the reality of spirits.

Hallywell defends the reality of spirits against the mechanical philosophy then rising in the Royal Society's circle. If matter and motion explain all, he warns, then soul, providence, and moral rule dissolve with the ghosts. The book catches the moment when England's learned men fought over whether the unseen world existed at all. His fear was pastoral as much as learned: a world without spirits leaves souls unguarded.
hering-guiding-symptoms-vol5-1881:
Volume V of the Guiding Symptoms came out in 1881, printed after Hering's death from his stored notes. The series gathers proven signs for hundreds of remedies, and this middle volume keeps the alphabetical march going. Headings split every entry by region, organ, and function.

Small marks beside a symptom carry the real craft of the set. They tell the reader which signs showed up again and again, and which ones cured in practice. Without them the pages would be a flood; with them a working doctor could find a remedy's keynote fast, even mid-consultation.
holmes-common-law-1881:
Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr published The Common Law in 1881, from lectures given in Boston. Holmes, a Civil War veteran soon to be a judge, was not yet forty. The book made his name and began a long shift in American legal thought.

Holmes opened with his famous line: the life of the law has not been logic, it has been experience. He traced crime, torts, and contracts from old Germanic and Roman roots to modern rules, showing law shaped by policy and need. Judges, he argued, make law while claiming only to find it. The book is read as a founding text of American legal realism and of Holmes's own road to the Supreme Court.
jacquier-flagellum-haereticorum-latin-15:
Nicolas Jacquier, a Dominican inquisitor, wrote his Flagellum haereticorum fascinariorum, the Scourge of Heretical Witches, in 1458. This text comes from the edition of 1581, which kept his argument in circulation. Jacquier's target is the old Canon Episcopi, whose skepticism about night flights he sets out to demolish.

He insists that witches truly gather, body and soul, at their assemblies. That claim made the sabbath real for learned theology. Scholars call his book the pivot of fifteenth-century demonology. After Jacquier, doubt needed defending and belief needed only citing. The Latin scourge turned learned opinion toward the burning dogma that shaped the great hunts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lulab-10181:
Lulab, the palm branch waved at the Feast of Tabernacles, is explained in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. The lulab joins with the etrog, or citron, among the four species of the festival. It is made of a folded palm shoot at least three handbreadths long. Three myrtle twigs and two willow branches are tied to its lower end.

The article describes how the lulab was used in the Second Temple. Worshipers waved it during the Hallel psalms, facing east and shaking it in every direction. That act confessed God's rule over nature. Processions circled the altar once each day and seven times on the seventh day. After the Temple fell, Johanan ben Zakkai ordered the rite kept everywhere for seven days. The entry remains a clear period account of the festival custom and its rules.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mantua-10381:
Mantua, the fortified Italian city on the Mincio, receives a Jewish history in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. It held 1,100 Jews in 1901, down from a peak of 2,523 in 1858. The first mention of Jews there comes from the twelfth century. Abraham ibn Ezra finished a grammar work in Mantua in 1145.

The article follows a community favored and squeezed by turns. A special tax of 2,000 ducats in 1459 was beaten down to 600 by protest. Two famous rabbis, Joseph Colon and Messer Leon, feuded and were both expelled in 1475. The Jews won leave to lend at interest, yet the prince ordered them to attend anti-Jewish sermons in 1485. A Jewish badge followed in 1496. Under the dukes a Jewish physician served at court, and an Ashkenazic synagogue was slowly approved. The entry shows Italian Jewish life balanced between princely favor and preachers' pressure.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meir-of-rothenb:
Meir of Rothenburg was the leading rabbi of Germany in the thirteenth century. Solomon Schechter and Louis Ginzberg profile him at length in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Worms about 1215 and studied at Würzburg and in the great French schools under teachers such as Jehiel of Paris. Back in Germany he drew bands of devoted pupils, some of them married men who left their families to study with him. He served in Kostnitz, Augsburg, Würzburg, Worms, Nuremberg, and Mayence, and, longest, Rothenburg, and died in the fortress of Ensisheim on May 2, 1293.

The article weighs his authority carefully. Later historians called him chief rabbi of Germany, but the entry doubts the office existed. His titles, “Chief” and “Father of Rabbis,” mark the leadership men granted his learning. His rulings on communal taxation ordered the finances of German Jewry for generations.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mengs-anton-raf:
Anton Rafael Mengs was a Bohemian-born painter who directed Rome's new Academy. Isidore Singer and Frank Cramer profile him in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Son of the painter Ismael Israel Mengs, he was drilled by his strict father toward art he at first showed little taste for. His father took him to Rome in 1741, and at sixteen he was made court painter at Dresden. To marry Margareta Guazzi, the peasant model of his "Holy Family," he left the Jewish faith. He joined the Roman Catholic Church. From 1752 Rome was his base, Madrid later his patron's court. His "Hall of Fame" ceiling for Charles III is called his masterpiece.

The criticism is balanced: an eclectic blending of Raphael, Titian, and Correggio. It is exquisite in taste, correct in drawing, and true in color, wanting only the originality of genius. Yet the work is ranked among the foremost of his age.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-michael-heimann:
Heimann Joseph Michael, born at Hamburg on April 12, 1792, was a Hebrew bibliographer whose private library became a landmark of Jewish scholarship. Isidore Singer and Isidor Warsaw wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906. A boy with a phenomenal memory, he began collecting books at twelve and read nearly everything he owned.

By his death in 1846 the library held 860 manuscripts and 5,471 printed works across all branches of Hebrew literature, and his unfinished catalogue of it appeared at Hamburg in 1848. Michael published little himself, but scholars such as Zunz, Luzzatto, and Delitzsch wrote to him constantly for information he never withheld. His one independent work, Or ha-Ḥayyim, appeared long after his death, in 1891.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mississippi-108:
Mississippi's Jews enter history through the state's changes of flag, as Cyrus Adler and Wolf Willner record in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. La Salle claimed the territory for France in 1682, and French law of 1724 expelled Jews outright; Spain's takeover in 1781 brought tolerance. A tombstone at Natchez named Harris, dated 1828, hints at settlers earlier still.

Congregations formed about 1840, cemeteries usually coming first — the article shows why. In 1849 three Jewish peddlers reached Woodville and one, Henry Burgance, died; his companions, unwilling to bury him among Christians, set about securing Jewish ground. The pattern repeats across the state's river towns: burial before synagogue, permanence declared over the dead before the living.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-morawczyk-10981:
Morawczyk, a name meaning the Moravians, was a family of Polish scholars of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board entered them in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jehiel Michael Morawczyk died at Lublin in 1593. He translated the German Wiener Gezerah into Hebrew as Gezerat Oestreich. He printed it at Cracow in 1582.

His chief work was a commentary on Abot, the Ethics of the Fathers. He compiled it from Rashi, Bertinoro, Abravanel, and others. It was printed three times under the title Minḥah Ḥadashah. A generation later, Moses ben Aaron Morawczyk taught school at Bisenz and then at Lublin. He wrote two manuals. They told teacher and pupil exactly how the Mishnah and the service should be studied.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-motal-benjamin-:
Benjamin ben Abraham Motal, of Constantinople, was a Turkish scholar of the first half of the seventeenth century. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He was said to be an exceptional grammarian, but his own grammatical works are lost. He is known instead as an editor.

In 1622, at Venice, Motal published the Tummat Yesharim in four parts. It gathers the responsa of Jacob Tam ibn Yahya, glosses on Alfasi, and works by Abraham ben David, Elijah ha-Levi, and Samuel Sirillo. He added his own notes and corrections to the Sifra and to Abot de-Rabbi Natan, with a preface. The entry preserves the name of a careful maker of books.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nahman-b-samuel:
Nahman ben Samuel ha-Levi was a rabbi of Busk in Galicia who joined the Frankists. The Jewish Encyclopedia article, by its editorial committee and Schulim Ochser, is brief. He lived in the first part of the eighteenth century. The Frankist movement drew him away from the rabbinate he had held.

In 1759 the administrator of the Lemberg archbishopric staged a disputation between Jews and Frankists. Nahman sat on the Frankist side as one of their delegates. Afterward he accepted baptism and took the Christian name Piotr Jacobski. The short notice fixes one rabbi's path into the Frankist schism and out of Judaism.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-national-farm-s:
The National Farm School trained Jewish boys in farming. Cyrus Adler and Joseph Krauskopf wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It stood at Doylestown, in Bucks County, Pennsylvania. Krauskopf proposed it in 1894 after visiting Russia's Pale of Settlement. Lectures raised the funds to buy the site.

The main building rose in 1896, and school opened in 1897. Eight pupils formed the first class there. By 1904 the school held forty-five pupils and ten buildings. Its course ran four years, mixing class work with field work. Boys learned crops, soils, stock care, and dairy work. Tuition was free, and any fit American lad could apply.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-neustadt-schirw:
Neustadt-Schirwindt was a district town of Russian Poland. Herman Rosenthal and A. Hyman Charlap wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Ladislaus IV built it in 1643. Its Polish name, Wladyslavow, honors that king. Under Prussian rule it bore the name Neustadt.

A well-ordered Jewish community stood there by 1740. Abba Dayyan served then as its first known rabbi. His line produced the Abelson and Bernstein families. His son Isaac claimed a prize for a stone house. Later rabbis include Nathan Stern, the iron head. Scholars of note filled the town from 1815 to 1850. Grammar, Talmud, and mathematics all found writers there. Of 4,000 people, over 3,000 were Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-noldeke-theodor:
Theodor Nöldeke was a German scholar of the East. Crawford Howell Toy and Joseph Jacobs wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Harburg on March 2, 1836. He studied at Göttingen, Vienna, Leyden, and Berlin. Göttingen made him assistant professor in 1864.

Kiel gave him a full chair four years later. Strasburg called him at its founding in 1872. He held that chair for the rest of his career. His fields were Persian, Arabic, and Syriac above all. Bible study also drew much of his labor. His book on Amalek appeared in 1864. Three grammars of Syriac tongues followed in time. His survey of the Semitic languages became a classic.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-orshanski-ilya-:
Ilya Grigoryevich Orshanski was a Russian jurist and author. Herman Rosenthal wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Yekaterinoslav in the year 1846. He died there on September 5, in 1875. His kin line held many famed rabbis and town workers.

At the age of four, Ilya entered the heder school. At ten he was well read in Hebrew works of thought. He read the Talmud with an uncle as his guide. He taught himself Russian and other tongues as he grew. At fifteen he read the hard tracts of the Cabala. In 1863 he went to Kharkov to read law. That year he wrote his first work of note. It treated tales of Alexander the Great in the Talmud.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pamplona-11881:
Pamplona is the chief and oldest town of Navarra, Spain. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Next to Tudela, it held the chief Jewish group there. The Jewry lay in the Navarreria, the oldest part of town. Hard years came when Navarra passed to Philip the Fair.

The folk of Pamplona would not bow to that king at first. French troops wrecked the Jewry in the fight of 1277. Houses were sacked and many Jews were slain then. In 1280 the town had to give back seized goods. It had to give new ground for homes to the Jews. A plan to rebuild the Jewry was set in 1319. The work was not in fact done till 1336. The new Jewry stood walled by the Magdalena bridge.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pedro-ii-pedro-:
Pedro the Second was emperor of Brazil for half a century. He was born in 1825 and died at Paris in 1891. Gotthard Deutsch and Meyer Kayserling wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He took full power in 1840 and lost his throne in 1889.

Pedro was a humane ruler and a serious scholar. He gave much of his spare time to Hebrew study. Shortly before his death he printed a small book. It held three Hebrew Provençal poems from the Jewish rite. He translated them into French with notes. He added his own version of Had Gadya too.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pfefferkorn-joh:
Johann Pfefferkorn was a German convert who attacked Jewish books. He was born in 1469 and died after 1521. Gotthard Deutsch and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Cologne's Dominicans took him up as their tool.

Pfefferkorn had been a butcher jailed for burglary. After baptism in 1505 he wrote pamphlet after pamphlet. The Judenspiegel led the pack in 1507. He won edicts from Emperor Maximilian in 1509. They ordered Jewish books seized and destroyed. Frankfurt's Jews surrendered their books the next spring. His campaign soon met Reuchlin's famous defense.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-piperno-settimi: Settimio Piperno was an Italian economist of Rome. Isidore Singer and Umberto Cassuto wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Rome in 1834. He taught statistics and economics at its Technical Institute. He also directed the Cesi Technical School there. He sat on the board of Rome's Jewish community. His books treat mutual aid societies and old-age pensions. One studies the new school of Italian penal law.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-poppers-meir-be:
Meïr Poppers was a Bohemian rabbi and student of Cabala, born at Prague. Kaufmann Kohler and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He learned Cabala under Israel Ashkenazi and Jacob Zemah. All his many books follow the teaching of Isaac Luria. He died at Jerusalem in 1662.

Thirty-nine of his books start with the word Or, meaning light. The word plays on his own name, Meïr. His Or Zaddikim sets out a mystic way of strict living. It rests on Luria, the Zohar, and other moral works. The book came out at Hamburg in 1690. A larger form came out later as Or ha-Yashar. His books shaped later readers of Luria's school.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rabbah-b-liwai-: Rabbah bar Liwai was a Babylonian teacher of the fourth set of amoraim. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived at the same time as Raba ben Joseph. Twice he showed that a ruling of Raba was wrong. Both times the ruling had to be wiped out. One saying of his has come down in the Talmud. Raba was stung by his sharp proof in public.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-raschkow-susski: Süsskind Raschkow was a German poet who died at Breslau. Herman Rosenthal and Isidor Warsaw wrote this short Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He died there on April 12, 1836. His works were Yosef we-Asenat, a drama from 1817, Hayye Shimshon, an epic poem from 1824, and Tal Yaldut, poems and proverbs from 1835.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rephaim-vale-of:
The Vale of Rephaim is a fertile plain in Judah. Emil G. Hirsch and Immanuel Benzinger wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. David fought his battles with the Philistines there. Isaiah also names the plain in his book.

The article places the vale near Bethlehem. The border of Judah and Benjamin crossed its northern end. It lay west or southwest of Jerusalem, they argue. Eusebius wrongly placed it north of the city. Josephus placed it between Jerusalem and Bethlehem instead. Since the 1500s scholars identify it with the plain Al-Bakah. That plain lies southwest of Jerusalem today. A German colony named Rephaim now settles there. The entry fixes a Bible battlefield on the modern map.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rivkin-miron-da:
Miron Davidovich Rivkin was a Russian writer born in Vitebsk in 1869. Herman Rosenthal and J. G. Lipman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. His father, a police department clerk, was a skilled Talmudist. Rivkin studied first in a heder.

The article traces his move through government Jewish schools. He entered the Teachers' Institute in Wilna in 1884. He graduated in 1889 and taught at Volozhin. Later posts took him to Molodejno and Minsk. In 1897 he joined Jewish schools in St. Petersburg. His first poems and plays date from student days. One poem treats Dorothea Mendelssohn, another John Hyrcanus. Sketches on the Volozhin yeshivah appeared in 1895. A collection of his sketches came out in 1900.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosenzweig-adol:
Adolf Rosenzweig was a German rabbi born at Turdossin, Hungary, on October 20, 1850. Isidore Singer wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia, working alone. He studied at Budapest and Presburg, then at Berlin's university and Hochschule.

Rosenzweig entered the rabbinate at Pasewalk on his twenty-fourth birthday, in 1874. He moved to Birnbaum, then to Teplitz in 1879, and reached Berlin in 1887. His books open with a guide to the books of Ezra and Nehemiah. Later works treat Josephus, Jerusalem and Caesarea, and the eye in Bible and Talmud. A last volume covers clothing and adornment in those same sources.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sackcloth-hebre:
Sackcloth, in Hebrew sak, is a coarse cloth usually woven of goat's hair. Joseph Jacobs and Wilhelm Nowack wrote the entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. The word came to name a garment worn by Israelites in mourning.

Such a garment also signaled submission, and prophets sometimes wore it. The Old Testament never describes its shape exactly, so scholars have guessed. Kamphausen pictured a corn-bag form, with openings for head and arms. Grüneisen saw the hairy mantle still used by the Bedouins. Schwally argued it began as a simple loin-cloth fastened round the hips.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schlesinger-wil:
Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Wilhelm S. Schlesinger. He was an Austrian physician. Schlesinger was born at Tinnye, in Hungary, in 1839. He studied at the University of Vienna. He took his medical degree there in 1864. He then set up practice in the Austrian capital.

In 1874 Vienna granted Schlesinger the right to lecture in gynecology. In 1878 he founded the Wiener Medizinische Blätter. He wrote many essays for that journal. His own studies treat the movements of the uterus. They also cover reflex motions and the nerve centers involved. Other works deal with blood tumors of the female pelvis. He also wrote on the structure of the female pelvis. The entry rests on Hirsch's biographical lexicon.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-seegen-josef-13:
Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Josef Seegen. He was an Austrian balneologist, a doctor of healing waters. Seegen was born at Polna on May 20, 1822. He studied medicine at Prague and Vienna. He took his degree in 1847. He became a privat-docent at Vienna in 1854 and assistant professor in 1859.

From 1854 to 1884 Seegen practiced each summer at Carlsbad. In 1856 he co-founded a society for the study of springs in Austria. His Compendium of healing springs appeared in 1857. A second edition followed in 1862. His later books treat diabetes mellitus. Others study how the animal body builds sugar and burns fuel. Pagel's lexicon of physicians supplies his record.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shin-13581:
Shin is the twenty-first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, the entry explains. Crawford Howell Toy and Isaac Broydé wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia piece on the letter. Its name seems tied to shen, the word for tooth. One sign carries two distinct sounds in Hebrew speech.

A dot on the right horn gives the sound sh. A dot on the left gives a plain s sound, called sin. How sin differed from samek stays unclear, scholars admit. Shin rarely serves as a building block in word forms. In later use it worked as a numeral too. There it stood for the number three hundred. Short as it is, the entry packs sound, sign, and number into one letter.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simeon-ben-gama:
Simeon ben Gamaliel the Second was a tanna of the third generation and Sanhedrin president. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. As a youth at Bethar he survived the Bar Kokba war. When Romans took that fortress, he escaped the massacre.

At Usha the restored college elected Simeon its president. He owed the honor to Hillel's house and his own worth. Half his many children learned Torah, half Greek philosophy. Simeon himself seems trained in Greek thought as well. He later ruled Scripture could be written only in Hebrew or Greek. His sayings also show knowledge of plants and animals. Natural science sat beside law in his learning. The entry portrays a leader rebuilding Jewish life after catastrophe.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solomon-ben-mos:
Solomon ben Moses ben Jekuthiel de Rossi was a writer and hymn composer. Wilhelm Bacher and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He flourished in Rome during the thirteenth century. He died after 1284, in the prime of life. He was the earliest literary member of the Rossi family.

His wife was Paola Anaw, a highly gifted woman. Solomon wrote a work of defense known by four titles. In its preface he warns against religious disputations as harmful. If forced to debate, he says, stay calm and only defend. The work protests Christian attacks on the Jewish view of the Messiah. He also wrote songs and a poem on an earthquake at Ancona.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-stade-13981:
Stade was a city in the province of Hanover, Prussia. Gotthard Deutsch and Abraham Lewinsky wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Its Jews are first mentioned in a charter from 1349. In 1613 they received a patent of protection from the archbishop. Their court Jew, Solomon Herscheider, was a physician living there.

Solomon later served as purveyor of silver for the mint. In 1620 he was jailed, apparently for embezzlement of funds. The Jewish cemetery at Stade became a garden in 1632. Protection taxes paid by Jews fell over the years that followed. A great fire in 1712 destroyed the Jewish street entirely. By 1905 only twenty-six Jews lived among 10,000 people.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-szold-henrietta:
Henrietta Szold was an American Jewish editor born at Baltimore. Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about her in 1906. She was the eldest daughter of Rabbi Benjamin Szold. Her work centered on the Jewish Publication Society of America. Since 1893 she served as its literary committee secretary.

Szold translated Darmesteter's work on the Talmud into English. It appeared at Philadelphia in 1897. She also translated Lazarus on the ethics of Judaism. That volume came out in 1900. With Cyrus Adler she edited the American Jewish Year Book. She wrote many articles for Jewish periodicals as well. For years she attended classes at New York's Jewish seminary. The entry catches a young editor early in a long career.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tedeschi-moses-:
Moses Isaac Tedeschi was an Italian Bible commentator born in 1821. Isidore Singer and Moses Beer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He was born at Triest on June 6. He lectured on Bible in his city's Talmud Torah. He died there on June 17, 1898.

Tedeschi's great work Ho'il Mosheh comments across the Bible. It covers the Earlier Prophets, Job, and Psalms. The Five Scrolls and Proverbs come in one volume. The Pentateuch and Minor Prophets followed in turn. Daniel, Ezra, Nehemiah, and Chronicles closed the set. He wrote ethical sermons drawn from Pirke Abot. A book on Hebrew synonyms appeared in 1879. He translated Mussafia's prose poem into Italian. His last work appends his own life story. The entry maps one teacher's shelf of commentary.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-throne-14381:
Throne carries two meanings in the Bible, and both are traced here. Joseph Jacobs and Judah David Eisenstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. A king sat on the throne of his kingdom. The throne named his power and his court of judgment.

Solomon's throne was the most splendid of all. Pharaoh told Joseph that only in the throne would he rank higher. Beyond earthly seats stands the Throne of Glory. From it God shows His majesty to all heaven. Micaiah and Isaiah saw that throne in visions. Its color matches the sapphire blue of the sky. Tradition says righteous souls rest hidden beneath it. Jacob's likeness was even engraved upon it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-transylvania-hu:
Transylvania, part of Hungary since 1867, had Jews since Roman Dacia days. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Traditions trace its first Jews to Persia or to King Decebalus. Firm records begin far later, in 1578. A decree then confined Jewish trade to set towns.

Gyulafehérvár became the one recognized Jewish residence. Turkish trade passed through Jewish hands at that frontier town. Gabriel Bethlen granted broad rights in 1623. Jews could settle in fortified cities and worship freely. Later rulers cut those rights back with badges and bans. The rules were never fully enforced, though. One official congregation, with a court by 1591, anchored the region.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-unger-joachim-j:
Joachim Jacob Unger was an Austrian rabbi who served Iglau, Moravia, from 1860. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Born at Homona, Hungary, in 1826, he took his doctorate at Berlin. His degree came in 1859, a year before Iglau called him.

His writings mix scholarship, sermons, and public questions. One essay treats Hebrew philology and Bible exegesis. Another studies Phoenician offering tablets from Marseille and Carthage. In 1874 he addressed the Jewish question in Prussia. Patriotic occasional sermons appeared in 1881 and again later. A volume of his poems came out in 1885. Festival and Sabbath sermons reached print in 1903. The entry shows a modern rabbi's wide range.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-verona-14681:
Verona is the chief city of its Italian province. Isidore Singer and Umberto Cassuto wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews lived there as early as the tenth century. An archbishop treated them harshly, and they were later expelled. Until 1408 they had no firm right to live in the city.

In 1408 Venice's rule brought a change. Jews gained leave to reside and to lend money. All other trades were barred to them. They lived in the San Sebastiano quarter and built a synagogue. Rules forced them to wear a yellow badge. In 1499 the council voted to banish them entirely. The entry follows these swings over five centuries.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-warrens-rosa-14:
Rosa Warrens was a Swedish poet and translator. She was born at Karlskrona on February 24, 1821. Isidore Singer and Regina Neisser wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. She died at Copenhagen on November 8, 1878. At age five she moved with her parents to Hamburg. She stayed there until her father's death in 1861.

Warrens devoted herself to Swedish literature and Norse myth. She translated northern folk songs into German. She kept their original meters in her versions. Her books cover Swedish, Danish, and Scottish songs. Later volumes add Norwegian, Icelandic, and Finnish ones. A book of her own poems appeared in 1873.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-we-ye-etayu-148:
We Ye'etayu is a hymn for the holiest days of the year. Isidore Singer and Francis L. Cohen wrote this short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Eleazar Kalir composed the piyyut long ago. The cantor chants it during the Musaf service. Northern rite congregations sing it on New Year and Atonement days.

Many German congregations leave the hymn out. Its one known traditional tune dates to the seventeen hundreds. The entry calls that tune weaker than its peers. Still, custom holds it firmly in place. Congregations prize its quaint sound at the season. The short note records text, author, and melody together.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wolf-max-14981:
Max Wolf (1840-1886) was an Austrian composer of light operas and stage songs. Isidore Singer and Newell Dunbar wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in Moravia, he came from a rich trade family. His father wished him to go into business. The boy showed a strong gift for music from the first.

He began to study how to write music at sixteen. He trained with teachers in Berlin and Vienna. A tale says a top general heard his work in Berlin. The general asked him for a march to put fire in the troops. His first stage works copied the style of Offenbach. Later works found a voice of their own. They played in Berlin, Vienna, and Gratz to good crowds.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yeshu-ah-jeshua:
Yeshuah ben Joseph ha-Levi was an Algerian Talmud scholar of the 1400s. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Tlemcen in the north of Africa. In 1467 Spain's troops slew Jews in that town.

The young man fled the town while the strife still ran. He meant to go back when calm came once more. By 1469 he had reached Toledo in Spain. A rich host there saw his deep Talmud lore. That host asked him to write a guide to the Talmud. The guide would serve as the set book for schools. His Halikot Olam came out in five gates or parts. Each gate treats one side of how the Talmud works.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zausmer-jacob-b:
Jacob ben Samuel Zausmer was a Polish rabbi and preacher of the 1600s. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He worked at the town that bears his name. His chief book bears the name Bet Yaakob in Hebrew.

That book came out at Dyhernfurth in the year 1696. It holds one hundred seventy-four court replies in its leaves. In its head note he names a second work of his. That work holds sermons on the Pentateuch in week order. Its name is Toledot Yaakob in the Hebrew tongue. The entry rests on two book lists of Hebrew works. It gives no facts of his birth or of his death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zedekiah-10481:
Zedekiah is a name borne by three men in the Hebrew Bible. Emil G. Hirsch and Ira Maurice Price wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The first was one of four hundred seers of King Ahab. He stood as a foe of the seer Micaiah in that court.

Ahab had called those seers to ask of a war to come. Micaiah spoke doom for that war in a sly tone. Zedekiah struck that man on the cheek for his words. He said a false ghost spoke through the four hundred then. The second man was a false seer in the exile years. The king of Babylon had him roasted in fire for his acts. The third was the last king of Judah on the throne. His true name was Mattaniah ere the king of Babylon changed it.
mesmer-precis-historique-1781:
Mesmer published his Précis historique in 1781 to set out the facts of animal magnetism as he saw them. The pamphlet is his own historical summary, written before the royal commissions of 1784 condemned his claims. It is a pivotal firsthand source for the birth of mesmerism.

Mesmer recounts his early cures and the resistance of the medical world. He presents case after case as proof of his unseen fluid. Rivals, jealous doctors, and blind prejudice explain, in his telling, every failure to win acceptance. The founder tells his story here in full, on his own terms. Later histories of the affair all lean on this defense.
michelson-relative-motion-ether-1881:
Albert A. Michelson, a young American physicist, ran this first ether test at Potsdam in 1881. He sought to catch the Earth in its flight through the ether. If the ether stood still, light should race at changed speeds as the Earth moved.

He built a fine tool that split a light beam and sent the parts on two paths. The beams came back with no shift at all, though his maths said a shift must show. The blank result was the first crack in the ether scheme, and it puzzled the field for years.
nasir-khusraw-sefer-nameh-schefer-1881:
Nasir-i Khusraw walked the Islamic world for seven years, and Charles Schefer's 1881 French version carries his Sefer Nameh to Western readers. The Persian traveler went from Central Asia to Mecca, Jerusalem, and Cairo. His precise, curious eye notes cities, shrines, markets, and roads along the whole vast way.

He measures walls, counts gates, and tastes local bread with equal care. Few travel books of the medieval Islamic world match its freshness. Faith and wonder guide his steps, yet fact fills his pages. The record stands as the finest travel account of its age and region, in a French dress that served scholars for generations.
nordenskiold-voyage-vega-vol2-1881:
Volume Two of the Vega voyage completes the first transit of the Northeast Passage. The English edition appeared in 1881, before the first volume. Nordenskiöld's ship had wintered within sight of her goal, held by the ice for ten months.

In July 1879 the Vega broke free and passed into the Pacific, to worldwide applause. The return sail visits Japan, China, and Ceylon, then home through Suez to a hero's welcome in Stockholm. Scientific results fill the closing chapters: charts, fossils, and notes on Arctic peoples. The voyage proved Asia could be circled by sea, a dream since the 1500s.
olcott-buddhist-catechism-1881:
Henry Steel Olcott taught the faith of the Buddha to the young in A Buddhist Catechism, his slim book of 1881. Olcott had moved to Ceylon, now Sri Lanka. He found schools there taught by faiths not of the isle. He wrote this guide to set the faith in plain words for its own youth.

Short asks meet short replies, in the mode of faith schools of the West. Heads of the faith on the isle passed the text as true. Schools there used it for years. Olcott is still held dear on the isle. The guide went through scores of print runs in its long life. Few books by a man of the West have shaped schools of the East so.
openalex-w2099735981:
Patricia Miloslavich, Eduardo Klein, Juan Manuel Diaz and colleagues reviewed marine biodiversity knowledge for South America's coasts. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2011. The continent has nearly thirty thousand kilometres of coastline. Its waters span the Caribbean, Pacific and Atlantic. Knowledge differs sharply between the ten coastal countries.

The review sums up what is known by region. It lists major gaps in species records and monitoring. Research effort and funding vary widely by country. Some coasts are well studied, others barely at all. Shared databases and training are among the needs named. The authors set priorities for filling the gaps. Better knowledge supports conservation along both coasts.
openalex-w2116492181:
Ricardo Cabezas, Marcos Avila, Janneth Gonzalez and colleagues reviewed the blood-brain barrier's role in Parkinson's disease. Their paper appeared in Frontiers in Cellular Neuroscience in 2014. The barrier tightly controls what enters the brain. Astrocytes, a type of brain support cell, help regulate it. Barrier failure may contribute to Parkinson's.

The review explains the barrier's cellular makeup. Endothelial cells form its main wall. Pericytes and astrocytes support and tune it. Astrocyte signals strengthen or loosen the barrier. In Parkinson's, those signals may go wrong. A leaky barrier could let toxins reach neurons. The authors discuss treatment ideas targeting astrocytes. Barrier repair is a possible therapy route.
openalex-w2195279081:
Peter Serina, Ian Riley, Andrea Stewart, and colleagues published this study in BMC Medicine in 2015. They improved the Tariff Method, a tool that assigns causes of death from verbal autopsies. Where death certificates are rare, interviewing families is the only practical way to learn why people died, and public health depends on those answers.

The method was trained on hospital-validated interviews with known true causes. When the first version was tested on community interviews, biases appeared. The team corrected the model for those biases and built Tariff 2.0. Its accuracy was then measured at both the individual and population level against the validated database, the standard yardstick for such tools.
openalex-w2252702481:
M. Aguilar, Damiano Aisa, B. Alpat, and colleagues published this measurement in Physical Review Letters in 2015. With the Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer on the International Space Station, they charted the flow of helium nuclei in primary cosmic rays. Helium is the second most common cosmic ray species after hydrogen, and its exact energy pattern tests ideas about cosmic ray origins.

The spectrometer sorted helium by rigidity, which links a particle's momentum to its charge. Coverage ran from just under two billion volts to three trillion volts. Knowing this spectrum precisely helps physicists model how cosmic rays are accelerated and how they wander through the galaxy before reaching Earth.
openalex-w2290369781:
Yunbi Xu published this review alone in Theoretical and Applied Genetics in 2016. He proposes envirotyping as a third pillar of crop science, alongside genotyping and phenotyping. As climate change bites harder into harvests, breeders need a systematic way to measure the environments their plants actually face.

Envirotype data come from multi-site trials, geographic and soil information systems, and direct sensing of soil and canopies. The data feed crop models, predict performance, and expose how genes answer weather signals. Uses range from describing test sites to precision farming and breeding. Xu imagines a four-dimensional crop profile joining genes, traits, environment, and time, built on future high-throughput sensing down to single plants.
openalex-w264334781:
Catherine W. M. Ong, Paul T. Elkington, and Sara Brilha, with colleagues, published this 2015 study in PLOS Pathogens. It investigates how tuberculosis destroys lung tissue and forms cavities. Those cavities carry huge numbers of bacteria and keep the disease spreading. Neutrophils, front-line immune cells, flood into TB lungs and are linked to poor outcomes.

The team found that neutrophils release an enzyme, MMP-8, that breaks down lung matrix. The enzyme was raised in patients and sat inside neutrophil traps and around real cavities. Sputum levels of MMP-8 matched how severe the disease looked on scans. A control switch called AMPK drove the enzyme's release. Doxycycline, a licensed drug that blocks such enzymes, stopped the collagen destruction in their model. The authors propose MMP-8 as a target for host-directed therapy, treating the damage rather than only the bacteria.
openalex-w2773939681:
Alexander Sczyrba, Peter Hofmann, and Peter Belmann lead a large consortium benchmarking metagenomics software in Nature Methods in 2017. Metagenomics reads DNA from whole communities, then software must assemble and sort the fragments. New algorithms appear constantly, and testing them individually is slow and can be biased. The CAMI initiative was built to judge them fairly, as a community.

CAMI ran a benchmarking challenge on datasets of unusual complexity and realism. It assessed assembly programs, binning tools, and taxonomic profilers against known answers. Community involvement shaped the datasets, metrics, and questions from the start. The portal stays open for new submissions, so the benchmark keeps living. Results show where current tools shine and where they stumble on hard community data. Such shared yardsticks steer developers toward the weaknesses that matter most.
openalex-w2782327081:
Raimunda do Socorro da Silva Azevedo, Jorge Rodrigues de Sousa, and Marialva Tereza Ferreira de Araújo lead a team studying fatal Zika microcephaly. Their study appeared in Scientific Reports in 2018. Zika infection during pregnancy caused babies to be born with abnormally small heads. How the virus damages the developing brain was the question. The team examined brain tissue from fatal cases directly.

They studied fifteen cases: ten Zika-positive newborns with microcephaly and five controls. Microcephaly brains showed meningoencephalitis, inflammation around vessels, and immune cells infiltrating tissue. Viral antigens appeared inside inflammatory cells and in brain tissue itself. Calcifications, gliosis, and dying neurons marked the damage pattern. The in situ immune response profile helps explain how infection injures the fetal brain. Such detail guides thinking about prevention and about protecting pregnancies during future outbreaks.
openalex-w2809684781:
Raouf Boutaba, Mohammad A. Salahuddin, and Noura Limam lead this 2018 survey of machine learning for networking, in the Journal of Internet Services and Applications. Machine learning has surged as data, algorithms, and computing power all grew together. Networks generate endless running problems where learning could automate decisions. Earlier surveys covered single techniques or technologies. This one spans the whole landscape.

The survey organizes learning methods by networking problem. Traffic prediction, routing, and classification come first. Congestion control, resource and fault management, quality of service, and security follow. For each area it explains which learning styles fit and where they have succeeded. It also catalogs limits honestly, with open challenges and future directions. The authors frame learning as the engine of self-managing networks. For researchers entering the field, this is the map of what exists.
openalex-w3088361581:
Dâmaris Silveira, Jose Prieto-Garcia, Fábio Boylan, and colleagues wrote this review in Frontiers in Pharmacology in 2020. It asks a plain question: is there evidence for herbal medicines as add-on symptom relief in COVID-19? The virus, first seen in Wuhan in late 2019, had killed hundreds of thousands by mid-2020.

Most patients face mild or moderate illness and manage at home with rest, fluids, and fever drugs. Guidelines said little about treating cough, a tiring symptom that also spreads the virus. No proven specific therapy existed when the authors wrote. They therefore sifted the evidence for herbal options used beside standard care, weighing both benefit and safety with care.
openalex-w4210630681:
Jacqueline Gerson, Natalie Szponar, Angelica Almeyda Zambrano, and colleagues studied mercury pollution in the Amazon, in Nature Communications in 2022. Small-scale gold miners use liquid mercury to separate gold from sediment, then burn it off. That makes this mining the world's largest source of mercury released to the air. Where that mercury lands, and what it does to forests, was poorly known.

As the title states, Amazon forests capture high levels of this airborne mercury near mining areas. Leaves and soils take the poison up and hold it. Many mining sites sit inside rich wildlife hotspots, so the pollution threatens species and local people alike. The study maps a hidden cost of informal gold mining.
openalex-w4414770781: Johan Rockström, Shakuntala Thilsted, Walter Willett, Line Gordon, Mario Herrero, and many colleagues authored the EAT-Lancet Commission on healthy, sustainable, and just food systems. Their commission report appeared in The Lancet in 2025. The preserved sample holds only the commission's long author list. It keeps no readable report text, so the commission's findings cannot be summarised from the sample.
openalex-w7206213381:
Raquel Romes Linhares and Regis Nunes Vargas present a simple method for sorting documents by how much they repeat their vocabulary. Their tool is Yule's K, a classic measure of how concentrated a text's word use is, paired with a clustering method that splits a set of documents into two groups. To test the idea, they ran thousands of simulated document sets with known mixes of the two kinds.

Across the simulations, the method recovered the true mix with high accuracy, correctly classifying nearly ninety-nine of every hundred documents on average. Errors grew only at the extremes, where one group was very small and the two kinds of text were hard to tell apart. The result is a checked, low-cost technique for researchers who need to separate repetitive writing from varied writing at scale.
openalex-w7213465981:
Thiago Moreira Rodrigues and a large team review iron supplements and brain development in young people. Their 2026 integrative review follows PRISMA and Cochrane guidance. It searches four major databases and grades evidence quality with standard tools, focusing on thinking skills and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder.

Thirteen studies were included. Iron treatment improved intelligence scores, attention, and memory on average. Gains were clearly larger in schoolchildren who began with iron-deficiency anaemia. Courses lasting four months or more worked better for lasting gains. For ADHD, evidence of low brain iron exists, but certainty about symptom benefit is weaker. The review separates solid findings from areas needing more research.
openalex-w7214090581:
Izadora Pala Toledo and colleagues study obesity as a risk factor for worsening type two diabetes in Brazil. Their 2026 ecological study uses public data on hospital morbidity and deaths from 2019 to 2023, plus national survey and statistics sources. Obesity and excess weight rose markedly among Brazilian adults across recent decades.

Tens of thousands of obesity hospitalizations and deaths were recorded in the period, concentrated in the Southeast and South. Diabetes cases and deaths numbered in the hundreds of thousands, again led by the Southeast and by women. Facing both conditions needs public policy, prevention, and health education, they argue, not clinical treatment alone.
openalex-w7214308181:
Nertan Ribeiro Batista led a seven-author team in a 2026 integrative review of negative pressure wound therapy for complex skin wounds. The treatment seals a wound and applies gentle suction, drawing out fluid. Complex wounds involve deep tissue loss, infection, or poor blood flow, and they often resist normal closure.

From thirty-two studies, the review found the therapy shrank wound area, encouraged healthy new tissue, and controlled fluid, while wider analyses linked it to fewer surgical site infections. It can also prepare a wound for final reconstruction, sometimes allowing simpler repair. Results depend on wound cause, depth, blood supply, and cleaning. The authors present it as a strong support tool, not a replacement for surgery and basic wound care.
openalex-w7220907181:
José Fernando Sales Gonçalves and three colleagues studied how literature is taught in Brazilian high schools, publishing their field study in 2026. Working at a full-time state school in Bom Jesus da Serra, Bahia, they asked whether classes still follow the old model. That model is built around literary periods, and they also asked how teachers and students see it.

Surveys of two teachers and forty-three first-year students showed the period-based order still structures lessons, alongside reading, discussion, and some technology. The authors describe a partial change rather than a break: literary history keeps its central place while newer ways of meeting the text grow around it. Their findings speak to anyone rethinking how schools introduce young readers to literature.
petit-albert-1881:
Household magic fills Le veritable petit Albert, in this 1881 printing of the great French folk grimoire. Secrets promise help with health, love, luck, and protection for ordinary folk. For three centuries the Petit Albert ranked among France's best-selling books of hidden knowledge, thumbed in farms and villages across the land.

Recipes, charms, and wonders pass from hand to hand in its pages. Joseph-Norbert Duquet's printing carried the old lore to new buyers here. Scholars trace its roots to the secrets ascribed to Albert the Great. The people's magic, plain and practical, survives in this little book, endlessly reprinted because readers kept finding their needs in it.
plos-pbio-0020081:
Yu Zheng, Richard J. Roberts, and Simon Kasif offered a fresh view of adaptation in PLOS Biology in 2004. Most genes in bacteria change slowly. A smaller set, tied to the cell surface and to defense, changes much faster. The authors call these segmentally variable genes.

Fast change in surface parts makes sense. Those are the parts that meet the world: hosts, rivals, and attackers. By naming and sorting this class of genes, the paper gives genome readers a new lens. Stretches that vary a lot may mark where a microbe is adapting right now. That idea can guide the hunt for vaccine targets and for clues about how pathogens keep ahead of immune systems.
plos-pone-0000081:
Phillip Endicott, Mait Metspalu, Chris Stringer, and their team read ancient DNA from the Andaman Islands in PLOS ONE in 2006. The islanders' maternal lineages, traced by mitochondrial DNA, bear on how early modern humans spread through South Asia. New typing methods let the team test many markers in scarce ancient samples at once.

Their results sharpen where the Andaman lineages fit among South Asian groups. That placement supports a very early settlement of the islands by seafaring people. Each such data point helps draw the map of the great coastal migration out of Africa. The method itself, packing many tests into little DNA, serves all ancient DNA work.
plos-pone-0000181:
Sari Voutilainen, Tomi-Pekka Tuomainen, Maarit Korhonen, and colleagues published this heart study in PLOS ONE in 2007. It comes from the Kuopio Ischaemic Heart Disease Risk Factor Study in Finland. The team examined a common variant of the COMT gene, Val158Met, alongside the risk of acute coronary events and blood levels of homocysteine.

COMT breaks down stress hormones and also handles homocysteine-related chemistry, both tied to heart risk. The authors test whether the gene variant, on its own or with homocysteine levels, predicts heart events. Findings of this kind feed the long effort to sort real genetic risk factors from noise.
plos-pone-0000281:
Frank Seebacher and Shauna A. Murray published this reptile physiology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Transient receptor potential ion channels are molecular sensors, some of which respond to temperature. The authors show these channels control thermoregulatory behaviour in reptiles, the basking and shade-seeking by which reptiles manage body temperature.

A reptile's behavior is its thermostat, so the sensors behind it matter. Linking TRP channels to that behavior connects a molecule to a whole-animal trait. The work helps explain how cold-blooded animals fine-tune their temperature, and how they might respond as their environments warm.
plos-pone-0000381:
André Catic and colleagues described a bacterial enzyme in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The enzyme, ElaD, is made by E. coli and belongs to the deubiquitinating proteases, enzymes that remove ubiquitin tags from proteins. In human cells, those tags mark proteins for destruction or change what they do, so enzymes that strip them off are powerful regulators.

Finding such an enzyme in a common bacterium raises questions about where it came from and what it does there. Bacteria are not thought to run a ubiquitin system like ours, so ElaD may act on the cells the bacterium infects. The paper opens a window on how microbes borrow or mimic host chemistry.
plos-pone-0000481:
João Carlos Sousa, Manuel João Costa, and Joana Almeida Palha wrote a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Their subject was the meeting point of hormone science and computing. Hormones regulate genes across the body, switching them on and off in patterns that shift with time and tissue. Bioinformatics, the computational study of biological data, offers tools to read those patterns.

Their theme is learning one field from the other. Hormone research gives bioinformatics real problems with clinical weight. Computation gives endocrinology a way to handle genome-scale data. Papers of this kind map a collaboration rather than report a single experiment, arguing that neither field can fully read hormone action alone.
plos-pone-0000581:
Simone Lemeer and colleagues took a census of enzyme action in growing zebrafish, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The enzymes are protein-tyrosine kinases, switches that embryos use to pass signals. The team profiled their action in embryos where one chosen kinase had been knocked down, turned low.

Census work like this counts what enzymes do, not just whether they are present. When one switch is dimmed, others may pick up the slack, and that response maps the web. Zebrafish embryos are clear and grow fast, which suits this kind of work. The lessons reach cancer drugs, many of which aim at these same switches.
plos-pone-0000681:
Yong-Gang Yao, Hans-Jürgen Bandelt and Neal S. Young warned about contamination in single-cell mitochondrial DNA work, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Many medical papers report mtDNA variation measured in single blood-forming cells, muscle fibers, eggs, tiny tumor samples, and degraded clinical specimens. At such tiny scales, stray DNA from outside is notoriously hard to avoid.

External contamination threatens the analysis itself: foreign DNA can masquerade as real variation. A false variant in a medical specimen could mislead diagnosis or research conclusions. The authors press the field to treat contamination as a central problem, not a footnote. Tiny samples demand strict controls, and this study explains why.
plos-pone-0000781:
John H. Malone, Thomas H. Chrzanowski and Pawel Michalak examined why hybrid male frogs are sterile, writing in PLOS ONE in 2007. Reproductive isolation defines populations as unique biological species. Yet very little was known about the gene expression basis for that isolation: which genes, behaving differently, make hybrids fail. Powerful molecular tools finally let researchers identify candidate genes in the act.

Their hybrids come from crossing Xenopus laevis with Xenopus muelleri, two African clawed frogs. Male hybrids are sterile, a common pattern in animal crosses. Comparing gene expression in hybrids against parents can locate the misregulated genes. Each candidate is a clue to how new species seal themselves off.
plos-pone-0000881:
Ketki Verkhedkar, Karthik Raman, Nagasuma Chandra and co-authors compared reaction networks in the germs behind tuberculosis and leprosy, for PLOS ONE in 2007. Scientists build many kinds of maps for living systems, from gene control maps to maps of chemical reactions. Each map gives a different view of how a cell runs.

Here the team built graphs from the metabolome, the full set of small chemicals in the cell, for Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium leprae. Comparing the two may show where their chemistry is shared and where it parts. Those differences matter, since one germ causes TB and the other leprosy, two very different diseases.
plos-pone-0000981:
Stina Enqvist, Knut Sletten, Fred Stevens and colleagues traced what decides which tissues amyloid strikes, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Amyloid is clumped protein deposited outside cells. About twenty-five proteins can form it, and the diseases range from Alzheimer's to type two diabetes. In AL amyloidosis, the clumps come from antibody light chains.

The team argue that both the germ line origin of the light chain and later somatic mutations shape which tissues get targeted. That would explain why patients with the same disease differ so much in which organs fail. A tissue logic could improve prognosis and treatment choices.
plos-pone-0001081:
Heiko Vogel and co-authors set plant gene answers to specialist and generalist insects side by side, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Plants guard their leaves with traits that are always on, and traits switched on by attack. A few hormone paths control the switched-on set.

The study plant is Boechera divaricarpa, a wild North American kin of the lab plant Arabidopsis. The team track gene use under feeding by specialists, which eat few plant kinds, and generalists, which eat many. Each pest may call for a different guard. A wild kin shows answers that lab strains, bred for ease, may have lost. The contrast guides thought on how to keep crops safe.
plos-pone-0001181:
Diarrhea, respiratory infection, and malaria cause much of the illness and death in sub-Saharan Africa, and their levels rise and fall over time. Daniel Medina and colleagues built forecasting methods for these diseases in Niono, Mali, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Their challenge is that the time series are non-stationary, meaning the patterns themselves keep shifting.

Forecasting tools that assume steady patterns fail on such data. The authors set out to model the real behavior of the three disease series in one district. Better forecasts let clinics and health programs prepare staff and supplies before a surge arrives.
plos-pone-0001281:
Blood tests for ovarian cancer markers can be thrown off by how the blood was handled before testing. Jason Thorpe and colleagues quantified that problem in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Biomarker studies compare serum protein levels between people with and without cancer, and efforts are usually made to standardize collection and storage.

The authors examined the effects of blood collection conditions on ovarian cancer serum markers. If handling differences mimic or mask disease differences, early detection studies can mislead. Their work tells researchers which pre-analytical steps matter most, practical knowledge for any biomarker program.
plos-pone-0001381:
Dafna Singer-Lahat, Dodo Chikvashvili, and Ilana Lotan published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how hormone cells release their cargo. Cells that make hormones let them out in a step called exocytosis. Ion channels in the cell wall help set the pace of that release. The team studied how one channel type works with a partner protein.

The authors show that the channel binds direct to the partner protein, and that this bond boosts release. Work done before had used added genes in rat cells. This study checks the pair as found in real cells. The finding adds a fresh route by which cells fine tune the flow of hormones and brain signals.
plos-pone-0001481:
M. Abid Hussain and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a stomach germ's protein and the immune reply. The germ, Helicobacter pylori, causes stomach swelling and ulcers and raises cancer risk. Many of its proteins had been flagged as harm factors. The team studied one enzyme of the germ in people with ulcers or stomach swelling.

They report that this enzyme can draw a strong antibody reply in such patients. A strong reply marks the protein as a lead for tests or shots. It may help labs tell who hosts the germ. It also adds to the map of how this germ provokes the stomach lining.
plos-pone-0001581:
Zoran Popmihajlov and Kendall Smith published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a self brake in T cells. A signal called IL-2 drives the growth of T cells picked by a germ cue. A second factor acts as a brake on that growth. The pair asked how the two are wired, since a sound brake keeps immune replies from running too far.

They found IL-2 itself turns on the brake factor after T cells fire. That forms a neat loop: the gas builds its own brake. Loops like this set the size and span of an immune reply. Faults in them may underlie ills where T cells attack the self.
plos-pone-0001681:
Linda M. Sanderson, Philip J. de Groot, Guido J. E. J. Hooiveld, and their co-authors set out a new way to study how dietary fat talks to genes, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Fats in food likely affect health by changing gene activity. Several gene switches, including SREBP-1c, NF-κB, and the PPAR family, respond to fatty acids. What stayed unclear was how much of the response each fat type drives.

Their answer is synthetic dietary triglycerides: fats built to exact designs, so each part can be varied alone. The full text explains the design, the feeding tests, and the gene activity readouts. Clean, controlled fats let nutrigenomics, the study of food-gene links, move past the mixed signals of natural diets.
plos-pone-0001781:
André F. A. Santos, Renan B. Lengruber, Esmeralda A. Soares, and their co-authors mapped neglected regions of the HIV genome in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Drug resistance data cover the first 400 amino acids of HIV's reverse transcriptase well. The C-terminal domains of Pol, named thumb, connection, and RNase H, were poorly understood, including what antiretroviral treatment does to them.

The team characterized conservation patterns in the connection and RNase H domains and identified new mutations in patients treated with NRTI drugs. The full text gives the patient sequences and the mutation map. Resistance can hide in unmonitored regions, so widening the map helps labs keep drug tests accurate.
plos-pone-0001881:
Hui Li and co-authors traced a gene choice shaped by past selection in East Asia in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The genes in view make alcohol dehydrogenase, a set of enzymes that break down alcohol in the body. One form of a gene in this set, known as ADH1B*47His, had been tied to a lower risk linked with drink.

The team studied how this form is spread across groups in East Asia and weighed signs that nature favored it there. Work like this tests how diet, drink, and local habits in the past can leave marks on genes today. It also helps explain why groups can react to alcohol in unlike ways.
plos-pone-0001981:
Deborah Tribouillard-Tanvier and co-authors found that a blood pressure drug fights prions, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Prion diseases are fatal, spreadable brain disorders with no cure, in animals and humans alike. Any drug already used in people that slows prions would be a fast lead.

The drug is guanabenz, long used for high blood pressure. As the title states, it was active in living animals against both yeast prions and mammal prions. Yeast may seem a far cry from brain disease, but their prions share core traits. A known, safe drug with anti-prion power is a rare and useful find.
plos-pone-0002081:
Abdisalan Noor and co-authors measured whether mosquito net use matches lower malaria in rural Somalia, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Across Africa, efforts and funding to scale up insecticide-treated nets had grown fast over five years. Yet little was known about how well the nets work in south central Somalia, a hard region for health work.

The team surveyed net use and tested for infection with Plasmodium falciparum, the deadliest malaria parasite, in rural communities. Local proof matters, since net habits, housing, and mosquito behavior vary by place. The study gives Somalia's malaria program data of its own.
plos-pone-0002181:
Ahmedin Jemal, Elizabeth Ward, Robert Anderson, and co-authors measured the gap in death rates between rich and poor Americans, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. From 1960 to 1990 that gap had widened, mostly because heart disease deaths fell more slowly among poorer groups than among richer ones. No study had checked the trend with data past that period.

The team examined death rates from 1993 to 2001 across socioeconomic groups. They report that inequalities in death rates from all causes kept widening in those years. Numbers like these shape health policy, since they show progress in survival is not shared evenly across the country.
plos-pone-0002281:
Gareth Weedall, Spencer Polley, and David Conway compared rates of protein change across malaria parasite species, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Comparing genomes across the Plasmodium genus can reveal which genes are under strong natural selection. A bottleneck was data: only partial, low-coverage genome sequence existed for the closest relative of the main human parasite, Plasmodium falciparum.

The team asked whether genes flagged for fast non-synonymous change, changes that alter the protein, in one species keep that signature in others. They found the signatures correlate poorly across the genus. The caution matters: selection signals in one malaria species do not transfer cleanly to its cousins.
plos-pone-0002381:
Li and co-authors published a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Jianxu Li, Hongbing Wu, Jing Hong, among others. Its subject is odorranalectin Is a Small Peptide Lectin with Potential for Drug Delivery and Targeting. Lectins are sugar-binding proteins that specifically recognize sugar complexes.

The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The full text is free to read, so any reader can check the work and follow the links to past work. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002481:
Bueti, working with fellow researchers, published a study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Domenica Bueti, Eelco V. van Dongen, Vincent Walsh, among others. Its subject is the Role of Superior Temporal Cortex in Auditory Timing. Recently, there has been upsurge of interest in the neural mechanisms of time perception.

The paper sets out the problem first and then the line of work the team chose to take. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002581:
Elemans and fellow authors published a research article through PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Coen P. H. Elemans, Andrew F. Mead, Lawrence C. Rome, among others. Its subject is superfast Vocal Muscles Control Song Production in Songbirds. Birdsong is a widely used model for vocal learning and human speech, which exhibits high temporal and acoustic diversity.

The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002681:
In 2008, Thorsten Pauly and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE. Their subject was Activity-Dependent shedding of the NMDA receptor glycine binding site by matrix metalloproteinase 3: a PUTATIVE mechanism of postsynaptic plasticity. Authorship is credited in the record to Thorsten Pauly and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Functional and structural alterations of clustered postsynaptic ligand gated ion channels in neuronal cells are thought to contribute to synaptic plasticity and memory formation. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front.
plos-pone-0002781:
In 2008, Miguel Gaspar and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE about multiple functions for ORF75c in murid herpesvirus-4 infection. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Miguel Gaspar, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. All gamma-herpesviruses encode at least one homolog of the cellular enzyme formyl-glycineamide-phosphoribosyl-amidotransferase. A further point appears in the abstract. Murid herpesvirus-4 (MuHV-4) encodes 3 (ORFs 75a, 75b and 75c), suggesting that at least some copies have acquired new functions. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002881:
Anthony Kong, Véronique Calleja, Pierre Leboucher and colleagues studied drug resistance in breast cancer cells in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Drugs that block the EGFR receptor often help only some patients, and EGFR levels alone do not predict who will respond. The role of the related receptor HER2 was their focus.

The team reports that HER2 can keep cancer growth going by switching on other HER receptors when EGFR is blocked. In the title's terms, HER2 function escapes EGFR inhibitors that way. The finding points drug makers toward blocking more than one receptor at once in such tumors.
plos-pone-0002981:
Mattia Zampieri, Nicola Soranzo, Daniele Bianchini and co-authors asked where gene co-expression patterns come from in 2008. Reverse engineering tries to infer gene networks from large sets of microarray data. Such networks are widely used to deduce, merge, and validate claimed physical interactions between genes.

The team tested the patterns found in E. coli and baker's yeast against what reverse engineering algorithms produce. Their question is whether co-expression reflects real regulation or artifacts of the methods. Published in PLOS ONE, the answer helps researchers judge how much trust inferred networks deserve. Readers can follow the full methods and data in the complete text of the article.
plos-pone-0003081:
Kerry Dwan, Douglas Altman, Juan Arnaiz and co-authors reviewed evidence on publication and outcome reporting bias in 2008. Growing use of meta-analysis in systematic reviews had highlighted biases arising during randomized trials. Study publication bias, where results decide whether a trial is published, threatens review validity.

The systematic review gathers empirical evidence on both publication bias and selective outcome reporting. Published in PLOS ONE, it is evidence about evidence: how much trust pooled results deserve. Trial registration and full reporting reforms rest on exactly this kind of audit. The article appeared in PLOS ONE, an open access journal anyone can read free online.
plos-pone-0003181:
Ran Taube, Quan Zhu, Chen Xu and colleagues describe a display platform based on lentiviruses in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Isolating human antibodies with current display tools can be limited by problems with protein expression, folding, and later modifications. The team describe a discovery platform that uses self-inactivating lentiviral vectors for surface display.

Their system shows human antibodies stably on the surface of human cells and virus particles. Readers get a method that keeps antibodies in a human cell setting, where folding is more natural. That could improve the search for antibodies for research and therapy.
plos-pone-0003281:
Ya-Chun Huang and Neal A. Hessler study social effects on reward neurons in songbirds in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Synaptic transmission onto dopaminergic neurons of the mammalian ventral tegmental area can be potentiated by acute or chronic exposure to addictive drugs. Because rewarding behaviour such as social affiliation can activate the same neural circuitry as addictive drugs, the team asked whether social context does the same in birds.

Their title reports that social modulation during songbird courtship potentiates midbrain dopaminergic neurons. Readers see courtship change the reward system at the synapse level. The work links social experience to the same machinery involved in addiction.
plos-pone-0003381:
Dru S. Dace and colleagues studied abnormal blood vessel growth in the eye in 2008. Such growth, called neovascularization, is a common cause of blindness. The team focused on interleukin-10, a signal that usually calms immune responses. They asked how it acts when a young eye is starved of oxygen.

Mice lacking the signal grew far fewer of the harmful new vessels. The signal seemed to steer how immune cells called macrophages react to low oxygen. With that steering gone, the vessel growth slowed down. The work names a surprising driver of eye disease and a possible drug target.
plos-pone-0003481:
Yongjun Guan and co-authors found T cells shielding themselves from HIV in this 2008 paper. CD4 T cells are the main target of HIV infection. Some T cells release chemicals that block the viral doorway CCR5. Those chemicals can guard nearby cells from R5 virus strains.
