The twist here is protection of the producing cell itself. Individual CD4 cells making those ligands defended their own surface. Such self-protection may let some cells resist infection from within. Understanding it could inspire therapies that copy the trick. Cells that guard themselves may also seed the viral reservoir that resists cure.
plos-pone-0003581:
Jindong Chen and co-authors removed a kidney gene in mice for this 2008 study. Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome is an inherited cancer syndrome. Its gene, FLCN, was found by positional cloning and acts as a tumor suppressor. Mutations cause kidney cancers, skin growths, and lung cysts.

Mice lacking FLCN in the kidney developed polycystic kidneys. They also developed renal neoplasia, abnormal kidney growths. The model confirms the gene's tumor suppressor role in living tissue. It gives researchers a system for studying this rare syndrome. Kidney tumors in this syndrome tend to grow slowly but return over time.
plos-pone-0003681:
Patricia Renesto, Clarisse Rovery, Jacques Schrenzel, and colleagues published this microbiology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Rickettsia conorii causes Mediterranean spotted fever and reaches people through tick bites. The skin sore at the bite, called an eschar, is where infection begins. The team read the bacterium's gene activity there.

They profiled which genes the bacterium switches on inside the eschar. That snapshot shows what the germ does first, while it is still at the entry point. Knowing those early moves can help explain how the infection spreads from skin to the rest of the body.
plos-pone-0003781:
Jasna Martinovic, Thomas Gruber, and Matthias M. Müller published this vision study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Recognizing an object means binding its separate features into one thing. Early steps of that process are thought to code features very fast, in distinct groups of neurons. Conjunctions of features come later.

The authors recorded brain activity while people processed visual objects. They compared how single features and feature combinations are coded in the human brain. The work probes the first steps by which scattered visual features turn into objects we can name and use.
plos-pone-0003881:
Marta Coll, Simone Libralato, Sergi Tudela, and co-authors assessed ocean fishing in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. Fishing removes mass and energy from the sea in every catch landed. That loss can no longer feed the higher levels of the food web. The authors call heavy removal of that kind ecosystem overfishing.

The paper weighs how much production fishing takes from marine food webs. It looks past single fish stocks to the whole system that supports them. The argument helps managers judge when total catch harms the wider ocean. It gives a frame for setting limits that protect more than one target species.
plos-pone-0003981:
Jayne Byakika-Tusiime, Leslie W. Chinn, Jessica H. Oyugi, and co-authors compared generic and brand HIV drugs in 2008. Generic therapy is the mainstay of HIV care in poor settings. Little proof existed that generics match brand drugs in the body. The team compared three drugs used together in Uganda.

Their PLOS ONE article measured steady-state drug levels in HIV-infected adults. The drugs were stavudine, lamivudine, and nevirapine. Matching levels support bioequivalence of the generic and innovator versions. Such proof underpins confidence in low-cost treatment programs worldwide. The study ran in PLOS ONE, an open journal read by labs around the world.
plos-pone-0004081:
Hayate Merad, Horea Porumb, Loussiné Zargarian, and co-authors examined HIV's DNA-inserting enzyme in 2009. Integrase inserts viral DNA into the host cell's DNA. That step makes HIV infection permanent in the cell. The team studied the enzyme's catalytic core structure.

Their PLOS ONE article identifies an unusual helix-turn-helix motif in that core. Spanning residues 149 to 186, it binds viral DNA and LEDGF. LEDGF is a host protein that guides integration. A defined binding motif offers a target for drugs blocking integration. The work appeared in PLOS ONE, with its methods and data open for all to see.
plos-pone-0004181:
Junwei Yang and colleagues published this infection study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Bleeding in the lungs is a major and often deadly feature of severe leptospirosis. Leptospirosis is a bacterial infection caught from animal-contaminated water, and the cause of its lung bleeding is unclear. The dangerous serovar Lai of Leptospira interrogans makes a protein that acts on platelet-activating factor, a blood signal.

Following that clue, the team measured the activity of the matching enzyme, PAF acetylhydrolase, in patients' blood. They propose its serum activity as a possible clinical marker for the lung bleeding form of the disease. An early warning marker could help doctors spot the patients most at risk.
plos-pone-0004281:
Sarah Parker and colleagues published this tuberculosis study in PLOS ONE in 2009. The cell wall of Mycobacterium tuberculosis is central to its success as a pathogen, and mycolic acids are key components of that wall. The genes that join the wall's building blocks sit in a cluster running from Rv3799c through at least Rv3804c.

The team characterised one gene in that cluster, Rv3802c. They report that it encodes a phospholipase and thioesterase, and that the antimycobacterial agent tetrahydrolipstatin inhibits it. An enzyme in the wall-building line that a drug can block is a lead for new tuberculosis treatments.
plos-pone-0004381:
Heads in backboned animals are built from two cell groups working side by side. Skull parts, tendons, and connective tissue come from neural crest cells. Most head muscles come from a second group, the cranial mesoderm. Julien Grenier, Marie-Aimée Teillet, Raphaëlle Grifone, and co-authors studied how the two groups relate. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Earlier work showed crest cells migrate in close company with mesoderm cells. The authors traced that pairing during head muscle growth in the embryo. Their aim was to map who builds what, and how the groups interact. The map helps explain normal face and jaw formation. It also frames birth defects where those tissues form wrong.
plos-pone-0004481:
Age and food change which genes are active in dog muscle, report Ingmar Middelbos, Brittany Vester, Lisa Karr-Lilienthal, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The team read gene activity in the thigh muscle of beagles using gene chips. Twelve female dogs took part: six aged one year and six aged twelve years, fed one of two test diets.

By comparing young and old dogs on each diet, the study separates the marks of aging from the marks of food. Genes that shift with age alone hint at how muscle weakens over time. Genes that shift with diet show where food can push back. Dogs age faster than people, so their muscle offers a sped-up view of changes that also matter for human aging and diet advice.
plos-pone-0004581:
A new antibody test measures hepcidin, the body's iron gatekeeper hormone, in human blood, report Vasiliki Koliaraki, Martha Marinou, Theodoros Vassilakopoulos, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Hepcidin is a small peptide built from twenty-five amino acids. When it rises, iron is locked away inside storage cells, which contributes to the anemia of chronic disease. When it falls, iron deficiency and overload states follow.

Measuring hepcidin well had been a bottleneck: the peptide is small and hard to assay. The team presents a novel immunological assay for quantifying it in serum. A reliable test lets doctors separate anemia types that look alike. It also helps track iron disorders where the hormone itself is the problem.
plos-pone-0004681:
Sarosh Fatakia, Stefano Costanzi, and Carson Chow used math tools to find linked spots in key drug targets, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The targets are a huge family of cell surface proteins that sense signals. They are the most common targets of drugs in use today.

Some spots in these proteins change together over time, which hints they work as a team. The team used shared change scores and graph methods to find tight groups of such spots. Knowing which spots move as a group can guide drug design. It can also help predict how a change in one spot affects the whole protein.
plos-pone-0004781:
Lionel Nowak and Pascal Barone showed that contrast adaptation helps keep orientation tuning steady in primate visual cortex, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Single neurons keep the same preferred orientation whether a pattern is faint or bold. Past studies used long stimulus times, which left room for adaptation to shape the result during each trial.

The team used shorter, controlled exposures in primate V1 cells. They found adaptation to contrast does help hold tuning width steady. Steady tuning lets the brain read shape regardless of light level. The work refines models of early vision. More work in larger samples can confirm how general the effect proves to be.
plos-pone-0004881:
Chao Zhang and colleagues reported S9, a novel anticancer agent interfering with PI3K Akt mTOR signaling and microtubules, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Deregulation of the PI3K Akt mTOR pathway plays central roles in tumor formation and progression, providing validated therapy targets. S9, a hybrid of lactone and indole compounds, exerts anti proliferative activity by simultaneously disrupting signaling and the microtubule cytoskeleton in cancer cell models.

Dual action may delay resistance emergence. Hybrid design merges two pharmacophores productively. Cell division and growth signals fall together. Further growth requires animal testing. Taken together, the findings mark a useful step for research in this area. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field. More tests with more samples will help show how strong the effect is.
plos-pone-0004981:
Protein domains are the building blocks of proteins. Members of one superfamily share a core shape. Yet their lengths can differ greatly. Sankaran Sandhya and colleagues studied those differences in PLOS ONE in 2009. They focused on superfamilies with large length variation. The variation exceeded thirty percent in the cases they examined.

Extra or missing pieces are called indels. The study asked how indels in a domain scaffold change structure and function. Some length changes matter greatly. Others are absorbed by the core without harm. The survey is a field guide to protein remodeling. It helps predict which changes a protein can tolerate.
plos-pone-0005081:
Male-pattern baldness is tied to the androgen receptor gene. The exact DNA change behind the link was unidentified. Joanna Cobb and colleagues tested one candidate in PLOS ONE in 2009. The candidate was copy number variation. Such variation duplicates or deletes large DNA segments. They ran a case-control study on androgenetic alopecia.

The study asked whether receptor copy changes explain the association. Their results probe that hypothesis directly. Even a negative answer narrows the hunt. The functional variant must lie elsewhere in or near the gene. Baldness genetics is a model for common trait genetics. Each excluded suspect sharpens the search. The work keeps that search honest.
plos-pone-0005181:
An enzyme called heparanase cuts through the mesh that surrounds cells. Most human cancers make too much of it, which helps tumors spread and grow new blood vessels. Zcharia and colleagues built mice with the heparanase gene removed and reported the results in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The new mice showed that heparanase and a second family of cutting enzymes, the matrix metalloproteinases, are controlled together. When one is gone, the other shifts as well. That linked control matters for drug design, since blocking one enzyme alone may not stop tumors from cutting their way out.
plos-pone-0005281:
Histoplasma capsulatum is a fungus that causes lung disease, and it secretes an enzyme activity called DppIV. Cooper and colleagues showed in PLOS ONE in 2009 that the fungus has two genes for that enzyme family, and one does most of the secreted work.

The enzyme can cut substance P, a human peptide that helps regulate immune responses. Cutting a host signal peptide could blunt the body's alarm against the fungus. The finding names a possible immune-evasion trick and a fungal enzyme that drugs might target. A germ that cuts a host alarm wire must first make the tool and send it out,. Each of those steps is a place where a new drug might jam its work.
plos-pone-0005381:
Cancer therapy needs agents that find tumors in the body and mark them for imaging or attack. Cuesta and colleagues built such an agent, a trivalent antibody fragment they call a trimerbody, and tested it in living animals in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The trimerbody joins a single-chain antibody fragment to a collagen-derived section that holds three arms together. Three binding arms grip tumor targets more firmly than one. In vivo tests showed the engineered fragments target tumors and support imaging, a step toward clinical scanners. Three arms cost more to make than one, so the gain must be real in the body. Not just in a dish, and the live tests here are the ones that count for that claim.
plos-pone-0005481:
David Schley, Simon Gubbins, and David Paton weighed the risks of local movement bans in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Foot-and-mouth disease can sweep through farm animals, so countries guard their disease-free status with care. When an outbreak is found, officials often ban animal movements nearby.

The authors asked how wide and how long such bans need to be, given the risk that infection has already spread. Bans protect herds but also halt trade and farm work. A clear view of the risk helps officials choose bans that stop disease without needless harm to farming areas.
plos-pone-0005581:
Mascha van 't Wout and co-authors studied social cue reading in schizophrenia in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. People read others' gaze and body motion quickly and without effort. That skill underlies smooth social life.

People with schizophrenia often struggle socially, and weak reading of basic cues may be part of the cause. The team used a new visual illusion to test quick, automatic attention to social signals in patients and in people at high risk. Gaps on such a basic test could help spot risk early. Quick cue reading can be tested without language, which makes the illusion useful across patient groups.
plos-pone-0005681:
Kevin Chen, Jonas Maaskola, Mark Siegal, and co-authors rechecked a popular tool for predicting microRNA targets in 2009. MicroRNAs are tiny RNA bits that tune gene activity by binding to messenger RNA. The PITA program scores targets by binding strength and by how open the site is.

Using population gene data from fruit flies, the team tested whether PITA's calls hold up. They found the program was less precise than its first report claimed. That gap matters, because labs spend months chasing predicted targets. A sharper test of prediction tools keeps that work aimed at sites most likely to be real.
plos-pone-0005781:
Anésia Santos and co-authors studied in 2009 how a plant defense receptor fine-tunes its own activation. The receptor NIK1 is a target of a virus protein that shuts down the plant's antiviral alarm. NIK1 belongs to a family of receptor-like kinases that guard cell surfaces.

The team found NIK1 adds phosphate tags to its activation loop in a step-by-step pattern. Single threonine spots in that loop play different roles in the kinase's power. Mapping those steps shows how the antiviral signal is dialed up. Plant viruses and their hosts are locked in an arms race, and the loop is one contested dial.
plos-pone-0005881:
Sarah Devantier and co-authors watched in 2009 how doctors sort patients when forced to choose which of two a third most resembles. Experts in many fields see the deep structure of a problem where novices see surface details. Whether that holds in clinical reasoning was less studied.

In the triad task, clinicians grouped patients, revealing how context shapes their categories. Their choices integrated background information into management thinking, not just symptoms. Understanding that integration helps train doctors and design decision aids. The study treats diagnosis as thinking, not mere pattern matching, and shows the context experts silently include.
plos-pone-0005981:
Regulatory T cells keep the immune system from attacking the body itself. Timothy Radstake, Lenny van Bon, Jasper Broen and colleagues asked whether those peacekeepers fail in systemic sclerosis, a disease that hardens skin and organs. Their 2009 PLOS ONE study compares patients with limited and with diffuse forms of the disease.

Patients had more regulatory cells, not fewer, but the cells worked less well. The flaw tracked with low levels of CD69 and of TGF-beta, two signs of a working peacekeeper. A larger but weaker guard force fits a disease of slow self-attack, and the named markers give clinics a way to gauge the failure.
plos-pone-0006081:
How a molecule leaves its pocket in a protein is as telling as how it enters. Dong Long, Yuguang Mu and Daiwen Yang simulated that exit in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper models ligand dissociation from liver fatty acid binding protein, a carrier that holds fatty acids and, unusually, can fit two molecules in its cavity at once.

Entry and exit routes for this protein family had puzzled the field for decades. A simulation can watch the exit frame by frame, which no bench test can do. The route it finds helps explain how the carrier loads and unloads its cargo, a basic step in how the liver handles fat and some drugs.
plos-pone-0006181:
Cells pause and repair themselves when their DNA is damaged, rather than dividing with broken instructions. Domenica Paparatto and colleagues studied two guard kinases, Chk1 and Cds1, in fission yeast for a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. They exposed the yeast to cisplatin, a cancer drug that harms DNA, and watched how the guards affected survival.

Both kinases proved important for yeast cells to live through the drug's damage. The guards delay division, buying time for repair work to finish. Yeast is a simple stand-in for the same safety system in human cells. Understanding it helps explain why some cancer cells resist drugs that attack DNA.
plos-pone-0006281:
Plague bacteria carry a versatile weapon called the V antigen on a small extra DNA ring. Tracy DiMezzo and colleagues tracked that antigen inside infected cells grown in the lab, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. V can quiet the host immune response and also helps switch on other attack proteins.

The team followed where V travels within cells during Yersinia pestis infection. Its route and timing were largely unmapped before this work. A clear trafficking map fills a gap in how plague disarms its host. The details may expose points where the process can be blocked.
plos-pone-0006381:
Low oxygen in tumors pushes cancer cells toward a mobile, spreading state. Ingrid Moen and colleagues gave hyperbaric oxygen to rats with mammary tumors in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Tumor hypoxia is relevant for growth, metabolism, and the transition that lets cells migrate.

Hyperoxic treatment induced the reverse transition, from mesenchymal back to epithelial character, in the rat adenocarcinoma model. Settled cells spread less readily than mobile ones. Oxygen therapy thus did more than feed tissue; it changed tumor identity. The result supports studying oxygen as an adjunct in cancer care.
plos-pone-0006481:
Dennis vanEngelsdorp and colleagues described colony collapse disorder in honey bees for PLOS ONE in 2009. Over two winters, large-scale losses of managed honey bee colonies in the United States had gone unexplained. No known cause fit the pattern. Beekeepers found hives empty of adult bees with food still present.

A descriptive study is the first step when a new syndrome appears. The authors set out what the disorder looks like and how cases can be defined. Clear definitions let later studies compare data across apiaries and states. The work helped organize the search for causes of a crisis for pollination and farming.
plos-pone-0006581:
Richard Piech, Jade Lewis, Caroline Parkinson, and colleagues scanned brains during food judgments in PLOS ONE in 2009. How much we desire a meal depends on both the constituent foods and how hungry we are. Not every meal becomes more desirable with increasing hunger, though. The brain therefore evaluates foods in a hunger-dependent way.

The team identified neural correlates of appetite and hunger-related evaluative judgments. Brain imaging shows which areas scale their response with hunger. Those areas are targets for understanding overeating and appetite loss. The study connects a daily experience, choosing food, to measurable brain activity.
plos-pone-0006681:
Dena L. Schanzer and colleagues modeled influenza testing in Canada for PLOS ONE in 2009. Public health systems watch the weekly share of lab tests positive for influenza. That share helps officials spot periods of flu activity. How well it works depends on the sensitivity of the testing itself. A test that misses cases can distort the picture of a season.

The team used modelling to estimate that sensitivity from national data. They drew on results from a national respiratory virus detection program. Their estimates show how much influenza laboratory testing likely catches or misses. Knowing the limits of the test helps interpret surveillance numbers honestly. It can also guide improvements in how Canada tracks flu each year.
plos-pone-0006781:
Christian Rabeling and his team found an ant whose queens need no mates in PLOS ONE in 2009. Sex rules in most of life, though it costs more than cloning. Mixing genes speeds change and clears bad gene faults. True cases of sex-free life are rare and prized as proof. The ant is Mycocepurus smithii, which farms fungus for food.

The team showed this ant breeds by thelytokous parthenogenesis. In plain words, females hatch from eggs no male has touched. Queens can fill a nest with daughters on their own. An ant that skips sex breaks the rules for social insects. It helps science weigh what sex is truly worth.
plos-pone-0006881:
Yuki Kawakubo and his team gauged blood flow in the front brain of youths with autism in PLOS ONE in 2009. Faults in that brain zone have long been tied to autism. Close kin of those with autism can show odd brain acts too. Tests of social skill bring some of those gaps to light. How the front brain grows up was less clear.

Growth of the front brain's blood flow lagged in autism. Kin with no autism shared part of that lag. A trait found in kin may mark a passed-down weak point. Blood flow tests are pain-free and safe for youths. The mark could help track growth and test early help.
plos-pone-0006981:
Pankaj Goyal, Antje Behring, Abhishek Kumar, and colleagues described a little-known enzyme in PLOS ONE in 2009. The human kinome holds hundreds of protein kinases. More than a hundred of them had unknown jobs at the time. One was STK35, a serine-threonine kinase in a small kinase family.

The team identified and characterized a form named STK35L1. They also traced its counterparts and close relatives across vertebrates. Mapping a kinase's family tree is the first step to finding what it switches on. Any of these unstudied kinases could later prove to be a drug target.
plos-pone-0007081: David Metzgar, Greg Skochko, Carl Gibbins, and colleagues evaluated and validated a real-time PCR test for human adenovirus 14 in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their assay was built to detect the virus in patient samples and to count how much was present. A validated test of this kind gives clinics and labs a trusted way to spot this adenovirus strain during outbreaks.
plos-pone-0007181:
Derek M. Dykxhoorn, Yichao Wu, Huangming Xie, and colleagues wrote a 2009 PLOS ONE paper on breast cancer spread. Cancer becomes most dangerous when cells leave the first tumor and colonize distant tissues. That last step, forming new tumors far away, is the least understood part of metastasis.

The authors study a small RNA molecule called miR-200 in mouse breast cancer cells. They report that miR-200 helps cancer cells colonize distant sites and form metastases. Their work points to colonization, not just invasion, as a step worth targeting in treatment research.
plos-pone-0007281:
Christopher R. Cederroth and Serge Nef studied early diet and adult sugar control in mice in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Dietary soy and its phytoestrogens may benefit fat and glucose metabolism. The authors had shown that males fed high soy from conception had lower weight and fat as adults.

The authors now examine fetal programming of adult glucose homeostasis. They ask how early soy exposure sets later blood sugar regulation. Their mouse work tests whether effects begin before birth rather than only through adult diet. The findings inform debates about soy feeding in early life.
plos-pone-0007381:
Nancy O. Duah, Helen A. Weiss, Annette Jepson, and colleagues used twins to study inherited control of malaria antibodies in 2009. Understanding how far genetics regulates acquired immunity to common infections is important. A classical twin study can estimate the heritable share of variation in measurable immune traits between pairs of twins.

The authors assess antibody isotype and subclass responses to Plasmodium falciparum antigens. Different antibody classes perform different defense jobs. They estimate heritability of those responses. Their PLOS ONE results show how much malaria immunity runs in families, which matters for vaccine design.
plos-pone-0007481:
Tamara Broderick and David MacKay published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on choosing items with only a single switch. Some users can produce just one reliable input: a button press, a blink, or a sip of air. Selection methods built for them are often slow and rigid. The same problem appears in mobile devices and in secure communication. The authors present a method meant to be both fast and flexible.

Their approach lets a user pick from many options using only that one repeated signal. Speed comes from how the options are organized and timed. Flexibility means the method adapts to different tasks and users. For people with severe motor impairments, faster selection means faster speech and writing. The paper is a design contribution to accessible computing, with uses beyond disability as well.
plos-pone-0007581:
Nidia Alvarez-Rueda, Marlène Biron, and Patrice Le Pape published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on Leishmania mexicana, a parasite that invades human cells. Invasion is a complex meeting of parasite and host machinery. Signals fire in both cells during the encounter. Little was known about protein kinase C and its relatives in the parasite during that meeting. The team measured a PKC-like activity as contact begins.

The parasite's infectivity tracked with that kinase-like signal. When the parasite touches a host macrophage, the signal switches on. That timing marks it as part of the invasion machinery rather than background noise. A trigger this specific is a possible weak point. Leishmania causes disfiguring disease across the tropics, and new drug targets are scarce. The study ties one measurable signal to the moment of entry.
plos-pone-0007681:
James Heron and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It asks how the brain tells self-made events from outside ones. When we act, our actions produce sights and sounds. The brain must judge which events it caused and which came from the world.

The team used time shifts to study this judgment. People adapted to an artificial delay between an action and its effect, and their sense of timing changed. The shift worked across senses, not just one. That points to a shared timing system that sits above sight and touch alone.
plos-pone-0007781:
Amy Englert and Michael Greene published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It asks how Brazilian free-tailed bats recognize their roostmates by smell. These bats are deeply social and crowd into roosts that can hold millions. Life in such crowds demands a way to tell friend from stranger.

The authors tested whether chemical cues guide both recognition and roost choice. Bats may use scent to find their own colony's roost among many. Chemical recognition in these vast colonies had barely been studied. The work adds smell to the story of how bat societies hold together.
plos-pone-0007881:
Ivo Ploemen and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It makes the malaria parasite's liver stage visible in real time. After a mosquito bite, Plasmodium parasites first grow inside the liver. That phase is important, yet hard to study.

Infection rates in lab animals and cultured cells are low. The methods to watch parasites develop inside cells were also complicated. The team used real time imaging to visualize and count the rodent malaria liver stage. Clear numbers from this phase can speed vaccine and drug tests. The liver stage is a tempting bottleneck to attack.
plos-pone-0007981:
Maria Gonzalez and colleagues tracked plant virus particles meeting immune scout cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. The particles come from cowpea mosaic virus, a plant germ now used as a carrier in vaccine design. To work, a carrier must first reach the cells that start an immune response.

Tests in dishes and in live animals showed how the scouts take the particles in and react. That meeting shapes how strong and what kind the later response will be. Knowing the details lets designers tune plant-virus carriers so vaccines built on them work better and safer.
plos-pone-0008081:
Edwin van Dellen and colleagues turned brain recordings into network maps in epilepsy patients for PLOS ONE in 2009. Temporal lobe epilepsy that resists drugs is often treated by surgery, usually after years of seizures. What those years do to local brain networks was little known.

Graph methods, which chart how points link, showed the networks around the seizure zone had changed their wiring over the long illness. The maps give surgeons and doctors a new way to read the cost of waiting. They may also help pick which patients gain most from surgery.
plos-pone-0008181:
Frank Norbert Gellerich and co-authors reported brain cell energy findings in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their work concerns mitochondria, the parts of cells that make most of the cell's energy. They studied how mitochondria in the brain respond to glutamate, a key signal chemical. The surprise lay outside the mitochondria themselves.

Calcium outside the mitochondria, at very low levels found in the body, switched on energy production. The effect was strong and worked only through this outside signal. It let mitochondria raise output on demand when glutamate was present. The finding changes how scientists picture energy control in brain cells.
plos-pone-0008281:
Andrew M. Prpich, Yuebiao Sheng, and Wei Wang asked a physics question in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Surface tension is a fundamental property of a liquid surface. It matters in natural, engineering, and biomedical processes. Research so far focused largely on the liquid side of a surface. Little attention went to the vapor side above it.

The authors asked which phase, liquid or vapor, matters more for surface tension. Their analysis reframes a classic concept in physical chemistry. The answer affects how scientists model droplets, bubbles, and films. It is a basic question with wide practical reach.
plos-pone-0008381:
Gerrit Volkmann and Xiang-Qin Liu presented a protein labeling method in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Site-specific labeling helps scientists study protein structure, folding, and interactions. Current methods for such labeling are few and limited. New methods are therefore needed by protein researchers. Their approach labels the tail end, the C-terminus, of a protein.

They combined a synthetic peptide with a split-intein to attach biotin. Biotin tags make proteins easy to pull out and track. Labeling only the tail end leaves the rest of the protein untouched. The method widens options for protein characterization.
plos-pone-0008481:
Helena Christiansen and co-authors study two collagen genes in zebrafish in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Collagens are strong proteins that shape tissues such as bone and cartilage. Most fibrillar collagens had been linked to human disease. Type XXVII collagen was a recent exception with no known role. The genes are called col27a1a and col27a1b in zebrafish. The team test what they do early in life.

They find both genes are needed to shape the notochord. The notochord is the early rod that guides spine growth. The genes also affect bone mineral buildup and later spine growth. Their loss thus disrupts the whole axial skeleton.
plos-pone-0008581:
Nathan Boles and co-authors study a checkpoint gene in blood formation in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Erythropoiesis is the process that makes red blood cells. It provides the body's oxygen transport system. It is highly regulated, yet few mechanisms behind it were known. Checkpoint Kinase 1, or Chk1, is best known for guarding DNA during cell division. The team test mice with only one working copy of Chk1.

Having half the normal dose causes anemia in those mice. Their red cell formation is defective as well. A DNA guard thus proves essential for making red cells. The finding links cell cycle control to a common blood disorder.
plos-pone-0008681:
Laetitia Chapel, Xavier Castelló, Claire Bernard, and colleagues used math to study dying languages. Their 2010 PLOS ONE article builds a simple model of two languages in direct rivalry. In the model, speakers drift toward the tongue they see as more useful or respected. Public action, like schooling or media support, can raise that standing.

The team tested two setups for how standing can change over time. They asked when a weaker language can hold on instead of vanishing. The model also shows how fast a language bounces back after a shock. Such work can guide real efforts to keep minority languages alive.
plos-pone-0008781:
Marla Keller, Pedro Mesquita, N. Merna Torres, and colleagues tested an HIV-blocking gel under real-life conditions. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The gel, called PRO 2000, is a vaginal microbicide meant to stop HIV. Trials usually test such gels in women who abstain from sex. Sex itself can spread or dilute a gel, though. Semen can also blunt antiviral action in lab tests.

The team measured gel levels and antiviral strength after intercourse. Both the amount present and the killing power mattered for protection. Their findings shape how future microbicide trials should be designed. Real-world checks prevent false confidence from abstinent-only studies.
plos-pone-0008881:
Malathesha Ganachari, Jorge Ruiz-Morales, Juan Gomez de la Torre Pretell, and colleagues tested a two-gene combination for tuberculosis risk. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. One gene, MCP-1, helps call immune cells to infection sites. A variant form of it raised TB risk in unvaccinated Mexicans and Koreans. A second variant, in the MMP-1 gene, might add to that risk. Whether the pair matters in BCG-vaccinated people was unknown.

Vaccinated carriers of both variants developed pulmonary TB more often. The joint effect exceeded either variant acting alone. Gene pairs, not single genes, may decide many infection outcomes. The result refines genetic risk testing for TB.
plos-pone-0008981:
Victoria Abraira and co-authors tested whether two proteins that stick together in a dish matter inside the ear, in PLOS ONE in 2010. One protein, Lrig3, sits in cell membranes and shapes how tissues form. The other group, the ErbB receptors, relays growth signals into cells. Lrig3 is needed for the inner ear to develop its normal shape.

In lab tests the proteins did bind to each other. But animals suggested that this binding is not what builds the inner ear. The ear formed its shape through some other action of Lrig3. Publishing a clear negative result like this saves other labs a wrong turn.
plos-pone-0009081:
Vyacheslav Furtak and co-authors showed that disturbing one cell protein weakens HIV, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Retroviruses such as HIV are obligate parasites that borrow host proteins to copy themselves. Host cells also hold proteins that restrict infection and defend them. Mov10 is part of P-bodies, the granules where cells store and process RNA.

Perturbing Mov10 sharply reduced HIV-1's infectivity in the team's tests. New virus particles still formed but were less able to infect fresh cells. The host factor thus helps the virus finish its life cycle properly. Blocking the help Mov10 gives is a possible new angle for antiviral drugs.
plos-pone-0009181:
Mariana Hecht and co-authors published this genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2010. It concerns American trypanosomes, the parasites that cause Chagas disease. DNA can sometimes pass from one species into another and then be handed down to offspring. Such transfers are major events in evolution, but proving one happened is hard.

The team adapted a sensitive DNA test to hunt for parasite sequences inside human DNA. They looked for cases where trypanosome DNA had entered human cells and then passed to the next generation. Documenting that inheritance would show the transfer is not a one-off accident. It would mean parasite genes can become a lasting part of a human family line.
plos-pone-0009281:
Xiaoling Gao and co-authors published this tuberculosis study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Tuberculosis remains a global health problem, and the BCG vaccine protects only unevenly. A kind of T cell defense, called type-1 immunity, is known to be vital for fighting the infection. Less clear was how different dendritic cell groups shape the fight.

The team took dendritic cells from mice infected with BCG, the vaccine strain. One subset, the CD8-positive cells, calmed the harmful reactions caused by a later challenge infection. The CD8-negative subset did not. That split suggests future vaccines should aim to engage the right dendritic cell subset, not just any immune response.
plos-pone-0009381:
John Tregoning and co-authors published this lung infection study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Respiratory syncytial virus, or RSV, is a major cause of lung illness in infants. CD8 T cells help clear the virus from the lungs. Too much T cell activity, though, causes part of the disease itself.

The team studied a chemical signal called MIP1 alpha, also known as CCL3. In mice, this chemokine set the balance between T cell groups in the lung. That balance decided how severe the illness became during a first infection. Tuning one signal might one day let doctors keep the cure while cutting the harm.
plos-pone-0009481:
Karlee Silver and colleagues studied malaria in pregnancy in PLOS ONE in 2010. When malaria infects the placenta, babies are often born too small. Low birth weight raises the risk of death and poor health. Proteins called angiopoietins guide the growth of blood vessels in the placenta. The team measured these proteins in infected mothers.

Levels of the two main angiopoietins were out of balance where malaria was present. That upset went with lower birth weight. The link suggests that broken vessel growth is one path from infection to harm. Guarding those vessel signals could be a way to protect unborn children.
plos-pone-0009581:
Carl Soulsbury compared mating and fatherhood across mammals in PLOS ONE in 2010. Larger testes are read as a sign of stronger sperm competition between males. In some groups, social mating systems match that pattern well. In others, the match is poor. Soulsbury gathered data on testes size, mating systems, and who actually fathers the young across mammal species.

The study tests whether size alone predicts real paternity patterns. Genetic fatherhood data give a firmer check than social labels do. Results of this kind refine a classic claim in evolution. They show where a simple body measure works as a guide, and where it misleads.
plos-pone-0009681:
Cytomegalovirus is a common virus that can hide in the body for life. Christopher Snyder and colleagues asked in 2010 how the immune system first learns to attack it. They worked with a mouse form of the virus. The mutant strain could infect cells but could not spread between them.

Even with spread blocked, the crippled virus primed most of the virus-specific killer T cells. The priming worked through cross-presentation, where one cell shows pieces of the virus to T cells. That result shows the immune system does not need a fully spreading infection to build strong defenses.
plos-pone-0009781:
Immunoassays are tests that use antibodies to detect specific targets in a sample. John Cooper and colleagues built a multiplex version on a CMOS microarray chip. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. CMOS is the chip technology used in most cameras and sensors.

Multiplex means the chip can run many tests at once. The team placed antibodies at set spots on the array in a targeted way. They then tuned the assay for sensitivity, using electrochemical detection to read results. Sensitive chip tests could speed medical and lab testing.
plos-pone-0009881:
Marriage can be modeled, feelings and all, with the tools of mathematics. José-Manuel Rey built a mathematical model of sentimental dynamics that ends in marital dissolution. The single-author study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

Sentimental dynamics means how feelings between partners rise and fall over time. The model tracks those shifts until they cross into breakup. The equations let small shifts build toward sudden endings. A model cannot capture a whole marriage, but it can expose tipping points. Such work shows how math can probe even intimate human bonds.
plos-pone-0009981:
Cells marked for orderly death carry molecular signatures that give them away. Angélique Godet and colleagues found a new such signature in the way proteins link up. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The signature is a combinatorial PP1-binding consensus motif, a short shared pattern in protein sequences. Combinatorial means the pattern mixes a few fixed and flexible parts. Apoptosis is the cell's tidy self-destruction program. PP1 is an enzyme that strips phosphate tags from proteins. A shared motif tied to apoptosis could help spot dying cells and new drug targets.
plos-pone-0010081:
Julian M Gluck is first author on a 2010 PLOS ONE methods paper for making tagged proteins in bacteria. Many animal and virus proteins carry a fatty tag, myristate, fixed by an enzyme bacteria lack. Labs need tagged protein in bulk for structure work, but old setups used two plasmids, small DNA rings, at once.

The new single-plasmid system makes both the enzyme and the target protein in one E. coli cell batch. Using Nef, an HIV protein, as the test case, the team got about twenty milligrams of fully tagged, pure protein per liter of culture. The approach should suit many other tagged proteins and large studies.
plos-pone-0010181:
The authors were Piotr Ruchala, Mohamad Navab, Chun-Ling Jung, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study built a peptide, a short protein chain, with anti-inflammatory action. Many Gram-positive bacteria release pore-forming toxins that share a short conserved segment. That segment binds cholesterol, and the team used its sequence as a template for their design.

Their peptide, named Oxpholipin 11D, binds cholesterol and oxidized phospholipids, damaged fats linked to inflammation. Soaking up those fats could calm harmful inflammation in blood vessels and elsewhere. The design shows how a toxin's own trick can be turned into a candidate therapy.
plos-pone-0010281:
The authors were Silvia Casarotto, Leonor Romero Lauro, Valentina Bellina, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study combined brain stimulation with brain recording. A magnetic pulse method, TMS, probes how excitable and connected the cortex is. Reading the response with dense EEG gives a direct, non-invasive measure in humans, useful for tracking disease and recovery over time.

The team found EEG responses shift when stimulation settings change. Responses also proved repeatable over time within a person. Both facts are needed before the method can track brain changes in clinics. The work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.
plos-pone-0010381:
Maria Sanchez-Vives and colleagues created a virtual hand illusion in PLOS ONE in 2010. Our sense of owning our body feels fixed, yet simple tricks can shake it. In the classic rubber hand trick, touch seen on a fake hand is felt as one's own. This team moved the trick into virtual reality. What the eyes saw and what the hand did were linked by computer.

When the virtual hand moved in step with the real one, people felt it was theirs. The brain, it seems, accepts a match between sight and movement as proof of ownership. Such illusions help scientists study body awareness and its disorders. They also matter for designing prosthetic limbs and remote robot hands. Ownership, the study shows, is a judgment the brain keeps updating.
plos-pone-0010481:
Yasuhiro Matsuo and Tetsu Kamitani reported a Parkinson's-linked protein inside melanoma tumors in PLOS ONE in 2010. Melanoma causes most skin cancer deaths worldwide. Parkinson's disease involves loss of brain cells and is tied to a protein called alpha-synuclein. Population studies had noticed the two diseases occur together more than chance allows. The team asked whether the brain protein shows up in melanoma.

Finding alpha-synuclein in melanoma tissue gives the population link a physical clue. Shared proteins might mean shared pathways between nerve decay and skin cancer. That could open odd but useful treatment ideas across fields. It also warns that drugs for one disease may affect the other. The study connects two specialties that rarely talk.
plos-pone-0010581:
Dawei Gou and colleagues studied gene silencing in fruit flies for PLOS ONE in 2010. Cells can switch genes off by adding small chemical marks to DNA, a process called methylation. In flies, most marking was thought to happen early, before hatching.

The team found that a protein named SETDB1 keeps methylation going after the embryo stage. Without it, marks faded and some silent genes became active. So the same system that sets up the pattern also maintains it through later life. The result widens the known role of SETDB1 in keeping the genome stable.
plos-pone-0010681:
Lindsay Edwards and colleagues measured muscle energy use in climbers on Everest, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Thin air at high altitude starves the body of oxygen. Healthy climbers offer a clean way to study low-oxygen stress without disease muddying the picture. The work was part of the Caudwell Xtreme Everest trip.

A scan method that tracks phosphorus in muscle showed how energy stores were spent and refilled. After time at altitude, muscle handling of energy had changed in clear ways. The shifts help explain weakness at altitude. They also model what happens in patients whose lungs or blood fail to deliver enough oxygen.
plos-pone-0010781:
Tricia Petruney and colleagues mapped who holds influence over HIV prevention policy, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Voluntary contraception by women living with HIV prevents more infant infections, at lower cost, than drug regimens alone. Yet prevention programs still focus almost wholly on drugs for mother-to-child transmission.

The team charted key officials, funders, and advocates and asked their views. Support for contraception as prevention was broader than expected, but a few gatekeepers held back wider adoption. Knowing exactly whose minds must change turns a vague advocacy hope into a list of meetings. The study treats influence itself as data for saving lives.
plos-pone-0010881:
Dmitri Chilov, Natalia Sinjushina, Jonna Saarimäki-Vire and co-authors published this mouse development study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Beta-catenin is a protein with two jobs: it relays signals from the Wnt family of growth cues and it helps hold cells together. The team studied what happens when beta-catenin is locked on in the developing mouse midbrain and the segment just behind it.

Stabilizing the protein strongly raised several Wnt target genes, including Fgf8, another key patterning signal, even in other tissues such as the limb. Oddly, the Wnt1 signal itself soon fell, hinting at a self-limiting feedback loop. Front-to-back and top-to-bottom patterning of the brain region went astray in step. Chilov and colleagues show how one protein coordinates a whole signaling network that lays out the early brain.
plos-pone-0010981:
Alexander Hoare, Stephen Kerr, Kiat Ruxrungtham and co-authors published this HIV modeling study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Access to first-line HIV treatment was expanding across Southeast Asia, but second-line drugs for patients whose virus becomes resistant were scarce. The authors built a mathematical model of a regional epidemic to forecast the hidden cost of that gap.

Their simulations show that after a decade of universal first-line treatment, up to a fifth of newly infected, untreated people could carry drug-resistant strains, depending on how fit those strains are. Adding yearly viral load testing, with real second-line therapy for those failing, cut transmitted resistance dramatically in the model. Hoare and colleagues warn that treatment scale-up without monitoring breeds the very resistance that makes HIV harder to treat.
plos-pone-0011081:
Buescher, Achberger, Amusan and colleagues published plant research in PLOS ONE in 2010. They studied Arabidopsis, a small plant often used in genetics labs. Different wild groups of this plant store minerals in their tissues at different levels, and the team asked whether genes explain the gap.

Comparing selected plant groups, the team linked natural gene differences to differences in mineral content. Those links point to genes that tune how plants take up and store key elements. The findings could help breed crops with better mineral value for people who eat them. They also show how wild variation can guide crop science.
plos-pone-0011181:
Zarate, Delhommeau, Wood and colleagues trained singers in PLOS ONE in 2010. The training taught people to hear very small pitch differences, finer than a normal note step. The team then measured singing accuracy and changes in brain responses after the practice.

Training improved how accurately people sang and altered brain activity tied to hearing. That shows adult brains remain flexible for sound skills with focused practice. The result supports music education with hard evidence of brain change. It may also help design training for people with hearing or speech difficulties.
plos-pone-0011281:
Rignell-Hydbom, Elfving, Ivarsson and colleagues studied womb exposure in PLOS ONE in 2010. Some long lasting chlorine based pollutants pass from mother to unborn child. Using a nested case control design, the team related mothers' exposure to later type 1 diabetes in their children.

Their analysis links prenatal exposure to raised diabetes risk. That adds the womb period to the list of times when environment shapes lifelong health. The evidence backs limits on pollutants that persist in bodies for years. Protecting unborn children is a strong reason to keep such chemicals out of food chains and homes.
plos-pone-0011381:
Gregory Schimizzi, Joshua Currie, and Stephen Rogers reported in 2010 that the amount of one cell enzyme changes how well common cancer drugs work. The drugs attack microtubules, the rods that cells use to divide, and tumors often resist them. The enzyme, a kinesin that takes microtubules apart, varies in amount from cell to cell.

Cells making more of the dismantling enzyme responded differently to microtubule drugs than cells making less of it. That link means a simple measurement of enzyme level could help predict which tumors a drug will hit hard. Oncologists need such predictors, since the same drug can shrink one tumor and barely touch another. The study turns a basic fact about cell structure into a practical clue for matching patients to treatment.
plos-pone-0011481:
Franziska Meier-Stiegen and co-authors showed in 2010 that the same master signal switches on different genes depending on the cell it reaches. Notch1 signaling tells embryonic cells which identity to adopt, and it is reused across many tissues. If the signal is constant, the variety of outcomes must come from the receiving cells, and the team tested that idea during early cell differentiation.

The genes Notch1 activated varied with cellular context, and the targets included both drivers of cell lineages and inhibitors that restrain them. Turning on a driver and its brake together is a way to keep development precise and reversible. The context lesson complicates any simple story in which one signal means one thing. Drug developers who target Notch must reckon with the tissue they are in, since the same drug can push different programs in different cells.
plos-pone-0011581:
Juliette Pavie and co-authors compared five rapid HIV tests in a real hospital clinic, publishing in PLOS ONE in 2010. Health officials in several countries were urging wider HIV testing at the time. Rapid tests licensed in Europe promised fast answers, but their accuracy on mouth fluid versus finger-stick blood was still unclear.

The team ran the five tests side by side on both sample types in routine care, rather than in a lab alone. Their comparison shows how sensitivity shifts with the sample used. For clinics choosing a kit, the results give practical guidance on which tests and samples can be trusted.
plos-pone-0011681:
Lin Chen and co-authors mapped insecticide resistance in Chinese mosquitoes, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Pyrethroid sprays are used heavily in China and worldwide to control disease-carrying pests. The mosquito Culex pipiens pallens has increasingly survived those sprays through a change known as knockdown resistance, tied to its sodium channel gene.

The team examined variation in that gene across mosquito populations. Their molecular survey shows how resistance is structured and spreading. Accurate monitoring like this lets control programmes choose sprays wisely and slow the loss of their main chemical weapon.
plos-pone-0011781:
James Fordyce offered a caution about a popular evolution statistic, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Family trees are increasingly used to infer how the pace of species formation changed through history. A common test compares observed branching times against a steady pure-birth expectation, using a measure known as the gamma statistic.

Fordyce shows a falling diversification rate does not necessarily signal an early burst of speciation. The same pattern can arise in other ways, so the standard reading overreaches. His interpretation guide keeps family-tree readers honest about what branches can and cannot say.
plos-pone-0011881:
Jean-François Pessiot and colleagues built in 2010 a software system called PeakRegressor for finding where a gene switch protein binds DNA. The switch in question is STAT1, which turns genes on during immune signaling. Knowing its true binding sites from sequence patterns alone is a standing puzzle in bioinformatics.

PeakRegressor combines motif pattern, position, and combinations of signals to pick out composite patterns that mark real binding sites. It also flags DNA variants that might disturb those sites and change gene control. Tools that read binding rules more accurately help explain why some harmless-looking DNA differences alter immune responses.
plos-pone-0011981:
Amandine Bemmo and co-workers profiled in 2010 how mouse breast tumors edit their gene messages as they gain the power to spread. Breast cancer kills mainly through metastasis, and changes in mRNA splicing, the editing of gene messages, are increasingly tied to cancer traits. The team compared tumors with different metastatic abilities at the level of individual exons.

The profiling revealed splicing changes specific to the more metastatic tumors. Each changed message can produce a protein version better suited to travel and colonization. A catalog of those edits gives researchers candidate switches behind spread, and candidate markers for judging how dangerous a tumor is likely to become.
plos-pone-0012081:
Marit Farenhorst and co-workers found in 2010 that a bug-killing fungus and a tired spray drug kill far more jointly than each does on its own. The spray, permethrin, is a main tool against the mosquitoes that spread malaria in West Africa, but the local kind can now shrug the drug off. Fungi that sicken and kill bugs are a known extra arm, long used on farm pests.

Put to the test on drug-proof mosquitoes, the fungus and the spray showed a true team effect: each made the other bite harder. That kind of team play can bring a cheap spray back from the dead, since the dose that fails alone may kill when a fungus has first sickened the bug. A fungus spray for house walls could thus stretch the life of the sprays malaria work now leans on.
plos-pone-0012181:
Zhengsheng Li, Megan Mulligan, Xusheng Wang, and co-authors traced wide differences between mouse strains to one gene change, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The gene makes COMT, an enzyme that clears dopamine and related messengers, shaping mood, thinking, and responses to drugs. A jumping piece of DNA landed in this gene in some mouse lines, changing how its message is built.

That one insertion explained broad differences in the enzyme's levels across the body and in behavior between strains. Studies using these mice to model human thinking or drug response must reckon with it. More broadly, the case shows how a single hidden variant can quietly drive many results blamed on other causes.
plos-pone-0012281:
Kwesi Frimpong-Boateng, Nico van Rooijen, and Ralf Geiben-Lynn studied how regulatory T cells blunt DNA vaccines in mice, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Regulatory T cells calm immune responses, a vital service against self-attack, but they may also muffle the first response to a vaccine and weaken it. Natural killer cells are among the earliest responders after vaccination, before the targeted defense assembles.

The team found the regulators suppress those early killer cells during plasmid DNA vaccination, weakening the later CD8 T cell response through a calming cytokine. If a vaccine's own brakes can be eased briefly, the same dose might protect better. That insight feeds the design of DNA vaccines, a platform long praised for safety but dogged by weak responses.
plos-pone-0012381:
Izabela Nowak, Edyta Majorczyk, Andrzej Wiśniewski and colleagues examined a natural killer cell gene in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. The gene, KIR2DS5, switches on killer cells of the immune system, though its exact target is unknown. It had been linked to outcomes after stem cell transplants, prompting the team to test its ties to several human diseases.

They compared how often the gene appears in patients and in healthy people across those diseases. The pattern suggests the gene may guard against some conditions while playing no role in others. Such clues help explain why immune gene mixes differ between populations, and they point to diseases where killer cell activity deserves a closer look.
plos-pone-0012481:
Carl Drews and Weiqing Han modeled wind-driven water drops at the Gulf of Suez and the eastern Nile Delta, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Wind setdown is the fall in water level when strong wind pushes surface water away for many hours. The effect is famous from accounts of sea crossings in the region, and the physics can be tested with modern weather and ocean models.

The authors simulated sustained winds over the shallow waters and measured how far levels fell and exposed land appeared. Their results show setdown of real consequence under the right wind. Beyond the historical debate, the modeling informs coastal flood science, where wind-driven water moves both ways.
plos-pone-0012581:
Vanessa De Vooght, Jeroen Vanoirbeek, Katrien Luyts and colleagues showed that mouse strain choice can sway asthma model results, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Occupational asthma arises from workplace exposures meeting individual susceptibility. Their chemical-induced asthma model uses a workplace-like sensitizer, but labs use different mouse strains, and genetic background can quietly rewrite outcomes.

Running the model across strains produced different severities and immune patterns. A model whose answer depends on the strain demands careful reporting and strain-matched comparisons. The work helps occupational health researchers design studies whose conclusions survive the move from one lab's mice to human workers.
plos-pone-0012881:
Moore, Goetz, Van Doornik and co-authors tracked young trout on their first trip from river to sea. Coastal cutthroat trout and steelhead trout meet and hybridise in streams along the North American Pacific coast. What the hybrid young do at sea was largely unknown when they wrote in 2010.

Their study followed the early marine migration of wild cutthroat, steelhead and their hybrids. Different migration timing or routes change which fish survive and breed. That knowledge helps managers protect both parent species and understand the hybrids' place.  Tagging let the team follow individual young fish at sea.
plos-pone-0332281:
Ranna Kíssia Alves das Neves and six colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It studies people in Rio de Janeiro who were hospitalized again after catching COVID-19 a second time, between 2020 and 2022. The authors examine associations with vaccination status and with sociodemographic and clinical factors, who patients were and what conditions they carried.

Reinfections that land people back in hospital are the costly core of repeat COVID waves. Knowing whether vaccination and which patient traits track with readmission helps hospitals plan for future surges. Brazilian public health officials and clinicians managing post-COVID care are the readers for this city-level record.
plos-pone-0332781:
Li and colleagues, in a 2026 paper, present a better way to measure the sludge blanket in sewage treatment tanks. Knowing how deep the settled sludge sits helps a plant run cleanly, but murky water confuses existing sound-based meters, which pick up noise and misread the boundary. The team tested their method at a Beijing treatment plant.

Their meter uses an array of sound sensors and hunts for the strongest echo of sound energy bouncing off the sludge surface. Filtering smooths stray spikes, and a peak-picking method separates the true signal from leftover noise. A fault check flags readings that stray too far. In plant tests, readings deviated from true values by a small margin and varied only slightly between repeats. The authors say the method holds up in turbid conditions where optical tools fail, offering plants a sturdier way to automate sludge control.
plos-pone-0335581:
Chloé Tavernier and co-authors compared bat activity in farm solar fields with nearby grasslands in 2026. Solar farms are spreading over farmland, bats are already under pressure, and whether panels displace bats was poorly known.

Detectors recorded calls at the edges of six solar fields and twelve control plots across the year. Every one of the seven species turned up less over solar fields, both in nights present and in calls recorded. Landscape features modified the pattern but never erased it. As solar fields multiply, the authors argue, monitoring bat numbers, not just activity at a moment, becomes essential.
plos-pone-0336281: Zanotti, writing alone, published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on a habit in retail forecasting: mixing models. Shops blend several forecasting models to predict sales, hoping the mix beats each part. Zanotti asks what that blending costs and whether it always pays off, using data from global retail. The answer matters because complex blends cost time and computing power for every planning cycle.
plos-pone-0337381:
Diego Lievano Parra and colleagues used rats with partial damage to the brain's dopamine system to watch walking problems emerge over time, modeling the hidden early phase of Parkinson's disease. A low dose of a toxin was placed on one side of the movement center. For six weeks the rats crossed a horizontal ladder while camera software tracked every step and slip.

Stepping errors rose after the lesion, peaked around the third week, and then eased somewhat while staying above normal. Walking speed changed less consistently, and patterns differed somewhat between males and females. Because early Parkinson's is nearly impossible to catch in people, a timed map of the first motor slips in animals gives researchers a window for testing protective treatments.
plos-pone-0343481:
Yusuke Takatsuru and three colleagues published this 2026 brain-imaging study on how food preference shows up while people eat. Some older adults lose appetite partly because they struggle to picture foods they might enjoy. Using a light-based brain scanner that works at the table, the team recorded front-of-brain activity in healthy young adults.

Each volunteer looked at and then ate a standard home-style meal and a favorite dish they had bought themselves. Brain signals during eating differed by dish, and preference ratings tracked those signals. Takatsuru suggests the readings could one day help clinics judge appetite in older patients without bulky equipment.
plos-pone-0344581:
Hao Pei and co-workers simulate the noise of a large urban electricity substation and design a package of fixes. Transformer hum can disturb nearby homes and offices, and builders need to know what works before concrete is poured. Their 2026 study models one city substation with standard sound software and tests layout changes, barriers, silencers, and stronger enclosure walls in the model.

Barriers and smart layout cut the transformer's noise by a fair band of decibels. Bolt-on silencers took off a further chunk. Improved enclosure walls gave the biggest single cut, enough to bring emissions within safe limits in the simulation. The recipe gives engineers a worked example for quieting substations in noise-sensitive districts.
plos-pone-0345881:
Yuthara Subasinghe leads a team of six interviewing gig workers in Sri Lanka about what keeps them going, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Fourteen workers earning through platforms such as Upwork and Fiverr described their skills and drives in depth. The authors were after the interplay between inner motivation, interest and autonomy, and outer motivation, pay and ratings, and how digital skill feeds both.

Digital skill turned out to be more than a technical asset: it acted as a psychological enabler, feeding feelings of autonomy, competence, and connection that power inner motivation. Inner and outer drivers sometimes reinforced each other and sometimes collided, producing distinct motivation profiles across workers. The resulting typology suggests platforms could design feedback and transparent metrics that support, rather than control, their workers. The authors note the Sri Lankan setting bounds how far the lessons travel.
plos-pone-0346581:
Aziza S Al Adhoobi, Saud M Al Jufaili, and co-authors mapped where two small killifish can live in Oman's desert streams, now and under a warming climate. These fish survive in wadis, the seasonal watercourses of an arid land, and both species are found almost nowhere else. Their 2026 study combined climate mapping software, field checks at twelve stream sites, and an audit of protected areas.

The southern species depended on monsoon moisture and stayed tightly restricted, while its northern relative ranged wider on winter rains. Climate projections pointed to shrinking habitat, and barely any of the best habitat sat inside protected areas. Surprisingly, streams ideal for the killifish held fewer other species overall, and dissolved oxygen proved the single most important water quality factor. The authors call for targeted protection of the best remaining streams.
plos-pone-0347081:
Alexander Cardaras led a team of eight authors on this 2026 paper about reading numbers out of bar charts in medical journals. Charts trapped as pictures inside PDF files block the large reviews that combine trial results. Their four-stage pipeline finds chart panels, reads labels, separates bars, and rebuilds the values from the axes.

Tested on eye disease trials against hand-checked values, the system recovered chart data with usable accuracy. Cardaras calls it a proof of concept: limited to bar charts and one field for now, but a step toward software that harvests published results at scale.
plos-pone-0347781:
Aleena Vikraman and colleagues study why lab-grown stem cells age, in this 2026 PLOS ONE cell biology paper. Stem cells taken from fat are prized for therapy, but under stress they senesce: they stop dividing and lose healing power, partly because their cleanup system for worn-out mitochondria falters.

Two familiar antioxidants, melatonin and coenzyme Q10, were tested for rescue. In stressed cells the pair restored the cleanup process and the upkeep of mitochondrial proteins, easing the senescent state and protecting the cells' ability to keep growing. If the effect holds up, simple antioxidant treatment could help laboratories keep therapeutic stem cells younger and more useful for longer.
plos-pone-0348081:
Eva Cappelli, Marianna Azzolini, and Cristina Ferrari studied nurses who face drug-resistant infections daily. Their study took place in two Italian intensive care units. It appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. Patients with resistant germs demand strict hygiene steps. Emergencies push staff to cut corners at the same time.

The team watched care in action for months. They also held twenty-one interviews with nurses, aides, and doctors. Resilience worked at three levels, they found. Personal resources mattered, and so did team habits. Backing from the hospital mattered most of all. Nurses bent the rules with care rather than dropping them. The authors urge hospitals to build resilience into staffing and training.
plos-pone-0348281:
George Agyei, Augustina Angelina Sylverken, and co-authors drew blood from nearly a thousand people in urban and rural Ghana to chart immunity to the coronavirus over time. Where people live can shape exposure and how long protection lasts. Their 2026 study sampled households across settings in 2023 and 2024, then retested a smaller group a year later for antibodies against two viral proteins and for virus-blocking power.

Past exposure proved equally common in city and countryside, at about forty-seven percent in each. Among those followed for a year, half carried both antibody types, showing combined traces of infection and vaccination. Paired antibody responses actually rose between visits, suggesting fresh boosting despite some fading. Nearly everyone tested had neutralizing antibodies. The authors see durable population immunity, maintained by ongoing exposure.
plos-pone-0348581:
Nan Zhang and co-authors improved three dimensional object detection from vehicle LiDAR in 2026. Self driving cars read the world as point clouds, which are sparse and uneven, so grouping points into objects is error prone.

Their method first separates ground from objects with a cloth simulation filter, then clusters with a tree structure that adapts its settings. An upgraded point network reads features at several scales with skip links. On two public benchmarks it reached high segmentation accuracy with fast per frame times. The pairing of careful clustering with deep reading is the design's answer to messy real road data.
plos-pone-0348681:
Hal Whitehead, Christine M K Clarke, and Ana Eguiguren report that sperm whales off the Galápagos Islands learned to relax around the research boats that photograph them. Photo identification is the backbone of whale science, but a wary whale ruins both the picture and the data. The team tracked how photographic quality and the distance whales allowed changed as individual whales accumulated encounters with the boats.

Experienced whales let boats come closer, and the share of poor, distant photographs fell, clear signs of habituation rather than growing stress. Tolerance made the research itself work better, yielding cleaner identification records. The authors recommend that any long-term wildlife study check for such learning, since animals that habituate, or the opposite, quietly change what the data mean and how ethical the disturbance is.
plos-pone-0348781:
Abel Jonathan Mussa and co-workers survey fungi in mountain soils in Tanzania that kill insects from within. These fungi help hold pest numbers down in nature, but their spread across tropical farm hills is barely mapped. Their 2026 study samples soils at three heights on the Uluguru slopes, in both farmed and fallow fields, and identifies fungi by DNA and by growing them.

Fourteen species turned up, led by two families known for insect killing. Farmed soils at middle and high levels held richer fungal life than fallow ones. In early lab tests, two species killed some fall armyworm caterpillars, a major crop pest. The survey gives farmers and scientists candidate fungi for gentler pest control.
plos-pone-0348881:
Safdar Abbas Kazmi and co-authors built a magnetic nanocomposite for cleaning dyed water with sunlight in 2026. Textile dyes resist breakdown, and a catalyst that works in visible light and can be fished out with a magnet afterwards is attractive.

Joining iron oxide with titanium oxide at the nanoscale improved charge separation, the step that usually wastes light energy. A tuned recipe removed most of a yellow reactive dye at neutral acidity, following predictable kinetics. Scavenger tests identified the active species doing the work. Machine learning helped predict performance. A recoverable catalyst answers the usual objection that nanopowders pollute while cleaning.
plos-pone-0349181:
RETRACTION NOTICE: The PLOS One Editors issued this 2026 notice withdrawing an earlier mouse study claiming that a careful balance of dietary fats eased a disease model of a protein disorder. Readers should not rely on the original findings. The notice grew out of questions about a key figure and about how the animal work was reported.

Part of one figure panel looked much like part of another said to show a different group. The author blamed a preparation error and sent fixes, but editors found still more concerns in the new panels and data. Error bars in several figures also looked unreliable on review. Details about humane endpoints and euthanasia had been missing from the paper as well.
plos-pone-0349281: Parthasarathy and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on a brain-based typing tool. A P300 speller lets a person pick letters by focusing on flashes on a screen, while sensors catch the brain's response. The team tested large language models to predict the intended letters. They compared several models against formal performance bounds. Better spellers could give people who cannot move or speak a faster voice.
plos-pone-0349381:
Yosué Vera and colleagues studied cancer patients who developed bloodstream infections at a referral hospital in Lima, Peru, asking how many died within a month and what raised the risk. They reviewed two hundred ninety-three patients treated between 2020 and 2024. Most had solid tumors, digestive cancers were the largest group, and most had active disease.

Nearly a third of patients died within twenty-eight days of the infection. The first antibiotics chosen matched the infecting germ in about four of five cases. Resistant bacteria are a growing problem in Peru, and this is among the first local studies to measure their toll in cancer care. The numbers give Peruvian oncologists a baseline for improving infection response.
plos-pone-0349781:
Kennedy Dodam Konlan, Hellen Akosua Asante, and Cecilia Eliason interviewed sixteen women in Accra, Ghana, about living with high blood pressure after childbirth, a dangerous and understudied phase of the condition. Their 2026 study recruited women from a regional hospital's postnatal clinic and explored their experiences in depth, sorting the conversations into themes.

Women swung between hope of recovery and fear of complications. Many felt confident following treatment yet struggled with lifestyle changes and home monitoring. Support from spouses, family, and health workers helped, while social stigma hurt. The authors recommend that midwives and nurses actively counter stigma and coach self-management, since the women's own accounts show the condition is managed socially as much as medically.
plos-pone-0349981:
Ying Liu and six colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It builds a workflow that runs from forecast to dispatch for a natural gas transmission network covering a whole region, planned a day ahead. Two parts anchor the workflow: station-level load prediction, forecasting gas demand at each station, and linepack target setting, deciding how much gas to store inside the pipes themselves.

Linepack is the network's built-in buffer, so setting its target well lets operators meet demand swings without strain. Joining forecast to dispatch in one workflow turns prediction into daily operating decisions. Gas network operators facing winter peaks are the readers for a day-ahead routine of this kind.
plos-pone-0350181:
Zoe Rand and colleagues charted forty years of killer whale sightings in Washington's Salish Sea, home to two very different kinds. Southern Resident whales eat fish and are endangered; Bigg's whales hunt marine mammals and answer to different pressures. Using detection records from nineteen seventy-eight to twenty twenty-two, the team modeled how each kind's presence changed across seasons and years.

The fish-eating Residents faded: their chance of being present fell steeply over the period, with the sharpest drop in summer, long their peak season. Bigg's whales moved the other way, rising from rare visitors to a likely presence. The opposite trends show the two groups cannot be managed as one, and they hint at deeper shifts in the food web that feeds the Residents.
plos-pone-0351081:
Filippos Sofos, Zoi Pana, and Dimitris Drikakis built a pneumonia detector for children's chest X-rays that shows its reasoning as one readable formula. Most image AI hides its logic inside huge networks, leaving doctors with a verdict they cannot inspect. Their approach evolves a compact equation from a handful of texture and shape measures taken from the X-ray, measures a radiologist can recognize, like entropy and solidity.

The formula sorted the main dataset with accuracy in the high eighties and held up on a filtered independent test set at just under eighty percent. It was also checked and retuned on a dataset from another source. With vastly fewer numbers inside than a deep network, the equation can be printed, debated, and audited, a different bargain for clinics weighing trust against raw accuracy.
plos-pone-0351181:
Liposarcoma, a cancer of fat tissue in limbs and the trunk, is treated mainly by surgery, yet kidney trouble and muscle loss may shape who survives. Julian Kylies and colleagues reviewed forty-seven adults treated with curative intent, in this 2026 PLOS One study.

Kidney function, muscle amount, and belly fat were measured from scans at diagnosis and again about eleven months later, alongside everyday functioning scores. Declining kidney function traveled with worse muscle measures, fading function, and higher death rates.
