The authors argue these treatable problems deserve routine tracking in sarcoma care, since catching them early could protect both strength and survival.
plos-pone-0351281:
Kholoud Saad Al-Saleh tackles a search problem created by the Arabic language itself, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Encrypted search systems let users query data without exposing it to the server. But Arabic builds dozens of word forms from one root. That bloats the encrypted index and hides matching documents behind spelling variants. The study compares four text preprocessing strategies, three stemmers and analyzers plus a segmenter, against plain normalization inside a working encrypted search scheme.

On a news corpus with benchmark queries, stemming shrank the vocabulary by up to eighty-three percent, with matching savings in index size and transfer cost. A surprise emerged on speed: the plain baseline answered fastest precisely because it retrieved the fewest documents, while better preprocessing found more and paid in time. Scaling tests reached tens of thousands of documents. The result is the first evidence based guide for choosing an Arabic preprocessor.
plos-pone-0351881:
Md Al Saber and a large team designed a candidate vaccine against mpox, the virus behind the twenty twenty-two global outbreak, entirely by computer. They compared sixteen viral genomes to find shared parts, then picked pieces of the virus's surface and envelope proteins most likely to train the immune system. Software stitched the chosen pieces into a single multi-epitope construct and simulated how it should behave.

The design aims for breadth, covering the strains circulating since the outbreak rather than one isolate. Computer checks covered immune targeting, shape, and safety flags, the usual first screen before any laboratory work. Nothing here has touched a cell or an animal, and the authors present it as a blueprint. Its value is speed: if an outbreak strain shifts, this pipeline can draft a matching candidate in weeks.
plos-pone-0352581:
Ahmad Rabbani and four colleagues develop plant-based food packaging films in this 2026 materials study. Their base material is cellulose acetate, spun into fine fibres. Aloe vera gel and lemongrass oil are blended in for flexibility and antimicrobial promise. Eleven formulations were produced under a structured experimental design. Strength, stretch, and stiffness were measured for each.

Cellulose acetate content drove most of the behaviour. More of it raised strength and stiffness but cut stretch. Aloe gel acted as a natural softener, trading stiffness for flexibility. Lemongrass oil helped only at low levels. Paired with high levels of the other ingredients, it weakened the films. Response models mapped these trade-offs, and the films were sorted into performance classes. Such classification helps manufacturers pick a recipe that fits a product's needs without endless trial batches.
plos-pone-0352681:
Sun and colleagues, in a 2026 simulation study, work on sealing coal fractures with particles made from captured carbon dioxide. Coal mines lose injected fluid through cracks, which wastes pressure meant to free gas. Their idea kills two birds: lock away the gas as a solid inside the coal, and use those solids as a temporary plug during fracturing.

The team built a computer model of coal pores and cracks from CT scans, and shaped the virtual particles from microscope images of the real solids. They then simulated fluid flow with particles plugging different spots under different injection settings. Plugging position changed the pressure built up inside the coal and how much fluid leaked away. From the runs, they fit formulas linking injection pressure, crack size, and plug position to pressure and leakage, with a very close fit. A lab setup was designed to check the simulation against real coal.
plos-pone-0352781:
Aloka Gnanasekara, Anuradha Jayakody, and Kasun Perera present this 2026 PLOS One survey study from Sri Lanka. It asks whether the state should adopt blockchain tools in its work. Senior IT directors answered a set survey. The authors read the answers through three classic lenses for adoption choices. The lenses cover the technology itself, the agency, and the world outside it.

All three lenses predicted intent to adopt. Trust in the tool mattered. So did fit with current systems, safety, and backing from top leaders. Funds on hand, rival pressure, and rules that support the move also mattered. Perceived edge over old tools did not matter. Neither did current IT stock or partner pressure. The authors turn the findings into a step-by-step adoption frame for Sri Lankan agencies.
plos-pone-0352881:
Santos-Lázaro and colleagues ran nationwide genetic surveillance of drug-resistant tuberculosis in Peru in a 2026 study. Peru carries the highest burden of multi-drug-resistant tuberculosis in the Americas. Tens of thousands of routine lab assay results from 2019 to 2022 were combined into genotype patterns for first- and second-line drug resistance.

Deeper sequencing of a chosen sample checked cases where resistance was only inferred. Mapping patterns by region shows where resistant strains cluster and spread. Surveillance at this scale helps health officials target testing and drug stocks. It also warns early when new resistance patterns emerge in a high-burden country.
plos-pone-0352981:
Catherine Jeanne Marguerite Meyer and five colleagues ask what tells a promising oil palm relative when to flower, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study from Brazil. Acrocomia palms could supply sustainable oil without clearing rainforest, but their flowering rhythm was blamed on the rains on shaky evidence. Six family lines from across South America, grown side by side in a research collection, were watched through three flowering seasons.

Flowering ran strongly from September to January, in step across lines and years. Day length, not rainfall or temperature, tracked the timing best; weather only nudged the years slightly apart. For growers, a day-length clock means flowering can be predicted and pollination managed — one more step toward domesticating this wild palm.
plos-pone-0353181:
Zhang and colleagues searched blood cells for a shared gene signature of autism and irritable bowel syndrome in a 2026 study. The two conditions often occur together, and stress hormone signaling is a suspected bridge. Gene data from both patient groups were mined with enrichment, network, and learning methods.

Genes responding to stress hormones were disturbed in similar ways in both conditions. Single-cell data located which blood cell types carry the signal, and drug databases suggested compounds that might reverse it. A shared signature could explain gut-brain links and point to treatments that calm both sets of symptoms at once.
plos-pone-0353381:
Mohan and colleagues, in a 2026 study, build an online simulation to measure how emergency doctors triage injured patients. Guidelines say the most hurt should go to trauma centers, but practice varies, and bad triage costs lives. There was no cheap, trustworthy way to measure a doctor's triage judgment, so the team recreated a small hospital's emergency department online.

Forty-five doctors worked through about twenty cases each, in a few minutes per case. Their answers were consistent across similar cases. Doctors also rated the cases as realistic. A behavioral analysis split each doctor's performance into sharpness of judgment and personal threshold for acting. Among doctors who saw enough real severe injuries each year, in-game sharpness matched their real-world record moderately well. The authors offer the simulation as a scalable yardstick for a skill that decides where ambulances should go.
plos-pone-0353481:
Peixoto and colleagues tested ways to use DNA prediction for a state-run soybean breeding effort in a 2026 study. Predicting yield and seed quality from DNA can cut field costs and speed new varieties. Trials at eight sites over two seasons supplied data on yield, protein, oil, and maturity for six prediction models.

A classic ridge model performed best overall in their tests. Training it on most of the population, chosen at random to keep variety wide, gave the steadiest predictions. A rank-based index also helped pick lines that raised yield and oil together. The guidance is practical: breeding teams can adopt DNA selection without exotic models or huge training sets.
plos-pone-0353681:
Sudhir Venkatesan led a team of eight authors fixing gaps in virus surveillance data, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Counts of respiratory infections arrive as time series with missing stretches, from reporting delays or testing changes. Yet officials need cumulative totals to judge the size of a wave while it is still moving.

Venkatesan's team developed methods to estimate those totals honestly from partial data, showing uncertainty instead of hiding it. Honest estimates let planners act without pretending the record is complete. The methods suit any disease reporting system with patchy data, which is most of them during a crisis. Better gap-filling also improves later research that compares waves across years and countries.
plos-pone-0353781:
Nik Zatul-Iffah Mohd Nabil and two co-authors check the first hurdle for a new dyslexia screening test aimed at secondary school students, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Older students with dyslexia often go unspotted because screening tools are built for young children. The team's twenty-eight-item test focuses on the thinking signs of dyslexia, and they asked whether its questions are clear and understandable.

Ten experts and ten students rated every item. Experts gave most items perfect clarity scores, and both groups' overall ratings beat the accepted benchmarks. A few items needed plainer wording. Passing this face-validity check clears the way for the harder statistical testing that must follow.
plos-pone-0353881:
Freidouny and colleagues measured stretch inside a false-limb socket liner in a 2026 early study. How a liner stretches against the skin affects comfort and fit for people who wear a leg prosthesis. Computer models often predict that stretch, but their guesses are rarely checked against direct measures.

One volunteer with a below-knee limb wore the liner through two stepping tasks while cameras tracked a dotted pattern on its surface. Camera measures were then set beside model predictions for the same tasks. Matching the two would build trust in models used to shape sockets. Even as a small first test, it shows a practical way to check fit science against real movement.
plos-pone-0354181:
Atsushi Mihara and seven colleagues test whether the order of two bone-building drugs changes how fractures heal, in this 2026 PLOS ONE mouse study. Both drugs help bones grow, but through different machinery: one mimics a parathyroid hormone signal, the other blocks a protein that brakes bone formation. Mice with a surgically cut shin bone received one drug alone, or one drug for a week and then the other.

Starting with the blocking antibody and switching to the hormone gave denser healing tissue and stronger bones than the reverse order, at equal total exposure. Cartilage lingered longer in the hormone-first groups, a sign of slower progress. Sequence, not just drug choice, may matter in fracture care.
plos-pone-0354681:
Gladys Estheysi Elías Solís and three colleagues published this 2026 review of gut-friendly supplements and childhood anemia. They gathered nineteen trials covering more than four thousand children, testing prebiotics, probiotics, and combined synbiotics against placebos or standard care, and rated how solid each result was.

Overall the supplements produced no meaningful gains in hemoglobin or iron stores, though one trial hinted probiotics might trim anemia rates. No serious side effects appeared. Elías Solís calls for larger, better trials in high-risk children before these products are promoted for anemia.
plos-pone-0354981:
Rudrajit Majumder and co-authors hunted for existing drugs that ultrasound could turn into weapons against glioblastoma. This brain tumour resists treatment partly because the blood-brain barrier blocks medicines. Sound-activated therapy can strike deep tissue without surgery, but proven activator drugs are scarce. Their 2026 pipeline pairs machine learning with printed tumour models.

A classifier trained without reliable negative examples scanned drug libraries for ultrasound-responsive candidates, including drugs first developed for Alzheimer's disease and ovarian cancer. Promising picks were then tested in three-dimensional printed tumour balls that mimic the real tumour's oxygen-starved core. Majumder and colleagues present the combined screen as a faster route to repurposed brain tumour treatments.
plos-pone-0355181:
Murat Akın and Orhan Kahveci compare in 2026 blood levels of a compound linked to vessel health in people with sudden hearing loss in one ear and in healthy peers. Patients were seen at diagnosis and again weeks after treatment, with hearing tested by standard tone methods. The question was whether the compound helps explain the illness or predict recovery.

Levels were higher in patients at the start and stayed high after treatment, even as hearing improved. Higher levels did not predict who recovered, though they did help separate patients from healthy people. The authors read the compound as a risk marker rather than a guide to outcome.
plos-pone-0355281:
Wei Sun and five colleagues published this 2026 pilot study of a possible warning marker for sudden worsenings of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Fifty people took part: patients mid-flare, patients stable, and healthy volunteers. The team measured how many neutrophil white blood cells carried a surface protein called PD-L1, alongside standard blood counts.

That neutrophil share ran higher in patients than in healthy people, and higher still during flares, where it also predicted flare status on its own. Sun calls the marker promising but insists larger multi-center studies must test it before clinical use.
plos-pone-0355381:
Hanan Ibrahim Alsharif led a team of eight authors testing a wild plant against stomach ulcers in animals, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Alcohol can injure the stomach lining and cause ulcers. The team gave an extract of Tragopogon coelesyriacus, a plant with traditional uses, in a live animal model of that injury.

Alsharif's group found the extract reduced the ulcer damage. They linked the effect to calmer oxidative stress, less inflammation, and less cell death in the stomach lining. A plant lead like this needs much more testing before human use. Still, it marks a candidate rooted in traditional knowledge that drug researchers can now examine with care.
plos-pone-0355481:
Khushbu Mishra and co-authors used national survey data from Nepal to test whether mothers' paid work improves young children's nutrition. Child undernutrition traps families in poverty across generations, so any lever matters. Their 2026 study applied matching and instrumental-variable methods to growth measures for children under five.

Maternal employment showed no statistically reliable effect on height, weight, or related growth scores. The authors explain that most mothers' work is informal, so income gains are small. Extra work also cuts time for feeding and care. Limited control by women over household money may further weaken the link. Mishra and colleagues caution against assuming mothers' jobs alone will fix child nutrition.
plos-pone-0355681:
Megumi Sato and colleagues examine in 2026 how baker's yeast turns a gene called YGP1 on and off as sugar runs low or stays plentiful. The gene makes a protein sent out of the cell and rises when food is scarce. Cell cycle timing and stress responses both come into play in the control system the team mapped.

When sugar was plentiful, a binding protein kept the gene active in a rhythm tied to cell division, partly through a second activator. When sugar ran out, two stress factors switched the gene on strongly. The plentiful sugar route also helped cells handle acid and live longer.
plos-pone-0355781:
Johannes Meyer zu Drewer and colleagues puzzled over extra hydrogen appearing in charcoal made with crushed rock. Such rock-enhanced biochar aims to store carbon twice over, by charring biomass and by letting minerals weather. Their 2026 study cooked wood with a silicate rock at two temperatures and many rock shares, then probed the products with advanced instruments.

Most mixtures barely changed carbon yield or char structure. One extreme batch, nearly all rock and cooked hottest, held far more hydrogen than expected. The team traces the surplus to three sources: hydrogen inside the rock itself, hydrogen clinging to mineral surfaces, and a pyrogenic coating over rock grains. The finding refines how such chars should be measured and credited.
plos-pone-0355981:
Ashley Shanahan, Gwenyth Eichfeld, Levi Todd, and Anzela Niraula charted how microglia, the brain's resident immune cells, behave across the stages of a standard laboratory model of multiple sclerosis-like damage. Their 2026 study fed mice a toxin that strips myelin from nerve fibers, then examined the brain's main white matter tract during early damage, peak damage, and early repair.

Microglia multiplied within a week and shifted into debris-clearing mode, eating damaged myelin while dialing down inflammatory signals, a profile tied to two genes involved in cleanup. In the retina, which has no myelin, the toxin still changed microglia directly, proving some effects bypass demyelination entirely. The timeline helps researchers separate helpful cleanup from harmful inflammation when testing therapies.
plos-pone-0356181:
Maia M. Sobejana and coauthors published a 2026 protocol in PLOS ONE for the Care for Muscle study, on exercise for people whose muscles are weak from rheumatic disease or age-related muscle loss. Endurance training is thought to feed the muscle's energy factories, while strength training builds the contractile machinery, but patients may respond differently depending on what is wrong inside their muscles. The trial randomizes just under seventy patients with rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, or sarcopenia to strength or endurance programs.

Training runs eight weeks, supervised sessions on cable and fitness equipment plus a weekly home session. The main outcome is peak muscle strength on a dynamometer, with ultrasound imaging of thigh muscle, biopsy-based measurement of mitochondrial function, blood inflammation markers, and walking endurance as supporting measures. By matching muscle biology to exercise response, rehabilitation might move toward schedules prescribed by disease mechanism rather than habit.
plos-pone-0356281:
Maheen Sughra, Aisha Irum, Muhammad Ibrahim, and Adnan Ahmad Khan re-tested a classic theory of health behavior against Pakistan's national survey. The survey covered more than fourteen thousand married women. The question was what really drives contraceptive use. Their 2026 study extended the Health Belief Model with fertility preferences and contact with the health system. It estimated the whole structure statistically across three nested versions.

Beliefs mattered, but modestly. Feeling threatened by pregnancy risks and seeing benefits in contraception each nudged use upward slightly. Contact with family planning providers mattered consistently. Fertility desires dominated everything, especially the wish to space births. The authors conclude programs in Pakistan should work through fertility goals and provider contact first. Belief campaigns are supporting players.
plos-pone-0356381:
Renato Luque-Benavides and colleagues reviewed eighteen years of patients with non-Hodgkin lymphoma arising around the eye at a Peruvian referral center, the largest such account from a Hispanic-Latino population. Their 2026 retrospective study covered ninety-eight patients treated between 2000 and 2017 and followed for a median of two decades, relating tumor type, stage, and treatment to survival.

The orbit was the commonest site, and slow-growing marginal zone lymphoma made up half the cases. Slow forms did very well, with roughly nineteen of twenty patients alive at five years, while aggressive forms lost far more ground. Older age independently worsened outlook in the slow group. The long follow-up gives Latin American eye cancer care a rare local benchmark.
plos-pone-0356481:
Joseph Harrison and Matthew Wallace estimate how long immigrants live, and how long they live free of disability, across England and Wales in this 2026 study. Using whole-population death records and three censuses, they built life tables for people born in thirty-seven different countries, measuring outcomes from age fifty. The aim was to test the popular idea of a healthy immigrant effect against both lifespan and healthy lifespan together.

Most migrant groups did outlive the England and Wales-born population and stayed disability-free longer. But several large groups broke the pattern: people born in Scotland and Ireland, and men born in Poland and Lithuania, had shorter lives and fewer healthy years. Women born in Pakistan and Bangladesh lived longer yet carried more disability. The authors stress that migrants are far from one group, and some need targeted public health attention.
plos-pone-0356781:
Yan Jiang and colleagues report a surprising amplifier of bacterial toxin damage in the mouse brain: albumin. Albumin is the commonest protein in blood. Their 2026 study injected mice with bacterial lipopolysaccharide. This molecule triggers fierce inflammation. Some mice got the toxin alone, and some got it pre-mixed with bovine albumin. The team then examined brain blood vessels and barrier leakage. It also examined a fiery form of cell death called pyroptosis.

At the lower toxin dose, the albumin mixture leaked more tracer into brain tissue. It injured more vessel cells. It raised more death and inflammation markers than toxin alone. At a high dose the advantage vanished, swamped by the toxin itself. Tests confirmed albumin physically carries the toxin into the brain. That mechanism may matter whenever infection meets a leaky barrier.
plos-pone-0356881:
Takefumi Yoshida and colleagues surveyed 587 Japanese elementary school students about refusing school, testing whether two strengths, resilience and solution building, the habit of constructing next steps toward goals, soften the behavior. Their 2026 study used self-report questionnaires and modeled the pathways separately for boys and girls.

For boys, resilience calmed refusal directly and also indirectly, by strengthening solution building. For girls, resilience worked only through the indirect route: it built solution skills, which in turn eased refusal. Both paths ended at the same place, children with more of both strengths resisted school less intensely. The authors suggest support programs teach concrete solution building to everyone, since it carries the benefit for both sexes.
plos-pone-0357181:
Shreya Battu and colleagues published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on how COVID-19 treated immunocompromised patients in intensive care as the pandemic changed. Reviewing nearly eight hundred Stanford ICU patients from 2020 to 2022, they split the timeline into pre-Delta, Delta, and Omicron periods and compared survival between immune-weakened patients and the rest.

Across the whole period, immunocompromised patients died more. But the gap reached significance only in the Omicron period, when their ninety-day mortality ran far above the comparison group's. They also made up a growing share of ICU admissions by then. The authors argue the pattern may reflect Omicron-era realities: vaccines and treatments helped the general population more, while the immunocompromised stayed exposed as precautions lifted. Protection strategies, they argue, should be timed to who remains at risk, not declared over for everyone at once.
plos-pone-0357281:
Zhonghui Zhu and colleagues probe whether the sympathetic nerves that support the aorta also protect it from tearing. A tear in the aorta's wall is deadly, and nerve signals help keep the vessel healthy, but their role in early disease was unclear. In mice given a chemical that weakens the aorta, nerve activity markers rose early and tracked with breakdown of the wall's elastic layers.

Removing a nerve hub in the neck did nothing on its own, yet it sharply worsened tearing once the weakening treatment began, raising ruptures and spreading damage. Muscle cells in the wall also showed signs of shifting type after the removal. Zhu and colleagues conclude that intact sympathetic support guards the aorta, and losing it early can hasten disaster.
plos-pone-0357381:
Fatemeh Gholamali Nezhad and coauthors published a 2026 protocol in PLOS ONE for a pilot trial of an unusual depression treatment: gentle electrical stimulation of the face muscles. Standard treatments fail about a third of people with major depression, so new mechanisms are needed. The idea grows from the notion that activating expression muscles can shift mood from the body upward. Earlier feasibility work suggested practicality, and this registered trial tests it properly.

Sixty participants will receive twenty sessions over four weeks, half with real stimulation and half with a sham version, with neither patients nor assessors told who got which. The trial tracks depressive symptoms, anxiety, quality of life, and sleep, plus dropouts and side effects as measures of tolerability and safety. As a pilot, its real product is design knowledge: effect sizes and practical lessons to shape a large multisite trial.
plos-pone-0357581:
Zelalem Addis and coauthors published a 2026 agronomy study in PLOS ONE on feeding hot pepper, a cornerstone of Ethiopian cooking, in the Amhara Region. Yields lag because soils are tired and losing organic matter. Over two seasons, six feeding regimes mixing liquid bio-slurry, a farm waste product, with standard nitrogen fertilizer in different proportions were compared, measuring soil chemistry and pepper yield in replicated plots.

Blends beat the extremes. Halves of each, and a quarter slurry with three quarters fertilizer, improved soil nutrients and produced the highest yields, above the unfed control, while returning the best profit per investment. The half-and-half blend is the headline recommendation for farmers with enough slurry, the quarter blend suiting those short on it. Farm waste, the study argues, can substitute for a large share of purchased fertilizer without sacrificing the harvest.
plos-pone-0357781: Wu and five co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE paper on software that grades a citrus fruit used in Chinese medicine. Fructus Aurantii is the dried young fruit. Their system, FAnet, is a light, end-to-end tool that names the fruit and grades its quality. Fast grading by camera could help herb markets sort stock fairly and spot poor or wrong material.
plos-pone-0358481:
Orsolya Csötönyi led a team of eight authors testing a painless way to read pig gut movement, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Stress changes how the gut moves, in pigs as in people, but measuring that usually needs invasive tools. The team tested surface electromyography, which reads electrical signals from the skin surface.

Csötönyi's method detects stress-induced changes in gut motility without surgery or swallowed devices. A painless, continuous window into the stressed gut helps researchers study welfare and feeding with less harm to the animals. Pig studies also inform human gut research, since the systems are alike. Farm science gains a tool that can run during normal housing, not only in a lab.
plos-pone-0358781:
Kimbley Asaso Omwodo leads a team of five testing whether low vitamin D tracks with preeclampsia in Kenyan mothers, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The dangerous blood pressure disorder causes about a fifth of direct maternal deaths in Kenya, and African data on the vitamin link are scarce. At a major referral hospital, the team matched fifty-nine women with the condition to fifty-nine without, pairing them by age, pregnancy stage, and number of previous births.

Blood vitamin D ran significantly lower in the preeclampsia group. Levels classed as suboptimal appeared in about a third of cases but in fewer than one in fourteen controls. Adjusted analysis confirmed higher odds of the condition among women with low levels. The study cannot prove the vitamin shortfall helps cause the disorder, but it strengthens the case for testing whether screening or supplementation in African pregnancies would prevent cases.
plos-pone-0359281:
Michael A Incze leads a team of eight describing a planned trial on hospital discharge for people with substance use disorders, in PLOS ONE in 2026. A hospital stay is a rare chance to start addiction treatment, yet many patients lose contact with care within days of leaving. The IntACT study tests a team based bridge: primary care clinicians meet patients in the hospital and keep following them after discharge.

The pilot will enroll seventy-five admitted patients at one site and assign them by chance to the team or to usual care. The team then supports each patient for four months, working on linkage to follow up medical and addiction care. Researchers will judge reach, acceptability, cost, and early signs of benefit over six months. The protocol lays groundwork for a larger trial if the model proves workable.
plos-pone-0359881:
Natnapa Heebkaew Padchasuwan and colleagues built and checked a new survey in 2026 that measures how well university students in Thailand handle sexual health facts. The skill has a name: sexual health literacy. It means being able to find facts about sexual health, grasp them, and use them well. Thailand had no survey made for this task among its own students.

The team's tool is known by the short name SHL-US. They put it through the standard checks that show a survey is sound: that its questions hang together and that scores stay steady. A sound tool lets schools spot which students are left in the dark. It also shows whether health classes truly raise what students know.
plos-pone-0359981:
Yifan Gu published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It studies cultural sustainability in Qing dynasty China, between 1644 and 1911. The lens is kinship networks, and the evidence is marriage strategies among literary lineages, families known for producing scholars and writers across generations.

The analysis is quantitative, counting and modeling how these families chose marriage partners. Marriages could spread a family's influence, guard its status, or keep literary culture alive through hard times. Historians of China and of family strategy gain a measured view of how elite culture reproduced itself for nearly three centuries.
plos-pone-0360081:
Mohsen Hesami, Mohammad Rahbari, and Ron Salzman studied in 2026 how maize plants change their gene activity after treatment with a natural biostimulant mixture. The mixture combines quillaja extract, from the bark of a South American tree, with fulvic acid, a substance from decomposed organic matter. Biostimulants are sold to help crops grow and withstand stress without being fertilizers themselves.

The authors track the plant's transcriptional responses, which genes switch on or off, over time and in response to particular stimuli. A time resolved picture shows whether the mixture triggers a quick alarm, a lasting adjustment, or both. Such evidence helps separate biostimulants that genuinely prime the plant from those riding on marketing, a live question in farm supply.
pmc-10364581:
Members of the GBD 2021 Diabetes group report how diabetes spread across the world from 1990 to 2021. Diabetes now ranks among the top causes of death and disability on the planet. It harms people in every country, at every age, and in both sexes.

Using the newest data and methods from the Global Burden of Disease study, the team built estimates for each country and region. They also project how common diabetes may become by the year 2050. Health leaders use such counts to plan care, set budgets, and judge whether prevention work is paying off.
pmc-13191781:
Ashley Toussaint, Om Panda, and Cheryl Graber present a 2026 case series of doctors who are twice exceptional, or 2e. The term means high brain power combined with conditions such as ADHD that can impair performance in standard settings. The idea is known in schooling but little discussed in medicine.

Five doctors at different career stages are profiled. Their conditions include ADHD, anxiety, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and a nonverbal learning disorder, alongside strong intellect. Themes repeat across cases. High achievement masked disability. Struggles were misread as poor professionalism. Support came late or never. Some thrived with mentors and structure, while others faced isolation and burnout. The authors urge training settings that affirm brain differences.
pmc-13196681:
Bhakti Hansoti and colleagues describe a 2026 framework for national public health institutes. These institutes are state agencies that lead and coordinate public health work. Many form by merging scattered units, yet weak structure can limit their impact.

The framework has a mapping step plus six modules. The modules cover strategy, partnerships, communication, workforce, finance, and governance, meaning how an agency is led and held to account. Each module starts with a check, then guided steps and good practice notes. Teams run each module as a sprint over three to six months. The tools aim to build skill that lasts through funding shifts and new health threats.
pmc-13197281:
Markus Johansson and colleagues present a 2026 sediment trap that reports hourly online. Sediment traps catch sinking particles in lakes to track flux and content. Classic traps gather samples for months and need costly upkeep, so fine timing is lost.

Their trap uses light-based scanning to gauge sediment volume as it settles, hour by hour. Lab tests showed a mean error of well under one milliliter. A trial unit in a Finnish bay caught short sediment pulses from shore building work. The solar unit sends data wirelessly, cutting field trips. Image handling still needs work for extreme sediment loads. The tool suits remote sites and fast-changing waters.
pmc-13198781:
Ouiam Taibi and colleagues present a 2026 case report on trapped air as a hidden cause of belly pain. Spontaneous pneumomediastinum means air collects around the heart and windpipe with no injury. It is rare and usually starts with chest pain, which makes a belly-pain presentation easy to misread.

Their patient was a 28-year-old man, a chronic smoker, with sudden severe upper belly pain. Exam and lung checks were normal. A belly scan ordered to rule out a burst ulcer found no gut problem. Further imaging instead showed the trapped air plus air under the skin of the neck. No trigger was found. The case warns that chest air leaks can pose as belly emergencies.
pmc-13199181:
Sabiha Farooq and colleagues studied a gene variant tied to obesity and blood chemistry in a 2026 case-control study. Large gene scans have linked TMEM18 to obesity, but its job in the body is unclear. The team asked whether one variant in that gene pairs with body measures and blood metabolites, the small chemicals of metabolism.

They enrolled 542 adults in Pakistan, split between overweight or obese cases and normal-weight controls. Blood DNA and serum chemistry were tested for all. The variant tied to five metabolites and to body mass index, body fat share, waist size, and weight. One version of the variant raised obesity risk. Carriers of two copies showed the clearest metabolite shifts.
pmc-13199681:
Abdalla Ahmed Elbashir and Khalid Malik M Hamid developed a 2026 lab method to measure two livestock dewormers at once. Triclabendazole and levamisole treat worms in cattle and sheep and ship as an oral liquid mix. Quality checks need a fast test that still works as drugs break down.

Their liquid chromatography method separates both drugs in minutes with a simple solvent blend. Validation checks covered accuracy, precision, detection limits, and toughness against small setting changes. Calibration lines stayed straight across wide ranges for both drugs. Stress tests showed breakdown products split cleanly from the real drugs, proving the test flags stale stock. The method now serves routine checks of the suspension.
pmc-13237281:
The editors of Microsystems and Nanoengineering mark their field's rapid growth with an editorial on its ten biggest ground-level challenges. Tiny devices now support smart medical sensing, precision checks in industry, and shrunken hardware for aircraft and spacecraft. They also sit inside the chips planned for the next wave of information technology.

Growth that fast leaves hard problems at ground level: making, measuring, powering, and trusting devices built at near-atomic scales. Naming the worst ten is an agenda-setting move, pointing young researchers and funders at the bottlenecks that matter most. Editorials like this shape a young field by agreeing, in public, on what must be solved next.
pmc-13237981: Abdelhamid and colleagues publish a correction to their study of medication habits among diabetic patients in Upper Egypt. The original paper linked how faithfully patients take their drugs with how they perceive their illness. The correction concerns the passage describing the adherence scale used, the MMAS-8, in the data collection section. It restates the scale's scoring: a total of eight marks high adherence, six or seven mark medium, and below six marks low. Journals record such fixes so later readers score the same tool the same way.
pmc-13240881:
Zewdie and a large Ethiopia-UK team explored what helps and hinders childhood vaccination across three Ethiopian regions. Ethiopia carries one of the world's largest groups of zero-dose children. The study ran eighteen focus groups, interviews with twenty-three mothers, and forty-two key informant talks. Eight districts in Amhara, Oromia, and Somali regions took part.

Shared barriers included distant services, low awareness, mothers' competing duties, and fear of side effects. Rough or disrespectful care also discouraged return visits. Beliefs differed by region, from delaying shots until after baptism to keeping young infants indoors. Engaging religious leaders and fathers, and timing sessions around local holidays, emerged as promising fixes.
pmc-13240981:
Chew and colleagues in the United Kingdom reanalyzed real-world data from Holly Health, a personalized coaching app for older adults. Users enrolled between August 2022 and January 2023. The secondary analysis tracked well-being, mental and physical health, and attitudes toward food. Acceptability was judged alongside the outcome changes.

After using the app, participants reported better self-confidence, energy, and mindfulness. Health mindset and both short- and long-term outlook also improved. Users rated the personalized tool as acceptable and engaging. The authors say such accessible apps could support healthy aging at scale.
pmc-13241181:
Mattioli and colleagues at the University of Pavia tested how introduced fish change fear reactions in alpine frog tadpoles. Six Western Italian lakes spanned fishless, fish-neighboring, and fish-filled settings. The young frogs faced rising doses of dragonfly predator scent in lab assays. Freezing time gauged how strongly each population sensed danger.

All groups froze more as scent grew stronger, confirming a graded response. Those from fish lakes reacted significantly even at the weakest scent levels. Surprisingly, fishless lakes near stocked waters showed the same raised sensitivity. The invasion's behavioral shadow, Mattioli argues, spills beyond the invaded lakes.
pmc-13241581:
Bueno and Souto in southern Brazil map how curcumin research for food science has evolved. Curcumin, the yellow pigment of turmeric, is held back by poor dissolving and weak uptake. The pair ran a counting study of Web of Science records. They added a focused review of ways to deliver and package it.

Output grew fast, with strong cross-border teamwork across the field. Focus shifted from drug-style action toward keeping curcumin stable and usable in foods. Tiny carriers, coatings, and carrier design lead both the full dataset and the uptake subset. The authors warn that proof stays scattered, and food makers need methods that scale, plus testing in real food matrices.
pmc-13242381:
Kechagia and colleagues in Athens followed two thousand Greek adults for twenty years of eating and diabetes outcomes. The ATTICA cohort began free of diabetes and cardiovascular disease. Validated food questionnaires separated animal from plant protein intake. Waist-hip ratio marked central adiposity throughout the analysis.

About a quarter developed diabetes across the two decades of follow-up. Red meat raised risk in both sexes with every daily serving increment. Animal protein harmed women only, roughly doubling risk among the centrally obese. Plant protein strongly protected younger women carrying excess abdominal fat.
pmc-13242581:
Wisdom Ikezogwo and co-authors built an AI triage system for microscope slides of colon polyps. Their paper appeared in Cancer Informatics in 2026. Colon specimens dominate their pathology service, and screening now starts at age forty-five, which adds volume. The team trained a transformer network on 1,191 slides spanning twelve diagnoses, from harmless polyps to invasive cancer. It had to sort neoplastic from non-neoplastic growths and attempt the full diagnosis.

The triage task worked well: on held-out slides and on a fresh set from routine service days, the system cleared ninety-five percent accuracy and specificity for spotting neoplasm. That performance supports using it as a first screen that pushes likely cancers to the front of the queue. The twelve-way diagnosis task is the harder problem and needs broader testing. The authors call for multi-center studies before wider clinical use.
pmc-13243181:
Xiao Wen and Kong Qingfei wrote a letter responding to a national study of frailty and surgical outcomes. Their letter appeared in Health Science Reports in 2026. The study they discuss, by Gonzalez and colleagues, used the Hospital Frailty Risk Score across surgical specialties and found frailty's heaviest toll in emergency operations. More than ninety percent of the highest-risk patients had undergone emergency surgery, leaving almost no time to strengthen them beforehand.

Wen and Kong praise the score as a practical screening tool while noting its blind spots. Because it is built from administrative codes, it can miss fixable problems such as muscle loss and functional decline. Their title states the agenda: from identification to intervention. Naming risk is only step one; hospitals must build care pathways that act on what screening finds. The letter is short, but it presses a large question in surgical care.
pmc-13244081:
Sarah Pangburn and colleagues compared malaria parasites of Caribbean lizards to learn how they eat blood. Their study appeared in Ecology and Evolution in 2026. Mammal malaria parasites digest hemoglobin inside red cells and lock the toxic leftovers into a brown crystal, hemozoin. Two of the three lizard species studied here break the pattern: they make no crystal. One has even moved into white blood cells, a niche no Plasmodium is supposed to occupy.

To see what changed, the team assembled and compared the parasites' genetic toolkits for hemoglobin digestion. The headline result is conservation: the core digestion genes persist across all three species, even in the ones that abandoned crystal making. That implies the non-crystal species evolved a different way to handle the toxic byproduct rather than losing the machinery outright. The work opens the understudied genetics of wildlife malaria, where most of the family's diversity actually lives.
pmc-13244381:
Tiffany Chang and colleagues report a hernia hiding behind a gynecologic disguise that nearly cost a woman part of her bowel. Their case report appeared in Case Reports in Obstetrics and Gynecology in 2026. The thirty-five-year-old mother arrived with two days of sharp abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. Scans suggested a tubo-ovarian abscess, so she received strong antibiotics and an attempted image-guided drainage that failed to help.

As she worsened, a camera operation found the truth: small bowel had slipped through a defect in the broad ligament, the sheet anchoring the uterus, and become trapped. The surgery widened into an open operation; the starved segment of ileum was removed and the bowel rejoined, and the ligament defect was repaired. The authors warn that internal hernias belong on the list for blocked bowels even without a surgical past. Delay invites strangulation.
pmc-13248081:
Komonski, Jouanneau, and Boureau tested home exercise for frail elders recovering from heart surgery, in this 2026 Journal of Rehabilitation Medicine feasibility study. Patients over seventy-five with weak physical performance are prone to decline after cardiac operations, and many cannot reach rehabilitation centers. At Nantes University Hospital, the team offered Vivifrail, a structured multicomponent home exercise program, and tracked recruitment, retention, and function over six weeks.

Of forty-five eligible patients, thirty-eight joined and twenty-nine returned for final testing, completing on average just over half the program. Walking, balance, and grip measures all improved meaningfully, and the most adherent patients ended least frail. The authors judge home-based rehabilitation feasible for this group and worth confirming in larger trials, especially for patients far from specialist centers.
pmc-13248981:
Du and a Chinese team tracked germs growing inside oxygen tubing, in a 2026 study of elderly patients. High-flow nasal cannula therapy delivers humidified oxygen comfortably for long stretches. The researchers sampled the circuits of one hundred two patients whose average age was about ninety-four, checking whether the tubing itself became a germ reservoir.

More than half the circuits grew microbes, including fungi and drug-resistant staph. Patients with colonized tubing developed lung infections far more often. In one case, genome sequencing proved the same Pseudomonas strain lived in the tubing and the patient's lungs. Analysis pointed to replacing tubing around ninety days to cut the risk.
pmc-13249681:
Karataş and a Turkish team asked whether air and weather trigger lung flare-ups differently by blood type, in a 2026 study. They reviewed three hundred fifty-four emergency visits for COPD exacerbations over one year and sorted each attack by the dominant white cell in the blood: neutrophilic, eosinophilic, or mixed. Daily pollution and weather records from official monitors were matched to visit dates.

Most attacks were neutrophilic and also the most severe. Overall attack counts showed no environmental pattern, but the eosinophilic type rose on days with more carbon monoxide and sulfur dioxide. Mixed attacks tracked humidity and wind instead. The authors argue flare-up warnings should be tailored by subtype, not issued for COPD as one block.
pmc-13250281:
Congjie He and co-authors test two plant compounds against prostate cancer in this 2026 study. A targeted radiation drug is used for advanced prostate cancer that no longer answers hormone treatment, but uneven tumours and natural radiation resistance limit how well it works.

In lab-grown cancer cells, adding genistein or baicalein, found in soy and in a Chinese herb root, made the radiation drug far more potent at low, gentle doses. The pairs raised cell damage signals, blocked DNA repair, and pushed cells into self-destruction. In mice, the combined treatment shrank tumours by half or more compared with the drug alone, with no clear side effects seen.
pmc-13250381:
Sampaio and co-authors pool trial evidence on simulation training for obstetric emergencies among health care students. Their 2026 Obstetrics and Gynecology International review searched four databases through September 2025 for randomized trials. Nine studies compared hands-on simulation teaching with traditional classroom methods for birth emergencies.

Seven trials, with a few hundred students in total, fed the combined analysis, and simulation produced clearly larger knowledge gains after training. Some trials also reported better teamwork and critical thinking among the simulation students. Results varied a lot between settings, and the range of plausible effects crossed zero, so benefits may depend on context. The authors call for studies on how long the skills last and whether patients fare better.
pmc-13250881:
Owusu-Boaitey and colleagues revisit whether early COVID-19 models or early antibody surveys better captured the pandemic's true size. Their 2026 Global Health Action discussion paper explains how seroprevalence studies, which track infection antibodies, first suggested lower fatality risks. Some early surveys undercounted the risk for children and for lower-income countries.

Later antibody studies that reached the right groups, plus corrections for known biases, lined up with the early modeling results. The authors say this agreement vindicates the models that guided policy at the time. They urge health authorities to tell the public plainly about that success and about the limits of early survey work. Clearer lessons, they argue, will help the public judge risks in future pandemics.
pmc-13253981:
Xueting Wu and colleagues describe a hard airway emergency in a 2026 case report. A 22-year-old man had acute epiglottitis, a fast swelling of the flap over the windpipe, with neck swelling and noisy breathing. Several tries to place a breathing tube failed because swelling hid the airway opening.

A mask still delivered air well, a state the team calls can ventilate but cannot intubate. Following airway guidelines, they stopped further tube tries and did a planned tracheostomy, an opening in the neck, at the bedside. His oxygen rose fast and he recovered with no complications, which the authors credit to early teamwork.
pmc-13254081:
Dirk Bauer and colleagues test how immune cells stick to an eye implant in a 2026 lab study. The PreserFlo MicroShunt is a tiny tube that drains fluid to treat glaucoma, made from a rubber-like material called SIBS. Human macrophages, immune cells that react to foreign materials, were grown on the shunts for 35 days.

Far more macrophages stuck to the SIBS shunts than to two common lens materials used as controls. The authors say surface traits of SIBS invite this sticking, which could affect long-term implant success, mainly in eyes with uveitis, an eye inflammation. Live studies are still needed.
pmc-13254681:
The EFSA Panel on Food Enzymes gives a safety verdict on a food enzyme in a 2026 opinion. Thermolysin is made by a non-genetically modified bacterium strain for use in three food manufacturing processes. The panel reviewed gene damage tests, a 90-day rat feeding study, and diet exposure estimates for European populations.

Exposure reached up to 0.874 milligrams per kilogram of body weight per day. No gene damage concern appeared, and the top rat dose showed no adverse effect. Safety margins were fine for most age groups, but the panel said the margin was too small to rule out concerns for children.
pmc-13256481:
Charlotte Lund Rasmussen leads a 2026 systematic review of questionnaires that ask parents and health workers what they think about young children's use of technology. The review covered peer-reviewed studies from January 2010 to September 2024, found through seven databases. It looked at children from birth to age five, and at how well the questionnaires themselves were built and tested.

In total, 85 studies were included, and all of them involved parents; none studied health professionals. Study quality was generally low, and only 15 of the 52 studies that reported questionnaire properties gave more than one measure of validity or reliability. Parents mostly backed digital devices as a help for learning, but worried about harm to children's physical health, emotions, and behavior.
pmc-13259581:
Mostafa Bondok, Kelly Serbu, and Anuradha Mishra offer five ways to support patients living with visual impairment. Their 2026 CMAJ practice piece starts from an access gap: people with sight loss report unmet health needs and extra cost barriers. Blind patients also face higher hospital admission and mortality rates.

First, introduce yourself each time and speak to the patient, not their companion. Ask before helping, describe examinations and images aloud, and offer an elbow rather than grabbing. Clinics should keep walkways clear, signage bold, and lighting strong. Information belongs in large print or accessible digital formats, and rehabilitation referrals round out the five.
pmc-13261081:
Koki Shigemoto and co-authors report a 2026 case of a fractured vena cava filter presenting as deep vein thrombosis. These filters sit in the body's largest vein to catch clots. Long-term filters can fracture and block the vein, causing new thrombosis years later.

Their patient was a 65-year-old Japanese woman with one month of pain and swelling in both legs. A filter had been placed 30 years earlier for thrombosis caused by uterine fibroids, and she was lost to follow-up. Her D-dimer was 10.5 μg/mL. Scans showed organized clot and calcification around the fractured filter, with chronic blockage of the vein and prominent backup veins. Edoxaban at 60 mg daily improved her symptoms. Filter removal and surgery were considered but deferred because the operative risk was high.
pmc-13261681:
Maulydia Maulydia and co-authors report a 2026 rat study of two amino acids in sepsis, a life-threatening reaction to infection. Glutamine and arginine can modulate inflammation and support immunity, and both often run low in sepsis. The team tested their combination's effect on inflammatory signals in gut tissue.

Seventy-two Rattus norvegicus rats received a sepsis trigger, then treatment starting at 6, 24, or 48 hours, given daily for three days. Jejunal tissue was collected two hours after the final dose. The combination changed cells expressing IL-8 in the 24-hour group (p = 0.026) and MMP-8 in the 6-hour group (p < 0.001). No differences appeared for the TNF-α or NF-κB signals at any start time, nor for other markers in the 48-hour group. The authors call for dose studies over longer periods to confirm these timing-specific effects.
pmc-13261981:
Delelegn Tsegaye Zikie and colleagues present a 2026 journal article on breastfeeding and family planning among new mothers in Northeast Ethiopia. Their focus is the lactational amenorrhea method, in which full breastfeeding can delay periods and help prevent pregnancy. They asked whether mothers who knew this method also breastfed in the way advised.

The team surveyed 607 mothers at four hospitals in 2023, using spoken questionnaires and statistical models that adjust for other factors. Good breastfeeding practice was found in 68.4 percent, and good knowledge of the method in 56.0 percent. Knowledge was linked to better breastfeeding. Schooling, marital status, age, and hospital type also mattered, so the authors urge structured lessons after birth.
pmc-13263681:
Desiana Radithia and colleagues test vitamin D's active form as a gel for healing mouth ulcers in rats. Traumatic oral ulcers are common and slow to close in a bacteria-rich environment. Their 2026 experiment wounds Wistar rats and compares calcitriol gel against no treatment across eight days.

Treated ulcers drew in more macrophages and lymphocytes by days six and eight, signs of an energized repair response. Fibroblasts multiplied faster, collagen packed denser, and new capillaries sprouted more richly. A vessel growth factor's expression rose alongside. By orchestrating inflammation, rebuilding, and blood supply together, the gel sped closure, supporting trials in human oral wounds.
pmc-13264581:
Danielle C Messias and co-authors published a 2026 study of risk signs for erosive tooth wear, the slow loss of tooth surface from acids not made by germs. They reviewed records at a university dental school in the Midwest United States. The aim was to spot which patients dentists should watch most closely.

They compared 2,482 patients with the wear against 2,967 without it, using records from 2019 to 2023. Wear linked to age 35 to 54, male sex, and habits like clenching or grinding the teeth. Eating disorders such as bulimia and anorexia showed the strongest link. No link appeared for dry mouth, reflux, alcohol use, sleep apnea, or brushing frequency. The authors say early spotting of these signs can guide tailored prevention.
pmc-13264981:
Jennifer Tsai published a 2026 study comparing three energy treatments for dry eye caused by faulty oil glands in the eyelids, a condition called meibomian gland dysfunction. Heat and light therapies can unclog the glands, and her clinic's records allowed a real-world comparison of radiofrequency, intense pulsed light, and both together.

The study covered 286 adults treated from 2022 to 2024. All three groups improved on symptom surveys, tear stability, and gland scores within a month, and gains held at three months. The combined group improved most on nearly every measure, with its main symptom score falling from 22.70 to 3.61. No serious side effects occurred. Tsai concludes that energy therapy works and the pairing works best, supporting tailored dry eye care.
pmc-13267981:
Pierre-Emmanuel Goetz and colleagues present a 2026 case report on shoulder repair with donor bone and cartilage grafts. A reverse Hill-Sachs lesion is a dent in the ball of the shoulder after a backward dislocation. When the dent covers a quarter to half the ball, the joint may not go back in place, and no standard fix exists. The team used fresh-frozen grafts from donors to rebuild the joint surface.

Two men were treated, aged 48 and 66, both with epilepsy, the trigger for their dislocations. Their defects covered about 43 and 42 percent of the ball. One graft came from a thigh bone end, the other from a donor shoulder ball. The paper reports how both shoulders worked and looked on imaging eight years later, adding rare long-term data for this graft choice.
pmc-13268181:
Khola Noreen and colleagues present a 2026 study building a Pakistan-ready tool for HPV vaccination research. The HPV vaccine prevents cervical cancer, yet uptake stays low in poorer countries, partly for cultural reasons. A global WHO framework lists the behavioral and social drivers of vaccination. The team adapted that framework for Pakistan through a qualitative survey across Punjab districts in 2025.

Participants included teenage girls, parents, health workers, teachers, school leaders, and religious scholars. Analysis kept the four WHO domains and found a fifth, cultural integration, covering local norms the global tool missed. Themes were mapped to the framework with supporting quotes. The finished tool was translated into Urdu by a bilingual expert. The authors offer it as a model for fitting global health tools to local culture before vaccine rollouts.
pmc-13269381:
P Soma, B B Kooverjee, and A Yika published a journal article in 2026 on genetic diversity in cattle in Gauteng province, South Africa. Local cattle are a valued resource because they cope with harsh weather and keep producing for years. Hair samples were tested with 11 standard DNA markers.

Samples came from 266 cattle in Western Gauteng, 132 in Lesedi, and 69 in Tshwane, with five local breeds and Angus as comparison groups. Diversity was high, with average expected variety of 75 percent. Inbreeding stayed low, with a mean near 0.015. More genetic difference sat within each population than between them. The authors offer the results as a baseline for breeding programs.
pmc-13269781:
Mai Tarek and co-authors published a trial report in 2026 on setting doses of two blood pressure drugs for patients with liver cirrhosis, scarring that changes how drugs are handled. Computer models of the body in cirrhosis first predicted lower doses by disease stage. Forty-four patients then took model-guided doses for three months.

Model doses fell sharply with severity, for example one drug dropping from 25 milligrams to about 2 in severe disease. In mild and moderate patients, both drugs were well tolerated and lowered blood pressure and heart rate. Liver and kidney tests stayed stable. One drug improved flow through the liver more, though it also caused more mild side effects. The authors back model-guided dosing.
pmc-13270681:
Muhammad Nauman Qureshi led a 2026 survey study on telemedicine, care given at a distance by phone or computer, for sorting patients in an emergency department. Sorting, called triage, decides who needs care first. The study asked staff, not patients, what they thought of the tool.

The team questioned 131 health workers at one of the largest hospitals in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. Doctors made up 62.6 percent of replies and knew telemedicine better than other staff. Most agreed it could help with first assessment, and AI-based triage was the most cited tool. Staff resistance, privacy worries, and lack of training were the main barriers named.
pmc-13271581:
Fang Lei is lead author of a 2026 pilot study of an online education programme meant to raise lung cancer screening uptake among high-risk people who smoke. Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death in the United States. Yet screening with low-dose CT scans stays underused, partly through limited knowledge, stigma, and false beliefs.

Twenty-five participants completed five self-directed online modules, with questionnaires before and after. Knowledge scores rose markedly. Stigma scores fell clearly. Beliefs about personal risk, benefits, and triggers to act also improved, as did intentions and confidence about screening. Screening uptake was checked by email three months later.
pmc-13273981:
Akiva Nachshon and colleagues wrote a 2026 authors' reply letter about using a bronchoscope during a bedside tracheostomy. A tracheostomy opens the windpipe to help a patient breathe, and a bronchoscope is a thin camera tube. Two commentators had questioned the team's earlier study of the procedure in intensive care patients.

In the reply, the authors restate their main finding: routine bronchoscopy did not cut major complications, deaths, or hospital stay, and it made preparation and the procedure take longer. They note no clear difference in oxygen drops between groups. They also explain their use of direct laryngoscopy in the other group and which bleeding risks kept patients out of the study.
pmc-13274781:
Sarah E Burstein and Howard I Maibach wrote a 2026 editorial arguing for stronger skin training for rural frontline doctors in the American Southeast. Skin cancer is common there, yet many rural counties have no dermatologist at all. Farm and outdoor work raise sun exposure, while poverty, distance, and low screening rates delay care.

That leaves primary care doctors as the first, and often only, clinicians judging suspicious spots. But dermatology is thinly taught in medical school and primary care training, and skin diagnosis leans on pattern recognition across many skin tones. The authors call better training a fast, practical fix: not replacing specialists, but equipping frontline doctors to spot, sort, and refer high-risk lesions sooner.
pmc-13275881: Christian Neumann and a large team of co-authors published the original study on quality of life after SARS-CoV-2 infection, the virus behind COVID-19. Their 2026 correction notice fixes a single error in that article. One author's name, Anna Schäfer, had been spelled incorrectly as Anna Horn in the first version. The notice states that the original article has now been corrected.
pmc-13277781:
Edgar Céléreau leads a 2026 brain imaging study of young people at risk for psychosis, a loss of contact with reality seen in disorders such as schizophrenia. A new scan method maps several brain chemicals across the whole brain at high detail. The team built a processing pipeline, a set of steps that cleans and aligns the maps, and tested it in two groups.

Chemical patterns matched well between the two samples and scanning sites, showing the method is stable. At-risk youth showed higher levels of one nerve-health chemical in frontal gray matter than controls. A subgroup also showed widespread rises in another chemical. Standard structure and wiring scans found no group differences, hinting the chemical maps may detect earlier change.
pmc-13279481:
Francesco Bertoldo and colleagues report a 2026 survey of fragility fracture care in Italian emergency departments. Fragility fractures are breaks from small falls in weak bone, and they are often missed in busy emergency rooms. Missed breaks lose the chance to start bone strength care and stop the next break. The team surveyed staff on how they spot and handle such breaks.

Thirty four health workers took part: ten emergency doctors, eleven radiologists and thirteen emergency nurses from many regions. A panel of experts built the survey on break checks, risk facts, records and referrals. Answers showed patchy checks of key risk facts across roles. Gaps stood out between what staff know and what they do each day. Set routines for spotting, writing and referral could close the gap.
pmc-13280581:
Alexis Aomreore and colleagues present a 2026 cross sectional survey of patient portal use in primary care in Ontario, Canada. Patient portals are digital programs that give patients access to their electronic health records and care tools. Portals are now widely used, yet desirability of their features is less known. The survey ran from December 2022 to March 2023 and captured use and anticipated use of five feature types, from messaging the practice to scheduling appointments.

A total of nine hundred seventy responses were obtained: seven hundred forty three patients and two hundred twenty seven caregivers. Portal access sat at fifty seven percent for patients and sixty two percent for caregivers. Features held communicating with the practice, viewing records, entering record information, receiving practice information and scheduling. Associations between socio demographic data and current use of features were tested. The profile of who uses what can guide portal design for equity.
pmc-13281281:
Amrita K Johal reviewed how hospitals pick adults for a last-resort heart and lung machine in a 2026 paper. The machine does the work of the heart and lungs for the sickest patients. It costs a lot, and who gets it shapes who lives. The review found few hospitals use firm written rules for the choice. Most studies on the topic were small and used unlike methods.

One scoring tool stood out as the best guide for most cases. A tweaked version, which adds a blood marker of strain, fit two hard groups better. Teams that decided as a full group, not by one or two doctors, saw better survival. The author calls for more proof tests of the scores. Fair, shared rules, the review argues, would help hospitals choose well.
pmc-13281881:
Ying-Xing Xiang and colleagues probed whether a common arthritis drug can drive lung disease in a 2026 study. The drug, methotrexate, calms the immune system and is used for joint and skin disease. COPD is a long-term lung disease that narrows airways and worsens over time. Past reports hint the drug might affect the lungs, but cause was unclear. The team worked two ways. Network maps predicted the drug's targets and paths. Gene data then tested for a cause-style link.

The maps tied the drug to nine proteins with strong binding fits. Those proteins steer swelling, stress response, and cell growth. The gene test found a clear positive link between drug use markers and COPD risk. The authors say the pair of methods points the same way. They frame it as a warning for long-term users. More direct clinical study is needed, they add.
pmc-13282081:
Parth Patel and co-authors tell of a 2026 case where a vein, not an artery, squeezed the gut. A sixty-year-old woman arrived with belly pain, nausea, and vomiting. Scans first raised concern for a rare syndrome in which the duodenum, the first part of the small gut, is pinched between the aorta and a major artery. Her images instead pointed to pressure at the level of the superior mesenteric vein, a large vein from the gut.

A camera exam down the throat showed outside pressure on the duodenum, with a pulsing mass and widening above the block. Surgeons then used robotic tools through small cuts to inspect the belly and free stuck bowel loops. They joined the duodenum to the next gut section, bypassing the squeezed spot. The authors highlight how this vein-based mimic can mislead even careful imaging, so direct inspection may be needed.
pmc-13282381:
Chengbin Liu and co-authors wrote a 2026 perspective on reading chemical tags in environmental DNA to monitor ecosystems more deeply. Environmental DNA, shed by organisms into water and soil, usually tells which species are present. It also keeps methylation tags, chemical marks that help control gene activity. The authors call this meth-eDNA and argue it could reveal traits of whole populations without catching any animals.

Three topics structure the piece: detecting the signals, how stable they stay in water, and uses as ecological indicators. Trait clues from tags could show stress, age structure, or adaptation that species lists miss. The authors expect that combining tag reading with other molecular layers and newer sequencing will sharpen precision. They frame the approach as a future tool for conservation and ecosystem management. Practical hurdles, such as signal decay outdoors, still need solving before routine use.
pmc-13282681:
Neyon Loku Gamage and co-authors present a 2026 study of heartworm-type parasites in dogs in Colombo District, Sri Lanka, and the bacteria living inside them. The parasites, Dirofilaria, spread by mosquitoes and can also infect people. The bacteria, Wolbachia, help the parasites survive and breed, making them a control target. Blood was collected from three hundred sixty-eight dogs between May and December 2025.

pmc-13282981:

They release factors that build vessels and drive spread traits. They also damp immune attack through suppressive signals and partner cells. High macrophage counts predict early return and poor outlook. The review maps treatment ideas that target these cells.
pmc-13283381:
Protein gas bubbles grown by microbes could carry ultrasound imaging into molecular territory, Ailin Cui and co-reviewers survey in 2026. Gas vesicles are tiny protein shells filled with gas from microbes. They can reflect ultrasound in ways that reveal tagged cells and tissues.

pmc-13284181:
A tiny tunable filter for heat-vision cameras is built by Tengfei Xu and colleagues in a 2026 device study. Long-wave infrared light suits passive imaging and material fingerprinting without added light. Filters in this band suffer from material absorption and few low-loss film choices.

A dual-channel demo paired spectral sensing with vision for object recognition. Hybrid sensing beat vision alone.
pmc-13284281: A 2026 correction notice in General Psychiatry fixes sample counts in an earlier study of brain connectivity, tobacco smoking, and psychosis risk, and carries no author byline. The baseline analysis is narrowed to participants with baseline MRI data: 364 high-risk non-smokers, 94 high-risk smokers, and 67 controls. Wording around the summary table is also corrected. Only the corrections themselves are given, so coverage stays brief.
pmc-13284881:

pmc-13285081:

Brain vessel gene work and cell tests under low oxygen tracked pathway changes and barrier stress. The results tie blood loss of the lipid to vessel strain.
pmc-13285681:
Blocking one chemokine may rescue immune therapy in kidney cancer, Ryuta Sobu and co-authors test in a 2026 study. Adding an IL-8 blocker, which cuts suppressor cell calls, tended to slow tumor growth beside PD-1 blockade.
pmc-13286081:
Sohaib Shujaat and colleagues draw policy lessons for national virtual hospitals in a 2026 viewpoint anchored on Saudi Arabia's Seha Virtual Hospital. Aging populations and packed wards push countries to move hospital care onto screens, yet whole-nation virtual hospitals stay rare. The authors gather world proof from remote intensive care, hospital-at-home, and stroke networks to judge what a national model must get right.

Saudi Arabia's hub, launched in 2022, now links hospitals across the kingdom for urgent consults, clinics, and case talks at national scale. Hard proof of its effect on deaths, costs, and fairness still lags behind its fast growth, the authors note. They urge built-in testing, sound funding, and care for access gaps as such systems spread.
pmc-13286281:
Farzin Tahvili, Martin Vinck, and Matteo Di Volo build a math model of brain rhythms in a 2026 theory study. Cortex gamma waves were long explained by a two-crowd dance of excitatory cells and generic blockers.
