The three-crowd system sings gamma on its own and matches lab quirks, including how light-pulse tricks on one cell type bend the rhythm. Trimming the math down shows the wiring pattern itself breeds the wave, no extra mechanism required. PV activity runs ahead of SOM activity, just as recordings show, because of who connects to whom. Modelers gain a firmer base for building large, cell-aware brain simulations.
pmc-13287081:
Narsimha Rao Keetha and co-authors pool studies on hidden celiac disease inside fatty liver clinics in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. Both conditions are rising and may share immune and gut-driven roots, yet how often they overlap was unclear. The team searched four databases for studies reporting celiac diagnoses among patients with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease.

Across the pooled studies, celiac disease appeared in about 3.8% of fatty liver patients, higher than general population expectations. Studies that confirmed the diagnosis with both blood tests and biopsies found more of it. Lower body mass, higher liver enzyme readings, lower hemoglobin, and lower platelet counts each leaned toward the overlap group. Disagreement between studies was extreme, so the authors urge selective screening and bigger, standardized prospective work rather than firm rules.
pmc-13287281:
Samuel Tundealao and colleagues built and piloted a talking digital guide in 2026 to help cancer survivors learn about inherited cancer risk and decide on genetic testing. Patients and at-risk relatives from varied backgrounds helped shape wording, layout, and privacy messages before a small feasibility trial.

Users rated the guide as easy to accept, with a usability score the authors report as 70.3. Testing uptake reached 73.3% with the guide, against 7.7% under enhanced usual care. Guide users also reported less conflict and regret about their choices. No guide user asked for pre-test counselling, against one in the comparison group. A larger randomised trial is proposed.
pmc-13287481:
Derk-Jan Dijk wrote a perspective in 2026 looking back over forty years of human experiments testing a classic two-part account of sleep control. In that account, a build-up of sleep pressure during waking interacts with a daily body clock to set when and how deeply people sleep.

Dijk sorts findings into those that fit the account and those that strain it. Points of tension include how the two parts truly interact and what they imply for brain recovery. His own doctoral work in Groningen during the 1980s helped test early predictions. The piece invites fresh work on how clock timing and sleep need jointly guard brain function.
pmc-13287681:
Qixiang Chen and co-authors used computer inverse design in 2026 to build a layered photonic surface that hides objects in visible light and in heat cameras at the same time. The structure draws on a material that flips state with temperature, vanadium dioxide, to change how it gives off infrared energy.

Colour across a wide band can be tuned over much of the print colour range without disturbing heat behaviour. Heat emission switches between two paired states in the two infrared bands. Precise heating also lets the surface send coded messages in infrared that ordinary cameras cannot see. Tests confirmed both hiding and signalling in one platform.
pmc-13288681:
Miriam Fornells-Ambrojo and colleagues present a 2026 protocol for a feasibility trial of narrative exposure therapy inside early psychosis services in England. Repeated personal trauma raises the chance of psychosis and slows recovery, yet trauma therapy rarely reaches first-episode patients, partly because services lack time and trained staff.

Fifty patients with first-episode psychosis and multiple traumas, cared for by two NHS trusts, will be assigned by chance to fifteen therapy sessions plus usual care or to usual care alone. Masked assessors will measure outcomes at the start, at four months, and at eight months, focusing on recruitment, retention, and completion. Interviews with patients and clinicians will probe acceptability, obstacles, and any harms, guiding a later full trial.
pmc-13288881:
Emsea Akers and co-authors plan a scoping review on injured children going home in 2026. Their piece is a protocol. Accidental injury fills children's wards worldwide. Families can hit a second crisis after discharge. Recovery at home can prove harder than expected. The team will gather caregiver views.

Four databases will be searched. English studies from 2000 to 2025 count. Patients must be under eighteen. Discharge views and improvement projects both count. Findings will sort through an access framework. Tables and summaries will expose challenges. Promising fixes will be named. Fairness checks will also be tracked.
pmc-13289081:
Alfonso Lagares and colleagues publish a 2026 study plan in Madrid, Spain. The IMPACTS-BRAINI study deals with mild brain injury. Two blood markers can rule out bleeds on scans. The markers are called GFAP and UCH-L1. Past work tested them in labs.

One hospital will run the study. Staff will log care before the test starts. They will log care after it starts too. Blood must be drawn within 12 hours of injury. Patients must meet set clinical marks. The team will count CT scans ordered. ER stay time will also be counted. Past patient data will serve as the contrast.
pmc-13289181:
Marta Simonetti and colleagues study nurse workloads and patient deaths in Chile in 2026. Their study covers public hospitals nationwide. Of 45 large hospitals, 43 took part. Nurses filled an online survey. Patient outcomes came from 2023 discharge data.

The data held 344,567 adult patients. Each ICU nurse covered 3.0 patients at once on average. Ward nurses cared for 10.1 at a time. Loads swung widely by hospital. Each extra patient raised the odds of death. That held in ICU and ward units. Ward stays also grew longer with load. Cutting loads could save lives, the authors say.
pmc-13289781:
Lisa Birzle and colleagues share a 2026 case series on endoscopic intermuscular dissection for early rectal cancers thought to invade deeply. The method cuts between muscle layers to remove lesions whole, fitting risk-based strategies that spare major surgery when safe. Sixteen patients at university hospitals in Augsburg and Bochum underwent the procedure with pre-procedure assessment guiding selection.

Every lesion came out in one piece without major complications in the series. Tissue review found a mix: deep or shallow invasive cancers with low-risk traits, pretreated cancer, one deeper cancer, benign growths with varied grades, a hormone-type tumor, and a vessel malformation. Margins were clear in fourteen cases overall. Two cases had deep margin concerns needing added care.
pmc-13290081:
Chrysanti Murad and coauthors test a 2026 lab question on whether a gum disease germ helps lung pneumococcal germs stick to airway cells by serotype. Porphyromonas gingivalis can raise a host receptor that pneumococci exploit, called PAFR. Lung lining cells were primed for 24 hours with fluid from the W83 strain, then exposed to four pneumococcal serotypes for adhesion counts.

Priming raised receptor gene activity clearly in the cell model. Adhesion jumped significantly for serotypes 4 and 7F after priming in the counts. Thick-coated serotypes 3 and 6A rose only slightly without statistical firmness overall. The mouth-lung partnership thus favors select pneumococcal types, shaping pneumonia risk by strain.
pmc-13290781:
A plant compound fed to pregnant mice protected their daughters from a fat-rich diet's metabolic fallout, Xueran Mei and colleagues report in an animal study from 2026. Mothers on a high-fat diet pass metabolic syndrome risk to offspring, and the team tested whether perinatal phlorizin could blunt that inheritance in females.

Daughters of high-fat-fed mothers showed disturbed sugar and fat handling at weaning and, as adults, gut imbalance, insulin resistance, and a leaky gut barrier despite no plain obesity. Transplanting gut microbes from protected daughters into antibiotic-treated males transferred much of the benefit. Mei and colleagues pitch phlorizin as a functional food candidate with effects across generations.
pmc-13291281:
Salt can coax a sea fungus to make new chemicals. Minh Van Nguyen leads a 2026 study of a marine Trichoderma strain. One strain can yield many compounds under changed growth. Bromide salt in the broth was the switch used here.

Salt-grown cultures turned darker in color. Their chemical mix grew richer as well. Extracts fought a key plant disease bacterium better. Fourteen compounds were pulled from the mix. Two were new to science, in the viridin family. Some compounds fought fungi, others fought bacteria. Fire blight signs on plants eased under treatment. Changing broth salts is a cheap discovery trick.
pmc-13291481:
A Chinese herbal mix may fight lung scarring disease. Yifan Ren leads a 2026 computer and lab study of Jingfang Granule. The disease, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, kills slowly. Few drug options exist for patients today.

Public gene data on the disease were mined first. Thousands of genes shifted in sick lung tissue. Network tools linked herb targets to disease targets. Five learning methods hunted for marker genes. Two genes, SPP1 and MMP1, stood out as key. Docking tests checked how herb parts bind them. Tissue stains backed the computer findings. The pair may guide new drug design for this disease.
pmc-13291781: Rosario Amato and co-authors put out a 2026 correction to their article on whether Lisosan G might serve as a glaucoma treatment. The notice says a preliminary version of panel A in Figure 4 was published by mistake. It supplies the corrected figure, showing retinal ganglion cell staining and density analysis in mouse retinas. The original article has been updated. Only this short correction is available here, so the underlying study's design and findings cannot be described from it.
pmc-13292981:
Mei-Mei Kuan and Javad Sarvestan build, in 2026, a forecast tool for hospital load from enterovirus in Taiwan. The virus sickens many children, and a post-pandemic rebound in 2023 and 2024 made planning harder for wards.

A random forest model trained on most of the period gave one-week-ahead forecasts for late 2024. Visits by the youngest children, ages 0 to 2 and 3 to 4, were the strongest clues. Weekly errors stayed modest, suggesting the tool could help plan beds and staff.
pmc-13293681:
Ameni Mehrez, Edouard Machery, and Valerio Capraro compare, in a 2026 study, how everyday Christians and Muslims view free will next to God's knowledge and power. Faith traditions have answered the tension in unlike ways for centuries, yet everyday belief may not follow doctrine.

Muslims differed: in abstract terms they held both free will and divine rule together, matching Qur'an teaching. In concrete cases, though, they played down free will. Lay faith thus blends doctrine with situation in complex ways.
pmc-13293781:
Yoko Takahashi and co-authors survey, in a 2026 study, local nurses 13 months after the 2011 Great East Japan Earthquake, asking whether losing their workplace harmed mental health apart from personal losses. Disaster research has centered on home and family loss, not workplace ruin.

A total of 414 nurses in coastal Miyagi Prefecture replied, giving rates of probable post-traumatic stress at 11.7% and depression at 24.6%, shares the authors report. Nurses from tsunami-wrecked hospitals looked worse in raw counts, yet the workplace link faded once personal burdens were counted. Death or loss of a family member stayed the strongest tie to severe stress symptoms.
pmc-13293881:
Tanuja Kistwal and colleagues report in 2026 that light can create quantum friction between carbon nanotubes and water. Stronger light cut diffusion by about 50%, and chemical tweaks that raised or lowered exciton numbers shifted diffusion up to twofold. When excitons were pinned by defects, the effect vanished. pmc-13293981:
Haobo Wang and colleagues present HiCapR in 2026, a protocol for mapping how viral RNA strands touch each other across a whole genome. pmc-13294681:
Yasemin Özdemir presents a 2026 dataset on birds at Karataş Lake in Burdur, Turkey, covering fieldwork from 2021 to 2022. pmc-13297381:
Metastatic prostate cancer care now favors early drug combinations over hormone treatment alone, and Takatoshi Somoto with co-authors mapped that shift in a 2026 review. Their account follows how landmark trials reshaped management of hormone-sensitive and castration-resistant disease.

Practical sequencing advice weighs blood reserve, other illnesses, and local access to monitoring.
pmc-13298181:
Why do buyers in Brazil call a bag of fine coffee worth its price? Ari Melo Mariano and his team model that call in a 2026 study. Their frame links what a product has, to the good it does the buyer, to the worth the buyer feels.

Survey replies came from 88 people, and the team fit the frame with a path model. The model made sense of 29.4% of the spread in felt worth. The traits of the coffee did most of their work through the middle step: gains that felt handy, useful, and smart. pmc-13298981:
Entropy, the mathematics of uncertainty, can grade how tamper-proof a blockchain really is, propose Lanlan Li and co-authors in a 2026 theoretical study. They model ledger states as probability distributions and track Shannon entropy on-chain, off-chain, and inside the virtual machines that run smart contracts.

pmc-13299281:

pmc-13299381:
Shingles reached both the brain and the bladder in an unusual case described by Jordan Pyatt and colleagues in 2026. A healthy 66-year-old man developed fever, severe headache, and light sensitivity, and only later did the telltale blistering rash appear over his sacrum.

pmc-13300381:
Staying active in old age tracks with feeling healthier, Keon Woo and two colleagues report from Korean survey data in a 2026 study. Active aging was split into health, participation, and security domains for regression analysis.

pmc-13300681:
Water near abandoned uranium mines on the Navajo Nation still carries cancer-linked metals, Christine Samuel-Nakamura and Abdul-Mehdi S. Ali report in a 2026 study from northwestern New Mexico. pmc-13301581:
A marine-derived lung drug candidate gets its full travel diary through the rat body in a 2026 pharmacokinetic study by Xiaochen Niu and colleagues. Binding, stability, and excretion studies complete a package meant to shape first human trial design.
pmc-13301781:

pmc-13302081:
Forever chemicals may bend the immune system through a shared set of genes, Katarina Baralić and colleagues argue in a 2026 in silico toxicology study. pmc-13302481:
When standard drugs fail stubborn obsessive-compulsive disorder, experts sometimes push doses past the guidelines, Mario Pinzi and colleagues document in a 2026 paper. pmc-13303081:
Higher body mass tracks with nineteen cancers and against three, Eleanor L. Watts and colleagues tally in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. pmc-13306581:
Hadi Shammout tested whether tablet coating pigments shield a light-sensitive drug during laser marking in a 2026 study. Laser marks help fight counterfeit medicines without solvents, yet the beam may harm drugs such as nifedipine inside the tablet.

Coatings held titanium dioxide or stand-ins including talc, chalk, zinc oxide and black iron oxide, plus a ready-made brown reference. Marks were burned at four wavelengths, 193 nm, 248 nm, 532 nm and 781 nm in the listed plan, with long daylight exposure as a comparison. Results guide safer coating choice for marked tablets.
pmc-13307181:

During pregnancy IgM stayed positive with brief virus returns, while fetal scans stayed normal and no virus DNA appeared in amniotic fluid in reported checks. pmc-13307681:

Firm trials with shared outcome rules must still prove how far the model can spread.
pmc-13307881:

pmc-13310781:
Ahmad Kaddoura and colleagues study early eye movement faults as warning signs in Huntington disease in a 2026 paper. Eye control often falters before clear motor diagnosis, and digital eye trackers could turn that fault into a useful marker. Which eye tasks matter most was unknown.

Data came from two large watch studies with 4,775 and 969 people in total. Up and down eye moves failed earlier and in more people than side to side moves. pmc-13310981:
Belle Gavriel-Fried led a 2026 interview study on how gambling disorder grows across the lives of United States veterans. Veterans face high trauma and stress loads that may feed gambling harm. Past talks on care barriers held rich life stories, so a second study mined them for path themes.

Talks covered 28 service members and veterans aged 27 to 73 years, met by video call. Three life stages framed the path: a childhood of want and longing for change, service years where broken promises raised risk, and civilian years where gambling sank deeper. Emotional weakness linked the stages, shaped by each setting.
pmc-13311081:
Pan Li and colleagues review new ways to attack the tuberculosis cell wall in a 2026 paper. Tuberculosis still kills over a million people a year, and drug resistant strains blunt old cures. The germ wall, built from linked sugars, wax acids, and protein mesh, has long been a proven drug target.

Classic drugs block wall building enzymes, but fresh plans go wider. Options disrupt wall strength, starve energy, jam transport of wall parts, enlist host defenses, and use nano carriers for delivery. Joining fronts may yield shorter, stronger cures that resist evasion. Most new paths still await human proof.
pmc-13311281:
Noellie Winkom Kpoda and co-authors, in 2026, map a study of snails that carry schistosomiasis in Burkina Faso's Volta Basin. Knowing where these snails live guides control of the worm disease.

Health teams can use the maps to aim snail control where risk is highest.
pmc-13311581:
Oisín Cleary and colleagues present a 2026 interview study on the impact of stroke at a young age, heard from survivors, caregivers, and clinicians. Stroke services are often built around older patients.

Thirty-six interviews were held online, with 22 young survivors, five caregivers, and nine health professionals, mostly in the United Kingdom. Four themes emerged, covering relationships and mood, lost work and money strain, feeling forgotten after discharge, and views on current care. The impact reached partners and wider family, not just survivors. The authors call for services shaped with young survivors, not one-size care.
pmc-13311681:
Austen El-Osta and co-authors survey British adults and health workers in a 2026 study on spatial computing for health and self-care. The term covers virtual, augmented, and mixed reality tools.

The online survey ran from January to August 2025 and drew 405 completed replies, 41 from health professionals. It asked how familiar people were with the tools, where they saw benefit across self-care areas, and what blocks uptake. Cost, proof of benefit, and fit with primary care were central worries. The results map public readiness for reality-based health tools and the hurdles services must clear first.
pmc-13311981:
Shuo Zhao and co-authors report two 2025 phase IIa trials of a new anti-VEGF antibody, called 601, for macular swelling after retinal vein blockage. Existing anti-VEGF drugs work, but more options are wanted.

Across 12 Chinese sites, 120 patients with branch or central vein blockage got eye injections of 601 or ranibizumab every four weeks to week twenty, then as needed. At week 24, vision gains were near equal: the new drug trailed by 1.27 letters in branch cases and 2.97 letters in central cases in this study. Retina thickness fell similarly. The results support larger trials.
pmc-13312081:
Rebekah J Nicholson and colleagues present a 2026 laboratory protocol for pulling sphingolipids out of human urine automatically and measuring them at scale. These fats may act as warning signs of kidney disease, but they occur in urine at far lower levels than in blood, which makes them hard to measure reliably.

The protocol walks through sample preparation and solid-phase extraction on an automated platform, then targeted tandem mass spectrometry for measuring the lipids. It replaces older single-step liquid methods that limited how much urine could be processed. The same setup can also prepare paired samples for broader metabolite and lipid profiling, and the authors note it can be adapted to other body materials beyond urine.
pmc-13312481:
Ariadna Tibau and co-authors comment, in a 2026 article, on the real clinical value of cancer drugs approved in Switzerland. Fast-track approvals increasingly rest on surrogate endpoints, which can leave the true benefit uncertain at launch. Switzerland gives patients unusually broad access to new oncology drugs, making the question of what that access buys especially sharp.

The authors discuss a meta-analysis of Swissmedic approvals from 2001 to 2020 covering 378 pivotal trials. Nearly 70 percent leaned on surrogate measures, mainly progression-free survival. Pooled results translated into modest absolute gains: a median of 2.4 extra months of overall survival and 3.5 months before progression. The authors stress the gap between strong relative effects and small absolute gains, and warn that shaky benefit evidence complicates pricing and reimbursement tied to value.
pmc-13312581:
Mercian Daniel and co-authors write a 2026 commentary on involving people with lived experience of mental illness in research in India. Such contributors are experts by experience who can sharpen a study's relevance and ethics. Global guidance now urges their inclusion across the research cycle, yet genuine engagement stays rare in India and similar low-resource settings.

The authors describe barriers drawn from their own work: stigma, both public and internalized, that undermines contributors' credibility and willingness to take part. The absence of organized lived-experience networks, which makes recruitment scattered and pay, continuity, and accountability hard to sustain. Borrowing the image of an engagement ladder, from token input up to lived-experience-led research, they recommend structured, context-sensitive strategies so participation becomes meaningful rather than decorative in Indian mental health science.
pmc-13313181:
Fanny Méjean leads a team that tested the order of three cancer drugs in kidney cancer, in work published in 2026. Their question was why pairing vessel-blocking drugs with immune therapy so rarely cures spread renal cell cancer, and whether the timing of each drug changes the result.

In mice with kidney tumors, a short course of axitinib first reshaped tumor blood vessels, eased low oxygen, and cut suppressive immune cells. A survivin vaccine given in that window drew in strong helper and killer T cells. When PD-1 blockade came with the vaccine, after axitinib rather than during it, the three-drug plan gave lasting control and many full cures. The result argues that sequence, not just drug choice, can turn a partial response into a cure.
pmc-13314581:
Tonio Lipkow and co-workers review tailored bone drug care for a rare bone disorder in a 2026 study. Fibrous dysplasia, with its McCune-Albright form, stems from a gene change after conception and brings pain, bent bones, and breaks.

Drugs such as denosumab and zoledronate slow bone loss, but proof is thin and denosumab carries a known rebound risk when stopped. Because disease drive varies so much between patients, fixed plans often fail. The team looked back at a single-center group of 42 patients cared for from 2014 to 2025, as counted in the report. They traced scans, tissue data, blood marks, pain scores, and side effects under plans tuned per patient, with denosumab and zoledronate swapped and timed by clinical need. The work backs personal pacing over set schedules.
pmc-13314781:
Ilaria Onofrio and Calman A. MacLennan review gonorrhea in a paper appearing in 2026, covering how the germ dodges immunity and drugs and why a vaccine is so hard. The bacterium, found only in humans, causes a major sexually passed infection across the world.

Control keeps slipping as resistance spreads across drug classes and as natural infection leaves no lasting guard. The germ varies its surface parts at high speed, blocks complement attack, bends the work of eating cells, and damps the adaptive immune arm, the authors write. Some of those tricks overlap with drug resistance paths. Lab infection models have shed light on the fight, and cross-guard from a meningitis B vaccine hints a gonorrhea shot is possible. The review maps the hurdles any vaccine must clear.
pmc-13314881:
Fulgence Kaboré and colleagues measure nerve-type pain in knee osteoarthritis in work published in 2026. Worn knees are known for mechanical pain, yet a share of patients hurt in a burning, shooting way that points to nerve involvement, and that share in their clinic was unknown.

The team studied 325 patients who met standard criteria at a referral hospital rheumatology clinic. Mean age was near 57.85 years as stated in the report. A screening score of 4 or more on the DN4 tool marked pain as nerve-like, and that pattern showed in a share of 32 percent of patients in the figures given. Those patients averaged higher pain scores, by the measures reported. Models then sorted which traits travel with nerve-like pain. Naming it matters, since nerve pain answers to different drugs than joint pain.
pmc-13315081:
Hong-Mei Chen leads a large team that links body makeup to physical performance in Chinese men, in work published in 2026. What the body is made of shapes health and fitness, yet its tie to many-sided performance in adult men was not well charted.

The team drew 2362 men from community fitness programs in Hengyang, as counted in the report. Body fat share, fat mass, fat-free mass, and muscle mass were read by an impedance device. Performance covered grip strength, push-ups, back strength, vertical jump, and estimated peak oxygen use. Rank correlations, pattern extraction, and adjusted models sorted the links, as the methods state. The map can guide training and health checks that prize muscle over mere weight loss.
pmc-13316181:
Oluwanifemi E Bolatimi and co-authors exposed mice in 2026 to low doses of a dioxin mixture for twelve weeks. They tested how sex and diet change liver and metabolic harm. Lasting organic pollutants link to liver disease, with population data hinting that men and women differ in sensitivity, yet mixture models were thin.

Male and female mice ate low-fat or high-fat diets and got weekly doses of three compounds at set nanogram levels, or a control. Low-fat fed females on the mixture showed lower liver weight but raised liver fat markers. Harm thus depends on both sex and food pattern.
pmc-13316281:
Ahinsa Ranaweera and co-authors dissect in 2026 how the HIV capsid and integrase play opposing yet cooperative roles in packing the viral genome complex into new virus cores. Using fast affinity capture to enrich native capsids, they tested what happens when integrase can no longer grip viral RNA, or when the capsid lattice is distorted.

Breaking integrase and RNA contact emptied cores of integrase, genome, and nucleocapsid, yet reverse transcriptase stayed. Distorting capsids with the drug lenacapavir or cross-linking instead kept the integrase and genome but lost other parts. Core assembly needs both partners balanced.
pmc-13316581:
Siyi Tang and colleagues used whole genome resequencing in a 2026 study of the Yunnan Partridge duck, a conserved local breed with spotted, gray, and yellow feather types. Feather color matters for breeding value and identity, yet its genetic basis in this breed was largely unknown.

The population showed moderate diversity and low inbreeding, and family trees split into three clusters matching color types. A genome scan pinned color to a stretch of chromosome 21, where the gene ASIP stood out as the main candidate. Two common gene block patterns separated spotted from gray birds with sharp clarity. Breeders now have marker tools to protect the breed and select color on purpose rather than by chance.
pmc-13316781:
Jacqueline Jennebach and many colleagues trace, in a 2026 process report, fifteen years of building Germany's national catalogue of learning objectives for medical students, the NKLM. The catalogue sets what every graduate must know, whatever specialty follows, and tries to align exams with teaching.

Work began in 2009 under shifting teams from education and faculty associations plus a research group. Over a thousand experts have revised the content, which shrank and sharpened across its first two versions. The next update is due in the summer of 2026, with a further version already in development. The authors frame the catalogue as a living document, kept current as medicine and teaching science move.
pmc-13316981:
Matthew R Parris leads a 2026 chemistry study shrinking a sea natural product, waixenicin A, down to its working core. The full molecule blocks the TRPM7 ion channel, a calcium gate tied to newborn brain injury from oxygen loss, but it is far too complex to make as a drug.

Guided by a design method that starts from the active shape, the team built stripped-down versions carrying only the suspected key ring feature. In electrical patch tests, the simple copies still blocked the channel, by 9 to 57 percent across the series in the reported runs. Weak but real activity maps the smallest structure a future drug must keep, a vital first cut for medicinal chemists.
pmc-13317781:
Apichaya Klaikaew and co-authors compare, in a 2026 case-control study, the urine microbe mix and acidity of women with and without overactive bladder, the urgent, frequent need to urinate without infection. The bladder was long thought sterile, and its resident microbes may play a role.

Twenty-three women with symptoms and twenty-three without, matched closely in age and body measures, gave midstream samples for pH and gene sequencing. Acidity matched between groups, and the overall microbe mix did not split either. Two genera, Corynebacterium and Rothia, ran more abundant in the symptom group. With small numbers, the authors frame the hints as starting points for larger, mechanistic studies.
pmc-13317981:
Hope A Townsend and colleagues present, in a 2026 methods paper, two algorithms that sharpen the hunt for active enhancers. These DNA switches give off faint RNA output that reveals which master regulators are at work. These signals are weak and jumpy, so ordinary tools miss or misname them.

One tool infers exact region lengths and counts reads fast, and the second, TFEA-LE, joins those counts with DNA motif clues to name responsive switches and their likely controllers together. On p53-driven tests it beat general tools on both precision and recall, and it untangled mixed regulator responses in lung cells. The pair held up on awkward data with outliers and skewed chemistry, aiding disease variant research.
pmc-13318781:
Sulian Gu and co-authors present a 2026 retrospective study of swallowing problems after severe stroke. Dysphagia is common and dangerous in this group. Records came from a neurointensive care unit at a large hospital. Admissions spanned January 2023 to August 2025.

Among 358 patients, 288 developed dysphagia, an incidence of 80.45 percent in the cohort. Five factors independently raised risk in their model. They were age 70 or older, deep brain lesion location, and a coma score of 8 or less. Mechanical ventilation and sedative use completed the list. A model built on those five factors reached an AUC of 0.864 for prediction in internal testing. The authors say outside validation is still needed before routine use.
pmc-13318981:
Sureewan Bumrungthai and colleagues present a 2026 community study in Thailand linking a gene variant to detection of human herpesvirus 6. The virus infects most people in childhood and then stays latent. A promoter variant in the TNF-α gene may tilt the host-virus balance. The sample covered 852 people aged 3 to 90 in Phayao Province.

Viral DNA was found in 12.8 percent of participants overall. Detection rose steadily with age. Carriers of the −308G>A variant had clearly higher odds of a positive test. The adjusted odds ratio was 3.21 in their model. Lower education also linked to detection, while psychological measures did not. The authors stress that long-term studies must test whether the link is causal.
pmc-13319081:
Mehdi Duyan and colleagues present a 2026 cross-sectional study of mindfulness and emotion control among female combat sports coaches. The sample held 398 women in a high-demand coaching setting. Self-report scales measured mindfulness, rumination, and control problems. Models tested whether rumination carried part of the effect.

The model fitted acceptably, with a CFI of 0.95 among its indices. Greater mindfulness predicted less rumination and fewer control problems. It, in turn, predicted more problems. The indirect path through it was significant, showing partial mediation. Coaches who dwelled less on negative thoughts gained extra emotional steadiness. The authors advise pairing mindfulness training with strategies aimed directly at such dwelling in coach support programmes.
pmc-13319481:
Serap BATI and Sibel KIYAK survey married women after a major quake in Türkiye in a 2026 study of death fears and plans for children. The quake struck on February 6, 2023 and left wide loss across the region. The team asked whether dread around death tracked with shifts in whether women still wanted a child.

A total of 294 women from the hurt region took part and filled in a short death distress scale plus a background form. Scores were higher for women who had changed their child plans, and grief linked parts scored highest of all. Age, income, past births, house damage, and being trapped all shaped distress. Post quake care should weigh these fears.
pmc-13320281:
Bingyuan Liu and co-authors cloak a drug loaded particle in immune cell skin for stroke care in a 2026 mouse study. Restoring blood flow after a stroke clot can itself harm the brain through a burst of cell stress and swelling. Their particle packs a proven guard drug inside a tea extract and iron core, then wraps it in skin from immune scout cells that home to harm.

The wrapped particle crossed into the brain, sought the starved zone, and soaked up harmful oxygen forms while blocking fat damage in lab tests. In mice with a blocked brain artery later freed, it shrank the dead zone, cut nerve cell death and swelling, and aided movement recovery and long term survival. The design merges shield and homing in one shot.
pmc-13320381:
Joaquin Ameller and co-authors present a data set on fresh vegetable flows into Brazzaville in a 2026 survey article. Knowing where a city food comes from helps plan transport, markets, and food safety, yet such maps for this capital had not been made since the 1990s. Sellers at the main wholesale and retail markets were asked face to face about stock on one day in each of the dry and rainy seasons.

Sixteen vegetables were tracked by price, weight, and source, from farm site and region down to middle sellers where they played a part. Clean shared fields join flows to supply nodes across the chain. The set can feed studies of city food reach, market webs, and truck routes, and can be set next to like sets from other African capitals.
pmc-13321281:
Yucui Ding and colleagues review calcium overload as a way to kill cancer cells in a 2026 article. Flooding cancer cells with calcium disrupts two linked cell parts, the endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria, and triggers programmed death. Clinical use is held back by weak tumour targeting, low build-up in tumours, and patchy mechanism knowledge.

The review maps how calcium sparks a self-feeding stress loop between the two organelles, centred on a channel chain across their contact sites. It also surveys calcium based nano carriers paired with sound or heat based therapies for stronger joint effects. Designs that respond to the tumour setting are flagged as the next step for safer, sharper treatment.
pmc-13322581:
Deep Sengupta writes a 2026 letter on anaesthesia outside the operating room for a child with Wilson's disease and autism. The case involved an 11-year-old boy weighing 32 kilograms who needed an MRI scan. Wilson's disease impairs the liver and copper handling, while autism with profound hyperactivity makes lying still for scanning impossible without deep sedation.

Published guidance, Sengupta notes, covers major surgery in Wilson's disease almost exclusively, stressing liver harm, kidney risk from copper, and odd responses to muscle relaxants. Guidance for sedation in an isolated MRI suite, above all with severe behaviour conditions added, is nearly absent. The letter presents intravenous propofol use in that gap and reviews the child's ongoing medicines.
pmc-13323681:
José Rodolfo Lopes de Paiva Cavalcanti and co-editors introduce a collection on the basal ganglia and their circuits, in a 2026 editorial. These deep brain nuclei, spanning striatum, pallidum, subthalamic nucleus and substantia nigra, were long cast as movement controllers alone.

Current views add cognition, motivation, reward and emotion to their remit, carried by dopamine, glutamate and GABA links. Classic direct, indirect and hyperdirect pathway models still frame debate, with the direct path easing movement and the indirect path holding it back. Featured work updates those models against disorders such as Parkinson's and Huntington's disease. The editors frame the set as a step toward circuit-level treatment ideas.
pmc-13324681:
Vladimir Aron and colleagues locate where exercise dulls pain in a 2026 experiment with healthy young men. One hard workout briefly lowers pain sensitivity, but whether the effect is body-wide or local was unclear.

Thirty-eight men aged 18 to 30 cycled for 25 minutes at strong effort or at light effort as a control. Before and after, the team tested pressure, heat, cold, and pinprick sensitivity in the worked legs and the resting arms. Hard cycling raised pressure pain thresholds only in the legs. Other measures barely moved, and hearing checks stayed flat. The pattern points to deep tissue sensors inside the working muscles as the main site of the effect.
pmc-13325081:
Rocco Malaspina and colleagues mix zinc oxide tetrapods into silk fibroin to make flexible sensing films in a 2026 materials study. Silk protein is body-friendly and breaks down safely, which suits wearable and medical devices.

After the solvent dried, the filler formed spheres, lines, or branched shapes depending on its amount in the silk matrix. Infrared checks showed the silk protein structure stayed unchanged by filler size or shape. Branched tetrapods stiffened the films most, hinting at a firm filler interface. A stretchable strain sensor built from the mix beat plain silk films on resistance change and gauge factor. Shape choice thus offers a tuning knob for soft sensors.
pmc-13327981:
Renjie Ji and a large team examine an immune checkpoint in spinal cord injury in a 2026 mouse study. Tim-3 sits on microglia, the cord's resident immune cells, and its role in post-injury inflammation was unclear. The team raised Tim-3 levels in microglia with a virus vector and tracked tissue damage, movement, and mood-like behavior.

Extra Tim-3 drove microglia to multiply and switch on, raising inflammatory signals and the enzyme iNOS, and injury damage and movement problems worsened, while mood-like behavior stayed unchanged. pmc-13328281:
Demet Yüksel Dal, Boran A Kilic, and Gurur Gamgam examine local brain network changes across cognitive decline in a 2026 study. Alzheimer's disease breaks links between brain regions, a disconnection pattern that may first trigger compensatory rewiring. The team measured node-level traits such as degree, strength, clustering, and centrality across disease stages.

Early-stage patterns matched the compensation idea, with local nodes reorganizing in ways that could briefly prop up thinking, while later stages showed structural decline dominating even as functional reshuffling persisted. Because the data are one-time snapshots of groups, the authors label compensation a working hypothesis needing repeat and longitudinal proof before any clinical use.
pmc-13328781:
Yong-Seok Jee writes in 2026 about how journal peer review is changing, with a focus on exercise rehabilitation. Review once acted mainly as a gate before publication, checking methods and novelty. In this field reviewers must also judge clinical value and real-world use, which makes the job broader.

Rising submission counts and demands for faster decisions now strain reviewers, editors, and publishers. Fatigue among reviewers is a growing worry, the essay notes. At the same time, open science brings calls for clearer decisions and more open debate after publication. Jee argues that review is becoming a shared duty for the research community, not just a filter before print.
pmc-13329381:
Jianyu Huang and co-authors study how a flavour compound binds to pumpkin seed protein in a 2026 report. The compound, tetramethylpyrazine, gives aroma to fermented foods but fades fast and breaks down quickly. Pumpkin seed protein was tested as a carrier that might hold and protect it.

Binding grew with dose and changed the protein shape, the team found. Light-based tests pointed to still binding driven by hydrogen bonds and weak surface forces, releasing heat as it formed. At apt levels the protein became more ordered and spread out. Computer models flagged key contact points on the protein. The mix also showed stronger antioxidant action and steadier emulsions. The authors propose the protein as a carrier for fragile flavours.
pmc-13329481:
Noah Williams and colleagues count personal costs of emergency care in Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada, in a 2026 study. Even under public funding, patients may pay for food, travel, and lost work. The team surveyed and interviewed people who visited four emergency departments, two rural and two urban, between March 2021 and July 2023.

Of 818 patients in the final group, 24 percent reported personal costs for a visit in the reported results. Stays of 4 hours or more raised the odds of any cost and of costs at or above 200 Canadian dollars in the adjusted models. City visits also linked to higher costs. Interviews stressed missed work and hard choices between care and daily needs.
pmc-13330481:
Quentin Marlier and colleagues test a new compound, DX243, in lab and mouse models of stroke in a 2026 study. Restoring blood flow is the only current care and reaches few patients in time. Cell models mimicked stroke stress with glutamate and with oxygen and glucose loss followed by return.

DX243 raised energy output after glutamate stress and kept neurons alive after the deprivation test in the reported results. In mice, one under-skin dose after an hour of artery blockage cut damaged brain area and preserved balance beam skill at 48 hours. Open field movement showed no clear change. The authors see repair-like promise and call for deeper preclinical and clinical work.
pmc-13330681:
Anna Carollo and colleagues write a 2026 letter on phone and video support for Parkinson patients between hospital stays. Their neuropsychology service at a hospital in Gravedona ed. Uniti, Italy, began regular remote check-ins after rehab admissions. Patients and caregivers were called to review training adherence and tackle fresh difficulties at home.

Rehab helps Parkinson care, yet structured follow-up between admissions is often missing, the letter notes. Caregivers joined calls both to clarify patient needs and to share their own strain and coping. The team reports high satisfaction, steady care continuity, and workable delivery in their summary. Remote contact can extend hospital rehab into daily life, they argue.
pmc-13331781:
Wareerat Prasitwiset and co-authors report a 2026 veterinary case from Chiang Mai Province, Thailand, the first documented dog infection with the parasite Leishmania martiniquensis. The dog had a small firm lump on the inner surface of its right ear, and needle sampling showed parasite forms inside cells.

The team grew the parasite in culture and confirmed its identity with several gene tests and family-tree analysis of a spacer gene region. Full checks of blood, chemistry, and belly imaging found no spread to inner organs, which fits a skin-only infection. Four weekly injections of amphotericin B straight into the lump cleared it. Alongside a review of animal infections worldwide, the case shows dogs can carry this parasite and raises questions about animal reservoirs and spread that need One Health study.
pmc-13333381:
E.M. Langner and co-authors mined smartphone data in 2026 for signs of behavioral stickiness that might flag mood episodes in bipolar disorder. Emotional inertia, the tendency to stay stuck, is tied to depression, but whether passively sensed behavior shows the same drag during mania was unexplored.

Data came from the BipoSense study: 29 patients, 10,587 observed days, covering 20 high episodes and 30 depressive ones. The team measured day-to-day carry-over and moving averages across activity, communication, sleep, and phone use. In depression, carry-over rose for activity and communication, strongest in later weeks of an episode, while average levels fell across activity, communication, and sleep. High episodes gave mixed carry-over signals but a clear average pattern: more activity, more contact, more phone use, and less sleep, matching the clinical picture. The authors say the two measures capture different sides of episode dynamics and need testing in bigger cohorts.
pmc-13333781:
Lluis Font-Vizcarra and Beatriz Sobrino-Díaz wrote a 2026 minireview on electrolytic cleaning as a way to strip biofilm from medical implants. Bacterial biofilms on metal surfaces shrug off antibiotics and immune attack, which makes implant infections hard to cure without removing hardware.

The authors explain this physicochemical basis, compare it with other electrical approaches that rely on pH shifts or reactive species, and weigh the experimental evidence gathered so far. Data remain early and clinical translation limited, but the physical mechanism offers a drug-free complement to debridement and antibiotics.
pmc-13336381:
You Na Song and co-authors fused a light-emitting platinum complex to its own host molecule to fix deep-blue OLED efficiency in a 2026 optoelectronics study. Deep-blue phosphorescent diodes lose energy in slow transfers between separate host and emitter molecules.

Their single molecule, Pt-SP-tCz, covalently joins a p-type host to a tetradentate platinum emitter, yet each half keeps its own photophysical and electrochemical identity, giving two recombination sites in one structure. The fused geometry shrinks donor-acceptor distance to molecular scale, enabling what the authors call zero-radius intramolecular energy transfer. Paired with an n-type host, a second zero-radius channel opens through exciplex formation. Together the shortcuts produced a record energy transfer rate of 3.64 times ten to the eighth per second in their device physics, pointing to brighter blue pixels.
pmc-13336481:
Xiangxi Kong and co-authors identified a macrophage subset that worsens Modic changes, the vertebral endplate lesions common in low back pain, in a 2026 study. The local immune environment drives these lesions, and the culprit cells were unknown.

Macrophages marked by THBS1, strongly inflammatory in character, crowded lesion sites in human specimens and in a mouse model induced by C. acnes. The bacterium and its metabolites switched THBS1 on through Toll-like receptor signaling, and deleting THBS1 only in macrophages slowed the disease. The secreted protein engages syndecan-4 on endplate cartilage cells, firing p38 and raising the NLRP3 inflammasome, which amplifies inflammation. Silencing that receptor calmed the response, nominating the THBS1-SDC4 pair as a drug target.
pmc-13336881:
Yingjun Liu and a large team toughen ultra-hot ceramics from inside their grains in a 2026 materials study. High-entropy borides promise parts for extreme heat, but they tend to snap: strength and toughness rarely come together. Outside reinforcements barely help because cracks start within grains.

Heavy direct current sintering with a titanium silicide additive packed the ceramic to over 93% density at a much lower 1000°C with heating above 5300°C per minute in the process runs. Selective atom movement rebuilt grain interiors with gradients and dislocation networks that block cracks. The ceramic hit 887 MPa for flexural strength and 7.1 MPa·m1/2 for fracture toughness in the reported tests. Inner rebuilding offers a path for heat-proof parts that resist breaking.
pmc-13337881:
Qing Li, Mingchen Gu, and Wei Li review exercise and brain circuits in early Alzheimer's disease for 2026. Early illness is framed as circuit failure alongside cell damage. Exercise slows decline, yet most explanations stay at the molecule or cell level.

Four vulnerable systems are covered: a memory entry circuit, a hippocampus to frontal link, a chemical signaling circuit, and the body clock axis. Direct circuit measures show breakdown in places, while many exercise effects rest on indirect signs such as behavior or chemistry. A multi-circuit view is proposed, where exercise steadies several networks at once to support memory, control, and daily rhythms.
pmc-13339181:
Peng Gao and colleagues test preventive steroid dosing in newborn heart surgery in a 2026 trial. Methylprednisolone is often given to calm inflammation from the heart-lung machine, yet benefit for newborn outcomes was unclear. Clinicians assigned treatment without randomization or blinding.

A total of 86 newborns operated between 2020 and 2023 were included as reported. The steroid group received 30 mg per kilogram after anesthesia began, while controls received saline. Blood inflammation markers and clotting marker D-dimer were the main measures. Steroid infants showed lower pro-inflammatory signals as reported, with combined outcomes such as death and organ injury also tracked for clinical meaning.
pmc-13339281:
Zheyue Peng and Ashley L Watts test two theories for why ADHD travels with other conditions in a 2026 study. One theory blames a shared common cause, while mutualism says symptoms feed each other over time. Youth data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study were used.

Four waves covered 11,878 youths starting at age 9 to 10 as reported. Results mostly backed the common cause account for links to both behavior and developmental spectra. Hyperactivity tied closer to behavior problems, while sluggish disengagement tied closer to developmental traits. ADHD is framed as bridging both domains rather than belonging to only one.
pmc-13339881:
Junrong Li and a large team predict depression in women with fatty liver disease from routine blood tests in a 2026 UK Biobank study. Fatty liver affects 38.9 percent of adults globally as cited, and depression alongside it raises death risk. Women face higher depression rates, sharpened after menopause.

Five years of records for women with the liver condition supplied blood, lifestyle, and reproductive data. A two-stage selection process using forest resampling picked stable predictors while balancing case and control traits. Several learning models were compared for accuracy. A light model from ordinary labs could flag women needing mental health checks during liver care.
pmc-13341181:
Risk grouping systems for thyroid cancer from two guideline bodies are compared by Won Gu Kim and Mijin Kim in a 2026 article. The 2025 American guidelines split patients into four risk tiers, adding a split within the old middle group, while the 2024 Korean system keeps three tiers.

That structural choice matters because the starting category steers decisions on radioactive iodine, hormone suppression, and how closely patients are watched afterward. The authors tabulate where the systems assign the same patient differently, including how each defines category boundaries. Clinicians who rarely see both documents side by side get a direct map of where practice could diverge.
pmc-13341481:
Frog toxin machinery repurposed against colon cancer is described by Xinqiang Xu and coauthors in their 2026 study. Colorectal tumors often dodge cell death by overproducing protective BCL-2 family proteins, and BH3-mimetic drugs work poorly in solid tumors, so the team tried delivering the death protein BAX directly.

Toad BAX bound human BCL-2 with a Kd of 12.7 µM and triggered mitochondrial rupture, cytochrome c release, and caspase activation in cancer cells. A redesigned triple mutant performed better still, and engineered exosomes carried it into tumors. Tests spanned cell cultures and several mouse models, including patient-derived grafts.
pmc-13342081:
Digital health messages do shift patient knowledge and behavior, in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis by Asma Alshanqiti's team. Studies from 2015 to January 2026 covered apps, websites, social media, telehealth, and AI-enabled tools aimed at patients.

The team took care to separate actual digital literacy skills from downstream outcomes like knowledge, behavior, clinical markers, and empowerment, a distinction earlier reviews blurred. Like outcomes were pooled under random-effects models with subgroup and sensitivity checks. Multi-component programs were assigned once by their dominant patient-facing channel to keep the comparisons honest.
pmc-13342181:
Moving more links to less loneliness in Yi schoolchildren, in a 2026 one-time study by Qingju Shao's team. Forms from 671 students aged 10 to 18 in Southwest China gauged activity beside anxiety, loneliness, and social anxiety, with age, sex, and school stage held in the model.

pmc-13342881:

pmc-13343881:

pmc-13345781:

pmc-13345881:

pmc-13347781:

pmc-13349781:

pmc-13349881:

pmc-13350181:

pmc-13351281:

pmc-13354381:

pmc-13355281:

pmc-13356581:

pmc-13359881:

pmc-13362181:

pmc-13364181:

pmc-13364281:

pmc-13374381:

pmc-13375581:

pmc-13377581:

pmc-13378881:

pmc-13378981:

pmc-13382081:

pmc-13382581:

pmc-13386881:

pmc-13388581:

pmc-13388981:

pmc-13391481:

pmc-13391981:

pmc-13392081:

pmc-13392281:

pmc-13393281:

pmc-13393581:

pmc-13394081:

pmc-13394381:

pmc-13394681:

pmc-13396081:

pmc-13396381:

pmc-13398481:

pmc-13400481:

pmc-13400581:

pmc-13400681:
